lessons.plain: Capital expense (capex) is money spent up front to buy something a business will own and use for years, such as its own servers and data center equipment. Variable expense is money paid as you go, in proportion to what you actually use. The AWS Cloud lets a business swap the first for the second. Instead of buying a room full of computers before it knows how busy it will be, it rents computing power by the hour or second, and the bill rises and falls with use. Think of buying a car versus taking taxis: there is no big purchase, but you pay for every trip.
lessons.guessPrompt: A new online shop expects somewhere between 100 and 10,000 customers next year. If it has to buy its own servers today, what goes wrong if it guesses too high, and what goes wrong if it guesses too low?
lessons.teach:
Capital expense (capex) is a large up-front payment for assets the company owns, such as servers, storage and networking gear. Variable expense is a cost that moves with consumption. Pay-as-you-go is the AWS pricing approach that creates it: you are billed for the resources you run, for as long as you run them. The value proposition is that a business stops paying ahead of time for capacity it might need and pays for capacity it actually turns on.

This matters because buying hardware forces capacity planning, which means guessing future demand months in advance. Guess too high and you own idle capacity, meaning machines that were paid for but sit unused. Guess too low and customers hit a slow or failing site until new hardware arrives.

Here is a worked example with made-up prices. A shop expects a holiday peak needing 10 servers, while normal months need 2. On premises, meaning in its own building, it buys 10 servers at $10,000 each, so it spends $100,000 before launch, and 8 of those servers sit idle for 11 months. In the cloud, a comparable rented server costs $1 per hour. A normal month is 2 servers × 730 hours × $1, about $1,460. The holiday month is 10 × 730 × $1, about $7,300. The year comes to roughly 11 × $1,460 + $7,300 = $23,360, paid month by month. If the shop fails in month three, it shuts everything down and stops paying, while the bought servers would already be sunk cost.

A common mistake is thinking variable expense means the cloud is always cheaper, or that you only pay when servers are busy. You pay for what you leave running, busy or not. A steady workload running at full use around the clock narrows the gap. In a running system, a forgotten test server keeps billing every hour, so the money saved on capex must be protected by watching the monthly bill.

questions.prompt:
A city library runs an online room-booking site. For the one month when summer courses open, it needs 6 servers; the other 11 months it needs 1. A rented cloud server in this made-up example costs $2 per hour, and a month is about 730 hours.

Step 1: A normal month costs 1 server × 730 hours × $2 = $1,460.
Step 2: The 11 normal months together cost 11 × $1,460 = $16,060.
Step 3: [missing] The peak month costs ...
Step 4: The year total is $16,060 plus the peak-month cost, paid month by month, with no large hardware purchase up front.

Which choice correctly completes Step 3?
choices: $1,460, because pay-as-you-go keeps the monthly bill fixed
5 × 730 × $2 = $7,300, counting only the servers added for the peak
6 × 8,760 hours × $2 = $105,120, because a rented server bills all year once started
questions.why: Under pay-as-you-go the library pays for all 6 servers it runs, for the hours it runs them, so the peak month is 6 × 730 × $2.

questions.prompt: A small accounting firm is reviewing its costs. Which of these is an example of variable expense, as opposed to capital expense (capex)?
choices: Signing for a fixed batch of servers sized to the firm's busiest week of the year
Paying $40,000 up front for storage gear the firm will own for five years
Buying a rack of networking equipment before a new office opens
A cloud bill that rises in tax season because more rented servers are switched on, then falls afterward
questions.why: Variable expense moves with consumption, so a bill that grows and shrinks with the servers actually running is variable, while the other choices are large up-front purchases of owned assets.

questions.prompt: A new ticketing startup has no idea whether it will get 100 users or 100,000 next year. Its founders consider renting cloud servers instead of buying their own. What does trading capex for variable expense mainly buy them?
choices: Servers that stop billing automatically whenever no customer is using them
A guarantee that the cloud will cost less than owning servers in every situation
They avoid guessing demand months ahead: they pay only for the capacity they turn on, and can shut it down and stop paying if the business fails
The ability to skip watching costs, since pay-as-you-go bills cannot grow unexpectedly
questions.why: Pay-as-you-go removes the up-front bet on future demand and the risk of idle or sunk hardware, but it does not guarantee lower cost, pause billing on idle servers, or remove the need to watch the bill.

questions.prompt: A developer at a logistics company starts 12 cloud servers for a two-day test, then forgets about them. Nobody uses them for the rest of the month. What happens to the company's bill?
choices: Only the two test days are billed, because billing ends when the test ends
The company keeps paying for all 12 servers for every hour they stay running, busy or not
The cost is a one-time capex charge already paid when the servers were started
Nothing, because the servers were idle and idle servers are free
questions.why: With pay-as-you-go you pay for what you leave running regardless of how busy it is, so forgotten servers keep billing every hour until someone shuts them down.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, in your own words, what it means that the AWS Cloud trades capital expense for variable expense, and name one situation where this trade helps less than people expect.
lessons.modelAnswer: Normally, a company buys its servers up front. That is capital expense: a big payment before it knows how much it will need. It has to guess demand. Guess high and you paid for idle machines. Guess low and customers suffer until new hardware arrives. With AWS you rent capacity pay-as-you-go, so the cost becomes variable. You pay for what you run, and the bill rises in busy months and falls in quiet ones. If a project fails, you switch things off and stop paying instead of being stuck with hardware. The limit is that variable does not automatically mean cheaper. You pay for anything left running, even when it is idle, so forgotten resources quietly add up. Also, for a steady workload that runs flat out all year, the savings over owning hardware shrink, so you still have to watch and manage the monthly bill.
rubricPoints: Defines capital expense as a large up-front purchase of owned assets.
Defines variable expense as cost that tracks actual usage, paid as you go.
Explains that up-front buying forces a demand guess, causing either idle capacity or shortages.
Notes you can stop paying when resources are shut down, unlike sunk hardware cost.
Names a limit, such as paying for idle running resources or smaller savings for steady full-time workloads.

suggested.rationale: A cost model in fictional credits would let the learner compare an up-front purchase against pay-as-you-go bills across changing demand and see how the shape of the cost changes.

lessons.plain: Global infrastructure means a cloud provider has already built data centers in many parts of the world and connected them, so you can rent space in any of them in minutes. Think of a hotel chain with buildings in dozens of cities: if you need to be in a city with no office, you book a room there instead of buying land and putting up a building. For a business, this buys two things. Speed: you can launch in a new location this week, not next year. Reach: you can put your application physically close to customers in another country, so it feels fast to them and can meet local rules about where data must live.
lessons.guessPrompt: A small online shop based in Ireland suddenly gets lots of customers in Australia who complain the site is slow. Without the cloud, what would the shop have to do to fix that, and roughly how long might it take?
lessons.teach:
Global infrastructure is the worldwide set of locations a cloud provider runs and lets customers use on demand. In AWS, a Region is a separate geographic area, such as Sydney or Frankfurt, that holds several data centers. An Availability Zone is one or more data centers inside a Region with its own power and networking. An edge location is a smaller site, often in a big city, that keeps copies of content close to users. Latency is the delay between a user's action and the response, and it grows with physical distance.

This matters because the provider has already paid for the buildings, hardware, network links and staff in each place. The customer only picks a location and starts paying for what they use. That changes two things. Deployment speed: a new location takes minutes, not a long building project. Reach: you can run close to users in new countries, which lowers latency. You can also keep data inside a country when local rules require it, called data residency.

Worked example. The Irish shop has Australian customers. Step one: on premises, it would need to lease rack space in Australia, buy servers, wait for delivery, hire local support and sign network contracts. That is months of work and a large upfront spend before knowing if the market lasts. Step two: in the cloud, it deploys a copy of its application in the Sydney Region the same day. Step three: it puts images and pages on edge locations so Australian pages load quickly. Step four: if the market fades, it shuts the Sydney copy down and stops paying.

A common mistake is thinking global infrastructure automatically makes your application global. Picking one Region gives you one Region. You must choose to deploy into others. A running system placed only in Ireland stays slow for Australian users no matter how big the provider's network is.

questions.prompt: A tutoring company based in Toronto runs its live-lesson app only in an AWS Region in Canada. It has just signed 2,000 students in Japan. Step 1: Japanese students report that lessons feel laggy. Step 2: The team recalls that latency, the delay between a user's action and the response, grows with physical distance, and Canada is far from Japan. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: Japanese students now get quicker responses, and the company pays only for what the new copy uses, which it can switch off if the Japanese market does not last. Which action belongs in Step 3?
choices: Do nothing, because the provider's worldwide network already makes the app global
Lease rack space in Tokyo, order servers and hire local staff to run a new data center
Deploy a copy of the app in an AWS Region located in Japan, which can be done the same day
Move the Canadian servers onto much larger machines so that every request is processed faster
questions.why: Running a copy of the app in a Region near the students shortens the physical distance, which cuts latency, and it takes minutes with pay-as-you-go pricing instead of months of building.

questions.prompt: A health insurer in Germany is told by local rules that its customer records must stay inside Germany. It already uses AWS in a Region in the United States. Which choice uses global infrastructure to meet the rule?
choices: Copy the records to edge locations around the world so they load faster
Store and process the records in an AWS Region located in Germany, which is called data residency
Keep the US Region, because one Region automatically covers every country
Split the records across two Availability Zones inside the US Region
questions.why: Data residency means keeping data inside a country, and the customer achieves it by choosing a Region in that country; Availability Zones and edge locations do not change which country the data lives in.

questions.prompt: A game studio launches its online game in a single AWS Region in Virginia, USA. Players in Singapore complain the game is slow. The producer says, "AWS has locations all over the world, so this shouldn't happen." What is the actual problem?
choices: The provider's network is too small to reach Asia
Picking one Region only gives you that one Region; the studio never deployed closer to Singapore, so the distance keeps latency high
The studio should have used more Availability Zones in Virginia to reach Singapore
Edge locations only work in the United States
questions.why: Global infrastructure is available, not automatic: the customer must choose to deploy into other Regions, so a game hosted only in Virginia stays slow for distant players.

questions.prompt: A clothing retailer wants to test selling in Brazil for three months and is unsure the market will last. How does using an AWS Region in Brazil change its costs compared with building its own data center there?
choices: It avoids a large upfront spend on buildings and hardware, pays only for what it uses, and can stop paying by shutting the copy down if sales fade
It pays a fixed yearly fee for the Region whether or not it runs anything
It must sign local network contracts and hire support staff before launching
It still pays for buildings and servers up front, but AWS delivers them faster
questions.why: The provider has already paid for buildings, hardware, network links and staff, so the customer swaps a large upfront investment for usage-based costs it can end at any time.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what using a cloud provider's global infrastructure actually buys a business that wants to expand into a new country, and name one limit or tradeoff of relying on it.
lessons.modelAnswer: The provider has already built Regions, which are geographic areas each containing several data centers, plus edge locations that cache content near users. So expanding into a new country stops being a building project and becomes a choice of location. We get speed, because we can deploy there in minutes instead of spending months leasing space and buying servers. We get reach, because running close to those customers cuts latency, and keeping data in-country helps with data residency rules. We can also try a market and walk away cheaply if it fails. The limit is that none of this happens on its own. If we deploy only in one Region, users far away still get slow responses. Running in several Regions also adds work and cost, such as copying data between them and paying for more running resources.
rubricPoints: Defines a Region and connects it to choosing a location near users.
Names deployment speed: minutes instead of months of buying and building.
Names reach: lower latency for distant users and meeting data residency needs.
Notes the provider prebuilt the sites, so there is no upfront build cost and you can exit easily.
States a limit, such as the need to deploy into each Region yourself or the extra cost and complexity of running in several.

suggested.rationale: The exam skill is turning a business situation into the specific benefit of speed and geographic reach, and explaining that back is the best practice for it; no listed mission or engine covers choosing Regions.

lessons.plain: These three words often get blurred into 'the cloud is flexible', but each answers a different question. High availability asks: does the service keep running when something breaks? Elasticity asks: does the amount of computer power grow and shrink to match demand, so you pay only for what you use? Agility asks: how fast can the team try something new? Think of a restaurant. High availability is having a second kitchen if one catches fire. Elasticity is calling in extra cooks for the dinner rush and sending them home after. Agility is testing a new dish tonight instead of next season.
lessons.guessPrompt: A shop's website crashes every year during its one-day holiday sale because too many visitors arrive at once, but it never goes down on normal days. Which of the three is the shop missing: staying up when equipment fails, adjusting capacity to demand, or speed to try new ideas?
lessons.teach:
High availability means a system keeps serving users even when one of its parts fails. It works by running copies of the system in separate places, so no single failure stops everything. On AWS those places are usually Availability Zones: separate groups of data centers, with their own power and networking, inside one geographic area called a Region.

Elasticity means capacity grows when demand rises and shrinks when it falls, ideally automatically. It works because cloud resources are rented by the hour or second, so releasing a server stops the charge. It differs from plain scalability, which only means the system can grow; elasticity also shrinks back, so the bill follows real demand.

Agility means the speed at which a team can get resources, experiment, and deliver change. It works because servers, databases and test setups arrive in minutes instead of weeks of purchasing, so a failed experiment costs little.

Worked example: a ticket-selling site. Step one, a power fault takes out one data center; traffic moves to a copy in a second Availability Zone and customers notice nothing. That is high availability. Step two, a popular concert goes on sale and visitors jump tenfold for an hour; extra servers start, then stop when the rush ends, and the bill rises only for that hour. That is elasticity. Step three, marketing wants to test a new seat-picker; the team builds a trial copy in an afternoon and deletes it when the test ends. That is agility.

The common mistake is assuming elasticity gives high availability. Adding twenty servers in a single location handles more visitors, but if that location loses power, all twenty go down together. In a running system, missing high availability shows up as outages, missing elasticity shows up as crashes during peaks or paying for idle machines, and missing agility shows up as slow delivery of new features.

questions.prompt: A small video-streaming company reviews three problems from last quarter and matches each to the cloud advantage it was missing. Problem A: during a football final, viewers jumped fivefold and the servers crashed under the load. Diagnosis: missing elasticity, because capacity did not grow with demand. Problem B: a new subtitle feature took three months to ship because the team had to wait for purchased servers to arrive. Diagnosis: missing agility, because getting resources was slow. Problem C: a networking fault hit the single Availability Zone that ran all of their servers, and the whole service was offline for four hours. Diagnosis: ______. Which choice correctly completes the diagnosis for Problem C?
choices: Missing elasticity; the fix is adding servers that start automatically inside that same zone
Missing agility; the fix is letting the team create servers in minutes instead of weeks
Missing high availability; the fix is running copies of the service in a second Availability Zone
Missing scalability; the fix is replacing the servers in that zone with larger, more powerful ones
questions.why: An outage caused by one location failing means there was no copy running in a separate place, which is exactly what high availability provides by spreading copies across Availability Zones.

questions.prompt: A payroll company's system can add servers when month-end processing begins, but those servers keep running, and keep being charged, for the rest of the month. Which statement best describes this system?
choices: It is elastic, because any system that can add servers is elastic
It is agile, because the servers were obtained quickly
It is scalable but not elastic, because it grows yet never shrinks back with demand
It is highly available, because it has extra servers ready if one fails
questions.why: Scalability only means the system can grow, while elasticity also shrinks capacity when demand falls so the bill follows real use, and this system never shrinks.

questions.prompt: A bank's product team wants to try three different designs for a loan-application form. They build a separate test setup for each in one morning, run them for a week, then delete the two that performed poorly. Which cloud advantage does this mainly show?
choices: Scalability, because the team was able to add more setups
Agility, because resources arrived in hours and failed experiments cost little
High availability, because three copies of the form were running at once
Elasticity, because the number of setups went up and then down
questions.why: Agility is the speed of getting resources and experimenting, and getting test setups in a morning and cheaply discarding the losers is that advantage.

questions.prompt: An online travel agency sets up automatic scaling that grows its fleet from 5 to 40 servers during busy holiday booking periods. All the servers run in one Availability Zone. What happens if that zone loses power during a holiday rush?
choices: Most of the servers keep running, because having 40 servers spreads the risk
Only the extra servers fail, because the original 5 are protected by elasticity
All the servers go down together, because elasticity added capacity but gave no protection from a single location failing
The site stays up, because automatic scaling moves traffic to another Region
questions.why: Elasticity adds capacity but does not provide high availability; servers in one location share that location's failures, so a power loss there takes them all down.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how high availability, elasticity, and agility differ, using one business example for each, and name one thing that adding more servers does not fix.
lessons.modelAnswer: They answer three different questions. High availability is about surviving failure: we run copies of the app in separate places, like two Availability Zones, so if one data center loses power the other keeps serving customers. Elasticity is about matching capacity to demand: during a flash sale servers are added automatically, and afterwards they are removed, so we pay for the peak only while it lasts rather than owning machines that sit idle. Agility is about speed of change: the team can spin up a test environment in minutes to try a new feature, and throw it away cheaply if it fails. The limit to remember is that adding more servers in one location gives capacity, not availability; if that location fails, every server fails with it. Elastic also means shrinking, not just growing, otherwise the cost benefit disappears.
rubricPoints: High availability means staying up when a component or location fails, achieved by copies in separate places such as Availability Zones.
Elasticity means capacity grows and shrinks with demand, so cost follows actual use.
Agility means the speed to obtain resources, experiment, and ship changes cheaply.
More servers in one location adds capacity but does not provide high availability.
Each idea is tied to a concrete business situation rather than a generic 'flexible' label.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests this by describing a business situation and asking which advantage applies, so reasoning through contrasting scenarios builds the distinction best.

lessons.plain: The AWS Well-Architected Framework is a set of questions and good habits AWS publishes for judging whether a cloud system is built well. It groups those habits into six areas called pillars: operational excellence, security, reliability, performance efficiency, cost optimization, and sustainability. Think of a home inspection. The inspector checks the wiring, the plumbing, the roof, and the heating separately, because a house can have perfect plumbing and a leaking roof. The pillars let a team inspect a system the same way, one concern at a time, so a gap in one area is not hidden by strength in another.
lessons.guessPrompt: If you had to check whether an online shop was built well, which separate things would you want to look at? Try to name about six different concerns.
lessons.teach:
The AWS Well-Architected Framework is a structured review method for cloud workloads. A workload is the set of resources and code that delivers one business function, such as a checkout system. The framework has six pillars. A pillar is one area of concern with its own design principles and review questions.

Operational excellence means running and improving the system day to day: automating changes, watching it with monitoring, and learning from failures. Security means protecting data and systems: controlling who can do what, encrypting data, and detecting threats. Reliability means the workload keeps doing its job correctly and recovers from failures, for example by running copies in more than one location. Performance efficiency means using computing resources well as demand changes, picking the right type and size of resource. Cost optimization means delivering the business value at the lowest sensible price, avoiding paying for idle capacity. Sustainability means reducing the environmental impact of running the workload, mainly by using less energy and hardware for the same result.

Why it works: splitting a review into six lenses stops a team from judging a system by one impressive feature.

Worked example: a team reviews a photo-sharing app. Operational excellence: deployments are manual, so they plan automation. Security: storage is publicly readable, so they lock it down. Reliability: one server in one data center, so a single failure stops everything; they add a second location. Performance efficiency: image resizing is slow on general-purpose servers; they choose better-suited ones. Cost optimization: test servers run all weekend unused; they schedule shutdowns. Sustainability: old photos sit on fast storage; they move them to lower-energy storage tiers.

A common mistake is treating the pillars as AWS services or as a one-time exam you pass. They are lenses applied repeatedly as the workload changes. Another frequent mix-up is reliability versus performance efficiency: reliability is about staying up and recovering, performance efficiency is about speed and fit of resources. In a running system, skipping a pillar shows up later as an outage, a breach, or a surprise bill.

questions.prompt: A regional bus company reviews its online ticket-booking workload pillar by pillar. Operational excellence: nobody is alerted when bookings fail, so they add monitoring and alarms. Security: every staff member shares one admin login, so they give each person their own limited permissions. Reliability: [missing finding]. Performance efficiency: seat searches slow down badly on Friday evenings, so they pick a resource type better suited to search. Cost optimization: a large reporting server sits idle except one hour a month, so they run it only when needed. Sustainability: ten years of old booking logs sit on hardware nobody uses, so they delete what is no longer required. Which finding best fills the reliability step?
choices: Payment records are stored unencrypted, so they switch on encryption for that data.
They enable the AWS service called Reliability so the framework review counts as complete.
Seat maps take six seconds to load, so they move the site onto faster, better-sized servers.
The booking database runs in one data center only, so they add a standby copy elsewhere.
questions.why: Reliability is about the workload continuing to do its job and recovering from failure, and a single-location database means one failure stops all bookings, so adding a copy in a second location addresses it.

questions.prompt: In the AWS Well-Architected Framework, what is a pillar?
choices: A separate AWS service you switch on to protect a workload
A one-time audit that a workload passes or fails permanently
A physical data center location where copies of a workload run
One area of concern, with its own design principles and review questions
questions.why: The framework defines a pillar as one area of concern with its own design principles and review questions; pillars are lenses, not services, audits, or locations.

questions.prompt: An insurance company's claims portal never goes down and always returns correct results, but each page takes nine seconds to load because it runs on servers too small and poorly matched to the work. Which pillar is the main concern?
choices: Operational excellence
Performance efficiency
Sustainability
Reliability
questions.why: The system stays up and correct, so reliability is fine; the problem is the speed and fit of the resources, which is performance efficiency.

questions.prompt: An online bookshop ran a Well-Architected review two years ago, scored well on all six pillars, and has not reviewed the workload since, even though it has added a new payments feature and a mobile app. What is the main problem with this approach?
choices: The pillars are lenses meant to be applied repeatedly as the workload changes, so the new parts have never been reviewed.
A good score on a past review stays valid, so the only risk is that the scoring rules have changed.
Only the security pillar matters once payments are involved, so the other five can be ignored now.
They should replace the review with a single AWS service that handles all six pillars automatically.
questions.why: The framework is not a one-time exam; the workload has changed, so skipping repeat reviews risks later outages, breaches, or surprise bills in the unreviewed parts.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what the six pillars of the AWS Well-Architected Framework are and what each one is about, and name one limit of the framework or one place where improving one pillar can cost you in another.
lessons.modelAnswer: The Well-Architected Framework is AWS's review method for checking whether a workload is built well, and it splits that check into six pillars. Operational excellence is about running and improving the system, like automating deployments and learning from incidents. Security is protecting data and access. Reliability is staying available and recovering from failure. Performance efficiency is using the right type and amount of resources as demand changes. Cost optimization is getting the value without paying for waste. Sustainability is cutting energy and hardware use. The point is to look at each concern separately so one strength does not hide a weakness. A limit is that it is guidance, not a guarantee or a service you switch on; you have to apply it repeatedly. And pillars can pull against each other: adding a second location improves reliability but raises cost.
rubricPoints: Names all six pillars correctly.
Gives an accurate one-line meaning for each pillar.
Describes the framework as a review method or set of lenses, not a product or service.
Notes it should be applied repeatedly as the workload changes.
Names a tradeoff between pillars, such as reliability versus cost.

suggested.rationale: Learning the six pillar names and what each covers is vocabulary to absorb first, and no current mission or planned engine exercises the framework directly.

lessons.plain: The AWS Well-Architected Framework is a checklist of six concerns, called pillars, for judging whether a cloud system is built well. Each pillar asks one question. Can we run and improve it? Is it protected? Does it keep working when parts fail? Does it use resources efficiently for the work? Does it avoid wasted money? Does it limit its environmental footprint? Think of a house inspector who checks wiring, plumbing and the roof separately. Each check owns its own question, and fixing one can make another worse. For example, adding a second boiler costs more.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company runs a second complete copy of its website in another part of the world, sitting mostly idle, just in case the first copy goes down. Which concern does this improve, and which concern does it make worse?
lessons.teach:
The AWS Well-Architected Framework is AWS's set of design questions for reviewing a cloud workload. A workload is the collection of resources that together deliver one business function. The framework groups its questions into six pillars, and each pillar owns one concern.

Operational excellence owns running and improving the system: deploying safely, monitoring it, and learning from incidents. Security owns protecting data and systems: who can access what, encryption, and detecting misuse. Reliability owns the system keeping its promised function when components fail or demand spikes, and recovering afterwards. Performance efficiency owns choosing and using the right type and size of resources to meet the demand. Cost optimization owns delivering the business value at the lowest sensible price, with no paying for idle or unneeded capacity. Sustainability owns reducing the energy and hardware the workload consumes.

The pillars help because a design decision often moves several of them at once, and naming the pillar exposes the tradeoff. Here is a worked example. A shop runs its store in one AWS Region, which is a separate geographic area of AWS data centers. Step one: the business asks for the store to survive a whole Region outage. That is a reliability concern. Step two: the team adds a standby copy in a second Region. Reliability improves. Step three: the standby servers and the copied data cost money even while idle, so cost optimization gets worse. The idle servers also use energy, so sustainability gets worse too. Step four: the team decides based on how much an outage would cost the business.

Security and performance can also pull apart. Encrypting and inspecting every request adds a small delay.

A common mistake is treating performance efficiency as reliability. A fast system can still go down completely, and a reliable system can still be slow. In a running system, optimizing one pillar blindly causes harm. Cutting all spare capacity to save money can turn a traffic spike into an outage. The pillars are a way to make tradeoffs on purpose, not a score where every pillar is maxed out.

questions.prompt: A photo-printing company runs its order website on twelve servers around the clock, even though most nights only three are busy. Trace this decision through the Well-Architected pillars. Step one: the finance team asks to stop paying for servers that sit idle. That is a cost optimization concern. Step two: the team removes all spare capacity and runs only the servers the normal load needs. Cost optimization improves, and because fewer idle machines draw power, sustainability improves too. Step three: missing. Step four: the team decides how much spare capacity to keep, based on how often sudden order surges happen and what an outage would cost the business. Which statement correctly fills in step three?
choices: Security gets worse, because running fewer servers means less of the data can be encrypted.
Performance efficiency improves, because the remaining servers must be faster to carry the same load.
Reliability gets worse, because with no spare capacity, a sudden surge in orders can turn into an outage.
Nothing else changes, because a decision made to save money only affects the cost optimization pillar.
questions.why: Reliability owns the system keeping its function when demand spikes, so removing all spare capacity trades reliability away for lower cost.

questions.prompt: A team is building a database that holds a large amount of data in memory. They compare several server types and pick one with extra memory and an average processor, because that matches what the database needs. Which Well-Architected pillar owns this decision?
choices: Sustainability
Reliability
Performance efficiency
Cost optimization
questions.why: Performance efficiency owns choosing the right type and size of resources to meet the demand placed on the workload.

questions.prompt: A concert-ticket website loads every page in under 100 milliseconds. Last month its only database server crashed, and the site was completely offline for three hours. A manager says, 'Our pages are fast, so we are clearly strong on reliability.' What is the best response?
choices: Speed shows the site is reliable, but the crash shows it is weak on security.
The outage is an operational excellence issue only, so performance and reliability are both fine.
The manager is right, because a fast system is one that keeps its promised function.
Speed is performance efficiency. Going fully offline when one component fails is a reliability weakness, and a fast system can still go down.
questions.why: Performance and reliability are separate concerns, and a site that goes offline when one server fails has a reliability problem no matter how fast its pages are.

questions.prompt: After a software release caused errors for customers, an online bookstore changes how it works. New releases now go out to a small share of users first while dashboards are watched, and every incident ends with a written review of what to change next time. Which pillar do these changes mainly strengthen?
choices: Security
Reliability
Performance efficiency
Operational excellence
questions.why: Operational excellence owns running and improving the system, which includes deploying safely, monitoring, and learning from incidents.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would tell the six Well-Architected pillars apart, and describe one real conflict between two pillars and how you would decide between them.
lessons.modelAnswer: Each pillar owns one question. Operational excellence asks whether we can run, monitor and improve the workload. Security asks whether data and access are protected. Reliability asks whether it keeps working through failures and recovers. Performance efficiency asks whether we picked the right resource types and sizes for the demand. Cost optimization asks whether we are paying for anything we don't need. Sustainability asks whether we are using more energy and hardware than necessary. They conflict because one change moves several pillars. Keeping a standby copy in a second Region raises reliability. It also lowers cost optimization and sustainability, because idle servers still cost money and use power. I'd decide by comparing the cost of an outage with the cost of the standby. The limit is that no design maxes every pillar, so the framework helps us choose tradeoffs deliberately rather than giving one right answer.
rubricPoints: Names the six pillars and gives each its own distinct concern.
Distinguishes reliability (keeps working through failure) from performance efficiency (right resources for the demand).
Gives a concrete conflict, such as redundancy raising reliability while lowering cost optimization.
Explains that the tradeoff is decided by business need, such as the cost of downtime.
States that the framework guides deliberate tradeoffs rather than maximizing every pillar.

suggested.rationale: Telling the pillars apart is best practised by reasoning through short business situations that ask which pillar a choice serves and which one it costs, as the exam does.

lessons.plain: Moving a company onto the cloud is less like flipping a switch and more like moving house: you decide what to bring, who packs what, and in what order, so nothing gets lost and the family can still eat dinner during the move. A cloud adoption strategy is that overall plan for how and how fast an organization starts using cloud services. The AWS Cloud Adoption Framework (AWS CAF) is a free planning guide from AWS that breaks the move into areas of responsibility, so the people, money, rules and technology all get ready together, not just the servers.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company moves all its servers to the cloud in one weekend, and the technology works fine. A month later, costs are out of control and staff keep making mistakes. Before reading anything, what do you think was missing from their plan?
lessons.teach:
A cloud adoption strategy is an organization's plan for how it will start using cloud services: what moves first, how fast, and who is responsible. Common shapes include a phased approach (start with a few low-risk workloads and expand), a cloud-first policy (new projects default to the cloud), and hybrid (some systems stay in the company's own data center and some run in the cloud). The AWS Cloud Adoption Framework (AWS CAF) is AWS's planning guide for building such a strategy.

AWS CAF groups the work into six perspectives, meaning areas of concern, each owned by different people. Three are business-facing: Business (making sure cloud spending supports company goals), People (training, roles and culture change), and Governance (budgets, cost control, risk and rules). Three are technical: Platform (designing and building the cloud environment), Security (protecting data and controlling access), and Operations (running and monitoring services day to day). It also suggests working in four repeating phases: Envision (decide what success looks like), Align (find gaps between the perspectives and agree on fixes), Launch (deliver small pilot projects), and Scale (expand what worked).

Why it works: a cloud move fails most often on the non-technical side, and the perspectives force those owners into the plan early.

Worked example: a regional retailer wants its online shop in the cloud. Envision: leaders state the goal of handling holiday traffic. Align: the People perspective finds staff have no cloud skills; Governance finds no spending limits exist. Launch: the team moves only the product catalog, trains staff, and sets budget alerts. Scale: after the pilot succeeds, checkout and inventory follow.

Common mistake: treating adoption as a purely technical project and only staffing the Platform perspective. The consequence in a running system is servers that work but nobody trained to operate them, no cost control, and access rules nobody owns, which leads to surprise bills and avoidable outages.

questions.prompt: A city library network wants to move its room-booking and e-book lending systems to AWS, using AWS CAF (the AWS Cloud Adoption Framework, AWS's planning guide that organizes cloud adoption into six perspectives and four repeating phases). Envision: the director sets the goal of letting patrons book rooms online at any hour. Align: the Security perspective finds that no one owns the rules for who can see patron records, and the Operations perspective finds no one is assigned to watch the systems after hours. Launch: [missing step]. Scale: after the pilot runs smoothly for three months, e-book lending moves over as well. Which choice best fills the Launch step?
choices: Hold more meetings to restate the goal before any system is moved.
Move only room booking as a small pilot, assign an owner for patron-record access, and put someone on after-hours monitoring.
Buy larger servers for the library's own building so the cloud move is not needed.
Move both systems at once so patrons get every improvement on the same day.
questions.why: Launch means delivering a small pilot while fixing the gaps Align found, here access ownership and monitoring, before Scale expands to more systems.

questions.prompt: A shipping company announces that every new application it builds will run in the cloud by default, unless there is a specific reason not to. Which cloud adoption strategy (an organization's plan for how it starts using cloud services) is this?
choices: A phased approach
A hybrid approach
A cloud-first policy
The Envision phase of AWS CAF
questions.why: A cloud-first policy means new projects default to the cloud, which is exactly what the company announced.

questions.prompt: While planning a cloud move with AWS CAF, an insurance firm discovers that nobody sets budgets for cloud spending and nobody reviews the risk of breaking industry rules. Which AWS CAF perspective (an area of concern owned by specific people) covers this gap?
choices: Operations, because it runs and monitors services day to day
Platform, because it designs and builds the cloud environment
Governance
People, because it handles training and roles
questions.why: Governance is the perspective responsible for budgets, cost control, risk and rules.

questions.prompt: A small software startup moves its customer portal to the cloud. Only its engineers who build the cloud environment (the Platform perspective) are involved; no one plans training, spending limits or access ownership. What is the most likely result once the portal is running?
choices: Working servers, but surprise bills and avoidable outages because no one is trained to operate them, controls cost or owns access rules
An automatic move into the Scale phase, because the technical work is finished
Slower servers, because the Platform perspective cannot build cloud environments alone
No problems, because a working cloud environment is all a cloud move needs
questions.why: Treating adoption as purely technical leaves the business-facing and operational concerns unowned, which leads to surprise bills and avoidable outages.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what the AWS Cloud Adoption Framework is for, name its six perspectives and four phases, and describe one limit or tradeoff of using it to plan a cloud move.
lessons.modelAnswer: AWS CAF is a planning guide for moving an organization onto the cloud. Its point is that a cloud move is not just a technical job. It splits the work into six perspectives: Business, People and Governance on the business side, and Platform, Security and Operations on the technical side, so each group of owners gets ready together. It runs in four repeating phases: Envision what success means, Align the perspectives and close gaps, Launch small pilots, then Scale what worked. A phased strategy fits it naturally because pilots expose problems cheaply. The limit is that CAF is guidance, not a tool that does the work: it tells you which questions to ask, but people still have to make the decisions. The tradeoff is time, since aligning six groups before launching is slower than just moving servers, though usually cheaper than fixing a rushed move.
rubricPoints: States that a cloud adoption strategy is the plan for what moves, how fast, and who owns it.
Describes AWS CAF as a planning guide that covers business and organizational readiness, not only technology.
Names the six perspectives, split into business-facing and technical groups.
Names the four phases: Envision, Align, Launch, Scale.
Names a limit or tradeoff, such as CAF being guidance only or alignment taking time.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests this by describing a business situation and asking which perspective or phase applies, so reasoning through scenarios builds the skill better than reading alone.

lessons.plain: The AWS Cloud Adoption Framework (AWS CAF) is a planning guide AWS offers to organizations moving to the cloud. It says the move should be judged by four business results, not by technology for its own sake: less risk, better environmental, social and governance (ESG) performance, more revenue, and smoother, cheaper day-to-day operations. Think of renovating a shop: nobody renovates just to own new shelves. You do it so the shop is safer, wastes less energy, sells more, and runs with less effort. CAF asks a cloud project to show which of those four results it delivers, and how.
lessons.guessPrompt: A retailer moves its online store to the cloud and can now launch a new product page in two days instead of two months. Which business result do you think that mostly serves: lower risk, better environmental performance, more revenue, or more efficient operations?
lessons.teach:
The AWS Cloud Adoption Framework (AWS CAF) is AWS's structured guide for planning a cloud move. A framework here means an organized set of questions and practices, not software. CAF argues that cloud adoption should be measured by business outcomes, meaning results a company's leaders care about, and it names four.

Reduced business risk: fewer chances of costly failure. Examples are better security controls, backups kept in more than one place, and systems that keep running when one data center fails.

Improved ESG performance: ESG stands for environmental, social and governance, the ways investors and regulators judge a company beyond profit. The cloud mainly helps the environmental part. Shared, heavily used data centers usually waste less energy than a half-empty private server room.

Increased revenue: more income, often because new products reach customers faster or the company can sell in new markets.

Increased operational efficiency: doing the same work with less cost, effort or delay, for example by automating routine tasks and paying only for capacity actually used.

The framing works because it turns a technical project into answers a non-technical decision maker can weigh. Each outcome can be tracked with its own measure.

Worked example: a bank runs reports on its own servers. Step 1: it moves backups to a second cloud location, so an outage no longer means lost data. That is reduced risk. Step 2: it retires an old, power-hungry server room, lowering the bank's carbon footprint. That is ESG. Step 3: report jobs now run automatically overnight instead of needing two staff, which is operational efficiency. Step 4: the freed staff build a new mobile feature that attracts customers, which is revenue.

A common mistake is lumping every benefit under "saves money." Saving money is efficiency only. Faster launches serve revenue, and resilience serves risk. On the exam, and in real planning, you should name the specific outcome a change delivers. If a migration is justified on cost alone, it can look like a failure even when it has greatly reduced risk or increased sales.

questions.prompt: A regional grocery chain with 40 stores moves its systems to AWS. Each change is matched to one AWS CAF business outcome (CAF, the AWS Cloud Adoption Framework, is AWS's organized set of questions and practices for planning a cloud move). Step 1: the checkout and inventory system now runs in two separate locations, so a storm that knocks out one data center no longer stops sales. That is reduced business risk. Step 2: stock reorders are now automated, cutting manual ordering work from 30 staff-hours to 5 per week. That is increased operational efficiency. Step 3: the chain shuts down its own server closet and its old cooling units, cutting electricity use. That is improved ESG performance. Step 4: the chain launches online ordering in three new towns within six weeks and gains customers it never reached before. Which outcome is Step 4?
choices: Increased operational efficiency, because the launch took only six weeks
Increased revenue, because a new product reaches new markets and brings in more income
Reduced business risk, because spreading into new towns lowers dependence on old stores
Improved ESG performance, because serving more towns helps the social part of ESG
questions.why: Getting a new offering to customers quickly and selling in new markets brings in more income, which is the increased revenue outcome, not efficiency, risk or ESG.

questions.prompt: In the AWS CAF outcome called improved ESG performance, what does ESG stand for, and which part does moving to the cloud mainly help?
choices: Environmental, social and governance; mainly the governance part
Energy, savings and growth; mainly the savings part
Environmental, social and governance; mainly the environmental part
Efficiency, security and growth; mainly the security part
questions.why: ESG means environmental, social and governance, and the cloud mainly helps the environmental part because shared, heavily used data centers usually waste less energy than a half-empty private server room.

questions.prompt: A video game studio moves its game servers to AWS. A year later, its monthly IT bill is about the same as before, but major outages fell from six a year to none. The finance director declares the migration a failure. What error is the director making, according to AWS CAF thinking?
choices: The director should have measured revenue only, since that is CAF's main outcome
Judging it on cost alone and ignoring the large reduction in business risk
None; if costs did not fall, the cloud move delivered no business outcome
Calling it a failure is right, because fewer outages count only as ESG
questions.why: Saving money is only the efficiency outcome; far fewer outages is reduced business risk, so judging the move on cost alone hides a real benefit.

questions.prompt: A delivery company used to buy enough servers to handle its December peak and leave most of them idle the rest of the year. On AWS it now pays only for the computing capacity it actually uses each month, doing the same work for less money. Which AWS CAF business outcome does this change mainly serve?
choices: Increased revenue
Increased operational efficiency
Improved ESG performance
Reduced business risk
questions.why: Doing the same work with less cost by paying only for capacity actually used is the definition of increased operational efficiency.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the four business outcomes AWS CAF targets, giving one concrete example of each, and name a limit or tradeoff in judging a cloud move this way.
lessons.modelAnswer: CAF says a cloud move should pay off in four business results, not in technology for its own sake. Reduced risk means fewer costly failures, for example backups kept in a second location so one outage does not destroy data. ESG performance means environmental, social and governance standing. The cloud mostly helps the environmental part, because shared, well-used data centers waste less energy than our half-empty server room. Increased revenue means more income, such as launching a product page in days and reaching customers sooner. Operational efficiency means the same work done for less cost or effort, like automating nightly jobs. One tradeoff is that the outcomes don't all show up at once or on the same budget line. A migration can raise costs at first while it lowers risk. If we judge it only on savings, we will undervalue it. So for each outcome we need its own measure.
rubricPoints: Defines AWS CAF as a planning framework that measures cloud adoption by business outcomes.
Names all four outcomes: reduced risk, ESG performance, increased revenue, operational efficiency.
Gives a distinct, concrete example for each outcome rather than calling them all savings.
Expands ESG as environmental, social and governance and links the cloud mainly to the environmental part.
Names a limit, such as outcomes needing separate measures, or cost savings alone understating the value.

suggested.rationale: The skill here is matching a business change to the right outcome and justifying it in words, which explaining back practices better than any existing hands-on mission.

lessons.plain: A migration strategy is the plan for what happens to each application when a company moves to the cloud. Think of moving house: some furniture you carry over as it is, some you repaint first, some you replace with new, some you throw out, and some stays in storage for now. AWS names seven such choices, often called the seven Rs. Moving a database is a special case because its data keeps changing while you move it. A replication service copies the data and then keeps the copy in sync, so the business keeps running until a short final switch-over.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company has a working application, a tight two-month deadline to leave its data center, and no budget to rewrite anything. Would you copy it over mostly as it is, or rebuild it to suit the cloud? Why?
lessons.teach:
A migration strategy is the decision about what happens to each application in a cloud move. AWS groups the options as the seven Rs. Retire means switching it off because nobody needs it. Retain means leaving it on premises for now, perhaps for compliance reasons or because it will soon be replaced. Rehost ("lift and shift") means copying servers unchanged onto cloud virtual machines. It is fastest with the least change, and it delivers the fewest cloud benefits. Relocate means moving a whole virtualization platform, such as VMware-based hosts, without changing the machines inside it. Replatform ("lift, tinker and shift") means moving with a few targeted changes. A common one is swapping a self-run database for a managed database service like Amazon RDS, where the provider handles patching and backups. Repurchase means replacing the application with software as a service (SaaS), a ready-made application rented over the internet. Refactor (re-architect) means rewriting the application around cloud-native services. It is the slowest and costliest option up front and brings the biggest long-term gain.

This works because each R trades effort now against benefit later. You match the R to the time, skills and appetite for change the business actually has.

Databases need replication. AWS Database Migration Service (DMS) is a managed replication service. It copies existing data from a source database to a target, then keeps applying new changes while the source stays live. This second stage is called continuous replication, or change data capture. When the database engines differ, for example Oracle to PostgreSQL, the AWS Schema Conversion Tool first translates table structures and stored code.

Worked example: a retailer's order system runs on an aging server, the deadline is two months, and there is no rewrite budget. First, the deadline rules out refactor. Second, the team wants to stop patching databases, so they replatform the database onto RDS. Third, DMS performs a full copy, then streams changes while orders keep flowing. Fourth, at a quiet hour the application is pointed at RDS, which means minutes of downtime instead of a weekend.

The common mistake is assuming everything should be refactored. Rewriting a stable system under a deadline risks outages. Skipping continuous replication forces a long cutover during which orders are refused or lost.

questions.prompt:
A university library's catalog database runs on Microsoft SQL Server in its own data centre. The library has six weeks and wants to stop doing its own database patching, so it will move to Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL, a managed database service, with only small application changes. Here is the plan, with one step missing.

Step 1: Because the change is a targeted swap to a managed database rather than a rewrite, the strategy is replatform.
Step 2: ???
Step 3: AWS Database Migration Service (DMS), a managed replication service, makes a full copy of the catalog data into the new PostgreSQL database.
Step 4: DMS keeps applying new loans and returns from the still-running source database (continuous replication).
Step 5: On a quiet evening the catalog application is pointed at RDS, so the outage lasts minutes.

What is Step 2?
choices: Copy the SQL Server machine unchanged onto a cloud virtual machine and stop there.
Rewrite the whole catalog application around cloud-native services before any data is moved.
Shut the SQL Server database down so that no new changes arrive while DMS is copying.
Use the AWS Schema Conversion Tool to translate the SQL Server table structures and stored code into PostgreSQL form.
questions.why: The source engine (SQL Server) differs from the target engine (PostgreSQL), so the Schema Conversion Tool must first translate the table structures and stored code before DMS can copy and replicate the data.

questions.prompt: A design agency runs its own timesheet application on an office server. It decides to switch that application off and instead pay a monthly subscription for a ready-made timesheet product that staff use through a web browser. Which migration strategy is this?
choices: Rehost, because the timesheet work continues in a new location
Refactor, because the timesheet system is rebuilt for the cloud
Retire, because the old server is switched off
Repurchase, because the application is replaced with software as a service (SaaS)
questions.why: Replacing an application with a ready-made product rented over the internet is repurchase; retire would mean nobody needs the function any more, but here the timesheet function continues.

questions.prompt: A logistics company runs 300 virtual machines on VMware-based hosts. It wants to move the whole virtualization platform to AWS quickly, without changing any of the machines running inside it. Which migration strategy fits best?
choices: Refactor, rewriting each workload around cloud-native services
Relocate, moving the entire virtualization platform as it is
Retain, keeping everything on premises until a later date
Replatform, swapping each machine's database for Amazon RDS
questions.why: Relocate means moving a whole virtualization platform, such as VMware hosts, without changing the machines inside it, which matches what the company wants.

questions.prompt: An online ticket seller migrates its booking database to a managed database. To save effort, the team uses only a one-time full copy and skips continuous replication (change data capture), which is the stage that keeps applying new changes from the live source. What is the most likely consequence for the running business?
choices: The provider will stop handling patching and backups on the managed database
The new database cannot accept any data until the application is fully refactored
A long cutover window during which the source must be frozen, so bookings are refused or lost
The Schema Conversion Tool will automatically take over and stream the changes
questions.why: Without continuous replication, any booking made after the full copy is missed unless the source is frozen, so the cutover becomes long and bookings are refused or lost instead of the switch taking only minutes.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose among the seven Rs for a workload, and why a database move usually uses a replication service instead of a one-time copy. Name one tradeoff between the fast strategies and the deep ones.
lessons.modelAnswer: Each application gets its own R based on time, budget and how much benefit we want. Unused systems get retired. Ones we can't move yet are retained. If speed matters most, we rehost, copying servers as they are, or relocate an entire VMware estate. If a small change pays off, we replatform, for example moving the database to managed RDS so we stop patching it. If a SaaS product already does the job, we repurchase. Refactoring, a full rewrite for cloud-native services, gives the biggest long-term gains but costs the most time and risk up front. That is the main tradeoff: fast moves carry over old inefficiencies, and deep moves delay the migration. For databases, DMS copies the data and then keeps replicating changes while the source stays live, so cutover takes minutes rather than a long outage. If the engines differ, the Schema Conversion Tool translates the schema first.
rubricPoints: Names the seven Rs and gives what each one means, at least for rehost, replatform, refactor and repurchase.
Matches the strategy to constraints such as deadline, budget, skills and desired benefit.
States the tradeoff that faster, low-change moves give fewer cloud benefits than refactoring, which costs more up front.
Explains that DMS does a full copy plus continuous replication so the source stays live and downtime is short.
Notes that the Schema Conversion Tool is needed when the source and target database engines differ.

suggested.rationale: Picking the right R and replication approach is a judgment call best practised by reasoning through exam-style business scenarios, and no current mission or planned engine performs a migration.

lessons.plain: A migration journey is the multi-step move of a company's applications and data from its own servers into the cloud. Few companies make that move alone, so AWS offers support in three kinds: people (AWS experts and partner firms you can hire), programs (structured plans that bundle guidance, training and sometimes funding credits), and tools (services that discover what you run, estimate cost and copy servers or databases across). Think of moving house: you can hire movers, follow a moving checklist, and rent a truck. Each helps a different part of the job, and none of them decides for you which furniture to keep.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company wants to move 300 servers to AWS but does not even have an accurate list of what those servers run. Before anything is copied, what kind of help do you think they need first: someone to move the servers, or something to find out what they have?
lessons.teach:
Resources that support a migration journey are the people, programs and tools AWS and its ecosystem provide to help a customer plan, fund and carry out a move to the cloud. Sorting them by kind makes exam questions easier.

People: AWS Professional Services is a team of AWS employees a customer can hire to advise on or deliver a migration. The AWS Partner Network (APN) is the community of independent companies (consulting firms, software vendors) that AWS has vetted; partners are not AWS staff, but many specialise in migrations.

Programs: the AWS Migration Acceleration Program (MAP) is a structured method in three phases (assess, mobilize, migrate and modernize) that combines guidance, training and, for qualifying projects, credits that offset some migration cost. AWS Prescriptive Guidance is a free library of tested patterns and step-by-step strategies. AWS Training and Certification upskills the customer's own staff.

Tools: AWS Application Discovery Service inventories on-premises servers and their dependencies. Migration Evaluator builds a business case by estimating cloud cost from current usage. AWS Migration Hub is a single dashboard that tracks progress across tools. AWS Application Migration Service copies whole servers into AWS; AWS Database Migration Service (DMS) copies databases while the source keeps running. The AWS Snow Family are physical storage devices shipped to move very large data sets when the network is too slow.

Worked example: a retailer with 300 poorly documented servers. Step one, Application Discovery Service maps what runs and what talks to what. Step two, Migration Evaluator turns that into a cost case for leadership. Step three, they join MAP and hire a partner for hands-on help. Step four, Application Migration Service and DMS move workloads, tracked in Migration Hub.

Common mistake: assuming copy tools come first. Moving servers before discovery breaks hidden dependencies, so an application that depended on an unlisted server fails after cutover and the migration stalls.

questions.prompt: A logistics company is moving its order system to AWS. Here is its plan, with one step left blank. Step 1: AWS Application Discovery Service, a tool that inventories on-premises servers and their dependencies, finds 40 servers. It also shows that the order database is read and written by three application servers around the clock. Step 2: Migration Evaluator, a tool that estimates cloud cost from current usage, produces a cost case, and leadership approves the move. Step 3: A 120 TB archive of scanned delivery receipts would take months to send over the office's slow internet link, so the company orders AWS Snow Family devices (physical storage devices shipped by courier) to carry it. Step 4: MISSING. The order database must be copied into AWS while it keeps taking orders. Step 5: AWS Application Migration Service copies the three application servers, and AWS Migration Hub tracks progress across every tool on one dashboard. Which resource completes Step 4?
choices: AWS Snow Family devices, because the database is large
AWS Prescriptive Guidance, because it has step-by-step database patterns
AWS Database Migration Service (DMS), which copies a database while the source keeps running
AWS Migration Hub, because it watches the database move
questions.why: DMS is the tool built to copy a database into AWS while the original keeps running, which is exactly what a database that takes orders around the clock needs.

questions.prompt: A furniture manufacturer wants hands-on help with its migration. It specifically wants an independent consulting firm that AWS has vetted, not a team of AWS employees. Which resource fits?
choices: AWS Professional Services
The AWS Partner Network (APN)
AWS Training and Certification
AWS Prescriptive Guidance
questions.why: The APN is the community of vetted independent companies, such as consulting firms, and many of them specialise in migrations. AWS Professional Services is staffed by AWS employees, so it does not fit.

questions.prompt: The finance director of a chain of dental clinics will not approve a cloud move until she sees an estimate of what AWS would cost, based on how the clinics' 25 servers are used today. Which tool is built to produce that business case?
choices: AWS Migration Hub
AWS Training and Certification
AWS Application Discovery Service
Migration Evaluator
questions.why: Migration Evaluator builds a business case by estimating cloud cost from current usage. Application Discovery Service only inventories servers and their dependencies, and Migration Hub only tracks progress.

questions.prompt: An insurance firm started its migration by copying its 60 servers into AWS straight away. After cutover, its claims application failed, because it depended on an on-premises licensing server that nobody had listed. Which change would most likely have prevented this?
choices: Running AWS Application Discovery Service first to map servers and what talks to what
Watching the copy on the AWS Migration Hub dashboard
Joining the Migration Acceleration Program (MAP) to receive credits
Shipping the data on AWS Snow Family devices instead of over the network
questions.why: Doing discovery first reveals hidden dependencies such as the licensing server. Skipping it and copying servers immediately is the common mistake that breaks applications after cutover.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the three kinds of migration resources AWS offers, give one example of each, and name a limit: something these resources do not do for the customer.
lessons.modelAnswer: AWS backs a migration with people, programs and tools. People means AWS Professional Services, which is AWS staff you hire, or a firm from the AWS Partner Network, which are independent vetted companies. Programs means structured help such as the Migration Acceleration Program, which walks you through assess, mobilize and migrate phases and can offer credits for qualifying projects, plus free Prescriptive Guidance and training for our own staff. Tools cover each stage: Application Discovery Service finds what we run, Migration Evaluator builds the cost case, Application Migration Service and Database Migration Service do the copying, Snow devices handle huge data, and Migration Hub tracks it all. The limit is that none of this makes the decisions or owns the outcome for us: we still choose which workloads to move and how, partners and Professional Services cost money, and tools only work well if discovery is done first.
rubricPoints: Groups resources into people, programs and tools.
Names at least one correct example in each group.
Distinguishes AWS Professional Services (AWS staff) from APN partners (independent firms).
Matches tools to stages such as discovery, business case, moving and tracking.
States a limit, such as resources not making decisions, costing money, or needing discovery first.

suggested.rationale: This objective is mainly a catalogue of AWS programs, people and tools to recognise and match to migration stages, which no current mission or planned engine exercises directly.

lessons.plain: A fixed cost is money you pay no matter how much you use something, like a monthly gym membership: the price is the same whether you go thirty times or never. A variable cost moves with use, like paying per visit: go more, pay more; go less, pay less. In computing, owning servers in your own building is mostly fixed cost, because you pay for the machines, space and power even when they sit idle. Renting computing from a cloud provider is mostly variable cost, because the bill follows what you actually run. Knowing which kind of cost you have tells you who carries the risk of guessing demand wrong.
lessons.guessPrompt: A shop's website is busy only during a two-week holiday sale and quiet the rest of the year. Would it rather pay a flat amount for enough servers to handle the sale all year, or pay only for the servers it runs each hour? Why?
lessons.teach:
A fixed cost is one that stays the same over a period regardless of how much you use. A variable cost is one that rises and falls with usage. Capacity means how much work your setup can handle; utilization means how much of that capacity you actually use.

In a company's own data center, most costs are fixed: purchased servers, building space, cooling, maintenance contracts and staff to look after hardware. You must buy enough capacity for your busiest moment, so in quiet periods you still pay for idle machines. In the cloud, most compute and storage are billed pay-as-you-go, meaning you are charged per hour, per second or per gigabyte actually used. The cost follows demand instead of a guess about demand.

Worked example in made-up credits. Option A: own 10 servers, costing 5,000 credits a month whether used or not. Option B: rent servers at 1 credit per server-hour (a month is about 720 hours). In a quiet month the shop needs 2 servers: 2 x 720 = 1,440 credits with B, versus 5,000 with A. In the sale month it needs 10: 10 x 720 = 7,200 with B, versus 5,000 with A. Over a year of eleven quiet months and one busy month, B costs about 11 x 1,440 + 7,200 = 23,040, while A costs 12 x 5,000 = 60,000. Variable wins because usage is uneven. If the shop needed all 10 servers every month, A would be cheaper, since steady, predictable use is where fixed costs can win.

A common mistake is assuming variable cost is always cheaper. It is cheaper when usage swings or is uncertain; for constant heavy use it can cost more. Another mistake is thinking only hardware purchases are fixed; leases, contracts and salaries are fixed too.

In a running system, variable billing means forgotten or oversized resources keep adding to the bill, and a traffic spike raises the bill along with it, so someone has to watch spending.

questions.prompt:
A concert-ticketing company is comparing two ways to run its booking website. Option A: own 6 servers for a fixed 4,000 credits a month, whether they are used or not. Option B: rent servers pay-as-you-go at 1 credit per server-hour, with a month counted as 720 hours. For 9 quiet months a year it needs only 1 server. For 3 busy concert-season months it needs all 6.

Step 1: Quiet month under B = 1 x 720 = 720 credits.
Step 2: Busy month under B = ?
Step 3: Year under B = 9 x 720 + 3 x (busy-month cost) = 6,480 + 12,960 = 19,440 credits.
Step 4: Year under A = 12 x 4,000 = 48,000 credits, so the variable option is far cheaper because usage is uneven.

What is the missing Step 2?
choices: Busy month under B = 6 x 720 = 4,320 credits
Busy month under B = 3 x 6 x 720 = 12,960 credits
Busy month under B = 4,000 credits, the same as the fixed monthly cost
Busy month under B = 1 x 720 = 720 credits
questions.why: Pay-as-you-go charges for each server-hour actually used, so 6 servers running all 720 hours of one month cost 6 x 720 = 4,320 credits, which matches the 12,960 used for the three busy months in Step 3.

questions.prompt: A small design agency is reviewing its monthly bills. Which one of these is a variable cost, meaning it rises and falls with how much the agency uses?
choices: The monthly lease on the room where the servers sit
The yearly salary of the technician who looks after the office servers
A hardware maintenance contract paid at the same price every month
A cloud storage charge billed per gigabyte of files actually stored
questions.why: The per-gigabyte storage charge goes up when the agency stores more and down when it stores less, while salaries, leases and fixed-price contracts stay the same regardless of usage.

questions.prompt: A payroll-processing firm runs the same heavy workload on the same number of servers around the clock, every month, and expects this to stay steady for years. Which statement best fits this situation?
choices: Owning the capacity at a fixed cost could be cheaper here, because steady, predictable use is where fixed costs can win
The firm should choose pay-as-you-go because its servers sit idle most of the time
Pay-as-you-go is guaranteed to be cheaper, because variable cost is always lower than fixed cost
Fixed and variable costs will always come out equal when usage is steady
questions.why: Variable billing saves money when usage swings or is uncertain; with constant heavy use the servers are fully used, so paying a fixed amount for owned capacity can cost less.

questions.prompt: A developer at a travel startup starts several large cloud servers billed per hour for a quick test, then forgets about them for a month. Nobody sends any traffic to them. What happens to the bill?
choices: A single one-time fee is charged when the servers are first started
The charge is capped at the same fixed monthly price an owned server would cost
Charges keep adding up for every hour the servers stay running until someone stops them
Nothing is charged, because cloud servers are only billed when they receive traffic
questions.why: With pay-as-you-go billing, forgotten or oversized resources keep adding to the bill for as long as they run, which is why someone has to watch spending.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between fixed and variable costs for computing, and say when paying a variable, usage-based price might actually cost more than owning the capacity.
lessons.modelAnswer: A fixed cost stays the same no matter how much we use, like servers we bought, the rack space, power and maintenance contracts. A variable cost moves with usage, like cloud servers billed by the hour. With our own hardware we have to size for our busiest day, so on normal days we pay for machines doing nothing. With pay-as-you-go cloud pricing, the bill tracks what we actually run, so idle capacity mostly disappears and we are not betting money on a demand forecast. The tradeoff: variable is not automatically cheaper. If a workload runs flat-out all the time, paying per hour can add up to more than owning the capacity. And variable billing needs watching, because a forgotten or oversized resource keeps charging, and a traffic spike raises the bill too.
rubricPoints: Defines a fixed cost as unchanged regardless of usage within a period.
Defines a variable cost as rising and falling with actual usage.
Explains that owned capacity must be sized for peak, so idle capacity is still paid for.
Links cloud pay-as-you-go billing to variable cost that follows demand.
Names a limit: steady, constant heavy use can make variable pricing more expensive.
Notes that variable bills need monitoring because unused or oversized resources keep costing money.

suggested.rationale: A cost model in fictional credits would let the learner change usage patterns and watch fixed and variable totals cross over, which is the core intuition here.
