lessons.plain: Running your own computers on-premises, meaning in a building you own or rent, comes with many hidden bills beyond the servers themselves. You pay for the room, electricity, cooling, locks and guards, spare parts, and staff who replace failed disks and swap out old machines every few years. Moving to the cloud means renting computing from a provider who already pays those bills across a huge shared facility. It is like moving from owning a house, where you fix the roof and pay the boiler repair, to renting a flat where the landlord handles the building. You still pay rent and still look after your own furniture.
lessons.guessPrompt: A small company runs 20 servers in a closet it built itself. Apart from the price of the servers, list three things it pays for every month or every few years just to keep those machines running.
lessons.teach:
An on-premises cost is any cost of running IT equipment in facilities you own or lease yourself. A cloud migration, meaning moving workloads onto a provider such as AWS, is meant to remove the costs tied to owning physical infrastructure. The main ones are hardware purchase and its periodic refresh, usually every three to five years. There is data center space, meaning rent, raised floors and racks. Power and cooling, which can rival the hardware bill over time. Physical security, such as badges, cameras and guards. Hardware maintenance contracts and spare parts. Overprovisioning, meaning buying enough machines for your busiest day and leaving them idle the rest of the year. And staff time spent racking, cabling and repairing equipment, work AWS calls undifferentiated heavy lifting because it does not make your product any better than a competitor's.

This works because the provider pays these costs once at enormous scale and spreads them across many customers. You rent only the capacity you use.

Worked example. A firm has 20 servers. Step one: the hardware refresh, about 100,000 every four years, goes away. Step two: closet rent, electricity and air conditioning go away. Step three: the maintenance contract and the technician's trips to replace disks go away. Step four: the servers sized for the December peak no longer sit idle all year. Step five: what remains is the operating system patching it still chooses to manage, its applications and data, software licenses, network transfer, and a new monthly cloud bill.

A common mistake is comparing only the server price with the cloud instance price and ignoring power, space and staff time. That makes on-premises look cheaper than it is. The reverse mistake is assuming a migration removes all IT work. In a running business, either error produces a wrong total cost of ownership, which is the full cost of a system over its life. The result is a migration that disappoints, or one rejected for the wrong reason.

questions.prompt: A small animation studio runs 30 rendering machines in a leased back room. It works out what moving the rendering work to AWS would remove. Step one: the machine replacement it budgets for every three years goes away. Step two: the back-room lease, the electricity and the portable air conditioners go away. Step three: the yearly repair contract and the spare graphics cards on the shelf go away. Step four: ______. Step five: what remains is the studio's own animation software and files, its software licenses, the cost of moving finished video out over the network, and a new monthly cloud bill. Which statement correctly fills step four?
choices: The studio no longer has to look after its own project files, because the provider takes full responsibility for its data.
The cost of sending finished video files over the network goes away, because data transfer is included free in every cloud bill.
The software licenses for its animation tools go away, because AWS supplies all software as part of the rental.
The extra machines it bought to survive the two-week crunch before each film deadline no longer sit idle the rest of the year.
questions.why: Overprovisioning, buying for the busiest period and leaving machines idle otherwise, is an on-premises cost a migration removes, while licenses, data and network transfer remain the customer's costs.

questions.prompt: An online furniture retailer's engineers spend many hours each month mounting new servers in racks, running cables and swapping failed power supplies. Under what name does AWS group this kind of work, and why?
choices: Overprovisioning, because the engineers are doing more work than the business needs.
Total cost of ownership, because it is the full cost of a server over its life.
Physical security, because the engineers must enter the server room to do it.
Undifferentiated heavy lifting, because it does not make the retailer's product any better than a competitor's.
questions.why: Racking, cabling and repairing hardware is work every company with its own equipment must do, so it gives no competitive edge, which is what undifferentiated heavy lifting means.

questions.prompt: A regional insurance office compares two numbers only: 8,000 to buy one new server versus the yearly price of a similar cloud instance. The server looks cheaper, so the manager rejects the migration. What is the main flaw in this comparison?
choices: It ignored the cloud bill entirely, since a migration removes all ongoing IT costs.
It left out power, cooling, floor space and staff time, so on-premises looks cheaper than it really is.
It counted the server's power and cooling twice, making on-premises look more expensive than it is.
It should have compared against two servers, because cloud instances always replace two physical machines.
questions.why: Comparing only server price to instance price omits the hidden on-premises costs, producing a wrong total cost of ownership and possibly rejecting the migration for the wrong reason.

questions.prompt: A law firm moves its case-management system from its own server closet to AWS. Which of these costs will the firm most likely still be paying after the migration?
choices: The electricity and air conditioning for the server closet.
The badge readers and camera on the server closet door.
The license fees for its case-management software.
The maintenance contract and spare hard drives for its servers.
questions.why: Software licenses stay with the customer after migration, while physical security, power, cooling and hardware maintenance are costs of owning infrastructure that the provider takes over.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate which on-premises costs a cloud migration actually removes, and name at least one cost or responsibility that does not go away.
lessons.modelAnswer: When we run our own servers, the price tag of the machine is only part of the bill. We also pay for the room they sit in, power and cooling, physical security, maintenance contracts and spare parts, and replacing everything every few years. On top of that we buy extra capacity for our peak day that sits idle most of the year. Then there is staff time spent racking, cabling and fixing hardware. Moving to AWS removes those physical ownership costs, because the provider carries them at scale and we rent only what we use. It is not free of cost or work, though. We still pay a monthly cloud bill, and we still pay for software licenses and data transfer. We still own our applications, our data and their configuration. So a fair comparison must count the hidden on-premises costs, and also the costs that stay after we move.
rubricPoints: Names physical costs removed: hardware purchase and refresh, space, power and cooling.
Mentions physical security and hardware maintenance or spare parts.
Mentions overprovisioning for peak capacity as a cost that goes away.
Mentions staff time on undifferentiated heavy lifting like racking and repairs.
Names at least one cost that remains, such as the cloud bill, licenses, applications, data or configuration.
Warns that comparing only server price against instance price gives a misleading total cost.

suggested.rationale: A cost model in fictional credits would let the learner list hidden on-premises line items and watch which ones vanish after migration, making the total cost comparison concrete.

lessons.plain: Much business software, such as an operating system or a database, needs a license, which is legal permission to run it and usually costs money. When you move to the cloud you have two ways to cover that. With license-included, the cloud provider supplies the license and folds its cost into the price you pay per hour of use. With bring your own license (BYOL), you reuse licenses your company already bought. It is like renting a car with insurance built in versus declining it because your own policy already covers you.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your company already paid for several years of database licenses and they are still valid. You are moving that database to AWS. Would you rather pay AWS an hourly price that includes a new license, or reuse the one you own? What might make reusing it harder than it sounds?
lessons.teach:
A software license is the legal right to run a vendor's product, such as Microsoft Windows Server, Microsoft SQL Server, or Oracle Database. On AWS you can cover that right in two ways.

License-included means AWS provides the license and adds its cost to the hourly or per-second rate of the resource. You buy nothing up front, you pay only while the server runs, and you can stop paying the moment you shut it down. This matches the cloud's pay-as-you-go model and suits new projects, short-lived workloads, or teams with no existing licenses.

Bring your own license (BYOL) means you reuse licenses you already own. You pay AWS only for the infrastructure, which avoids paying twice for software you already bought. The catch is that the vendor's license terms still apply. Some licenses are counted per physical processor socket or core, so they may require Dedicated Hosts, which are physical servers reserved only for your company so you can see and count the hardware. You also carry the job of tracking compliance. AWS License Manager is a service that records how many licenses you have and warns you before you use more than you own.

Worked example with made-up numbers: a company owns 10 database licenses valid for three more years. Step one, it checks whether the vendor's terms allow cloud use. They do. Step two, it compares costs. The license-included rate is 2.00 credits per hour, while infrastructure alone is 1.20 credits per hour. Step three, the 0.80 hourly difference is money already spent on licenses, so BYOL saves it. For a new test environment that will run only two weeks, license-included is simpler, because there is nothing to track.

A common mistake is assuming any owned license can move to any cloud server. If the terms forbid it, or demand dedicated hardware you did not plan for, the company risks a failed vendor audit and unexpected fees. BYOL trades lower cost for more responsibility, while license-included trades a higher rate for simplicity and flexibility.

questions.prompt: A design studio owns 6 Windows Server licenses that stay valid for two more years, and it wants to run 6 servers on AWS for that whole period. Step one: it reads the vendor's license terms. Cloud use is allowed, but the licenses are counted per physical processor core. Step two: ______. Step three: it compares the infrastructure-only price, including that hardware, against the license-included hourly rate. Step four: it records its 6 licenses in AWS License Manager, a service that tracks license counts and warns before the company uses more than it owns. Which choice best fills step two?
choices: Switch to license-included, because licenses counted per core can never be brought to AWS
Run the servers on ordinary shared hardware, because AWS takes over compliance tracking for BYOL
Plan for Dedicated Hosts, physical servers reserved for the studio, so the cores can be seen and counted
Buy license-included servers and keep the owned licenses as a backup, paying for both
questions.why: Per-core licensing terms mean the company must be able to see and count the physical hardware, which is what Dedicated Hosts provide, and that hardware cost has to be included in the comparison in step three.

questions.prompt: On AWS, what does a license-included option mean for a server running a vendor product such as SQL Server?
choices: You reuse a license you already own and pay AWS only for the infrastructure
The vendor bills you separately each month, whether the server runs or not
AWS provides the license and adds its cost to the server's running rate, so you pay only while it runs
You buy the license up front from AWS and then pay a lower hourly rate for the server
questions.why: License-included means AWS supplies the license and folds its cost into the hourly or per-second rate, which matches pay-as-you-go.

questions.prompt: A new nonprofit owns no software licenses. It needs a Windows Server machine for a three-week fundraising data project and then will shut it down. Which licensing approach fits best, and why?
choices: Buy long-term licenses now in case the project grows later
License-included, because nothing is bought up front, billing stops at shutdown, and there are no licenses to track
BYOL, because it always costs less than license-included
BYOL on a Dedicated Host, so the hardware can be counted
questions.why: With no existing licenses and a short-lived workload, license-included gives simplicity and lets the nonprofit stop paying the moment the server is shut down.

questions.prompt: A logistics company moves its owned Oracle Database licenses onto ordinary shared cloud servers without reading the vendor's terms. The terms actually require dedicated hardware. What is the most likely consequence?
choices: AWS automatically converts the servers to license-included at no extra cost
A failed vendor audit and unexpected fees
The servers stop running until AWS License Manager approves them
Nothing, because owning a license means it can run on any cloud server
questions.why: Under BYOL the vendor's terms still apply and the customer carries compliance, so ignoring a dedicated-hardware requirement risks a failed audit and unexpected fees.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between bring your own license and license-included on AWS, and tell them when you would choose each, including the tradeoff or limit that comes with BYOL.
lessons.modelAnswer: Both options answer one question: who pays for the right to run software like Windows or a commercial database. With license-included, AWS supplies the license and bakes its cost into the hourly price. We pay nothing up front, pay only while it runs, and have no license counting to do, so it suits new or short-lived workloads. With BYOL we reuse licenses we already own and pay AWS only for the infrastructure, which avoids paying twice and is usually cheaper if we hold valid licenses. The limit is that the vendor's terms still bind us. Some licenses count physical cores or sockets, so we might need Dedicated Hosts, meaning physical servers reserved for us. We are also responsible for staying compliant, and a tool like AWS License Manager helps track usage. Choose BYOL when we own eligible licenses and the workload is long-running. Choose license-included for simplicity and flexibility.
rubricPoints: License-included means AWS provides the license and its cost is built into the usage price.
BYOL means reusing licenses the company already owns and paying AWS only for infrastructure.
BYOL can lower cost by avoiding paying twice for the same software.
The vendor's license terms still apply under BYOL and may require dedicated hardware such as Dedicated Hosts.
Under BYOL the customer carries compliance tracking, which AWS License Manager can help with.
License-included fits new, short-lived, or flexible workloads where no licenses are already owned.

suggested.rationale: The skill is picking the right licensing option for a given business situation, so reasoning through exam-style scenarios that weigh owned licenses, workload lifetime, and compliance duties teaches it best.

lessons.plain: Rightsizing means matching the size of the computers and storage you rent to what your work actually needs, then adjusting as that need changes. In the cloud you pay for the capacity you choose, whether you use it or not, so an oversized server wastes money every hour. Think of renting a moving van. A truck twice the size you need costs more for no benefit, and one too small leaves furniture behind. Your needs keep changing too, with more customers, new features and quieter seasons, so the right van size changes. That is why you check again on a regular schedule.
lessons.guessPrompt: A server you rent by the hour shows its processor is about 10 percent busy all month. Do you think you pay less for it than for an identical server that is 90 percent busy, and what would you do about it?
lessons.teach:
Rightsizing is the practice of choosing the smallest, cheapest resource configuration that still meets a workload's performance needs, and then revisiting that choice over time. A workload is the application or job you are running. A resource is anything you rent by size. That includes a virtual server, a database, or a storage volume. On AWS a virtual server is an Amazon EC2 instance, and its instance type sets how many virtual CPUs and how much memory it gets. Overprovisioning means renting more capacity than you use. Underprovisioning means renting too little, so users see slowness or errors.

Rightsizing works because cloud pricing follows the size you pick, not how hard you use it. A server at 10 percent CPU costs the same per hour as the same server at 90 percent. You find the gap by measuring utilization, which is the share of capacity actually in use. A monitoring service collects those measurements. On AWS, Amazon CloudWatch gathers the metrics, and AWS Compute Optimizer analyses them and suggests sizes.

Worked example. A team launches a server with 8 CPUs and 32 GB of memory to be safe. Two weeks of metrics show average CPU of 10 percent, peaks of 25 percent, and 6 GB of memory used. Step one is to size for the peak plus headroom, not for the average. A peak of 25 percent of 8 CPUs is 2 CPUs' worth of work. Step two is to pick a type with 4 CPUs and 16 GB, which keeps the peak near 50 percent. Step three is to watch that server's cost roughly halve, because size and price move together. Six months later users double and peaks hit 90 percent on the new size. Rightsizing now means moving up.

Rightsizing recurs because workloads grow, shrink and change shape. AWS also keeps releasing new instance types that may do the same work for less. A size that was right last quarter can be wasteful or too tight today.

One common mistake is sizing from the average alone. Another is treating rightsizing as a launch-day task. In a running system, the first causes slowdowns at peak. The second lets waste or overload creep back unnoticed.

questions.prompt: A small accounting firm runs its reporting database on a virtual server (an Amazon EC2 instance) with 16 virtual CPUs and 64 GB of memory. Three weeks of Amazon CloudWatch metrics show average CPU of 5 percent, peaks of 20 percent, and 12 GB of memory in use. Step one: size for the peak plus headroom, not the average. A peak of 20 percent of 16 CPUs is about 3.2 CPUs' worth of work. Step two is missing. Step three: watch the monthly cost for this server fall, because a smaller size means a lower price. Which choice is the missing step two?
choices: Pick a type with 8 CPUs and 32 GB, which keeps the peak near 40 percent and leaves room for the 12 GB of memory.
Pick a type with 4 CPUs and 16 GB, which keeps the peak at about 80 percent and memory at 75 percent.
Keep the 16 CPU, 64 GB type, because a 20 percent peak shows the server is coping well.
Pick a type with 2 CPUs and 8 GB, because the average of 5 percent of 16 CPUs is less than 1 CPU of work.
questions.why: About 3.2 CPUs of peak work on 8 CPUs runs near 40 percent with headroom, and 32 GB comfortably holds 12 GB, so it is the smallest choice that still meets peak needs.

questions.prompt: A marketing agency rents two identical virtual servers of the same instance type for the same number of hours. One averages 15 percent CPU and the other averages 85 percent. How do their compute charges compare?
choices: They cost the same, because cloud pricing follows the size you rent, not how hard you use it.
The 15 percent server costs much less, because you pay only for the CPU you use.
The 85 percent server costs less, because busy servers get a utilization discount.
The 15 percent server costs more, because idle capacity carries an extra fee.
questions.why: Price follows the chosen size, so equal sizes and hours cost the same no matter the utilization, which is why a lightly used server is waste worth rightsizing.

questions.prompt: An online bookshop carefully rightsized its web servers 14 months ago. Since then, seasonal traffic has dropped, and AWS has released newer instance types. The finance lead says, "We already rightsized, so we're done." What is the best response?
choices: Agree, but only revisit the size if users start reporting errors.
Agree, because a careful rightsizing exercise only needs to be done once at launch.
Disagree, because workloads change and newer types may do the same work for less, so the size should be measured and reviewed again.
Disagree, but only because new instance types appeared; changes in traffic never affect the right size.
questions.why: Rightsizing recurs because workloads grow, shrink and change shape and new instance types keep arriving, so last year's right size can be wasteful or too tight today.

questions.prompt: A ticketing company sizes a new server by looking only at average CPU, which is 12 percent, and picks a much smaller type that the average fits into neatly. On busy on-sale days, demand spikes far above the average. What is the most likely result in the running system?
choices: Nothing changes, because CPU usage averages out over the month.
The server automatically becomes overprovisioned, wasting money during the spikes.
Costs rise sharply, because smaller instance types cost more per hour during spikes.
Users see slowness or errors at peak, because the server is underprovisioned for its highest demand.
questions.why: Sizing from the average alone ignores peaks, so the server has too little capacity when demand spikes, which is underprovisioning that shows up as slowdowns or errors.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what rightsizing is and why your team should put it on a recurring schedule instead of doing it once at launch. Include one risk or tradeoff of shrinking a resource too aggressively.
lessons.modelAnswer: Rightsizing means picking the smallest resource size that still handles our workload, because in the cloud we pay for the size we rent, not for how busy it is. An idle 8-CPU server costs the same as a busy one. We decide using measured utilization, such as CPU and memory over a few weeks. We size for the peak plus some headroom, not the average. It has to recur because our traffic grows, shrinks and changes over time, and AWS releases newer instance types that may be cheaper for the same work. Last quarter's right size can be wasteful or too tight today. The tradeoff is that cutting too close to the peak saves money but leaves no room for a spike, so users get slowness or errors. We should keep headroom and keep watching the metrics after each change.
rubricPoints: Defines rightsizing as matching resource size to actual need at the lowest cost that meets performance.
Explains that cloud cost follows the size chosen, not how busy the resource is, so idle capacity is waste.
Says the decision is based on measured utilization and sized for the peak plus headroom, not the average.
Gives reasons it recurs, such as changing workloads and new, cheaper instance types.
Names the risk of underprovisioning, where shrinking too far causes slowness or errors at peak.

suggested.rationale: A cost model lets the learner resize resources against changing usage figures and watch the bill and the headroom move each period, which shows why rightsizing has to be repeated.

lessons.plain: Automation means letting software do the repetitive setup and operating work that a person would otherwise do by hand: creating servers, configuring networks, deploying new versions, adding capacity when traffic rises. In the cloud, everything is controlled through software requests, so almost every task can be written down once and replayed. Think of a bakery recipe versus a baker who improvises each morning. The recipe gives the same loaf every time, any trained person can follow it, and mistakes can be fixed in the recipe instead of being repeated. Automation buys speed, consistency, fewer human errors, and staff time for more valuable work.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team builds its test environment by clicking through a web console for two days, then must build an identical production environment. What could go wrong if they repeat the clicks by hand, and what would you do instead?
lessons.teach:
Automation is replacing manual, repeated operational steps with software that performs them the same way every time. It works in the cloud because every resource, whether a server, a virtual network, or a database, is created and changed through an API (an application programming interface, a defined way for software to send requests to a service). Anything a person can click, a script or template can request.

The main form is infrastructure as code (IaC): describing the resources you want in a text file, called a template, which a tool reads and builds for you. On AWS, CloudFormation is the managed service that does this; you hand it a template and it creates, updates, or deletes the whole set of resources together. Other automation includes deployment pipelines that test and release code without manual steps, and automatic scaling, which adds or removes capacity based on measured load.

The benefits to name are: speed (environments in minutes, not days), consistency (every copy is identical), fewer human errors (no forgotten step), repeatability (rebuild after a failure or in a new Region), auditability (the template is a written record that can be reviewed and versioned), and lower operating cost because engineers stop doing toil.

Worked example. A company needs dev, test, and production environments. First, an engineer writes one template describing a network, two servers, and a database. Second, CloudFormation builds dev from it in about fifteen minutes. Third, the same template builds test and production, identical except for a size setting. Fourth, a security fix is made once in the template and applied to all three. Done by hand, each environment would take days and slowly drift apart, meaning their settings quietly differ.

A common mistake is treating automation as the same thing as elasticity. Elasticity is capacity matching demand; automation is the broader practice of removing manual work, and automatic scaling is just one use of it. Another mistake: automating a flawed process simply repeats the flaw faster. In a running system, unautomated environments drift, so a release that passed testing can fail in production because the two were never truly the same.

questions.prompt: A small online ticketing company runs its booking system in one AWS Region (a geographic area containing AWS data centres). Step 1: an engineer writes a CloudFormation template describing a load balancer, four servers, and a message queue. Step 2: CloudFormation builds the whole set in the company's main Region in about twenty minutes. Step 3: a major outage takes that Region offline, and the business needs the booking system running again quickly. [MISSING STEP] Step 4: an auditor later reads the template's version history to confirm exactly what was built and when. Which choice correctly fills the missing Step 3 action?
choices: Engineers rebuild the servers by hand in a second Region, following a written checklist of the original setup steps
The team edits the template to remove the message queue so the rebuild finishes faster in a second Region
The same template is handed to CloudFormation in a second Region, which builds an identical copy of the stack
Automatic scaling adds more servers in the main Region until the measured load returns to normal levels
questions.why: Because the template is a reusable description of the resources, CloudFormation can rebuild the same environment in a new Region quickly and identically, which is the repeatability benefit.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm keeps a text file that describes its virtual network, servers, and database, and a tool reads that file to create and update those resources. What is this practice called?
choices: Configuration drift
Infrastructure as code
Elasticity
Manual provisioning
questions.why: Infrastructure as code means describing resources in a text file, a template, that a tool reads and builds for you.

questions.prompt: An insurance company's staging and production environments were each set up by hand over several months. A software release passed every test in staging but failed in production because a network setting differed between them. Which automation benefit most directly addresses this problem?
choices: Speed, because new environments would be ready in minutes, not days
Lower operating cost, because engineers would spend less time on toil
Elasticity, because capacity would have matched demand in production
Consistency, because environments built from one template stay identical
questions.why: Hand-built environments drift apart; building both from the same template keeps their settings identical, so what passes testing behaves the same in production.

questions.prompt: A media company's manual release process skips a step that checks whether backups actually work. The team automates the process exactly as it is, and releases now happen five times faster. What is the most likely result?
choices: The skipped backup check is now repeated faster and more often
Automatic scaling fixes the problem by adding more servers
Releases become auditable, so the backup flaw disappears
The automation detects and adds the missing backup check on its own
questions.why: Automating a flawed process does not correct it; it simply repeats the same flaw faster and more consistently.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, in your own words, what automation buys a company running on AWS, using infrastructure as code as your example, and name one limit or tradeoff of automating.
lessons.modelAnswer: Automation means letting software do the setup and operations work we would otherwise do by hand. Because every AWS resource is created through an API, we can write our infrastructure down as code, for example a CloudFormation template, and have the service build it. That gives us speed, since a full environment appears in minutes; consistency, since dev, test, and production come from the same file and do not drift apart; fewer human errors, since nobody skips a step; and repeatability, since we can rebuild after a failure or in another Region. The template also acts as a reviewable record of what exists. The tradeoff is up-front effort: someone has to write and maintain the templates and learn the tooling. And automation is not judgment. If the template contains a mistake, it reproduces that mistake everywhere, quickly, so templates still need review and testing.
rubricPoints: Defines automation as software performing repeated manual operational steps.
Explains infrastructure as code as describing resources in a template a service builds, such as CloudFormation.
Names specific benefits such as speed, consistency, fewer human errors, and repeatability.
Notes that identical environments prevent drift between test and production.
Names a limit, such as up-front effort or a flawed template spreading errors everywhere.
Does not confuse automation with elasticity.

suggested.rationale: The unit skill is naming the specific benefit automation delivers in a business situation, so reasoning through exam-style scenarios teaches it best.

lessons.plain: Economies of scale means that the more of something you produce, the less each single unit costs you. A bakery making ten thousand loaves a day pays less per loaf than a home baker. It buys flour by the truckload, and its ovens and staff are shared across far more bread. AWS runs computing for millions of customers, so it buys hardware, electricity and buildings in enormous volume and spreads its overhead very thinly. Because those per-unit costs fall, AWS can charge lower pay-as-you-go prices than most companies could reach by running their own small data center.
lessons.guessPrompt: A small company runs 200 servers in its own room, and a cloud provider runs millions of servers. Both must pay for security guards, cooling and a building. Which of them do you think pays less for overhead per server, and why?
lessons.teach:
Economies of scale is the drop in cost per unit that comes from operating at very large volume. Two forces cause it. The first is spreading fixed costs, meaning costs that stay the same whatever the output, such as a building, a cooling plant or a security team. The second is purchasing power, the bigger discounts a buyer gets when ordering servers, network gear and electricity in huge quantities.

Here is a worked example in fictional credits. Company A runs its own server room, and its fixed overhead is 2,000,000 credits a year. It has 200 servers, so overhead per server is 2,000,000 divided by 200, which is 10,000 credits. A cloud provider runs one large site with overhead of 20,000,000 credits a year, ten times as much, but that site holds 100,000 servers. Its overhead per server is 20,000,000 divided by 100,000, which is just 200 credits. The provider also pays less for each machine because it buys in bulk.

The customer sees this benefit through price. AWS's total usage is the combined demand of all its customers, and that combined demand keeps growing. As it grows, AWS's unit cost falls, and AWS has passed part of those savings on by cutting prices many times over the years. A small customer renting one virtual server gets a price built on the provider's scale, not their own.

A common mistake is to confuse economies of scale with elasticity. Elasticity is the ability to add or remove capacity as demand changes. Economies of scale is about the price of each unit, not about how much capacity you can get. A second mistake is to think a customer must be large to benefit. The scale belongs to AWS, so even tiny workloads pay the lower rate.

For a running business, the result is a lower and steadily falling cost for the same computing work, with no purchasing or facilities effort of its own.

questions.prompt:
A regional hospital runs its own data room. Its fixed overhead (costs that stay the same however many servers it runs, such as the room, cooling and staff) is 900,000 credits a year, and it runs 150 servers. A cloud provider's large site has fixed overhead of 45,000,000 credits a year and holds 300,000 servers.

Step 1: Hospital overhead per server = 900,000 / 150 = 6,000 credits.
Step 2: Provider overhead per server = ?
Step 3: Compare. The provider spends 50 times more in total on overhead, yet each of its servers carries far less overhead than each hospital server. The provider can price its virtual servers from this lower unit cost.

Which choice correctly completes Step 2?
choices: 6,000 credits, the same as the hospital, because overhead per server is fixed
45,000,000 / 150 = 300,000 credits, so the provider is far more expensive per server
45,000,000 - 900,000 = 44,100,000 credits of extra overhead per server
questions.why: Overhead per server is the provider's own total fixed overhead divided by its own server count, so 45,000,000 / 300,000 = 150 credits, much lower than the hospital's 6,000.

questions.prompt: A finance manager asks what "economies of scale" means for a cloud provider. Which answer is correct?
choices: The cost of each unit falls as the provider operates at very large volume, because fixed costs are spread over more units and bulk buying earns bigger discounts
The provider builds sites in many countries so customers can reach users worldwide
The customer pays only for the resources it uses, with no up-front purchase
The provider can add or remove capacity for a customer as that customer's demand rises and falls
questions.why: Economies of scale is the drop in cost per unit from operating at huge volume, driven by spreading fixed costs and by purchasing power.

questions.prompt: A two-person design studio rents a single small virtual server from AWS for its website. A colleague says the studio is far too small to benefit from economies of scale. What is the best response?
choices: Correct; economies of scale only help customers whose traffic changes a lot during the day
Partly correct; the studio benefits only if it signs a long contract to commit to volume
Incorrect; the scale belongs to AWS, whose combined customer demand lowers its unit cost, so even one small server is priced from that lower cost
Correct; the studio must grow to thousands of servers before any scale discount applies
questions.why: The scale comes from the combined demand of all AWS customers, so even a tiny workload pays a price built on AWS's scale, not its own.

questions.prompt: A logistics company's traffic triples every December, and AWS lets it add servers for that month and remove them in January. A team member calls this "economies of scale". What is wrong with that label?
choices: Nothing; any benefit of using the cloud is an example of economies of scale
It describes purchasing power, which is separate from economies of scale
It describes elasticity, the ability to add or remove capacity as demand changes, while economies of scale is about the lower price of each unit
It describes spreading fixed costs, because the company's December servers are a fixed cost
questions.why: Adding and removing capacity with demand is elasticity; economies of scale concerns the falling cost per unit from very large volume, not how much capacity you can get.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, in your own words, how AWS's size turns into a lower bill for your small team, and name one limit of this benefit or one thing it is often confused with.
lessons.modelAnswer: Economies of scale means that cost per unit falls as volume rises. AWS serves a huge number of customers, so its fixed costs, like buildings, cooling and security staff, are spread across an enormous number of servers. It also buys hardware and power in bulk at bigger discounts. Both effects lower AWS's cost for each unit of computing, and AWS shares part of that saving through lower pay-as-you-go prices, which it has cut repeatedly as total usage has grown. Our team gets those prices even though we are small, because the scale is AWS's, not ours. One limit is that this lowers the unit price but does not stop waste. If we leave oversized or idle resources running, we still pay for them. It is also not the same as elasticity, which is about adjusting capacity, not about price.
rubricPoints: Defines economies of scale as lower cost per unit at higher volume.
Names spreading fixed costs and bulk purchasing power as the causes.
Explains that the savings reach customers as lower usage prices and repeated price reductions.
Notes that even small customers benefit because the scale belongs to AWS.
Names a limit or confusion, such as waste still costing money or mixing it up with elasticity.

suggested.rationale: The exam and the unit goal both test whether a learner can state precisely how provider scale becomes a lower customer price, which is best practised by explaining it back.

lessons.plain: The shared responsibility model is the agreement that splits cloud security between AWS and you, the customer. AWS protects the cloud itself: the buildings, the machines, the cables and the software that runs its services. You protect what you put in the cloud: your data, who can log in, and how you set things up. Think of renting an apartment in a guarded building. The landlord secures the front door, walls and wiring. You lock your own unit, choose who gets a key, and decide what you leave lying on the table.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your company stores files with AWS, and an employee accidentally changes a setting so one file can be read by anyone on the internet. Whose responsibility is that mistake: your company's or AWS's? Why do you think so?
lessons.teach:
The shared responsibility model divides security work into two parts. Security OF the cloud is AWS's job. It covers the physical data centers (the guarded buildings full of servers), the hardware, the networking between them, and the virtualization layer, which is the software that lets one physical machine be safely split into many separate rented virtual machines. Security IN the cloud is the customer's job. It covers your data, your user accounts and permissions (who is allowed to do what), your configuration settings, and your choices about encryption, which means scrambling data so only holders of a key can read it.

Why split it this way? Each side secures what it actually controls. You cannot walk into an AWS building to check a lock, and AWS cannot see inside your data or guess who in your company should have access. The line sits where control changes hands.

Worked example: a company runs a website on a rented virtual server (Amazon EC2). Step one, a guard checks badges at the data center: AWS. Step two, a failed hard drive in the physical host is replaced: AWS. Step three, security updates (patches) for the operating system installed on the virtual server: customer, because the customer chose and runs that operating system. Step four, a firewall rule deciding which internet traffic may reach the server: customer. Step five, deciding which employees can log in: customer. Step six, whether stored customer records are encrypted: customer.

The common mistake is assuming that anything hosted on AWS is automatically secured by AWS. AWS gives you the locks; it does not decide to turn them on for you. In a running system this shows up as data leaks from storage someone set to public, or servers broken into through an unpatched operating system. The underlying cloud stayed secure the whole time, yet the breach still happened, and it is the customer's to own and fix.

questions.prompt: A veterinary clinic chain runs its appointment-booking app on three rented virtual servers (Amazon EC2) and sorts each security task by owner. Task A: badge checks at the doors of the building that holds the physical servers. Owner: AWS, because it is the physical data center. Task B: deciding which receptionists may log in to the booking app. Owner: the clinic, because this is about user accounts and permissions. Task C: switching on encryption for stored pet-owner records. Owner: the clinic, because encryption choices sit inside the cloud. Task D: fixing a flaw in the virtualization layer that could let one customer's virtual machine peek into another customer's virtual machine on the same physical host. Owner: ?
choices: Both sides equally, because the flaw affects AWS hardware and customer data
The clinic, because anything that might leak its data is its job to fix
AWS, because the virtualization layer is part of the cloud that AWS runs
The clinic, because the flaw could expose the clinic's own virtual servers
questions.why: The virtualization layer, the software that splits one physical machine into separate virtual machines, is security of the cloud, which AWS controls and must secure.

questions.prompt: Under the AWS shared responsibility model, which of these tasks counts as security OF the cloud and is therefore AWS's job?
choices: Deciding whether to encrypt a table of supplier invoices
Choosing which contractor accounts are allowed to delete project files
Securing the network links that connect AWS data centers to each other
Setting a firewall rule that allows web traffic to a rented server
questions.why: The networking between AWS data centers is part of the physical cloud AWS controls; the other three are permissions, encryption and configuration choices that belong to the customer.

questions.prompt: A bakery chain keeps 40,000 online order records in an AWS storage service. An employee changes a setting so the storage can be read by anyone on the internet, and the records leak. Who is responsible for this breach?
choices: The bakery, because the public setting was its own configuration choice
AWS, because the records were hosted on AWS infrastructure
AWS and the bakery equally, because the leak used an AWS service
Nobody in particular, because the underlying cloud was never breached
questions.why: Configuration settings are security in the cloud, so the bakery owns the leak even though the AWS infrastructure itself stayed secure.

questions.prompt: A game studio's rented virtual server is broken into through a known weakness in its operating system, which the studio installed itself and has not updated in eight months. Which statement best describes what went wrong?
choices: AWS failed to patch the server, because patching is part of security of the cloud
AWS's physical hardware was compromised, which let attackers into the server
The breach was shared, because the server and the operating system both run on AWS
The studio skipped its own job of patching the operating system it chose and runs
questions.why: Patching an operating system the customer chose and runs on a virtual server is security in the cloud, so the studio owned that work and the breach.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says, "We moved to AWS, so security is their problem now." Explain the shared responsibility model to them in your own words, give one task on each side of the line, and name a limit of the model, such as where it does not protect you.
lessons.modelAnswer: Not quite. AWS and we split security. AWS handles security of the cloud: the data center buildings, the physical servers and network, and the virtualization layer that keeps our virtual machines separated from other customers'. We handle security in the cloud: our data, who has accounts and permissions, our configuration, patching any operating system we run, and whether we turn on encryption. For example, replacing a failed disk in a host is AWS's job, but locking down a firewall rule on our server is ours. The limit is that AWS only guarantees its own layer. If we leave storage open to the public or skip patches, AWS's infrastructure stays perfectly secure while our data still leaks, and that breach is on us. Moving to the cloud removes some work but does not hand over our share.
rubricPoints: States that AWS is responsible for security of the cloud: physical facilities, hardware, network and virtualization layer.
States that the customer is responsible for security in the cloud: data, access permissions, configuration and encryption choices.
Gives at least one correct example task on each side of the line.
Explains the line falls where control passes from AWS to the customer.
Names a limit: a customer misconfiguration can cause a breach even though AWS's layer is secure.

suggested.rationale: The skill this objective builds is sorting concrete security tasks to the right owner, which is best practiced by reasoning through short exam-style scenarios and then explaining the choice.

lessons.plain: When you rent space in the cloud, keeping it safe is a team job split between you and the provider. Think of renting a flat in a secure building. The landlord looks after the locks on the front door, the walls, the wiring and the fire alarms. You decide who gets a key to your flat, whether you lock your own door, and what you keep inside. Some jobs are split: the landlord fixes the boiler, but you must not tamper with it. AWS works the same way. It guards the buildings and hardware, you guard your data and who can reach it, and a few jobs are done by both.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a company stores customer records on AWS and an employee accidentally makes that storage readable by anyone on the internet, whose responsibility was it to prevent that: AWS's or the company's? Why?
lessons.teach:
Responsibilities on AWS fall into three groups. AWS responsibilities are the things only AWS can touch: the physical data centers, guards and badge readers, power and cooling, the servers, storage disks and network cables, and the virtualization layer (the software that splits one physical machine into many rented virtual machines). Customer responsibilities are everything you put into or switch on in the cloud: your data, who has access (user accounts, passwords, permissions), whether data is encrypted (scrambled so only key holders can read it), firewall-style network rules, and the operating system and applications on any virtual server you run.

The third group is shared controls, where each side does its own half of the same job. AWS names three. Patch management (applying security fixes): AWS patches its infrastructure, you patch your guest operating system and apps. Configuration management (keeping settings correct): AWS configures its devices, you configure your databases, servers and apps. Awareness and training: AWS trains its staff, you train yours. Two related terms help. Inherited controls are ones you get entirely from AWS, such as physical and environmental security; you simply benefit from them. Customer-specific controls are entirely yours, such as deciding how data flows and is separated inside your own environment.

Worked example: a team runs a web app on a rented virtual server. A new vulnerability appears in the server's operating system. Step one: is the flaw in AWS hardware or the virtualization layer? No, it is in the guest operating system. Step two: who installed and controls that operating system? The team. Step three: so applying the patch is the team's half of the shared patching control.

A common mistake is assuming "it's in the cloud, so AWS secures it." AWS never sees or manages your permissions or data choices. In a running system, that mistake shows up as public storage, unpatched servers, or weak passwords leading to a breach that AWS's secure buildings did nothing to stop.

questions.prompt: A logistics company stores shipment records on AWS. One night a physical storage disk inside an AWS data center fails. Trace who is responsible for replacing it. Step one: is the problem in AWS hardware or the virtualization layer? Yes, it is a physical disk in a data center. Step two: [missing]. Step three: so replacing the failed disk is AWS's responsibility, and the company inherits that protection. Which choice best fills step two?
choices: Is the disk part of a shared control? Yes, so each side replaces half of it.
Who installed the guest operating system? The company did, so the disk is its job.
Who encrypted the shipment records? The company did, so it must replace the disk.
Who owns and controls that hardware? AWS does, since customers cannot touch data center equipment.
questions.why: Physical disks sit inside AWS data centers that only AWS can touch, so the deciding question is who controls that hardware, and the answer is AWS.

questions.prompt: A small video-editing startup on AWS never hires security guards, buys fire suppression, or installs badge readers, yet its workloads are protected by all of these in AWS data centers. What is this kind of control called?
choices: A customer-specific control, because the startup chose the AWS Region
A shared control, because both sides split the work of physical security
A configuration management control, because AWS keeps device settings correct
An inherited control, because the startup gets it entirely from AWS
questions.why: Inherited controls are ones the customer receives entirely from AWS, such as physical and environmental security, and simply benefits from.

questions.prompt: A regional bank moves its systems to AWS and hires 12 new engineers. Under the shared control for awareness and training, what is the bank's half of the job?
choices: Training its own 12 engineers on security practices, while AWS trains AWS staff
Training AWS data center staff on how to handle the bank's servers
Nothing, because AWS training covers anyone who uses AWS services
Asking AWS to train the bank's engineers, since training is shared
questions.why: In awareness and training, each side trains its own people: AWS trains its staff and the customer trains the customer's staff.

questions.prompt: A design firm stores 4,000 client drawings in AWS storage and sets the storage so anyone on the internet can read it. The files leak. Which explanation is correct?
choices: AWS is at fault, because access settings are an inherited control
It is a shared failure, because AWS should have patched the storage service
The firm is at fault, because deciding who has access to its data is a customer responsibility
AWS is at fault, because anything stored in the cloud is secured by AWS
questions.why: Access permissions on your data are a customer responsibility, so AWS's secure data centers do nothing to stop a leak caused by the customer making storage public.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how security work is split between AWS and the customer, including what a shared control is, and name one limit of relying on AWS's side to keep you safe.
lessons.modelAnswer: AWS secures the parts we can't touch: data centers, physical guards, hardware, networking cables and the virtualization layer that carves servers into virtual machines. We secure everything we put in or configure: our data, user accounts and permissions, encryption choices, network rules, and the operating system and apps on any server we run. Some jobs are shared controls, where each side does its half: patching, configuration management, and staff training. AWS patches and configures its infrastructure and trains its people; we patch and configure our own systems and train our team. Physical security is an inherited control we just benefit from. The limit is that AWS's strong physical and infrastructure security does nothing if we leave a storage bucket public, skip patches, or hand out broad permissions. Most cloud breaches come from the customer's side, so we can't outsource that thinking.
rubricPoints: States that AWS owns physical facilities, hardware, network and the virtualization layer.
States that the customer owns data, access permissions, encryption choices and their own operating systems and apps.
Defines a shared control as one job where each side handles its own part.
Names at least one shared control such as patching, configuration management or training.
Names a limit: AWS's side cannot prevent customer misconfiguration or weak access control.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests this by describing a security task and asking who owns it, so reasoning through short scenarios builds the sorting skill best.

lessons.plain: Every AWS service splits security work between you and AWS, but the split moves depending on how much of the machine AWS runs for you. Think of housing: renting an empty flat (Amazon EC2, a virtual server) means you fix the locks and wiring inside; a serviced apartment (Amazon RDS, a managed database) means staff handle the boiler and repairs; a hotel room (AWS Lambda, run-your-code-only) means you just bring your luggage. In every case you still decide who gets a key and you look after your own belongings, meaning your data and who can access it.
lessons.guessPrompt: A security patch is released for the operating system underneath your application. Who do you think installs it if the app runs on a virtual server you launched yourself, and who installs it if the app runs as a function where you only upload code?
lessons.teach:
The shared responsibility model says AWS secures the cloud itself (buildings, hardware, the hypervisor that splits hardware into virtual machines) and you secure what you put in it. How far up AWS's half reaches depends on the service type.

Amazon EC2 is infrastructure as a service: you rent a virtual server and get full control of it. AWS secures the physical host and hypervisor. You own the guest operating system (OS) and its patches, installed software, the firewall rules called security groups, encryption choices, and your data.

Amazon RDS is a managed service: AWS runs a database engine such as MySQL for you. AWS now also patches the underlying OS and the database software, runs backups on the schedule you set, and handles the hardware. You still own database users and passwords, who can reach the database over the network, whether to turn on encryption, and the data.

AWS Lambda is serverless: you upload a function (a piece of code) and AWS runs it when triggered, with no server for you to see. AWS handles the OS, the language runtime it provides, scaling and capacity. You own your code, its third-party libraries, the permissions the function is given, and the data it touches.

Worked example, an OS security patch. On EC2: you log in to your instance and apply it, because the OS is yours. On RDS: AWS applies it during the maintenance window you chose. On Lambda: AWS applies it with no action from you. Now trace a different task, granting access. In all three, you write the permissions and decide who can connect. That task never moves to AWS.

The common mistake is believing "managed" means "AWS handles all security." A team on RDS that leaves the database open to the whole internet with a weak password has made its own failure; AWS patched the engine, but the open door was the customer's. In a running system that mistake leads to leaked data, and it is the customer's responsibility to prevent it. The rule: the more AWS manages, the less infrastructure you patch, but your data, identities and access settings always stay with you.

questions.prompt: A veterinary clinic chain runs three workloads and learns about a security flaw. Trace who fixes each piece. Step 1: The appointment system uses PostgreSQL that the clinic's team installed themselves on an Amazon EC2 virtual server. Installed software on EC2 belongs to the customer, so the clinic's team updates PostgreSQL on that server. Step 2: The billing system uses Amazon RDS, a managed database service, running PostgreSQL, and the same flaw is in the database engine. ??? Step 3: A reminder function on AWS Lambda, which runs uploaded code with no visible server, bundles a third-party code library that also has a flaw. Libraries the customer adds to its code are the customer's, so the clinic updates the library and re-uploads the function. Which statement correctly fills in Step 2?
choices: No one needs to act, because a managed service cannot have flaws in its database software.
The clinic's team must log in to the RDS database server's operating system and install the PostgreSQL fix themselves.
The clinic must fix it by restricting network access, since patching the engine is never anyone's job on RDS.
AWS applies the database engine fix, during the maintenance window the clinic chose.
questions.why: On a managed database service like RDS, AWS patches the underlying operating system and the database software, applying fixes during the maintenance window the customer selects.

questions.prompt: Across Amazon EC2 (a rented virtual server), Amazon RDS (a managed database) and AWS Lambda (serverless functions), which set of responsibilities stays with the customer no matter which service is used?
choices: The hypervisor that splits hardware into virtual machines, and the data center buildings
Database engine patches, automated backups, and scaling capacity up and down
Their data, the identities that can use it, and the access settings that decide who can connect
The guest operating system patches, the language runtime, and the physical hardware
questions.why: The more AWS manages, the less infrastructure the customer patches, but data, identities and access settings always remain the customer's job.

questions.prompt: A travel startup writes an AWS Lambda function that resizes photos. To save time, a developer gives the function permission to delete anything in every storage area the company owns. A bug later deletes 4,000 customer files. Under the shared responsibility model, who owned the decision that allowed this?
choices: No one, because permissions are shared equally between AWS and the customer
The startup, because the permissions given to a Lambda function are the customer's to set
AWS, because the language runtime that ran the code is provided by AWS
AWS, because Lambda is serverless and AWS handles the function's security
questions.why: On Lambda, AWS handles the operating system, runtime and scaling, but the customer owns its code and the permissions the function is given.

questions.prompt: A logistics company moves its tracking app onto Amazon EC2 virtual servers. The team assumes AWS keeps everything patched, and for eight months nobody updates the guest operating system on those servers. An attacker then exploits a known operating system flaw. What went wrong?
choices: AWS failed its duty, since it patches the operating system on every service including EC2
The team misread the model: on EC2 the guest operating system and its patches belong to the customer
The flaw was in the hypervisor, so the attack proves AWS's half of the model broke
EC2 is a managed service, so the team should have chosen a maintenance window for AWS to patch it
questions.why: EC2 is infrastructure as a service, where AWS secures only the physical host and hypervisor while the customer owns the guest operating system and its patches.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how security responsibility differs between running an app on Amazon EC2, a database on Amazon RDS, and code on AWS Lambda, and name one tradeoff of moving toward the more managed options.
lessons.modelAnswer: It's a sliding scale. On EC2 we rent a virtual server, so AWS only covers the hardware and hypervisor; we patch the operating system, manage installed software, set security group firewall rules and protect our data. On RDS, AWS also patches the OS and database engine and runs backups, but we still control database accounts, network access and whether encryption is on. On Lambda, AWS runs the whole platform including OS and runtime, so we just own our code, its libraries, its permissions and the data. What never moves: our data, our identities and access decisions are always ours. The tradeoff is control. Managed services take patching work off us, but we can't log in to tune the OS, install custom agents, or pick exactly when every update lands, so if we need that control, EC2 gives it at the cost of more work.
rubricPoints: States that on EC2 the customer patches and secures the guest operating system and software.
States that on RDS AWS patches the OS and database engine while the customer controls database access, network exposure and encryption settings.
States that on Lambda AWS manages the OS and runtime while the customer owns code, libraries and function permissions.
Says data and access control remain the customer's responsibility in every case.
Names a tradeoff, such as less control or customization in exchange for less operational work.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests this by giving a service and a security task and asking who owns it, so reasoning through several such situations builds the skill best.

lessons.plain: AWS Artifact is a free download library inside your AWS account where AWS keeps the official proof of its own security. Independent auditors regularly inspect AWS's data centers, hardware and processes, then write reports and certificates. Artifact is where you fetch copies of that paperwork. It also holds certain legal agreements you can review and accept online. Think of a restaurant's health inspection certificate: you don't inspect the kitchen yourself, but you can ask to see the inspector's signed report. When your own auditor asks, "How do you know your cloud provider is secure?", Artifact is where you get the answer.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your company's auditor asks for proof that the data centers running your AWS workloads passed an independent security audit. You cannot visit those buildings. Where do you think you would get that proof, and who do you think wrote it?
lessons.teach:
AWS Artifact is a self-service portal in the AWS Management Console (the web interface for your account) that gives you on-demand access to AWS's compliance evidence. Compliance means meeting a published set of rules, such as a security standard or a law. Evidence is the documentation that proves it. Artifact has two parts. Artifact Reports holds audit reports and certifications written by third-party auditors, meaning independent firms that are not AWS. Examples include SOC reports (System and Organization Controls reports, which describe how well a provider's security controls work), the PCI DSS attestation (proof AWS meets the payment-card industry's security standard) and ISO certificates (international security management standards). Artifact Agreements lets you review and accept legal agreements with AWS, such as a Business Associate Addendum (BAA), which is required under the US health-privacy law HIPAA before you store patient health data.

Why this works: under the shared responsibility model, AWS secures the cloud itself, and you cannot inspect that part. So AWS pays auditors to check it and publishes the results to customers, which saves every customer from running its own data-center audit.

Worked example. A clinic is moving its booking app to AWS. Step one: its compliance officer signs in and opens Artifact Agreements, reads the BAA and accepts it for the account. Step two: the officer opens Artifact Reports, searches for the SOC 2 report and downloads it, accepting the terms that keep it confidential. Step three: the officer hands that report to the clinic's external auditor as evidence for the AWS side.

Common mistake: believing Artifact makes your workload compliant or scans your resources. It does neither. Its reports cover only AWS's responsibilities. Your own configuration, access rules and data handling still need your own controls and evidence. Another mistake is forwarding downloaded reports publicly; many are confidential and may only be shared under the terms you accepted.

On the exam, when a question asks where to find AWS compliance reports or accept agreements like a BAA, the answer is AWS Artifact.

questions.prompt: A small online shop called Pinecrest Tea runs its checkout on AWS and accepts credit cards. Its payment bank asks for proof that the AWS infrastructure under the checkout meets the payment-card industry's security standard (PCI DSS). The shop's operations lead works through it like this. Step one: she signs in to the AWS Management Console and opens AWS Artifact. Step two: [missing]. Step three: she sends the document privately to the bank's reviewer, staying within the confidentiality terms she accepted, and keeps a note that the shop's own checkout settings still need their own evidence. Which action belongs in step two?
choices: Open Artifact Agreements and accept the Business Associate Addendum (BAA), since that agreement is what proves PCI DSS compliance to a bank
Open Artifact Reports, find the PCI DSS attestation and download it, accepting the terms that keep it confidential
Start an Artifact scan of the checkout servers so the tool can mark the shop's own workload as PCI DSS compliant
Post the PCI DSS attestation on the shop's public website so the bank and customers can both read it
questions.why: The PCI DSS attestation is a third-party audit document, so it lives in Artifact Reports and is downloaded under confidentiality terms before it is shared privately.

questions.prompt: AWS Artifact has two parts. Which statement correctly describes what each part is for?
choices: Artifact Reports holds audit reports and certifications from independent auditors; Artifact Agreements lets you review and accept legal agreements with AWS
Artifact Reports holds the legal agreements you sign with AWS; Artifact Agreements holds SOC reports and ISO certificates
Artifact Reports is where AWS's own staff publish their internal audits; Artifact Agreements is where you upload your company's audit results
Artifact Reports scans your resources for problems; Artifact Agreements lists the fixes you must apply to become compliant
questions.why: Reports holds third-party audit reports and certifications such as SOC, PCI DSS and ISO, while Agreements is where you review and accept legal agreements like a BAA.

questions.prompt: A US physiotherapy chain plans to keep patient treatment notes in an AWS account. Its lawyer says a Business Associate Addendum (BAA) must be in place first, as required by the health-privacy law HIPAA. Where in AWS does the chain review and accept this agreement?
choices: By running a compliance scan that signs the BAA automatically
Artifact Agreements, in the AWS Management Console
Artifact Reports, by downloading the latest SOC report
A third-party auditor's website, since AWS does not offer the BAA itself
questions.why: Legal agreements with AWS, including the BAA needed under HIPAA, are reviewed and accepted in the Agreements part of AWS Artifact.

questions.prompt: An engineering team at a logistics firm downloads AWS's SOC 2 report from AWS Artifact and tells management, "Our shipment-tracking app is now fully compliant, so we don't need any controls or evidence of our own." What is wrong with this claim?
choices: Nothing is wrong, because downloading a report from Artifact makes the workload that uses it compliant
The report covers only AWS's responsibilities; the team's own configuration, access rules and data handling still need their own controls and evidence
The claim would be true only if the team also forwarded the report publicly to its customers
SOC 2 reports only apply to payment-card systems, so the team downloaded the wrong document
questions.why: Under the shared responsibility model, Artifact's reports prove AWS's side only; Artifact does not scan or certify your own workload.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says, "We downloaded our SOC report from AWS Artifact, so our app is compliant now." Explain to them in your own words what Artifact actually provides and what it does not cover.
lessons.modelAnswer: AWS Artifact is a free portal in the console where we download compliance evidence about AWS itself, and accept certain legal agreements. The reports, like SOC reports, the PCI DSS attestation and ISO certificates, are written by independent auditors who checked AWS's data centers, hardware and processes. The Agreements section is where we'd accept something like a Business Associate Addendum if we handled US health data under HIPAA. The limit is that all of this covers only AWS's half of the shared responsibility model. The SOC report proves AWS's infrastructure controls work; it says nothing about how we configured our app, who has access, or how we protect our data. Artifact doesn't scan our resources either. So the report is one piece of our audit evidence, and we still need our own controls and proof for our side. Also, many reports are confidential, so we shouldn't share them outside the terms we accepted.
rubricPoints: Artifact is a self-service console portal for AWS compliance reports and agreements.
The reports are written by independent third-party auditors, with examples like SOC, PCI DSS or ISO.
Artifact Agreements is where agreements such as a HIPAA BAA are reviewed and accepted.
The evidence covers only AWS's side of the shared responsibility model, not the customer's workload.
Artifact does not make you compliant or check your own resources.
Many reports are confidential and must be shared only under the accepted terms.

suggested.rationale: This objective is about knowing a service's purpose and what it contains, which is factual recall best learned by reading rather than a hands-on mission or engine.

lessons.plain: Compliance means following the rules that outside authorities set for how data must be handled. Those rules are not the same everywhere. A country or region can require that personal data stay inside its borders. An industry such as healthcare, card payments or government work adds its own rules on top. And on AWS, each individual service is checked against each rule set separately, so one service may be approved for a given rule set while another is not yet. Think of moving house: your new country, your profession and each appliance you bring all come with their own regulations.
lessons.guessPrompt: A hospital wants to put patient records on a cloud provider that says it is 'compliant.' What questions would you ask before assuming the hospital's own rules are satisfied?
lessons.teach:
A compliance obligation is a rule an outside authority imposes on how you store, process or protect data, which you must be able to prove to an auditor (an independent checker). On AWS, these obligations vary along three separate axes, and you must check all three.

Geography: laws differ by where people and data are. The EU's GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation) governs personal data about people in the EU. Some countries require data residency, meaning certain data must physically stay in that country. On AWS you control this by choosing the Region, a geographic area of AWS data centers. AWS does not move your data out of the Region you pick, but picking the right one is your decision.

Industry: some sectors add rules regardless of location. Examples are HIPAA for US health information, PCI DSS (Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard) for card data, and FedRAMP for US government cloud use.

Individual services: AWS gets services assessed program by program. A service is 'in scope' for a program once it has been assessed for it. A new or niche service may not be in scope yet, even if many others are.

Worked example: a German clinic plans to store patient files. Step one, geography: personal data of EU patients, so keep it in an EU Region such as Frankfurt. Step two, industry: health data carries extra sector rules, so identify which apply. Step three, services: confirm that the storage, database and every other service the files touch is in scope for those programs. Only then is the design ready for review.

Common mistake: assuming 'AWS is compliant' means your workload is. AWS's certifications cover AWS's own part; how you configure and use services is yours. The consequence in a running system is real: regulated data placed in an out-of-scope service or the wrong Region can fail an audit and bring fines, even if everything works technically.

questions.prompt: A US online ticket seller stores customers' credit card numbers on AWS. It wants to send those card records to a newly launched AWS analytics service. Its compliance review so far: Step 1, geography: customers and data are in the US, and the team has picked a US Region on purpose. Step 2, industry: card data is involved, so PCI DSS (the payment card industry's security standard) applies. Step 3: ??? Only after Step 3 is the design ready for an auditor. What belongs in Step 3?
choices: Confirm that the new analytics service, and every other service the card data touches, is in scope for PCI DSS.
Run a test load to make sure the analytics service processes the card records correctly and quickly.
Move the card data to an EU Region so that GDPR protections also apply to the transactions.
Skip this step, since AWS holds PCI DSS certification and that certification covers every workload customers run on AWS.
questions.why: Services are assessed program by program, so a new service may not yet be in scope for PCI DSS even if many other AWS services are.

questions.prompt: On AWS, what does it mean for a service to be "in scope" for a compliance program such as HIPAA or FedRAMP?
choices: The service has been assessed for that specific program.
The service is available in every AWS Region worldwide.
The customer has configured the service correctly for that program.
The service automatically encrypts all data stored in it.
questions.why: AWS gets each service assessed program by program, and a service is in scope for a program once that assessment has happened.

questions.prompt: A bank in a country whose law requires customer records to physically stay inside that country is moving those records to AWS. Who makes sure the data stays in the country, and how?
choices: AWS's own certifications guarantee data residency for every customer, so no action is needed.
The bank does it by choosing an AWS Region located in that country; AWS keeps the data in the Region chosen.
AWS does it automatically by detecting where the bank's customers live and storing their data there.
The bank does it by choosing a service that is in scope for an industry program such as PCI DSS.
questions.why: Data residency is controlled by Region choice, which is the customer's decision, and AWS does not move data out of the Region picked.

questions.prompt: A US health app team stores patient records on AWS. Their reasoning: "AWS has HIPAA-related assessments, so our app is compliant." They put the records in a niche AWS service that was never assessed for HIPAA. Everything works technically. What is the most likely outcome?
choices: No problem, because AWS's HIPAA work covers how every customer configures and uses its services.
AWS will automatically move the records to a HIPAA-assessed service before an audit.
The only risk is slower performance, since compliance depends on choosing the right Region.
The app can fail a HIPAA audit and the company can face fines, because the records are in an out-of-scope service.
questions.why: AWS's certifications cover only AWS's part; putting regulated data in an out-of-scope service is the customer's choice and can fail an audit even when the system works.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why 'we're on AWS, so we're compliant' is not enough, covering geography, industry and individual services, and name one tradeoff of keeping data in a single Region for residency.
lessons.modelAnswer: Compliance rules come from outside authorities, and they vary three ways. Geography: laws like the EU's GDPR, or data-residency rules, depend on where the people and data are, and we satisfy them partly by choosing the right AWS Region, which is our choice, not AWS's. Industry: health, card payment or government work add rules like HIPAA, PCI DSS or FedRAMP. Services: AWS assesses each service per program, so we must confirm every service our regulated data touches is in scope; a new service might not be. AWS's certifications cover its side only; our configuration is ours. A tradeoff: pinning data to one Region for residency limits where we can place copies for disaster recovery or serve distant users quickly, and some services may not be offered there.
rubricPoints: Compliance obligations differ by geography, such as GDPR or data-residency laws.
Industries add their own rules, such as HIPAA, PCI DSS or FedRAMP.
Each AWS service is in scope for a program only once assessed, so check service by service.
