The customer chooses the Region and is responsible for compliant use; AWS's certifications cover only AWS's part.
Names a real tradeoff, such as residency limiting Region choice for recovery, latency or service availability.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests this through scenarios where you must weigh location, industry and service scope together, so reasoning through situations teaches it best.

lessons.plain: Think of a building with four kinds of security help. An inspector walks the halls checking for weak locks and broken windows before anyone breaks in. A guard watches the cameras for someone acting suspiciously right now. A security office collects every report from the inspector, the guard and the others into one dashboard. A crowd barrier stops a mob from blocking the front door. On AWS, Amazon Inspector checks your software for known weaknesses. Amazon GuardDuty watches activity for signs of an attack. AWS Security Hub gathers everyone's findings in one place. AWS Shield protects against floods of junk traffic.
lessons.guessPrompt: If one tool checks your servers for outdated software with known security holes, and another tool watches account activity for strange behaviour like logins from an unusual country, which one would you expect to notice a stolen password being used?
lessons.teach:
These four services each answer a different security question. A finding is a report that a service has spotted a possible problem. A vulnerability is a known weakness in software, such as an unpatched library.

Amazon Inspector is a vulnerability scanner. It examines virtual servers (EC2 instances), container images and Lambda functions, compares the installed software against public lists of known vulnerabilities, and flags unintended network exposure. It answers: what weaknesses exist in what I run?

Amazon GuardDuty is a threat detection service. It reads activity records such as account API logs (from CloudTrail), network traffic records (VPC Flow Logs) and DNS lookups. It uses threat intelligence and pattern analysis to spot behaviour like a server contacting a known malicious address or credentials used from an odd location. It answers: is someone attacking or misusing my account right now? You turn it on; you install no agents and manage no log pipeline.

AWS Security Hub is an aggregator. It pulls findings from Inspector, GuardDuty and other tools into one prioritised view, and runs automated checks against best-practice standards. It answers: what is my overall security posture?

AWS Shield protects against DDoS (distributed denial of service) attacks, where many machines flood a site with traffic to knock it offline. Shield Standard is automatic and free for all customers. Shield Advanced is a paid tier that adds stronger protection, attack reporting, access to an AWS response team and cost protection against scaling charges caused by an attack.

Worked example: a company asks for one tool to warn that a server runs an old web library, and another to alert when that server starts talking to a cryptocurrency-mining address. Step one: the old library is a known weakness, so Inspector. Step two: the outbound traffic is suspicious behaviour, so GuardDuty. Step three: to see both alerts together, add Security Hub.

Common mistake: swapping Inspector and GuardDuty. Inspector looks at what is installed; GuardDuty looks at what is happening. Also, Inspector, GuardDuty and Security Hub mostly report problems and do not fix them for you, so findings nobody reads leave the system just as exposed.

questions.prompt: A small online game studio is planning security for its launch weekend, and its engineer has worked through most of the plan. Step one: they worry that thousands of machines could flood the game's login site with traffic and knock it offline. That is a DDoS attack, so the protection comes from AWS Shield. Step two: the studio wants more than basic protection. It wants an AWS response team it can call during an attack, reports on attacks, and protection from the extra scaling charges an attack could cause. ??? Step three: they also want their Lambda functions (small pieces of code AWS runs on demand) checked for software with known weaknesses, so they turn on Amazon Inspector. Which choice correctly completes step two?
choices: Rely on Shield Standard, because it is automatic and free and already includes the response team and cost protection
Subscribe to Shield Advanced, the paid tier that adds attack reporting, the AWS response team and cost protection against attack-driven scaling charges
Turn on AWS Security Hub, because it gathers findings into one view and so blocks the attack traffic
Turn on Amazon GuardDuty, because it watches network traffic and stops floods of incoming requests
questions.why: Shield Advanced is the paid tier of Shield that adds attack reporting, access to the AWS response team and cost protection, none of which come with the free Shield Standard.

questions.prompt: A logistics company has turned on Amazon Inspector and Amazon GuardDuty, and it also uses some other security tools. Its security lead says: "I don't want to check five separate screens. I want one prioritised list of findings, plus automatic checks that tell me how our setup compares with best-practice standards." A finding is a report that a service has spotted a possible problem. Which AWS service fits this request?
choices: Amazon Inspector
Amazon GuardDuty
AWS Security Hub
AWS Shield Advanced
questions.why: Security Hub is the aggregator: it pulls findings from Inspector, GuardDuty and other tools into one prioritised view and runs automated best-practice checks.

questions.prompt: At a university research lab, a virtual server (an EC2 instance) that normally sits quiet starts sending traffic to an internet address that appears on threat intelligence lists as a known command-and-control server for attackers. The software installed on the server has no known weaknesses. Which AWS service is designed to spot this kind of activity?
choices: Amazon Inspector, because it compares installed software against public lists of known vulnerabilities
AWS Shield Standard, because it automatically protects every customer from attacks
AWS Security Hub, because it is the service that reads network traffic records directly
Amazon GuardDuty, because it analyses activity records such as network traffic and DNS lookups for suspicious behaviour
questions.why: GuardDuty is the threat detection service that watches what is happening, using records like VPC Flow Logs and DNS lookups plus threat intelligence, while Inspector only looks at what is installed.

questions.prompt: A travel booking firm turned on Amazon Inspector and Amazon GuardDuty eight months ago, but nobody was assigned to look at their output. Last week attackers broke in through an outdated software package that Inspector had flagged in its very first scan. What is the main lesson?
choices: Inspector and GuardDuty mostly report problems rather than fix them, so findings nobody reads and acts on leave the system just as exposed
The firm should have used AWS Shield Advanced, because it scans software for known vulnerabilities
GuardDuty should have patched the outdated package automatically once Inspector reported it
Inspector failed because it only works on servers that have a manually installed agent and a log pipeline
questions.why: These services detect and report problems but mostly do not fix them, so the flagged weakness stayed open because no one acted on the finding.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how Amazon Inspector, Amazon GuardDuty, AWS Security Hub and AWS Shield differ, and name one limit, such as what these tools do not do for you or the tradeoff between Shield Standard and Shield Advanced.
lessons.modelAnswer: Each one covers a different job. Inspector scans our EC2 instances, container images and Lambda functions for known software vulnerabilities and network exposure, so it tells us what weaknesses exist. GuardDuty watches activity data such as CloudTrail API logs, VPC Flow Logs and DNS queries for suspicious behaviour, like a server talking to a known bad address, so it tells us when something is actively going wrong. Security Hub collects findings from those tools and others into one dashboard and checks us against best-practice standards. Shield defends against DDoS floods: Standard is free and automatic, while Advanced costs money but adds a response team, attack reporting and cost protection. The limit is that the first three mostly report rather than fix, so someone still has to patch software and respond to alerts. Shield is protection, not a scanner.
rubricPoints: Inspector scans workloads for known software vulnerabilities and exposure.
GuardDuty detects threats by analysing activity such as API, network and DNS logs.
Security Hub aggregates findings into one view and checks against best-practice standards.
Shield protects against DDoS attacks, with free Standard and paid Advanced tiers.
Names a limit, such as findings needing human action or Advanced's cost versus its extra support.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests this by giving a short security scenario and asking which service fits, so reasoning through mixed situations that separate scanning, detection, aggregation and DDoS protection builds the skill best.

lessons.plain: Encryption scrambles data so only someone holding the right key can read it. Data spends its life in two situations: sitting still on a disk (at rest) or moving across a network (in transit). Protecting one does not protect the other, so you decide each separately. Think of sending valuables: a locked safe at home protects them while they sit there, and an armoured van protects them on the road. Owning a safe does nothing for the trip, and hiring a van does nothing for the jewels once they are back on your shelf. In the cloud, you usually switch on or configure both.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a website uses HTTPS (the padlock in your browser), do you think the files it saves on its servers are automatically encrypted on disk? Why or why not?
lessons.teach:
Encryption at rest means data is stored scrambled on disks, in databases, in backups or in object storage, so a stolen drive or leaked backup file is unreadable without the key. Encryption in transit means data is scrambled while it travels between two points, such as a browser and a server or one service and another, so someone listening on the network sees only noise. The usual technology for in-transit protection is TLS (Transport Layer Security), the protocol behind HTTPS.

They are separate because they defend against different threats. At rest guards against someone getting the stored copy. In transit guards against someone intercepting the conversation. Each is switched on in a different place, with different settings.

On AWS, at rest is typically a setting on the storage service, such as Amazon S3 (object storage), Amazon EBS (virtual disks) or Amazon RDS (managed databases). The keys are often held by AWS KMS (Key Management Service), a managed service that creates, stores and controls the use of encryption keys. In transit relies on TLS certificates, digital files that prove a server's identity and enable the encrypted connection. AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) issues and renews these certificates for you.

Worked example: a user uploads a photo to an app that stores it in S3. Step one, the browser sends the photo to the app over HTTPS, so it is encrypted in transit. Step two, the app forwards it to S3, ideally over TLS again, which is in transit a second time. Step three, S3 writes it to disk, and with default encryption on and a key from KMS, it is encrypted at rest. Remove any one step's protection and that stage is exposed.

Common mistake: believing that HTTPS on the front door means stored data is safe, or that an encrypted database means traffic to it is safe. In a running system that gap is exactly where a leaked backup or a sniffed internal connection exposes customer data. Under the shared responsibility model, choosing and configuring both protections is generally the customer's job, even though AWS supplies the tools.

questions.prompt: A delivery company tracks parcels. Each stage is checked for which protection applies. Stage 1: drivers' phones send delivery records to the company's API over HTTPS, so the records are encrypted in transit. Stage 2: the API saves the records in an Amazon RDS managed database with encryption switched on and a key held in AWS KMS, so the stored records are encrypted at rest. Stage 3: a reporting server inside the company's network reads the records from the database over a plain, unencrypted connection. What is the correct assessment of Stage 3?
choices: Exposed at rest, so the fix is to enable KMS encryption on the reporting server's disk.
Safe, because the database is encrypted at rest, which also covers anything read out of it.
Safe, because Stage 1 already used HTTPS, so the records stay protected for the rest of their journey.
Exposed: this hop has no encryption in transit, so it should use TLS.
questions.why: Encryption at rest protects only the stored copy and earlier HTTPS protects only that earlier hop, so a new unencrypted connection leaves this conversation open to anyone listening on the network unless it uses TLS.

questions.prompt: A charity keeps donor records in a database. An old backup file of that database is accidentally posted to a public file share. Which protection would keep the donor data in that leaked file unreadable?
choices: Encryption at rest on the database and its backups
A TLS certificate issued by AWS Certificate Manager
Switching the charity's website from HTTP to HTTPS
Encryption in transit using TLS between donors' browsers and the website
questions.why: A leaked backup is a stored copy of the data, and only encryption at rest protects stored copies; TLS, certificates and HTTPS protect data only while it travels.

questions.prompt: A small bookshop runs its online store on AWS and wants visitors' browsers to connect over HTTPS. It needs a TLS certificate, a digital file that proves the server's identity, and it wants that certificate renewed automatically. Which AWS service does this job?
choices: Amazon EBS (virtual disks)
AWS Certificate Manager (ACM)
Amazon S3 default encryption
AWS KMS (Key Management Service)
questions.why: AWS Certificate Manager issues and renews TLS certificates for encryption in transit, while KMS manages keys for encryption at rest and EBS and S3 are storage services.

questions.prompt: A startup turns on encryption for its Amazon EBS virtual disks and says: 'Our data is encrypted now, so the traffic between our servers is protected too, and anyway AWS handles that part.' What is wrong with this statement?
choices: Disk encryption protects only traffic, so the stored data on the disks is still exposed.
Disk encryption protects only stored data, and setting up TLS for traffic is generally the startup's own job.
Nothing is wrong, because EBS encryption covers both stored data and network traffic.
AWS automatically encrypts all traffic between customer servers, so only the disk setting was the startup's job.
questions.why: At rest and in transit are separate settings that defend against different threats, and under the shared responsibility model choosing and configuring both is generally the customer's job, even though AWS supplies the tools.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why encryption at rest and encryption in transit are two separate decisions, give an example where one is on and the other is off, and name a tradeoff of turning them on.
lessons.modelAnswer: Encryption at rest protects data where it is stored: disks, databases, backups and S3 buckets. If someone steals a drive or a backup file, they cannot read it without the key, which AWS KMS can manage for us. Encryption in transit protects data while it moves, usually with TLS, so anyone intercepting traffic sees only scrambled bytes. ACM can provide the certificates. They block different threats and are configured in different places, so one never implies the other. For example, a site can use HTTPS while writing customer records to an unencrypted database. The traffic is safe, but a copied backup is readable. The reverse also happens: an encrypted database reached over a plain connection on an internal network. The tradeoffs are some extra setup, key and certificate management, possible key usage costs, and a small performance overhead. Choosing and configuring both is usually our job as the customer.
rubricPoints: Defines at rest as protecting stored data and in transit as protecting data moving over a network.
States that each defends against a different threat, so enabling one does not cover the other.
Names TLS or HTTPS for in transit and a storage setting with managed keys such as KMS for at rest.
Gives a concrete example where one protection is present and the other is missing.
Names a tradeoff such as key or certificate management effort, cost, or performance overhead.
Notes that configuring encryption is generally a customer responsibility using AWS tools.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests whether you can look at a scenario and spot which stage of the data's journey is unprotected, so reasoning through situations teaches this best.

lessons.plain: Once your systems run in the cloud, you need to know four things: is everything healthy, who changed something, what did it look like before the change, and who still has access. AWS has a separate tool for each question. Amazon CloudWatch watches health and performance. AWS CloudTrail keeps a record of every action someone takes. AWS Config keeps a history of how each resource was set up. IAM access reports list who holds keys and passwords and what they actually use. Think of a building: CloudWatch is the thermostat and smoke alarm, CloudTrail is the sign-in book at the front desk, Config is the archive of floor plans, and access reports are the list of who holds keys.
lessons.guessPrompt: Someone deleted an important database last night and your manager asks who did it. Would you look at a tool that graphs performance numbers, or a tool that records every action and the person who took it? Why?
lessons.teach:
These four tools answer four different questions about your AWS account.

Amazon CloudWatch is a monitoring service. It collects metrics, which are numbers measured over time such as CPU use or request count. It also collects logs. You can set alarms, which are rules that notify you or take an action when a metric crosses a threshold. It answers "how is it performing right now?"

AWS CloudTrail is an audit service. It records API calls, meaning every request made to AWS through the console, the command line or code. Each record shows who made the call, when, from where, and what was asked. It answers "who did what?"

AWS Config is a configuration-history service. It saves a record of a resource's settings every time they change. It can also check those settings against Config rules, which are desired-state checks such as "storage buckets must not be public." It answers "what did this look like before, and is it compliant now?"

Access reports come from IAM (Identity and Access Management, the service that controls who can do what). The credential report is a downloadable list of every user with the status of their password and access keys. Last-accessed information shows which services a user or role actually used. Together they answer "who has access, and do they still need it?"

Worked example: at 09:58, a security group (a virtual firewall rule) on a web server is opened to the whole internet. Config records the new setting, keeps the old one, and flags the rule as noncompliant. CloudTrail shows the API call came from user Dana at 09:58. CloudWatch shows traffic to the server spiking afterward and fires an alarm. Later, the credential report shows Dana's access key has not been rotated in a year. Last-accessed data shows she never uses most of her permissions, so you trim them.

A common mistake is choosing CloudWatch for "who deleted the database?" CloudWatch measures behaviour, while CloudTrail records actions by identities. If you mix them up in a running system, you end up with graphs but no culprit, or with an audit trail but no warning that a server is failing. AWS provides these tools, but turning them on, reviewing them and acting on what they find is the customer's job.

questions.prompt:
A small logistics company runs its orders database on AWS. At 14:20 on a Tuesday, someone switches off automatic backups for that database. Complete the investigation by choosing the missing Step 2.

Step 1: AWS Config shows the database's backup setting changed from enabled to disabled at 14:20. It keeps the earlier setting on record and flags the company's rule "databases must have backups enabled" as noncompliant.

Step 2: ???

Step 3: Amazon CloudWatch shows the database's request count and CPU use stayed normal all afternoon, so there was no performance problem, only a risky setting change.

Step 4: IAM last-accessed information shows the user who made the change almost never uses their database-admin permissions, so the team removes them.

Which action belongs in Step 2, to find out which identity made the change?
choices: Download the IAM credential report, because it lists each change a user has made to resources.
Search AWS CloudTrail for the API call that changed the backup setting, which shows user Ravi made it at 14:20 and from which location.
Read the CloudWatch metrics for the database, because a dip in the graph at 14:20 names the user who made the change.
Set a new Config rule, which will reveal who changed the setting.
questions.why: CloudTrail records every API call with who made it, when and from where, so it answers "who did what?" CloudWatch measures behaviour, the credential report shows password and access-key status, and Config records what the settings were.

questions.prompt: A design agency is tidying up permissions. It wants to see which AWS services one of its roles has actually used, so it can remove the permissions the role never touches. Which tool answers this most directly?
choices: Amazon CloudWatch metrics
AWS Config rules
IAM last-accessed information
AWS CloudTrail alarms
questions.why: Last-accessed information, one of the IAM access reports, shows which services a user or role actually used. That is exactly what you need to trim permissions nobody uses.

questions.prompt: An online gaming company wants to be notified automatically whenever the average CPU use on its game servers stays above 85% for ten minutes. What should it use?
choices: An AWS CloudTrail record of API calls made to the servers
The IAM credential report, downloaded every ten minutes
An Amazon CloudWatch alarm on the CPU metric
An AWS Config rule that saves the servers' settings each time they change
questions.why: CPU use is a metric, a number measured over time. A CloudWatch alarm notifies you or takes an action when a metric crosses a threshold.

questions.prompt: A startup's manager says: "AWS offers CloudTrail, CloudWatch and Config, so AWS will watch our account for us and warn us about anything suspicious." What is wrong with this statement?
choices: These tools only work for AWS's own staff, so customers cannot use them at all.
AWS provides the tools, but turning them on, reviewing what they record and acting on the findings is the customer's job.
Nothing is wrong. Once an account exists, AWS reviews these logs and contacts the customer about problems.
Only CloudWatch is the customer's job. AWS reviews CloudTrail and Config on the customer's behalf.
questions.why: AWS supplies these governance and audit tools. The customer is responsible for enabling them, reviewing their output and acting on it.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate keeps mixing up CloudWatch, CloudTrail, Config and IAM access reports. In your own words, explain which question each one answers. Give one limit: something a tool cannot tell you on its own, so you would need another tool alongside it.
lessons.modelAnswer: Think of them as four questions. CloudWatch answers "how is it running?" It collects metrics and logs and fires alarms when a number crosses a threshold. CloudTrail answers "who did what, and when?" It records every API call with the identity behind it. Config answers "what did this resource look like before, and does it follow our rules now?" It keeps a history of settings and flags noncompliant ones. IAM access reports answer "who has credentials, and what do they actually use?" The credential report lists key and password status, and last-accessed data shows which services an identity really touches. The limit is that none of them tells the whole story alone. Config can show a firewall rule changed, but not who changed it, so you need CloudTrail for that. CloudTrail shows the change, but not that traffic then spiked, which is CloudWatch's job. Also, AWS supplies the tools, but enabling and reviewing them is our responsibility.
rubricPoints: CloudWatch monitors performance and health with metrics, logs and alarms.
CloudTrail records API calls, showing who did what, when and from where.
AWS Config records configuration history and checks resources against rules for compliance.
IAM access reports show credential status and which services identities actually use, which supports trimming access.
Names a limit, such as each tool answering only one question, so you must combine them.
Notes that enabling and reviewing these tools is the customer's responsibility.

suggested.rationale: The core exam skill is matching a governance question to the right tool, which is best practised by reasoning through short scenarios rather than by any single hands-on engine.

lessons.plain: Logs are the written record of what happened: who did what, when, and from where. In the cloud, security logs come from several places, because different things leave different traces. One log records every request made to manage your account, another records network traffic, and another records what your own programs and servers report. Think of an office building. There is the front-desk visitor book, the door-badge records and each department's own notebook. When something goes wrong, you need to know which book to open. Most of these logs are not kept by default, so you must turn them on and store them somewhere safe before you need them.
lessons.guessPrompt: Someone deleted an important storage bucket in your cloud account last night. Before any teaching, guess which kind of record would tell you who did it: the bucket's own contents, a list of network connections, or a record of every management request made to the account?
lessons.teach:
A security log is a time-stamped record of events that you keep so you can investigate, alert, or prove what happened. On AWS the main sources each answer a different question.

AWS CloudTrail records API calls. An API call is a request to the AWS control system, such as creating a server or deleting a bucket, whether it comes from the console, the command line or code. CloudTrail answers who did what, when and from which address. The event history keeps the last 90 days of management events to view for free. To keep records longer you create a trail, which continuously delivers log files to an Amazon S3 bucket. S3 is AWS's managed object storage.

Amazon CloudWatch Logs is a managed log store for text that your applications, operating systems and some AWS services write. Examples are login failures on a server or errors from a function. You can search these logs and alarm on them.

VPC Flow Logs record metadata about network traffic in your virtual private cloud (VPC), which is your private virtual network. Each record holds the source, the destination, the port and whether the traffic was accepted or rejected. It does not hold the contents. The records go to CloudWatch Logs or S3.

Some services also keep their own access logs. S3 server access logs record requests to a bucket. Load balancer access logs record requests reaching your load balancer.

Worked example: a firewall rule disappeared. First, open CloudTrail and filter for the event that changes security group rules. Second, read the identity, the time and the source address. Third, check VPC Flow Logs to see whether traffic was rejected before the change and accepted after it. Fourth, read CloudWatch Logs on the server to look for suspicious logins.

A common mistake is expecting CloudTrail to show what happened inside a server or inside network packets. It only sees requests to AWS itself. A second mistake is never creating a trail, so evidence older than 90 days is simply gone. Storing logs in a separate, locked-down S3 bucket keeps an attacker from erasing their tracks.

questions.prompt: A small online bookshop finds that one of its S3 storage buckets, which holds customer invoices, was switched from private to public last week. The team also suspects that strangers downloaded files while it was open. Their investigation plan has three steps. Step 1: open AWS CloudTrail and filter for the API call that changed the bucket's access policy. Step 2: read who made that call, when, and from which address. Step 3 is missing. It should answer this question: which individual files were requested from the bucket while it was public, and by whom? What should Step 3 be?
choices: Check VPC Flow Logs, because they show the contents of every file that left the network.
Look in Amazon CloudWatch Logs on a web server, because CloudWatch automatically records every bucket download.
Check the S3 server access logs for that bucket, which record the requests made to it.
Open the CloudTrail event history and read the contents of each invoice file to see which ones changed.
questions.why: S3 server access logs are the bucket's own record of the requests made to it, so they show which files were requested and by whom; CloudTrail covers the policy change, and flow logs never hold contents.

questions.prompt: A hospital's IT team thinks an unknown machine is repeatedly trying to connect to one of its servers on port 3389 inside its virtual private cloud (VPC), its private virtual network on AWS. They want to see the source address of these attempts and whether each one was accepted or rejected. Which log source answers this?
choices: S3 server access logs, because they track all connections in the VPC
VPC Flow Logs, because they record the source, destination, port and accept or reject result of traffic
AWS CloudTrail, because it records every network packet sent to a server
VPC Flow Logs, because they capture the full contents of each connection attempt
questions.why: VPC Flow Logs record traffic metadata, including source, destination, port and whether traffic was accepted or rejected, but not the contents.

questions.prompt: An auditor asks a logistics company to show who deleted a user account in its AWS account about seven months ago. The company has only ever used the free CloudTrail event history and never created a trail. What is the most likely result?
choices: The record is likely gone, because the event history keeps only the last 90 days of management events
The record is still in the event history, because CloudTrail keeps all management events forever at no cost
They can find it in VPC Flow Logs, which keep a copy of every API call
They can create a trail now, and it will bring back the older events
questions.why: Without a trail delivering log files to an S3 bucket, CloudTrail only keeps 90 days of management events, and a new trail does not bring back older ones.

questions.prompt: A game studio runs its own login software on a virtual server. The developers want to search for repeated failed login attempts that this software writes as text, and to raise an alarm when the failures spike. Where should these log lines be sent?
choices: Amazon CloudWatch Logs, a managed log store that can search application and system logs and alarm on them
VPC Flow Logs, because they record which usernames were used in each login
The CloudTrail event history, because it holds 90 days of application error messages
AWS CloudTrail, because it records every login attempt that happens inside a server
questions.why: CloudWatch Logs stores the text that applications and operating systems write and supports searching and alarms; CloudTrail only sees requests to AWS itself, not activity inside a server.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate where you would look in AWS to investigate a suspected break-in, which log answers which question, and one limit of these logs that could leave you without evidence.
lessons.modelAnswer: I'd look in three places, because each records something different. CloudTrail is the record of API calls made to the AWS account: who changed or deleted a resource, when, and from which address. Its event history only covers the last 90 days, so we should have a trail that delivers the logs to an S3 bucket for long-term keeping. CloudWatch Logs holds what our applications and servers write, such as failed logins or app errors. VPC Flow Logs show network connections in our virtual network: source, destination, port and whether each was accepted or rejected. They never show the contents. The big limit is that most of this isn't captured unless we turn it on ahead of time. Flow logs, a long-lived trail and app logging can't be switched on after the incident and then fill in the past. The logs should also live somewhere the attacker can't delete them.
rubricPoints: CloudTrail records API calls to AWS: who did what, when and from where.
CloudTrail event history covers only 90 days, so long-term records need a trail delivering to S3.
CloudWatch Logs collects application and operating-system log output.
VPC Flow Logs record network traffic metadata, not packet contents.
Logging must be enabled in advance and stored somewhere tamper-resistant.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests matching a security question to the right log source, so reasoning through incident scenarios builds that mapping better than reading a list of products.

lessons.plain: AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) is the free, built-in system that decides who can get into your AWS account and what each person or program may do there. Think of an office building. A user is a named person with their own badge. A group is a department whose members all get the same door access. A role is a temporary visitor badge that anyone authorized can borrow for a short while. A policy is the written list of which doors a badge opens. In this system, nobody gets through any door unless a policy says yes.
lessons.guessPrompt: A new developer joins a team of five developers who all need exactly the same access. Would you grant the newcomer each permission one at a time, or is there a faster and safer way? What would it be?
lessons.teach:
IAM is AWS's identity and authorization service. On every request it answers two questions. The first is authentication: who are you, proven by a password or a key. The second is authorization: are you allowed to do this? IAM is global, meaning it is not tied to one Region (a geographic area of AWS data centers), and it costs nothing extra.

An IAM user is a long-lived identity for one person or application. It can have a console password and/or access keys, which are a key ID plus a secret that programs use to sign requests. An IAM group is a collection of users. Permissions attached to the group apply to every member. A group cannot sign in, and groups cannot contain other groups. An IAM role is an identity that has permissions but no permanent password or keys. A trusted user, AWS service, or other account assumes the role and receives temporary credentials that expire automatically. A policy is a JSON document (structured text) made of statements. Each statement has an Effect (Allow or Deny), Actions (operations such as reading a stored file), and Resources (the specific items affected).

Why it works: everything is denied by default. A request succeeds only if some policy explicitly allows it, and an explicit Deny always beats any Allow.

Worked example: Priya belongs to the group Developers. Its policy allows reading from the storage bucket app-logs. When she reads a file there, four things happen in order. First, IAM authenticates her signed request. Second, it gathers the policies on her user and her groups. Third, it finds no Deny. Fourth, it finds the group's Allow, so the read succeeds. When she then tries to delete the file, no policy allows deleting, so the default deny refuses the request.

Common mistake: pasting a user's access keys onto a virtual server so an application can call AWS. Those keys never expire, so an attacker who takes over the server keeps working credentials. Attach a role to the server instead. The application then gets short-lived credentials that renew automatically, which limits how long any leaked credential stays useful.

questions.prompt: At a small travel company, Tomás is in the group Analysts. The Analysts group policy allows deleting files in the storage bucket quarterly-reports. Tomás's own user also has a policy with Effect Deny for deleting files in quarterly-reports. He tries to delete a file there. Step 1: IAM checks his signed request and confirms who he is (authentication). Step 2: IAM gathers every policy on his user and on the Analysts group. Step 3: IAM sees the Allow from the group and the Deny on his user. Step 4: ___ Which choice correctly completes Step 4?
choices: The delete succeeds, because once IAM finds any Allow for the action it stops checking and lets the request through.
The delete is refused, because no policy allows deleting, so the default deny applies.
The delete succeeds, because a permission attached to a group applies to every member and overrides that member's own policies.
The delete is refused, because an explicit Deny always beats any Allow, no matter where the Allow comes from.
questions.why: When a matching explicit Deny exists, it overrides every Allow, so the group's Allow cannot rescue the request.

questions.prompt: In AWS IAM, which kind of identity has permissions but no permanent password or access keys, and instead hands out temporary credentials that expire automatically to whoever is trusted to assume it?
choices: An IAM user
An IAM group
An IAM policy
An IAM role
questions.why: A role has no long-lived credentials; a trusted user, service, or account assumes it and receives short-lived credentials that expire on their own.

questions.prompt: A delivery startup runs an order-processing application on a virtual server in AWS. The application must write messages to a managed queue. What is the safer way to give the application AWS permissions?
choices: Put the application's server into an IAM group that has queue permissions.
Attach an IAM role with the needed queue permissions to the server, so the application gets short-lived credentials that renew automatically.
Copy an administrator's console password into the application's settings so it can sign in.
Create an IAM user for the application and save that user's access keys in a file on the server.
questions.why: A role gives temporary credentials that expire and renew automatically, so a leaked credential stays useful only briefly, unlike access keys that never expire.

questions.prompt: An administrator at a museum creates a brand-new IAM user named gallery-scanner. She gives it access keys but attaches no policies and adds it to no groups. The program using those keys tries to read a file from a storage bucket. What happens?
choices: The request is refused, because everything is denied by default and no policy explicitly allows the read.
The request succeeds, because a correctly signed request from a real user is allowed until a Deny says otherwise.
The request succeeds only in the Region where the user was created, because IAM users are tied to one Region.
The request is refused, because users with access keys must first be placed in a group before they can authenticate.
questions.why: Authentication only proves who the caller is; without an explicit Allow, the default deny refuses the action.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, in your own words, how IAM users, groups, roles, and policies fit together, and when you would choose a role instead of a user. Name one limit or tradeoff along the way.
lessons.modelAnswer: IAM controls who can do what in our AWS account. A user is a permanent identity for one person or app, with a password or access keys. A group bundles users so we attach permissions once and every member inherits them, which is easier than managing each person separately. Groups cannot nest or log in, though. A policy is the JSON rulebook: Allow or Deny, which actions, on which resources. Everything is denied unless a policy allows it, and an explicit Deny always wins. A role has permissions but no permanent credentials. Someone or something assumes it and gets temporary credentials. I'd use a role for an application on a server or for access from another account, because long-lived keys can leak and keep working. The tradeoff is that roles need a trust setup deciding who may assume them, which is one more thing to configure correctly.
rubricPoints: A user is a long-lived identity for one person or application with its own credentials.
A group applies the same permissions to many users at once and cannot sign in or contain other groups.
A role grants temporary credentials to whoever is trusted to assume it, with no permanent keys.
A policy is a JSON document of Allow/Deny statements covering actions and resources.
Access is denied by default and an explicit Deny overrides any Allow.
Names a limit or tradeoff, such as the risk of long-lived keys or the extra trust configuration a role needs.

suggested.rationale: An authorization policy evaluator would let the learner attach policies to users, groups, and roles and watch default deny and explicit deny decide real requests.

lessons.plain: A policy is a written rulebook that says what a person or program may do in your AWS account. AWS offers ready-made rulebooks, called managed policies, for common jobs such as read-only access. You can also write your own, called custom or customer managed policies, that fit one exact task. Least privilege means giving only the permissions a job truly needs. Think of keys in an office building. A master key is quick to hand out, but if it is lost, every door is exposed. A key cut for one room takes more effort, but a lost one does little harm.
lessons.guessPrompt: A reporting app only needs to read files from one storage bucket. AWS offers a ready-made policy that lets it read every bucket in the account. Should you attach that ready-made policy, or write your own? What could go wrong with each choice?
lessons.teach:
A policy is a document that lists permissions. It is written in JSON, a simple text format made of labelled fields. Each statement in a policy has three main parts. Effect says Allow or Deny. Action names the operations, for example s3:GetObject, which means read a file from Amazon S3, AWS's object storage service. Resource names the specific things the statement covers, using an Amazon Resource Name (ARN), which is a unique address for each resource. Anything a policy does not allow is denied by default.

An AWS managed policy is written and maintained by AWS for common jobs, such as ReadOnlyAccess or AmazonS3FullAccess. You can attach it to users, groups or roles, but you cannot edit it. AWS may also update it when new actions appear. A customer managed policy is one you write and store in your own account. You can attach it to many identities, and you control every line. An inline policy is a third option. It is embedded in a single identity and is deleted along with that identity, so it is less reusable.

Least privilege means granting only the actions, on only the resources, that a job needs. It works because a stolen key or a buggy script can do only what its permissions allow. Smaller permissions mean less possible damage.

Worked example: a reporting app must read files from one bucket called sales-reports. Step 1: you check the AWS managed policies. AmazonS3ReadOnlyAccess fits loosely, but it can read every bucket in the account, including payroll. Step 2: you write a customer managed policy with Effect Allow, Actions s3:GetObject and s3:ListBucket, and Resource limited to the sales-reports bucket and its contents. Step 3: you attach that policy to the app's role. The app can now read sales reports and nothing else.

A common mistake is attaching a broad managed policy like AdministratorAccess just to make something work, then never tightening it. In a running system, one leaked credential with that policy could delete databases or launch expensive servers. Managed policies are a quick starting point, and custom policies are how you finish the job to least privilege.

questions.prompt: A bakery chain runs a nightly backup script that must save files into one S3 bucket called bakery-backups, and nothing else. The team is writing a customer managed policy (one they write and control in their own account) for the script's role. So far the statement says Effect: Allow, and Action: s3:PutObject, which means write a file into S3. The role will have no other policies attached. One part is still missing: the Resource field. What should it contain to follow least privilege?
choices: The ARN (unique address) for the contents of the bakery-backups bucket only
The ARN of every bucket the bakery owns, so the script still works if backups are moved later
A wildcard (*) meaning every resource in the account, because the action is already limited to writing
Nothing at all, because anything not listed is denied by default, so the Resource field is optional
questions.why: Least privilege means only the needed actions on only the needed resources, so the Resource must point at the bakery-backups contents rather than all buckets.

questions.prompt: A clinic's IT team attaches the AWS managed policy ReadOnlyAccess to a group, then decides it should not include one particular action. What can they do?
choices: Write their own customer managed policy with exactly the permissions they want and attach that instead
Edit that line inside ReadOnlyAccess, since anything attached to their group belongs to their account
Turn ReadOnlyAccess into an inline policy so it can be changed later
Ask AWS to remove the action, because AWS managed policies only change on customer request
questions.why: AWS managed policies are written and maintained by AWS and cannot be edited by you, so the way to control every line is to write your own customer managed policy.

questions.prompt: A logistics company has 12 roles that all need the same carefully trimmed set of permissions. They want to change those permissions in one place later. Which kind of policy fits best?
choices: An inline policy embedded separately in each of the 12 roles
A different AWS managed policy for each role, so each role is isolated
An AWS managed policy such as AdministratorAccess, since AWS keeps it updated
One customer managed policy attached to all 12 roles
questions.why: A customer managed policy is stored in your account, can be attached to many identities and is fully under your control, while inline policies live inside single identities and are less reusable.

questions.prompt: A university's grading script has exactly one policy: Effect Allow, Action s3:GetObject (read a file from S3), Resource limited to the exam-scans bucket contents. A bug makes the script try to delete a file in that same bucket. What happens?
choices: The delete succeeds, because the script already has access to that bucket
The delete succeeds only for files the script has read before
The delete is allowed until someone adds an explicit Deny statement for it
The delete is denied, because no policy allows the delete action and anything not allowed is denied by default
questions.why: Permissions are denied by default, so the script can only do what its policy allows, which here is reading, which limits the damage a buggy script can do.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between an AWS managed policy and a customer managed policy, and how least privilege decides which one to use. Name one tradeoff of each.
lessons.modelAnswer: A policy is a JSON document listing which actions are allowed or denied on which resources. Anything not allowed is denied by default. An AWS managed policy is pre-written and kept up to date by AWS for common roles, like read-only access. It is fast to use and needs no upkeep from us. The tradeoff is that we can't edit it, and it is usually broader than our task. A customer managed policy is one we write and store ourselves. We can limit it to exact actions and exact resources by their ARNs, and reuse it across users, groups and roles. The tradeoff is that we have to write it carefully and maintain it. Least privilege means granting only what the job needs, so a leaked key or a bad script can do less harm. In practice, we start from a managed policy if one fits, and switch to a custom one when the managed policy grants more than the task requires.
rubricPoints: Defines a policy as a document of allowed or denied actions on resources, with deny as the default.
States that AWS managed policies are written and maintained by AWS and cannot be edited.
States that customer managed policies are written and controlled by you and can be scoped to specific resources.
Defines least privilege as granting only the actions and resources a task needs.
Names a tradeoff: managed policies are convenient but often too broad, while custom policies are precise but need effort and maintenance.
Explains that tighter permissions limit damage from leaked credentials or faulty code.

suggested.rationale: An authorization policy evaluator would let the learner compare a broad managed policy with a narrow custom one and see exactly which requests each allows or denies.

lessons.plain: When you open an AWS account, the email address and password you signed up with become the root user. This is the account's master identity, and it can do anything in the account, with no way to switch that off. Think of it as the deed and master key to a building. You lock it in a safe, hand day-to-day keys to staff, and take the master out only for the few jobs that need the owner in person. Protecting the root user means locking that master key away. It also means knowing the short list of jobs only the owner can do.
lessons.guessPrompt: If one login could do absolutely everything in your company's cloud account, including closing it, how often do you think people should use it, and what would you do to protect it?
lessons.teach:
The root user is the identity created with a new AWS account, tied to the sign-up email address. It has complete, unrestricted access to every resource and setting. Ordinary permission policies cannot shrink its powers. These are the IAM (Identity and Access Management) rules that say what an identity may do. So if root is stolen, the attacker owns the account.

Protecting it follows a few habits. Use a long, unique password. Turn on MFA (multi-factor authentication), which asks for a second proof such as a code from a phone app or a hardware key. Do not create root access keys, which are long-lived secrets that let programs act as root, and delete any that exist. Create a separate administrator identity in IAM or IAM Identity Center for daily work. Keep the root email mailbox secure, because it can be used to reset the password.

Root should come out only for tasks nothing else can do. The commonly tested list is short. Changing account settings such as the root email, account name or root password. Closing the account. Changing or cancelling the AWS Support plan. Restoring access when an administrator accidentally locked every IAM identity out. Turning on IAM access to the billing console. Registering as a seller in the Reserved Instance Marketplace. Enabling MFA delete on an Amazon S3 storage bucket.

Here is a worked example of setting up a new account. Step 1: sign in as root and enable MFA. Step 2: create an administrator identity with broad permissions. Step 3: sign out of root and work as the administrator. Step 4: a month later, finance asks to upgrade the support plan. Check the list: that task is root-only, so retrieve root, make the change, and sign out.

A common mistake is treating root as a personal admin login, or saving root access keys in a script. In a running system, one leaked key or phished password then gives total control: deleted data, surprise bills, even a closed account.

questions.prompt:
Mira runs the AWS account for a small architecture firm, Lindqvist & Ortega. She does her daily work as an IAM administrator identity. The root user is locked away with MFA turned on. On Monday she sorts three requests by checking whether each task is root-only.

Request 1: start two new virtual servers for a client project. This is not a root-only task, so she does it as the administrator, and root stays locked away.

Request 2: the partners want the account renamed to the firm's new name. The account name is an account setting, and changing it is root-only. So she retrieves root, makes the change and signs out.

Request 3: the bookkeeper has her own IAM identity and has been granted billing permissions, but she still cannot open the billing console at all.

Missing step: what should Mira do for Request 3?
choices: Retrieve root, turn on IAM access to the billing console, then sign out of root
Create root access keys and paste them into the bookkeeper's accounting software
Share the root password with the bookkeeper so she can view the bills herself
As the administrator, attach a broader permission policy to the bookkeeper's identity, with no need to touch root
questions.why: Turning on IAM access to the billing console is on the short list of root-only tasks, so Mira briefly uses root for that one change and then signs out.

questions.prompt: The security lead at a regional hospital writes an IAM permission policy meant to stop the root user from deleting storage buckets, and attaches it. (IAM permission policies are the rules that say what an identity may do.) What is the effect on the root user?
choices: None: ordinary permission policies cannot shrink root's powers, so root still has full access
Root can no longer delete buckets but keeps every other power it had
The policy starts limiting root only after MFA is turned on for root
The policy limits root only when root signs in through the web console
questions.why: The root user has complete, unrestricted access, and ordinary permission policies cannot reduce it.

questions.prompt: An administrator at a logistics company works through four tasks. Which one requires signing in as the root user instead of using the administrator identity?
choices: Deleting an old, unused storage bucket
Creating a new IAM user for a newly hired engineer
Downgrading the AWS Support plan from Business to Developer
Setting up a new virtual network for a test environment
questions.why: Changing or cancelling the AWS Support plan is on the root-only list, while the other three tasks can be done by a properly permissioned administrator.

questions.prompt: A developer at a games studio saved the root user's access keys in a build script. Access keys are long-lived secrets that let programs act as an identity. The script was then pushed to a public code repository. What is the realistic risk?
choices: Nothing serious, because the root user's MFA blocks anyone who tries to use the keys
Very little, because the keys expire on their own after about a day
Only the build pipeline is exposed, because access keys are restricted to the few resources the script actually touches
Anyone who finds the keys can act as root, with total control over data, spending and even closing the account
questions.why: Root access keys carry root's unrestricted power and are long-lived, so one leaked key can hand an attacker total control of the account.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate asks why they can't just use the root login for everyday work since it never hits permission errors. Explain in your own words how to protect the root user, which tasks truly need it, and the tradeoff of locking it away.
lessons.modelAnswer: Root is the identity created with the account. It can do everything, and permission policies can't limit it. That's exactly why it's dangerous for daily use: if its password or keys leak, the attacker has total control. So we give it a strong unique password and MFA, never create root access keys, and secure the sign-up email. We then do daily work through a separate administrator identity. Root comes out only for the few jobs nothing else can do. Those are changing account settings like the root email or password, closing the account, changing the support plan, restoring locked-out IAM access, enabling IAM billing access, and S3 MFA delete. The tradeoff is some friction: the MFA device must be stored safely and reachable. If it's lost, recovery takes time, so the people who hold it must be planned in advance.
rubricPoints: Root has full, unrestricted access that permission policies cannot limit.
Protect it with a strong password and MFA, and secure the sign-up email.
Avoid root access keys and use a separate administrator identity for daily work.
Name several root-only tasks, such as closing the account, changing the support plan, or changing root account settings.
Note a tradeoff, such as friction or the risk of losing the MFA device.

suggested.rationale: This objective is mostly a short set of habits and a fixed list of root-only tasks to recognise, which careful reading and recall cover best.

lessons.plain: Authentication is how a system checks that you are who you claim to be before it lets you in. On AWS, three ideas matter. Multi-factor authentication (MFA) asks for a second proof, such as a code from your phone, on top of your password. AWS IAM Identity Center gives people one sign-in that opens the door to many AWS accounts. A cross-account role lets someone in one account borrow a temporary badge to work in another. Picture an office: a keycard plus a PIN, one front-desk badge that works in every building, and a visitor pass that expires at the end of the day.
lessons.guessPrompt: A colleague needs to work in five separate AWS accounts. Would you give them five separate logins with five passwords, or look for another way? What could go wrong with five logins?
lessons.teach:
Authentication means proving identity. It comes before authorization, which decides what that identity may do. An AWS account is a separate container for resources and billing, and larger organizations often run many of them.

Multi-factor authentication (MFA) requires two different kinds of proof. One is something you know, such as a password. The other is something you have, such as an authenticator app on a phone or a hardware security key. It works because a stolen password alone no longer opens the door. MFA is strongly recommended on the root user (the account's original, all-powerful login) and on every human login.

AWS IAM Identity Center, formerly called AWS Single Sign-On, is a central sign-in service. A person signs in once and sees a portal listing the accounts and access levels assigned to them, then picks one. Those access levels are defined as permission sets, which are reusable bundles of permissions applied to accounts. Identity Center can keep its own user directory or connect to a company's existing one. It hands out short-lived credentials, so nobody keeps long-term passwords in each account.

An IAM role is an identity that has permissions but no permanent password or keys. Someone assumes the role and receives temporary credentials that expire. A cross-account role lives in one account. Its trust policy, a rule attached to the role, names another account that is allowed to assume it.

Worked example: Priya works in Account A (tools) and needs to read logs in Account B (production). Step 1: an admin in B creates a role called LogReader with read-only log permissions. Step 2: LogReader's trust policy names Account A. Step 3: Priya, signed into A with MFA, asks to assume LogReader. Step 4: AWS checks the trust policy and Priya's own permission to assume the role, then issues credentials valid for a limited time, for example one hour. Step 5: she reads the logs, and the credentials expire.

A common mistake is to create a separate IAM user with long-term access keys in every account instead. In a running system those keys get copied, forgotten and leaked. Removing a departing employee then means hunting through every account. Roles and Identity Center leave nothing permanent behind to steal.

questions.prompt:
Harbor Freight Labs runs 7 AWS accounts (an AWS account is a separate container for resources and billing). It uses AWS IAM Identity Center, a central sign-in service, connected to the company's existing staff directory. Trace how an auditor gets in.

Step 1: An admin creates a permission set called AuditViewer. A permission set is a reusable bundle of read-only permissions.
Step 2: The admin assigns AuditViewer to the audit group in 3 of the 7 accounts.
Step 3: Lena, an auditor, signs in once with her password plus a code from her hardware security key, which is MFA (multi-factor authentication).
Step 4: ???
Step 5: She picks the Payments account and receives short-lived credentials that expire on their own.

Which choice correctly fills Step 4?
choices: She signs in again with a separate IAM user password stored in each of the 3 accounts
Identity Center issues her long-term access keys that she saves for future audits
She sees a portal listing the 3 accounts where she has AuditViewer access
She writes a trust policy in each account that names her own login
questions.why: After one sign-in, Identity Center shows a portal of the accounts and permission sets assigned to that person, and she picks one from there, with no per-account passwords and no long-term keys.

questions.prompt: A clinic's IT lead wants staff logins to use multi-factor authentication (MFA), which requires two different kinds of proof. Which sign-in combination actually meets that definition?
choices: Two different passwords, each one at least 16 characters long
A long password that is changed every 30 days
A password plus a one-time code from an authenticator app on the user's phone
A password plus an answer to a security question like 'first pet's name'
questions.why: MFA needs something you know (the password) and something you have (the phone running the authenticator app). The other options only use things you know.

questions.prompt: A game studio keeps its build servers in Account Dev and its player-data storage in Account Live. The admin in Live creates an IAM role named DataExporter. An IAM role is an identity with permissions but no permanent password or keys. The admin wants only people from Account Dev to be able to assume this role. What on the role controls which other account may assume it?
choices: A long-term access key created for DataExporter and shared with Dev
The role's trust policy, which names Account Dev as allowed to assume it
A permission set assigned to Account Dev in IAM Identity Center
An MFA device registered to the root user of Account Live
questions.why: A cross-account role's trust policy is the rule attached to the role that names which other account is allowed to assume it.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm has 12 AWS accounts. Instead of using roles or Identity Center, each engineer has a separate IAM user with long-term access keys in every account. One engineer leaves the company. What is the main problem this setup creates?
choices: The keys expire automatically after about an hour, so nobody can rebuild the engineer's past work
Someone must find and remove that engineer's keys in all 12 accounts, and any copy that is missed can still be used
Only authorization is affected, because long-term keys play no part in authentication
Turning on MFA for each account's root user would fully cancel the engineer's remaining keys
questions.why: Long-term keys never expire on their own. They get copied and forgotten, so offboarding means hunting through every account, while roles and Identity Center leave nothing permanent behind to steal.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how MFA, IAM Identity Center and cross-account roles each make sign-in safer, when you would reach for each one, and one limit or tradeoff that comes with them.
lessons.modelAnswer: Authentication is proving who you are. MFA adds a second kind of proof, like a phone app code or a security key, on top of a password, so a stolen password isn't enough. It belongs on the root user and on every human login. IAM Identity Center is one central sign-in for many accounts. People log in once, pick an account and a permission set, and get short-lived credentials, so we never manage separate passwords in each account. A cross-account role is for when someone or something in one account needs to act in another. The role's trust policy names the allowed account, and assuming the role gives temporary credentials that expire. The tradeoffs: MFA adds friction and needs a recovery plan if a device is lost. Identity Center becomes a central dependency. Roles need their trust set up carefully, because a trust policy that is too broad lets the wrong account in.
rubricPoints: Authentication proves identity and is separate from authorization, which decides what that identity may do.
MFA combines something you know with something you have, so a stolen password alone fails.
IAM Identity Center gives one sign-in across many accounts, using permission sets and short-lived credentials.
A cross-account role is assumed through a trust policy and gives temporary, expiring credentials.
Roles and Identity Center avoid long-term keys scattered across accounts.
Names a real limit, such as lost MFA devices, a central dependency, or an overly broad trust policy.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests choosing the right authentication method for a described situation, so reasoning through short scenarios (many accounts, a stolen password, another account needing access) builds the skill best.

lessons.plain: Credentials are the secrets that prove who you are to AWS or to your own systems: passwords for people, access keys for programs, and things like database passwords your apps use. Handling them well means keeping them out of places where they can leak, making them strong, and changing them regularly. Think of a hotel: instead of taping a room key under the doormat, you keep keys at the front desk, which hands them out only to the right guest and can re-cut them anytime. In AWS, protecting your credentials is your job, not AWS's, and AWS gives you managed stores and rules to help.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your application needs a database password to start up. Would you type that password directly into the program's source code, or store it somewhere else? What could go wrong with the first option?
lessons.teach:
Credential handling means creating, storing, using and replacing secrets safely. Under the shared responsibility model, this is the customer's job; AWS supplies the tools.

An access key is a long-term credential for programs calling AWS. It has two parts: an access key ID (like a username) and a secret access key (like a password). Because it never expires on its own, you should rotate it, meaning create a new one, switch over, then delete the old one. Where possible, prefer temporary credentials from a role over long-term keys.

A password policy is an account-wide rule set for human IAM user passwords: minimum length, required character types, how often passwords expire, and whether old ones can be reused.

AWS Secrets Manager is a managed secret store: it encrypts secrets such as database passwords and API tokens, hands them to authorized apps on request, and can automatically rotate them on a schedule. It charges per secret stored and per API call.

AWS Systems Manager is a toolkit for operating servers; its Parameter Store feature holds configuration values, including encrypted ones called SecureString parameters. The standard tier is free, but it does not rotate secrets automatically.

Worked example: an app needs a database password that must change every 30 days. Step one, store the password in Secrets Manager. Step two, turn on rotation every 30 days. Step three, give the app permission to read only that secret. Step four, the app fetches the current password at startup, so rotation never requires a code change. If the value were a plain setting like a feature flag, Parameter Store would be the cheaper fit.

Common mistake: pasting access keys or passwords into source code and committing them to a shared repository. Automated scanners find leaked keys quickly; attackers then launch resources on your account, running up bills and possibly reading data, until you deactivate the key.

questions.prompt: A small hotel chain is sorting out three credentials on AWS. Value A is a token for a third-party booking API that the vendor requires to change every 60 days. Decision: store it in AWS Secrets Manager (a managed, encrypted secret store) with automatic rotation every 60 days, and let only the booking app read it. Value B is a non-secret setting, the default check-out hour of 11. Decision: store it in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store (a configuration store whose standard tier is free) because it needs no rotation. Value C is the sign-in password for each of the 40 front-desk staff who log in as IAM users, and management wants every password to be at least 14 characters and to expire every 90 days. Decision for value C: ____
choices: Set an account-wide IAM password policy with a 14-character minimum and 90-day expiry
Store each staff password as a Secrets Manager secret set to rotate every 90 days
Give each staff member an access key and rotate the keys every 90 days
Store each password as an encrypted SecureString parameter in Parameter Store
questions.why: Rules for human IAM user passwords, such as minimum length and expiry, are set account-wide by a password policy, not by storing each password in a secret or parameter store.

questions.prompt: A data team's reporting script calls AWS using a long-term access key. Which pair of parts makes up that access key?
choices: A username and a sign-in password for the AWS console
A Secrets Manager secret name and a rotation schedule
An access key ID and a secret access key
A role name and a temporary session token that expires
questions.why: An access key has an access key ID, which works like a username, and a secret access key, which works like a password.

questions.prompt: A developer at a delivery startup accidentally pushes a file containing an AWS access key to a public code repository. What is the right first move, and why?
choices: Wait for the key to expire on its own, because access keys time out after a short period
Report it to AWS and let them fix it, because credential handling is AWS's job under shared responsibility
Delete the file from the repository, because once it is removed the key can no longer be used
Deactivate the leaked key right away, because attackers can use it to run resources on the account until it is deactivated
questions.why: Access keys never expire on their own and scanners find leaked keys quickly, so the key keeps working for attackers until the customer deactivates it.

questions.prompt: A clinic runs an app on AWS that uses an API token for a lab-results service. Under the shared responsibility model, who is responsible for making sure that token is stored safely and replaced regularly?
choices: AWS, because it owns the servers where the token is stored
Nobody, because tokens stored in AWS are protected automatically
The lab-results vendor, because it issued the token
The clinic, using AWS tools such as Secrets Manager to store and rotate it
questions.why: Credential handling is the customer's job under shared responsibility; AWS supplies tools like Secrets Manager, but the customer must use them.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would handle a database password and an AWS access key for a new app, and when you would pick Secrets Manager over Systems Manager Parameter Store, naming a tradeoff.
lessons.modelAnswer: Credentials are our responsibility, not AWS's, so first rule: nothing secret goes in code or the repo. For the database password I'd use Secrets Manager, which encrypts it, lets only our app's identity read it, and can rotate it automatically on a schedule, so the app just fetches the current value. The tradeoff is cost: Secrets Manager charges per secret and per call. For plain config values, or secrets we're happy to rotate by hand, Systems Manager Parameter Store with a SecureString is cheaper, since the standard tier is free, but it won't rotate anything for us. For AWS access, I'd avoid long-term access keys and use temporary role credentials; if a key is unavoidable, rotate it and delete old ones. Humans get a password policy enforcing length, complexity and no reuse.
rubricPoints: States that credential handling is the customer's responsibility.
Describes an access key as ID plus secret, long-lived, needing rotation, with temporary role credentials preferred.
Explains a password policy as account-wide rules for human user passwords.
Names Secrets Manager for encrypted storage with automatic rotation.
Names Parameter Store as a cheaper store without automatic rotation, giving the tradeoff.
Warns against hardcoding or committing secrets and states the consequence of a leak.

suggested.rationale: That mission makes the learner wire a secret into a deployment without leaking it, which practices the exact habit this objective tests.

lessons.plain: Federated identity management means letting people sign in to AWS with an account they already have somewhere else, such as their company login or a social account, instead of creating a separate AWS username and password for each person. AWS agrees to trust another system to vouch for who someone is. Think of a hotel that accepts your passport rather than issuing you its own ID card: the passport office checks who you are, and the hotel decides which rooms you may enter. One identity, kept in one place, works across many systems, so there are fewer passwords to manage and forget.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your company already has a directory where every employee has a login. If 500 employees need access to AWS, what problems might you run into by creating 500 new AWS logins, and what might be a better approach?
lessons.teach:
Federation is an arrangement where AWS trusts an outside identity provider to confirm who a person is. An identity provider (IdP) is the system that holds user accounts and checks passwords, for example a corporate directory like Microsoft Active Directory, or a public login like Google. AWS does not store that person's password; it accepts a signed statement from the IdP saying who the user is. Those statements travel in standard formats: SAML 2.0, common for workforce logins, and OpenID Connect (OIDC), common for web and mobile apps.

Why it works: after AWS accepts the statement, it lets the user take on an IAM role, which is a set of permissions anyone trusted can temporarily assume. The user receives temporary credentials, meaning access keys that expire on their own, often within an hour, instead of long-lived passwords or keys stored in AWS.

Worked example: Priya opens her company sign-in page and enters her normal work password. The corporate IdP checks it and sends AWS a signed SAML statement saying "this is Priya, in the Finance group." AWS has been configured to map the Finance group to a read-only billing role. Priya is granted that role with temporary credentials and lands in the AWS console. When she leaves the company, IT disables her directory account, and she can no longer sign in to AWS.

Two AWS services do this work. AWS IAM Identity Center connects your workforce directory to one or many AWS accounts and gives employees a single sign-on portal. Amazon Cognito handles sign-in for customers of your own app, including social logins.

A common mistake is creating an individual IAM user for every employee anyway. The result is duplicate accounts, permanent passwords and keys that can leak, and forgotten access that stays active after people leave. Under the shared responsibility model, setting up federation and its permissions is the customer's job, while AWS secures the services that perform it.

questions.prompt: A logistics company, Harbor Freight Lines, has set up federation between its corporate directory and AWS. Its directory group "Warehouse-Analysts" is mapped to an IAM role that can only read data in one storage bucket. Trace what happens when an analyst, Tomas, signs in. Step 1: Tomas opens the company sign-in page and types his usual work password. Step 2: The corporate identity provider checks the password and sends AWS a signed SAML statement saying "this is Tomas, in Warehouse-Analysts." Step 3: ??? Step 4: Tomas reaches the AWS console and can read the bucket, and about an hour later his access keys stop working on their own unless he signs in again. Which choice correctly fills in Step 3?
choices: AWS compares Tomas's password with a copy of it stored in AWS, then creates a permanent IAM user for him.
AWS issues Tomas long-lived access keys that he must store safely and rotate himself.
AWS accepts the statement, matches Warehouse-Analysts to the read-only role, and gives Tomas temporary credentials for it.
AWS forwards the statement to Amazon Cognito, which adds Tomas to the company's public customer pool.
questions.why: In federation AWS trusts the identity provider's signed statement, maps the user's group to an IAM role, and hands out temporary credentials that expire on their own, which explains why Tomas's keys stop working in Step 4.

questions.prompt: A small studio is building a mobile puzzle game. It wants players to create accounts or sign in with their existing Google login, without the studio storing their passwords itself. Which AWS service fits this job?
choices: Microsoft Active Directory
Amazon Cognito
AWS IAM Identity Center
An individual IAM user for each player
questions.why: Amazon Cognito handles sign-in for the customers of your own app, including social logins like Google, while IAM Identity Center is meant for an organisation's own employees.

questions.prompt: A university IT team connects its staff directory to AWS. It decides that the directory group "Research-Admins" should map to a role with full access to the research account. Under the shared responsibility model, who is responsible for deciding and configuring that mapping and its permissions?
choices: Nobody, because federated users bypass IAM permissions
The identity provider vendor, because it issues the signed statement
AWS, because federation is a managed AWS feature
The university, as the AWS customer
questions.why: Setting up federation and choosing which permissions each role grants is the customer's job, while AWS only secures the services that perform it.
