questions.prompt: An engineer at a logistics company says: 'Our order system runs across three Availability Zones, so we are already protected if the entire Region goes down.' What is wrong with this statement?
choices: Nothing; three Availability Zones are enough to survive the loss of a whole Region
Protection against a regional outage needs at least five Availability Zones
Availability Zones only reduce latency and offer no protection against failures at all
All three Availability Zones belong to the same Region, so a regional disaster can take them all out; another Region is needed
questions.why: Availability Zones protect against one facility failing, but they all sit inside one Region, so only a second Region covers a regional disaster.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate when a workload should run in more than one AWS Region instead of just multiple Availability Zones, covering the four common reasons and naming at least one cost or tradeoff.
lessons.modelAnswer: Multiple Availability Zones protect us from one data centre group failing, but they all sit inside a single Region, so a regional outage still takes us down. We go multi-Region for four reasons. Disaster recovery: keep a copy of data and systems in another Region so we can restore if ours is lost. Business continuity: have that second Region ready to actually carry traffic so the business keeps working. Latency: put a Region near distant users so responses are faster. Data sovereignty: pick the Region inside the country where the law says data must stay, and be careful not to copy regulated data out to other Regions. The tradeoff is real: a second Region roughly doubles some infrastructure, adds charges for moving data between Regions, and makes deployments and testing more complex, so we only do it when one of these needs justifies it.
rubricPoints: Distinguishes Availability Zones (survive one facility failing) from Regions (survive a whole-area failure).
Names disaster recovery and business continuity as reasons, noting continuity may need a ready-to-serve second Region.
Explains latency as distance-driven delay solved by placing a Region near users.
Explains data sovereignty as choosing a Region in the required jurisdiction and not copying regulated data elsewhere.
Names a tradeoff such as added cost, cross-Region transfer charges or operational complexity.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests this through short scenarios where the learner must spot which of the four needs applies and reject the single-Region multi-AZ near-miss, which scenario reasoning practises best.

lessons.plain: An Amazon EC2 instance is a virtual server you rent from AWS by the hour or second. AWS offers many sizes and shapes of these servers, grouped into instance families. Each family is tuned for a different balance of processing power, memory, fast local disk, or special chips such as graphics processors. Think of renting a vehicle. A family car handles most trips, a sports car is built for speed, a moving van carries bulk, and a tow truck has special equipment. You pick the one that matches the job, so you are not paying for capacity you never use.
lessons.guessPrompt: A video company converts thousands of uploaded clips into smaller formats every night. The servers run their processors flat out but use little memory. Would you rent servers with extra processing power or servers with extra memory, and why?
lessons.teach:
Amazon EC2 (Elastic Compute Cloud) is the AWS service that rents virtual servers, called instances. An instance type is one specific size, such as m7g.large. The leading letter names its instance family, a group of types that share the same ratio of resources. Those resources are the vCPU (a virtual processor core), memory (RAM, the fast working space a program holds data in), local storage, and sometimes extra hardware.

There are five families to know. General purpose (M and T types) has balanced processor and memory and suits web servers, small databases and development machines. Compute optimized (C) gives more processor per unit of memory and suits batch processing, video encoding, game servers and scientific modelling. Memory optimized (R and X) gives large RAM and suits in-memory databases and real-time analysis of big datasets. Storage optimized (I and D) has very fast local disks for heavy reading and writing, and suits data warehousing and distributed file systems. Accelerated computing (P, G, Inf and Trn) adds graphics processors or custom chips for machine-learning training and graphics rendering.

This works because you pay for every resource the instance includes. Matching the family to your bottleneck, the resource that runs out first, means you are not paying for idle capacity.

Here is a worked example. A transcoding job shows processor use at 100% and memory at 30%. First, find the bottleneck, which is the processor. Second, pick the family that is rich in that resource, which is compute optimized. Third, reject the near miss. Memory optimized would leave most of the RAM you paid for sitting unused, and the job would still wait on the processor.

A common mistake is reading storage optimized as "needs lots of storage space." It actually means fast input and output on local disks. Plain capacity is better handled by separate storage services. In a running system, a wrong choice shows up as either slow performance or an inflated bill. You can stop an instance and change its type later, but that change means some downtime.

questions.prompt: A regional grocery chain runs a real-time pricing analysis service that keeps a 400 GB product dataset in RAM (memory, the fast working space a program holds data in). Monitoring shows memory use at 92% and vCPU (virtual processor core) use at 25%. Step 1: The bottleneck, the resource that runs out first, is memory. Step 2: Choose the memory optimized family (R or X types), which is rich in RAM. Step 3 is missing: explain why compute optimized (C types) is the wrong near miss. Which statement completes Step 3?
choices: Compute optimized is wrong because it has no local disk at all, so there would be nowhere on the instance to keep the 400 GB dataset.
Compute optimized is wrong because that family is reserved for game servers and video encoding, so it cannot run analysis software of any kind.
Compute optimized is wrong because it always costs more than every other family, whatever the workload actually needs from the instance.
Compute optimized gives more processor per unit of memory, so the processor capacity you pay for would sit mostly idle while the dataset still runs short of RAM.
questions.why: The workload is short on memory, and compute optimized spends its resource ratio on processor, so you would pay for idle vCPUs and still hit the memory limit.

questions.prompt: An engineer sees the Amazon EC2 (Elastic Compute Cloud, the AWS service that rents virtual servers) instance type r6i.xlarge. What does the leading letter "r" tell them?
choices: The size of the instance within its group.
Whether the instance is reserved or rented by the hour.
The AWS region where the instance is running.
The instance family, a group of types sharing the same ratio of resources.
questions.why: The leading letter of an instance type names its family, which groups types with the same balance of processor, memory, storage and extra hardware.

questions.prompt: A university research group needs EC2 instances to train machine-learning models on millions of medical images, and the work depends on graphics processors. Which instance family fits best?
choices: Compute optimized, because training is heavy on the processor.
Memory optimized, because the image collection is very large.
Storage optimized, because the images must be read from disk.
Accelerated computing, because it adds graphics processors or custom chips.
questions.why: Accelerated computing (P, G, Inf and Trn types) is the family that adds graphics processors or custom chips for machine-learning training, which plain processor-heavy compute optimized types do not provide.

questions.prompt: A logistics company needs to keep 50 TB of old shipment logs that are almost never read. A team member picks a storage optimized EC2 instance because "it is the family for lots of storage." What is wrong with this choice?
choices: Storage optimized instances cannot hold more than a few gigabytes, so the logs would not fit and the company would need a memory optimized instance instead.
The choice is wrong only because instance types can never be changed later, so the company would be locked in permanently.
Nothing is wrong; storage optimized is the correct family whenever the amount of data is large, no matter how often it is read.
Storage optimized means very fast reading and writing on local disks, not plain capacity; rarely read data is better handled by separate storage services, so this choice mainly inflates the bill.
questions.why: Storage optimized is about fast local disk input and output, so paying for that speed on data that is almost never read wastes money when separate storage services suit plain capacity.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose an EC2 instance family for a new workload, and name one limit or tradeoff of that choice.
lessons.modelAnswer: First I'd figure out which resource the workload runs out of first. That might be processor, memory, fast disk access, or something that needs a graphics or machine-learning chip. Then I'd pick the family rich in that resource. Compute optimized fits encoding or batch jobs. Memory optimized fits in-memory databases. Storage optimized fits heavy local disk input and output. Accelerated computing fits ML training or rendering. If nothing stands out, general purpose is the sensible default, for things like web servers or dev boxes. The tradeoff is that each family is lopsided by design. If I guess wrong, I either pay for resources that sit idle or the app crawls on its real bottleneck. Storage optimized is also about speed, not raw capacity. Changing the type later is possible, but it needs a stop and restart, so some downtime.
rubricPoints: Identifies the workload's bottleneck resource as the basis for the choice.
Names the families and matches each to a typical workload.
Treats general purpose as the balanced default.
Notes that storage optimized means fast local I/O, not just capacity.
States a tradeoff such as paying for idle resources or slow performance from a mismatch.
Mentions that resizing later is possible but requires stopping the instance.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests this as short scenarios where you match a described workload to a family and reject the near miss, so reasoning through situations adds the most.

lessons.plain: A container is a sealed package holding an application plus everything it needs to run, so it behaves the same on any machine, like a standard shipping container that fits any ship or crane. Running a few by hand is easy; running hundreds needs a coordinator that starts them, restarts failed ones and spreads them across machines. AWS offers two such coordinators. Amazon ECS is AWS's own, simpler design. Amazon EKS runs Kubernetes, the popular open-source coordinator, for you. Both run your containers. They differ in which coordinator you want to learn and live with.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company already runs its containers on Kubernetes in its own data center and wants to move them to AWS while keeping the same Kubernetes tools and skills. Which would you guess fits better: Amazon ECS or Amazon EKS?
lessons.teach:
A container is a lightweight, isolated package of an application and its dependencies, built from a container image (a read-only template). An orchestrator is software that decides where containers run, keeps the requested number running, replaces failed ones and scales them. A cluster is the group of machines an orchestrator manages.

Amazon ECS (Elastic Container Service) is a managed container orchestrator designed by AWS. It works in AWS-native terms and fits closely with other AWS services, so there is less to learn. Amazon EKS (Elastic Kubernetes Service) is a managed Kubernetes service. Kubernetes is an open-source orchestrator that runs in many clouds and on-premises. EKS runs and maintains the Kubernetes control plane for you. The control plane is the "brain" that makes scheduling decisions. Because Kubernetes is a common standard, EKS suits teams that already use it or want to run the same way across clouds.

Both services need somewhere for containers to actually run. You can use EC2 instances (virtual servers) that you manage, or AWS Fargate, which supplies the compute so you never handle servers. Fargate is not an orchestrator. It is a place for ECS or EKS to run containers.

Worked example. Need: "A small team wants to run containerized web apps on AWS, has no Kubernetes experience, and wants the simplest option." Step 1: it is containers, so the choice is ECS or EKS. Step 2: is Kubernetes required or already in use? No. Step 3: is simplicity and AWS integration the priority? Yes. Answer: ECS, possibly on Fargate to avoid managing servers. The near-miss, EKS, would add Kubernetes complexity the team does not need.

A common mistake is treating Fargate as a rival to ECS and EKS. It is a compute option underneath them. Another mistake is choosing EKS because it sounds more powerful. In a running system, an unneeded Kubernetes setup means more upgrades, configuration and skills to maintain. Pick EKS when Kubernetes compatibility or portability is the stated need, and ECS when AWS-native simplicity is.

questions.prompt:
A logistics company already runs about 40 containerized services on its own Kubernetes setup in its data center. It is moving them to AWS, wants its engineers to keep using the same Kubernetes tools and skills, and would rather not manage any servers. Here is the reasoning, with one step missing.

Step 1: The workloads are containers, so the orchestrator choice is between Amazon ECS and Amazon EKS.
Step 2: Is Kubernetes already in use? Yes, across all 40 services.
Step 3: ???
Step 4: The company does not want to manage servers, so it should run the containers on AWS Fargate rather than on EC2 instances it manages itself.

Which statement correctly fills Step 3?
choices: Choose EKS, because Kubernetes compatibility is the stated need and EKS runs the Kubernetes control plane for them.
Choose EC2 instances, because Kubernetes containers can only run on servers the customer manages.
Skip both orchestrators and choose Fargate, because it already removes the need to manage servers.
Choose ECS, because it is the simpler option and fits most closely with other AWS services.
questions.why: The team already relies on Kubernetes, so EKS, the managed Kubernetes service, keeps their tools and skills, while Fargate in Step 4 is only the compute underneath it, not a replacement for it.

questions.prompt: An engineer at a media company says, "We should pick between ECS, EKS and Fargate." Which statement best describes what AWS Fargate actually is?
choices: An open-source orchestrator that runs in many clouds and on-premises
A managed orchestrator designed by AWS that replaces ECS
A compute option that supplies the machines where ECS or EKS run containers, so you never manage servers
A read-only template from which containers are built
questions.why: Fargate is not an orchestrator and not a rival to ECS or EKS. It is a place for them to run containers without you handling any servers.

questions.prompt: An insurance firm wants to run the same container orchestration approach on AWS, on another cloud provider, and in its own data center, so its teams work the same way everywhere. Which AWS service fits this need best?
choices: Amazon ECS
EC2 instances without any orchestrator
Amazon EKS
AWS Fargate on its own
questions.why: EKS is managed Kubernetes, and Kubernetes is an open standard that runs in many clouds and on-premises, which gives the portability the firm asked for.

questions.prompt: A three-person nonprofit tech team has never used Kubernetes and runs only on AWS. They chose Amazon EKS because it "sounded more powerful" than Amazon ECS. What is the most likely consequence for their running system?
choices: Their containers will not run, because EKS cannot use Fargate
Nothing changes, because ECS and EKS need the same upgrades and skills
They take on extra Kubernetes upgrades, configuration and skills to maintain that ECS would have spared them
They will lose the ability to replace failed containers automatically
questions.why: An unneeded Kubernetes setup brings more upgrades, configuration and skills to maintain. ECS is the better fit when AWS-native simplicity is the need.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between Amazon ECS and Amazon EKS, when you would pick each, and one tradeoff or limit of each choice.
lessons.modelAnswer: Both are managed orchestrators. That means they start, place, restart and scale containers across a cluster of machines. ECS is AWS's own orchestrator. It is simpler to learn and tightly tied to other AWS services, so it is the default when a team just wants containers running on AWS. The tradeoff is that its way of working is AWS-specific, so moving to another cloud means relearning. EKS runs Kubernetes, the open-source standard, and AWS manages the control plane. Pick it when the team already uses Kubernetes or wants the same tooling across clouds and on-premises. Its cost is complexity: more concepts, configuration and upgrades to handle. Either one can run containers on EC2 instances you manage or on Fargate, which removes server management. Fargate is where containers run, not a third orchestrator.
rubricPoints: Defines a container and an orchestrator in plain terms.
States that ECS is AWS's own orchestrator, simpler and AWS-integrated.
States that EKS is managed Kubernetes, suited to existing Kubernetes use or portability.
Names a tradeoff: ECS is AWS-specific, while EKS brings more complexity.
Notes that both can run on EC2 or Fargate, and that Fargate is compute, not an orchestrator.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests choosing between ECS, EKS and Fargate from a described need, and no listed mission or engine runs containers, so reasoning through scenario situations builds that skill best.

lessons.plain: Serverless compute means you run your code without renting, patching, or sizing the machines underneath it. Servers still exist, but the cloud provider manages them, and you pay roughly for the work actually done rather than for idle machines. AWS offers two main kinds. AWS Lambda runs short pieces of code, called functions, whenever an event happens, such as a file arriving. AWS Fargate runs containers, which are packaged applications, without you managing the virtual machines they sit on. Think of Lambda as calling a taxi for each trip, and Fargate as leasing a car with someone else handling the maintenance.
lessons.guessPrompt: A photo-sharing app needs to make a small thumbnail each time someone uploads a picture, which takes about two seconds per photo, and uploads arrive unpredictably. Would you rather keep a server running all day waiting for uploads, or have code that starts only when a photo arrives? Why?
lessons.teach:
Serverless compute is a model where the provider runs and scales the underlying servers and you supply only your code or container. You do not choose instance sizes, apply operating system patches, or pay for idle capacity in the usual way.

AWS Lambda is a function-as-a-service offering: you upload a function, which is a small unit of code, and attach a trigger, which is an event that starts it, such as a file landing in Amazon S3 object storage or a web request. Lambda starts as many copies as the events require, scales back to zero when nothing happens, and bills per request plus the time and memory used. Each run is limited to 15 minutes.

AWS Fargate is a serverless compute engine for containers. A container is an application packaged with everything it needs to run. Fargate works underneath Amazon ECS or Amazon EKS, the AWS container orchestrators (services that schedule and manage containers). With Fargate you state the CPU and memory a container needs and AWS supplies the capacity, so you never manage the EC2 virtual machines beneath it. Containers can run for hours or indefinitely.

Worked example. Need one: make a thumbnail when a photo is uploaded. Step one, the work is triggered by an event. Step two, each job lasts seconds. Step three, traffic is irregular. Lambda fits; EC2 would mean paying for a server sitting idle. Need two: an existing containerized web API that serves traffic all day, and the team does not want to patch servers. Step one, it is already a container. Step two, it runs continuously. Fargate fits; Lambda is a near miss because the app is a long-running container, not short event-driven functions.

A common mistake is choosing Lambda for a batch job that takes an hour. In a running system the function is stopped at the 15-minute limit, the job never finishes, and retries repeat the same failure. Long jobs belong on Fargate, or on EC2 when you need full control of the machine.

questions.prompt: A small veterinary clinic wants to send a text-message reminder each time a receptionist books an appointment in its online system. About 40 bookings arrive on a busy day, at unpredictable times, and sending one reminder takes about 3 seconds. The clinic does not want to manage or pay for a server that sits idle. Worked reasoning: Step one, the work is started by an event (a new booking). Step two: [missing]. Step three, traffic is irregular, so a service that scales back to zero between bookings avoids paying for idle capacity. Conclusion: AWS Lambda fits. Which statement correctly fills in step two?
choices: The code is packaged as a container, so it has to run on AWS Fargate.
The clinic must first pick an EC2 instance size large enough for 40 bookings.
Each run lasts a few seconds, well under Lambda's 15-minute limit per run.
Each run is short, but Lambda bills a fixed amount per hour of uptime.
questions.why: Lambda limits each run to 15 minutes, so checking that a 3-second job fits easily inside that limit is the missing step before choosing it.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes what AWS Fargate does?
choices: It gives you EC2 virtual machines whose operating system you patch yourself.
It runs containers under Amazon ECS or EKS; you state CPU and memory and AWS supplies the servers.
It is object storage that triggers code when a file is uploaded.
It runs small functions in response to events, each limited to 15 minutes.
questions.why: Fargate is a serverless compute engine for containers: it works underneath the ECS or EKS orchestrators, you specify CPU and memory, and you never manage the EC2 machines beneath it.

questions.prompt: A shipping company has a nightly job, already packaged as a container, that builds route reports and takes about 90 minutes to finish. The team does not want to patch or manage any servers. Which choice fits best?
choices: AWS Fargate, because it runs containers for long periods without you managing servers
Amazon S3, because the reports will be stored there once they are built
AWS Lambda, because it scales to zero when the job is not running
Amazon EC2, because long jobs always require a virtual machine you manage
questions.why: The job is a container that runs well past Lambda's 15-minute limit, and the team wants no server management, which rules out EC2 and points to Fargate.

questions.prompt: A media startup moves a video-conversion task that takes about 40 minutes per file into an AWS Lambda function, with automatic retries switched on. What happens in the running system?
choices: Lambda notices the long job and extends the time limit so the file finishes.
Each run is stopped at 15 minutes, the file never finishes, and every retry fails the same way.
The job finishes, but the bill is higher because Lambda charges for idle time.
Lambda moves the job to a larger EC2 instance once it passes 15 minutes.
questions.why: Lambda stops any run at the 15-minute limit, so a 40-minute job never completes and retries simply repeat the failure; long jobs belong on Fargate or EC2.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between AWS Lambda and AWS Fargate, how you would decide between them for a new workload, and name one limit or tradeoff of going serverless.
lessons.modelAnswer: Both are serverless, meaning AWS manages the servers, patching and scaling while we just bring code. Lambda runs short functions in response to events, such as a file upload or an API call. It scales to zero when idle and bills per request and run time, so it is great for spiky, event-driven tasks. Fargate runs containers for ECS or EKS without us managing the EC2 instances underneath, so it suits long-running services or apps already packaged as containers. To decide, I ask whether the work is a short reaction to an event or a continuously running container. The tradeoff is less control: Lambda caps each run at 15 minutes, and with either one we cannot tune or log into the underlying machine the way we could with EC2. If we need that control or very long jobs, EC2 or Fargate is the better pick.
rubricPoints: Defines serverless as the provider managing servers, scaling, and patching.
Describes Lambda as event-triggered functions that scale to zero and bill per request and duration.
Describes Fargate as running containers for ECS or EKS without managing EC2 instances.
Gives a decision rule: short event-driven work to Lambda, long-running or containerized apps to Fargate.
Names a limit such as Lambda's 15-minute maximum or reduced control over the underlying machine.

suggested.rationale: This domain is tested by matching a described need to the right service and rejecting near misses like EC2, so reasoning through exam-style scenarios builds the skill best.

lessons.plain: Elasticity means your computing capacity grows when demand rises and shrinks when demand falls, so you pay only for what you need at each moment. Auto scaling is the machinery that makes this happen without a person watching. It keeps an eye on how busy your servers are and adds or removes them automatically. Think of a supermarket that opens extra checkout lanes when queues get long and closes them when the store goes quiet. The lanes are servers, the queue length is the signal, and the manager who opens and closes lanes by rule is auto scaling.
lessons.guessPrompt: A shop's website runs on two servers that are nearly idle at night but overloaded every lunchtime. Without buying more hardware, what would you want the cloud to do automatically at noon and again at night?
lessons.teach:
Auto scaling is the service that automatically adds or removes compute capacity in response to demand, and it is how AWS delivers elasticity. Elasticity is the ability to match capacity to load in both directions, up and down, over minutes. On AWS the main form is Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling, which manages virtual servers called EC2 instances.

It works through an Auto Scaling group: a named collection of identical instances built from a launch template, which is a saved recipe saying what kind of server to start. The group has three numbers. Minimum capacity is the fewest instances allowed, maximum capacity is the most allowed, and desired capacity is how many should run right now. A scaling policy is a rule that changes desired capacity. A common type, target tracking, says something like keep average CPU (processor busyness) near 50 percent. The group also runs health checks, replacing any instance that stops responding.

Worked example: a group has minimum 2, maximum 10, desired 2, with a target of 50 percent CPU. At noon traffic jumps and average CPU hits 90 percent. The policy raises desired capacity to 4, two new instances start from the template, and CPU drops toward 50 percent. At night CPU falls to 10 percent, so desired capacity returns to 2 and the extra instances are terminated, which stops their charges. It never goes below 2 or above 10.

A common mistake is treating a load balancer as the thing that scales. A load balancer only spreads incoming requests across the servers that already exist; auto scaling changes how many servers exist. They are often used together, but they do different jobs. Another mistake is setting the maximum too low: in a real surge the group stops growing at the cap, and users see slow or failed requests even though auto scaling is switched on.

questions.prompt: A bakery chain runs its online ordering site on an EC2 Auto Scaling group with minimum 3, maximum 8, and desired 3. A target tracking policy aims to keep average CPU near 40 percent. Trace the morning rush. Step 1: Orders spike before breakfast and average CPU climbs to 85 percent. Step 2: The policy calculates that about 11 instances would bring CPU back near 40 percent and tries to raise desired capacity. Step 3: ??? Step 4: Later, CPU falls back below 40 percent, desired capacity drops, and the extra instances are terminated, which stops their charges. Which choice correctly fills Step 3?
choices: Desired capacity becomes 11 and eleven instances run, because a scaling policy overrides the maximum during a surge.
Desired capacity stops at 8, so only 8 instances run, and customers may see slow or failed orders until demand drops.
The load balancer creates the extra servers it needs to bring CPU down to 40 percent.
Nothing changes, because the group only adds instances when an existing instance fails its health check.
questions.why: An Auto Scaling group never goes above its maximum capacity, so it stops growing at 8 even though the policy asked for more, and the leftover load can show up as slow or failed requests.

questions.prompt: A city transit app sees heavy use at rush hour and very little at 3 a.m. Its team wants capacity that grows during the rush and shrinks again overnight, within minutes, without anyone touching it. What is this ability called, and which mechanism delivers it on AWS?
choices: Elasticity, delivered by auto scaling adding and removing instances as demand changes.
Elasticity, delivered by a launch template that stores the server recipe.
Fault tolerance, delivered by health checks replacing broken instances.
High availability, delivered by a load balancer spreading requests across servers.
questions.why: Elasticity means matching capacity to load in both directions, and auto scaling is the mechanism that adds or removes compute capacity to do it.

questions.prompt: A small game studio already has a load balancer in front of its two EC2 instances. During a weekend launch, both servers run at nearly full CPU and players complain about lag. A teammate says, "We have a load balancer, so it will handle the extra load." What is the best response?
choices: Wrong, because a load balancer only works for databases, not game servers.
Wrong, because a load balancer only spreads requests across existing servers; they need auto scaling to add more servers.
Correct, because the load balancer will start new servers once CPU passes a threshold.
Correct, as long as the load balancer has health checks turned on.
questions.why: A load balancer distributes traffic among servers that already exist, while auto scaling is what changes how many servers exist, so adding capacity needs auto scaling.

questions.prompt: A museum's ticketing site uses an Auto Scaling group with minimum 4, maximum 12, and desired capacity currently 6. Overnight, visits drop almost to zero and average CPU sits around 5 percent, well below the policy's target. How many instances will the group run overnight?
choices: 0, because with almost no traffic the group terminates every instance to stop all charges.
4, because desired capacity falls but never below the minimum.
12, because the group keeps the maximum ready in case traffic returns.
6, because desired capacity only ever increases and must be lowered by hand.
questions.why: Scaling in lowers desired capacity as load falls, but the group never goes below its minimum capacity, so 4 instances keep running.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, in your own words, how auto scaling delivers elasticity, and name one limit or tradeoff they should keep in mind when configuring it.
lessons.modelAnswer: Elasticity means capacity follows demand both up and down, so we are not paying for idle servers at night or falling over at peak. Auto scaling is what does that automatically. We define an Auto Scaling group with a launch template, plus minimum, maximum and desired instance counts, and attach a scaling policy, for example keep average CPU around 50 percent. When load rises, the policy raises desired capacity and new instances launch; when load drops, extras are terminated and their cost stops. Health checks also replace broken instances. It is not the same as a load balancer, which only spreads traffic over existing servers. The tradeoff is in the limits: the maximum caps both cost and capacity, so set it too low and a big surge still overwhelms us, and new instances take a little time to start, so scaling is not instant.
rubricPoints: Defines elasticity as capacity matching demand in both directions.
Identifies auto scaling as the automatic mechanism that adds and removes instances.
Mentions an Auto Scaling group with minimum, maximum and desired capacity and a scaling policy driven by a metric.
Distinguishes auto scaling from a load balancer, which only distributes traffic.
Names a limit such as the maximum capping capacity during a surge or startup delay of new instances.
Notes the cost benefit of terminating unneeded instances when demand falls.

suggested.rationale: Tuning minimum, maximum and target values and watching instance counts respond to changing load is the most direct way to feel how auto scaling produces elasticity.

lessons.plain: A load balancer is a traffic director that sits in front of a group of servers and hands each incoming request to one of them. Picture a busy restaurant host at the door. Instead of letting every guest crowd one waiter, the host seats people across all the waiters who are free, and stops seating anyone at a table whose waiter has gone home sick. Users see one address and never need to know how many servers are behind it. The result is that no single server gets overwhelmed, and a broken server can quietly drop out without the website going down.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your website runs on three identical servers, and one of them suddenly crashes. If a load balancer sits in front of all three, what do you think happens to the visitors who would have been sent to the crashed server?
lessons.teach:
A load balancer is a service that receives incoming network requests at a single address and spreads them across several back-end machines, called targets. On AWS the managed version is Elastic Load Balancing (ELB). AWS runs and scales the balancer itself, so you do not patch it or size it.

It works because of health checks. A health check is a small test request the balancer sends to each target every few seconds. A target that answers correctly is marked healthy. A target that fails several checks in a row is marked unhealthy and gets no new traffic until it recovers. Targets can sit in different Availability Zones, which are separate data-centre groups within one AWS Region. So the balancer can also keep serving users when one whole zone has trouble.

ELB comes in types. An Application Load Balancer understands web traffic (HTTP and HTTPS) and can route by the content of the request, for example sending /images to one group of servers and /api to another. A Network Load Balancer works at the lower connection level (TCP and UDP) and suits very high volumes or very low delay.

Worked example: a shop runs on servers A, B and C. Requests arrive at the balancer's single address and are passed in turn to A, B, C, A, B, C. Server B's disk fills and it stops answering. Its health checks fail, the balancer marks B unhealthy, and from then on traffic alternates only between A and C. Customers notice nothing. When B is fixed, it passes its checks again and rejoins the group.

A common mistake is thinking a load balancer adds capacity. It only shares out the servers you already have. Adding or removing servers as demand changes is the job of auto scaling, which usually works alongside it. Another near-miss is Route 53, the AWS DNS service, which turns names into addresses. A load balancer is the one that hands individual requests to healthy targets. Without a load balancer, one failed server means failed requests for every user pointed at it.

questions.prompt: A ticket-booking site runs four servers behind an Elastic Load Balancing (ELB) load balancer, the AWS managed service that spreads incoming requests across back-end machines called targets. Servers P and Q are in one Availability Zone (a separate data-centre group within a Region), and servers R and S are in a second zone. Step 1: Buyers' requests arrive at the balancer's single address and are shared across P, Q, R and S. Step 2: A power problem hits the first zone, and P and Q stop answering. Step 3: ??? Step 4: New requests go only to R and S, and buyers keep booking tickets without errors. Which choice correctly fills Step 3?
choices: Route 53 changes the site's name so it points straight at server R, and server R then passes some of the requests on to S.
The balancer keeps sending requests to all four servers, and buyers whose requests fail just retry until they reach R or S.
P and Q fail several health checks in a row, so the balancer marks them unhealthy and stops giving them new requests.
The balancer starts two new servers in the second zone to replace P and Q, so that the group is back to four healthy targets.
questions.why: Health checks let the balancer find the failed targets and send new requests only to the healthy ones, and it does this without creating servers or changing DNS names.

questions.prompt: A video-learning company runs one website. It wants requests for /video to go to a group of servers tuned for streaming, and requests for /checkout to go to a separate group that handles payments. Both kinds of request are ordinary web traffic over HTTPS. Which AWS option fits best?
choices: Route 53, because the DNS service turns the site name into an address for each group
An Application Load Balancer, because it understands web requests and can route by their content
A Network Load Balancer, because it handles connection-level traffic at very high volume
Auto scaling, because it adds servers to whichever group is getting the most requests
questions.why: An Application Load Balancer understands HTTP and HTTPS and can send requests to different target groups based on the path, such as /video or /checkout.

questions.prompt: A small charity has two web servers and expects five times its normal visitors during a fundraising week. A staff member says: "We'll put a load balancer in front of the two servers, so we can handle the extra visitors." What is wrong with this plan?
choices: A load balancer only shares out the two existing servers, so adding servers needs auto scaling
A load balancer only works with servers spread across at least three Availability Zones
A load balancer must be patched and sized by the charity, so it would be too much work
Nothing is wrong, because a load balancer adds capacity whenever the number of visitors grows
questions.why: A load balancer spreads requests across the servers you already have, so handling more visitors means adding servers, which is the job of auto scaling.

questions.prompt: An online magazine uses Route 53, the AWS DNS service, and also has a load balancer in front of six web servers. One of the six servers crashes. Which service makes sure that new requests from readers go only to the five servers still working?
choices: The load balancer, because its health checks find the failed target and it stops sending that target new requests
Auto scaling, because its main job is to share out each reader's request across the remaining servers
None of them, because readers whose requests went to the crashed server will keep getting errors
Route 53, because turning the magazine's name into an address also checks each server's health
questions.why: Route 53 turns names into addresses, but the load balancer is the service that hands each request to a target that is passing its health checks.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, in your own words, what a load balancer does for an application and how it decides where traffic goes. Then name one thing it does not do on its own.
lessons.modelAnswer: A load balancer gives users one address and spreads their requests across a group of servers, which it calls targets, so no single server is swamped. On AWS this is Elastic Load Balancing, a managed service, so we don't run the balancer ourselves. It keeps checking each target with health checks. If a server stops answering correctly, the balancer stops sending it traffic until it passes again, so a failure doesn't reach users. Spreading the targets across several Availability Zones means even a zone problem can be absorbed. An Application Load Balancer can route web requests by path, and a Network Load Balancer handles raw connections at very high volume. The limit is that it doesn't create capacity. If all the servers are full, it just shares out the overload. You pair it with auto scaling to add servers. It also isn't DNS, which is Route 53's job.
rubricPoints: States that a load balancer spreads incoming requests across multiple targets behind one address.
Explains that health checks remove unhealthy targets from rotation automatically.
Connects this to availability, including targets spread across Availability Zones.
Names Elastic Load Balancing and distinguishes the Application Load Balancer from the Network Load Balancer.
Notes the limit that it does not add capacity, which is auto scaling's job, or that it is not DNS.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests this by describing a need and asking you to pick a load balancer over near-misses like auto scaling or Route 53, so reasoning through scenario questions builds the skill best.

lessons.plain: When your application needs a database on AWS, you have two broad choices. You can rent a virtual server (Amazon EC2) and install and run the database software yourself, or you can use a managed database service, where AWS runs the database software for you and you simply connect to it. It is like choosing between owning a car, where you handle the oil changes, tyres and repairs, and leasing one with a full service plan. The service plan costs less of your time but gives you less freedom to modify the engine.
lessons.guessPrompt: A three-person team needs a standard PostgreSQL database with nightly backups and automatic recovery if the server fails, and nobody on the team wants to patch servers. Would you guess they should install PostgreSQL on a virtual server they manage, or use a database service that AWS operates? Why?
lessons.teach:
A self-managed database on EC2 means you launch an Amazon EC2 instance, which is a virtual server you rent by the hour or second, then install, configure and run the database engine on it yourself. A managed database means AWS operates the engine for you. Amazon RDS (Relational Database Service) is the main example: you choose an engine such as MySQL or PostgreSQL, and AWS handles the server underneath.

The difference is about the shared responsibility model, the split of duties between AWS and you. On EC2, AWS secures the physical hardware, but you own the operating system patches, database installation and upgrades, backups, replication (keeping a copy in sync on another server), failover (switching to that copy when the main one dies), and scaling. With a managed service, AWS takes over most of that list, often through settings: turn on automated backups, choose a standby in another Availability Zone (a separate data centre group), pick a bigger size. You still own your data, your schema, your queries and who is allowed to connect.

Worked example. The team above needs standard PostgreSQL, nightly backups and automatic recovery. Step one: is the engine offered as a managed service? Yes. Step two: do they need anything the managed service blocks, such as logging into the operating system? No. Step three: who will do patching and failover? Nobody wants to. So the managed service fits. Now change one fact: a legacy application needs a database version AWS does not offer, plus a custom agent installed on the operating system. Managed services do not give you operating system access, so EC2 is the right answer, accepting the extra work.

A common mistake is believing managed means AWS handles everything. If you grant open network access or write a bad query, that is still yours. In a running system, choosing EC2 without staffing the operations work leads to missed patches, untested backups, and long outages when a single server fails.

questions.prompt: An online bookshop with two developers and no database administrator needs a standard MySQL database. It also needs a standby copy in a second Availability Zone (a separate data centre group) so it keeps running if one copy fails. The team is deciding between running MySQL themselves on an Amazon EC2 instance (a rented virtual server) and using Amazon RDS, AWS's managed relational database service. Step one: is MySQL offered as a managed engine? Yes. Step two: ??? Step three: who will apply patches and handle failover (switching to the standby when the main copy dies)? Neither developer has time, so the managed service fits. Which choice correctly fills in step two?
choices: Check whether AWS will also write and tune the shop's queries, which it does because the service is managed.
Check whether they can install their own monitoring agent on the database server's operating system, which a managed service allows.
Check whether an EC2 instance costs less per hour, and if it does, choose EC2 whatever the staffing.
Check whether they need anything a managed service blocks, such as logging into the operating system. They don't, because plain MySQL with a standby is enough.
questions.why: Before choosing the managed service, you confirm that nothing you need, such as operating system access, is blocked by it, and this shop needs nothing of that kind.

questions.prompt: A travel agency moves its PostgreSQL database from a self-managed EC2 instance to Amazon RDS, a managed database service. Under the shared responsibility model (the split of duties between AWS and the customer), which task is still the agency's job after the move?
choices: Deciding which networks and users are allowed to connect
Applying operating system patches to the database server
Building replication to a standby server by hand
Installing database engine upgrades on the server itself
questions.why: A managed service takes over server work such as patching, replication and upgrades, but the customer still owns access control, along with its data, schema and queries.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm runs an old warehouse application. It needs a database engine version that AWS does not offer as a managed service, and the vendor requires a special agent to be installed on the database server's operating system. Which option fits, and why?
choices: Amazon RDS, because AWS will add the missing engine version when you ask
A self-managed database on Amazon EC2, because it gives operating system access and any engine version, at the cost of the firm doing the operations work
Amazon RDS, because managed services let you install any agent you need
A self-managed database on EC2, because AWS then patches and backs up the database for you
questions.why: Managed services do not give you operating system access and only offer the engine versions AWS supports, so EC2 is the answer, and the firm takes on patching, backups and failover itself.

questions.prompt: A startup runs its PostgreSQL database on a single EC2 instance. Nobody is assigned to operations work, and no one has set up replication or tested backups. Eight months later, that server fails. What is the most likely result?
choices: AWS automatically switches the database to a standby in another Availability Zone
No real impact, because AWS secures the physical hardware and therefore protects the database
AWS restores the database from its own nightly backup within minutes
A long outage, and possibly lost data, because no standby or tested backup was set up
questions.why: On EC2, backups, replication and failover are the customer's job, so if nobody does that work, a single server failure means a long outage.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, in your own words, how you decide between running a database yourself on EC2 and using a managed AWS database, and name the tradeoff you accept with each choice.
lessons.modelAnswer: The question is who does the operations work. If I put a database on an EC2 virtual server, I install it and own operating system patching, upgrades, backups, replication, failover and scaling. If I use a managed service like Amazon RDS, AWS runs the engine and gives me those things as settings, such as automated backups or a standby copy in another Availability Zone. I still own my data, schema, queries and access controls either way. I default to managed when the engine and version are offered and I do not need special control, because it saves time and reduces mistakes. I pick EC2 when I need operating system access, an unsupported engine or version, or unusual configuration. The tradeoff: managed costs me flexibility and control; EC2 gives me full control but costs me ongoing effort and the risk of doing it badly.
rubricPoints: Defines self-managed on EC2 as running the database software yourself on a rented virtual server.
States that a managed service like Amazon RDS has AWS handle patching, backups and failover.
Notes the customer still owns data, schema, queries and access control with a managed service.
Gives a valid reason to choose EC2, such as needing operating system access or an unsupported engine or version.
Names the tradeoff: managed trades control for less operational work, EC2 the reverse.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests this by describing a team's needs and constraints, so reasoning through short scenarios about who does the operations work builds the decision skill best.

lessons.plain: A relational database stores information in tables of rows and columns, like a set of linked spreadsheets, and you ask it questions using SQL, a standard query language. Running one yourself means installing it, patching it, backing it up and fixing it when a disk fails. Amazon RDS (Relational Database Service) is a managed relational database: AWS does those chores while you design tables and write queries. Amazon Aurora is AWS's own relational engine inside that family, built for the cloud to be faster and more resilient. Think of RDS as hiring a building manager for a familiar house, and Aurora as a house the manager designed and built.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company runs an existing Microsoft SQL Server database and wants AWS to handle patching and backups without rewriting the application. Would you guess Amazon Aurora or Amazon RDS fits, and why?
lessons.teach:
Amazon RDS is a managed service for relational databases. Relational means data lives in related tables with a fixed structure, called a schema, and is queried with SQL. Managed means AWS handles provisioning the server, operating system and database patching, automated backups and hardware replacement. RDS supports several engines, meaning the database software itself: MySQL, PostgreSQL, MariaDB, Oracle, Microsoft SQL Server and IBM Db2, plus Aurora.

Amazon Aurora is an AWS-built engine that is compatible with MySQL or PostgreSQL, so applications written for those usually work unchanged. Its storage layer keeps six copies of your data across three Availability Zones (separate data centers in one Region), grows automatically, and AWS advertises it as several times faster than standard MySQL or PostgreSQL. An option called Aurora Serverless adjusts capacity automatically for unpredictable load.

Two RDS features matter. Multi-AZ keeps a standby copy in another Availability Zone and fails over to it automatically if the primary fails; this is for availability. Read replicas are extra copies that serve read-only queries to spread load; this is for performance.

Worked example: a need says, the app uses PostgreSQL, traffic is heavy, and the team wants the most resilient, highest-performance relational option. Step one: data is tabular and uses SQL, so relational, not a NoSQL service like DynamoDB. Step two: the engine is PostgreSQL, which Aurora supports. Step three: the stress on performance and resilience points to Aurora over standard RDS PostgreSQL. Answer: Aurora. If the engine were Oracle, Aurora would be wrong, because Aurora only speaks MySQL and PostgreSQL; RDS for Oracle fits.

Common mistake: confusing Multi-AZ with read replicas. A standard Multi-AZ standby does not serve your reads, and read replicas are mainly for scaling reads, not automatic failover. In a running system, choosing only read replicas for a critical database can leave you with an outage when the primary fails.

questions.prompt:
A regional dental clinic chain keeps patient appointments in related tables and queries them with SQL. Its booking software runs on Microsoft SQL Server. The clinic wants AWS to handle patching and backups, and the database must keep running on its own, without anyone stepping in, if the server it runs on fails.

Step 1: The data is tabular and uses SQL, so the need is relational. That rules out a NoSQL service such as DynamoDB.

Step 2: The engine (the database software) is Microsoft SQL Server. Aurora only works with MySQL or PostgreSQL, so Aurora is out, and Amazon RDS for SQL Server fits.

Step 3: ???

Answer: Amazon RDS for SQL Server with Multi-AZ turned on.

Which choice correctly completes Step 3?
choices: Switch to Aurora Serverless, because it adjusts capacity automatically and so keeps the database online.
Turn on Multi-AZ mainly so the standby copy can also answer the clinic's read queries and share the load.
Add read replicas, because a read replica automatically takes over as the primary when the main server fails.
Keeping the database running through a server failure is an availability need, so turn on Multi-AZ. It keeps a standby copy in another Availability Zone and fails over to it automatically.
questions.why: Automatic failover to a standby copy in a separate Availability Zone is what Multi-AZ provides for availability, while read replicas are for scaling reads and Aurora does not support SQL Server.

questions.prompt: A colleague says Amazon RDS is a "managed" relational database service. In that description, what does "managed" mean?
choices: You no longer write SQL queries, because AWS generates the queries for your application automatically.
AWS takes care of provisioning the server, patching the operating system and database software, running automated backups, and replacing failed hardware.
The database has no fixed schema, so tables can change shape freely without you planning a structure first.
AWS runs the physical hardware, but you are still responsible for patching the operating system and setting up your own backups.
questions.why: In RDS, managed means AWS handles provisioning, OS and database patching, automated backups and hardware replacement, while the data stays relational with a schema and is still queried with SQL.

questions.prompt: An online ticket-resale startup runs its app on MySQL. Traffic is quiet most days, then jumps sharply and without warning when popular concerts go on sale. The team wants its existing MySQL code to keep working unchanged, and wants capacity to adjust automatically. Which option fits best?
choices: Amazon DynamoDB, because a NoSQL service is the only kind of database that scales automatically.
Amazon RDS for MySQL with Multi-AZ, because the standby copy adds capacity whenever traffic spikes.
Amazon Aurora Serverless, because Aurora is MySQL-compatible and the Serverless option adjusts capacity automatically for unpredictable load.
Amazon RDS for Oracle, because a commercial engine handles sudden traffic spikes better.
questions.why: Aurora is compatible with MySQL, so the code works unchanged, and Aurora Serverless is the option built to adjust capacity automatically when load is unpredictable.

questions.prompt: A logistics company runs its critical shipment-tracking database on Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL. To protect it, the team added three read replicas and did not turn on Multi-AZ. One night the primary database server fails. What is the most likely problem, and why?
choices: The company risks an outage, because read replicas are mainly for spreading read-only queries and are not set up for automatic failover the way a Multi-AZ standby is.
There is no problem, because read replicas and Multi-AZ are two names for the same failover feature.
There is no problem, because RDS turns on Multi-AZ automatically for any database that has more than two read replicas.
The read replicas take over writes automatically, but backups stop, because backups only run on Multi-AZ databases.
questions.why: Read replicas exist to scale reads, while automatic failover to a standby in another Availability Zone comes from Multi-AZ, so relying only on read replicas can leave a critical database down when the primary fails.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate when you would pick Amazon RDS, when you would pick Amazon Aurora, and name one limit or tradeoff that decides between them.
lessons.modelAnswer: Both are managed relational databases: AWS handles patching, backups and hardware, and we write SQL against tables. RDS is the umbrella service and runs familiar engines like MySQL, PostgreSQL, MariaDB, Oracle, SQL Server and Db2, so it's the choice when we must keep a specific commercial engine such as Oracle or SQL Server. Aurora is AWS's own engine, compatible with MySQL or PostgreSQL, with storage copied six times across three Availability Zones that grows on its own, and better performance. The deciding limit is engine support: Aurora cannot run Oracle or SQL Server. Either way, Multi-AZ gives automatic failover for availability, while read replicas spread read traffic for performance, and we shouldn't confuse the two. If the data isn't relational at all, neither fits and we'd look at a NoSQL service.
rubricPoints: States that both RDS and Aurora are managed relational databases queried with SQL.
Lists that RDS supports multiple engines including Oracle and SQL Server.
Explains Aurora is AWS-built, MySQL/PostgreSQL compatible, with higher performance and replicated storage.
Names the engine-compatibility limit as a deciding factor.
Distinguishes Multi-AZ for failover from read replicas for read scaling.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests choosing between RDS, Aurora and near-miss services from a described need, so reasoning through scenario questions builds the skill best.

lessons.plain: Amazon DynamoDB is a database that AWS runs entirely for you. It is built for one job above all: storing lots of small records and fetching any one of them very quickly by its key. It is called NoSQL because it does not use the classic model of rigid tables joined together with the SQL query language. Think of a huge coat check. You hand over a coat and get a ticket number. Later you show the number and get your coat back at once, whether the room holds ten coats or ten million. Records can differ in shape, and you never pick or patch servers.
lessons.guessPrompt: A mobile game stores each player's profile and looks it up by player ID millions of times a day, and different players have different fields. Which fits better: a database built around fixed tables joined together, or one built around fast lookups by a single key? Why?
lessons.teach:
Amazon DynamoDB is AWS's fully managed, serverless NoSQL database. NoSQL means a database that does not use the relational model, where fixed tables are joined together and queried with SQL. DynamoDB instead stores key-value pairs and documents. Fully managed and serverless mean AWS runs the servers, patching and replication, and you never choose an instance size.

Data lives in tables. A table holds items, which are like rows, and each item holds attributes, which are named fields. Every item needs a primary key. The primary key always includes a partition key, the value DynamoDB uses to decide where the item is stored. It can also include a sort key, which orders items that share a partition key. Apart from the key, items in the same table can carry different attributes, so there is no fixed schema.

Why it works: every read and write goes straight to an item by its key. That lets DynamoDB spread data across many storage partitions and keep responses in single-digit milliseconds, whether the table holds a thousand items or billions. It automatically copies data across three Availability Zones. You can choose on-demand capacity, where you pay per request with no planning, or provisioned capacity with auto scaling. Global tables replicate a table to several Regions. DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) adds an in-memory cache for microsecond reads.

Worked example, a shopping-cart service. Step 1: the Carts table uses userId as its partition key. Step 2: user u-42 adds a book, and the app writes an item keyed u-42 holding a list of products. Step 3: at checkout the app reads that item directly by u-42, one fast lookup with no joins. Step 4: a holiday sale brings ten times the traffic, and in on-demand mode DynamoDB absorbs it without anyone resizing servers.

Common mistake: choosing DynamoDB for work that needs joins across many tables, complex ad-hoc SQL reports or a strict relational structure. That is the job of Amazon RDS or Aurora. In a running system, forcing relational queries onto DynamoDB leads to slow full-table scans and higher cost. Also, Amazon ElastiCache is a cache placed in front of a database, not the main durable store, so it is not a substitute for DynamoDB.

questions.prompt: A fitness-tracker company stores heart-rate readings in DynamoDB, and each device sends many readings per day. The steps below are worked through, with Step 2 missing. Step 1: create a table named Readings with deviceId as the partition key. Step 2: [missing]. Step 3: the app asks for device d-7's readings, and DynamoDB returns them in time order because they share the same partition key. Step 4: a newer device model also sends a batteryLevel attribute, and DynamoDB stores it next to older items that lack it, with no table change. What is Step 2?
choices: Add timestamp as the sort key, so readings that share a deviceId are kept ordered by time
Define a fixed schema so that every reading item must carry exactly the same attributes
Make timestamp the only partition key instead of deviceId, so each reading lands in its own place
Store the readings in Amazon ElastiCache as the main store and copy them to DynamoDB later
questions.why: A sort key orders items that share a partition key, so deviceId plus timestamp keeps each device's readings together and in time order.

questions.prompt: In a DynamoDB table, what is the job of the partition key?
choices: It is the value DynamoDB uses to decide where the item is stored
It picks the instance size of the server that holds the table
It fixes the list of attributes that every item in the table must have
It sets which other tables the item can be joined to in a SQL query
questions.why: The partition key is the part of the primary key that DynamoDB uses to decide where each item is stored, so it can spread data across many partitions.

questions.prompt: A ticket-booking startup expects traffic that swings wildly. On a quiet day it gets a few hundred requests, but during a concert on-sale it may get fifty times that. The team does not want to forecast capacity or resize anything. Which DynamoDB choice fits best?
choices: Provisioned capacity set to the quiet-day level, adjusted by hand
DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX), so the cache absorbs every write
On-demand capacity, paying per request with no capacity planning
Global tables, so that a second Region takes the extra load
questions.why: On-demand capacity charges per request and absorbs traffic spikes without anyone planning or resizing capacity.

questions.prompt: A finance team needs to join customer, invoice and payment tables and run complex ad-hoc SQL reports on a strict relational structure. A colleague suggests DynamoDB. What is the best response?
choices: Use DynamoDB, because its single-digit millisecond lookups make any query fast, including joins
Use DynamoDB with global tables, because copying to several Regions adds join support
Use Amazon RDS or Aurora instead, because DynamoDB is not built for joins and ad-hoc SQL, which would lead to slow, costly full-table scans
Use Amazon ElastiCache as the main database, because an in-memory store suits reporting
questions.why: Joins across tables and ad-hoc SQL on a relational structure are the job of a relational database such as RDS or Aurora. DynamoDB is fast only for direct reads and writes by key.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, in your own words, when you would pick Amazon DynamoDB for a new feature, and name one kind of need where it is the wrong choice and what you would use instead.
lessons.modelAnswer: DynamoDB is AWS's fully managed, serverless NoSQL database. We don't run or patch any servers. We create a table, give every item a primary key built around a partition key, and read or write items by that key. Because every access goes straight to a key, it stays in single-digit milliseconds even at huge scale. It also replicates across three Availability Zones automatically. With on-demand capacity it absorbs traffic spikes without capacity planning. Items can have different fields, so the schema is flexible. That makes it a strong fit for things like shopping carts, user sessions, game profiles or device data looked up by an ID. The tradeoff is that it isn't built for joins or ad-hoc SQL reporting across related tables. For that, a relational service like Amazon RDS or Aurora fits better. If we only need a fast temporary cache, that's ElastiCache.
rubricPoints: Defines DynamoDB as a fully managed, serverless NoSQL key-value and document database.
Explains that items are accessed by a primary key and partition key, giving consistently fast lookups at any scale.
Mentions flexible schema and automatic scaling or on-demand capacity with no servers to manage.
Gives a fitting use case such as carts, sessions or profiles looked up by ID.
Names the limit: poor fit for joins and complex SQL queries, where RDS or Aurora is the better choice.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests picking DynamoDB over near-miss options like RDS, Aurora or ElastiCache from a described need, so reasoning through scenario situations builds that skill best.

lessons.plain: Amazon ElastiCache is a managed in-memory cache: a fast, temporary holding area that keeps copies of frequently read data in a server's memory (RAM) instead of on disk. Your application checks the cache first and only goes to the slower main database when the answer is not there. Think of a librarian who keeps the ten most-requested books on the front desk instead of walking to the back shelves every time. AWS runs the cache servers for you, handling setup, patching and replacing failed nodes, so you get speed without operating the machinery yourself.
lessons.guessPrompt: An online shop's product page asks the database for the same product details thousands of times a minute, and the database is getting slow. Without changing the database itself, what could you put in front of it so most of those repeated questions get answered faster?
lessons.teach:
Amazon ElastiCache is a managed service that runs in-memory data stores for you. In-memory means the data lives in RAM, the computer's working memory, which answers in well under a millisecond, far faster than reading from disk. Managed means AWS provisions the servers (called nodes), patches them, and can replace a failed node. ElastiCache offers open-source engines you may see named: Redis OSS, Valkey (a community fork of Redis) and Memcached, which is a simpler key-value cache.

Why it works: many applications read the same data far more often than they change it. Keeping a copy close and in memory removes repeated work from the main database, called the source of truth, which is the durable store that holds the real record.

Worked example. A product page reads from an Amazon RDS relational database, taking about 40 ms per query. Step 1: a visitor requests product 42; the app asks ElastiCache and gets a cache miss (not found). Step 2: the app queries RDS, gets the answer, and writes it into the cache with a TTL (time to live) of 60 seconds, after which the copy expires. Step 3: the next thousand visitors within that minute get a cache hit, answered from memory in under a millisecond, and RDS does none of that work. Step 4: after 60 seconds the entry expires and the cycle repeats, picking up any price change.

Common mistake: treating the cache as the main database. Memory is temporary, and caches evict or expire data, so anything you cannot afford to lose belongs in a durable store such as RDS or Amazon DynamoDB. The near-miss on the exam is DynamoDB: it is a fast, durable NoSQL database, not a cache in front of another database.

Consequence in a running system: a cache lowers database load and latency, but readers may see slightly stale data until the TTL runs out. Also, if many entries expire at once, a flood of misses can hit the database together.

questions.prompt: A city transit app shows bus timetables stored in an Amazon RDS relational database, and each timetable query takes about 25 ms. The team adds Amazon ElastiCache, a managed in-memory store, in front of it. Step 1: a rider opens route 7, the app checks the cache, and gets a cache miss (the entry is not there). Step 2: ??? Step 3: for the next five minutes, riders opening route 7 get a cache hit, answered from memory in under a millisecond, and RDS does no work for them. Step 4: after five minutes the copy expires, so the next request misses again and fresh timetable data is loaded. Which choice correctly fills in Step 2?
choices: The app queries RDS, returns the timetable, and stores a copy in the cache with a TTL (time to live) of 300 seconds.
The app queries RDS on every later request and never writes to the cache, so riders always see fresh data.
The app writes a new timetable into ElastiCache only, since the cache is now the main record for route 7.
The app returns an error to the rider, because a cache miss means the timetable data no longer exists anywhere.
questions.why: On a miss the app reads the source of truth (RDS) and writes the result into the cache with a 300-second TTL, which is what makes the later hits and the expiry in Steps 3 and 4 possible.

questions.prompt: A team asks why Amazon ElastiCache can answer requests much faster than their disk-based database. Which explanation is correct?
choices: ElastiCache compresses every record so the database has less data to scan.
ElastiCache stores data permanently on faster disks than the database uses.
ElastiCache keeps data in RAM, the computer's working memory, which responds in well under a millisecond, far faster than reading from disk.
ElastiCache replaces the database entirely, so there is no source of truth to consult.
questions.why: In-memory means the data lives in RAM, which answers far faster than disk, so repeated reads skip the slower database.

questions.prompt: An online ticket seller must record every completed purchase and must never lose one, and it needs fast reads and writes at large scale. A colleague proposes storing purchases only in Amazon ElastiCache. What is the better choice?
choices: Keep ElastiCache only, because Memcached is a simpler engine that does not evict data.
Keep ElastiCache only, but set a very long TTL so purchases never expire.
Store purchases in a durable database such as Amazon DynamoDB, a fast NoSQL database, and use a cache only to speed up reads if needed.
Keep ElastiCache only, because a managed service replaces failed nodes, so no data can be lost.
questions.why: Caches live in temporary memory and can evict or expire data, so records you cannot afford to lose belong in a durable store like DynamoDB.

questions.prompt: A sports score website caches match results in Amazon ElastiCache with a TTL of 120 seconds in front of its main database. A score changes in the database at 10:00:00, but some visitors still see the old score until about 10:02. What explains this?
choices: The main database is slower than the cache, so its write takes two minutes to finish.
ElastiCache always waits for the database to push every change before expiring an entry.
Readers can see slightly stale data until the cached copy's TTL runs out, after which the next miss loads the new score from the database.
The cache has failed and AWS is replacing the node, so it is serving a backup from disk.
questions.why: A cached copy keeps being served until its TTL expires, so a cache trades a little freshness for lower latency and database load.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what Amazon ElastiCache does and when you would add it to an application, and name one limit or tradeoff they must accept if they do.
lessons.modelAnswer: ElastiCache is AWS's managed in-memory cache, running engines like Redis OSS, Valkey or Memcached for us. We put it in front of a slower database such as RDS. The app checks the cache first; on a hit it answers from RAM in under a millisecond, and on a miss it reads the database and stores a copy with a TTL so later reads are fast. It suits read-heavy data that is asked for repeatedly, like product details or session data. The tradeoff is freshness and durability: cached copies can be stale until the TTL expires, and memory is not a safe permanent home, so the real record must stay in a durable database. If we need a fast durable database itself, that points to DynamoDB, not a cache. We also need to watch for many keys expiring at once and hammering the database.
rubricPoints: States that ElastiCache is a managed in-memory cache using engines such as Redis OSS, Valkey or Memcached.
Explains the hit and miss flow in front of a slower source-of-truth database.
Names a fitting use case such as read-heavy, repeatedly requested data.
Identifies a tradeoff such as stale data until TTL expiry or lack of durability.
Distinguishes it from a durable database such as DynamoDB or RDS.

suggested.rationale: Working the cache stampede incident shows a cache in front of a database in a live system, including what happens when many entries miss at once.

lessons.plain: Moving a database to the cloud is like moving a busy shop to a new building without closing for weeks. AWS gives two helpers. AWS Database Migration Service (DMS) is the moving crew. It copies your data from the old database to the new one and keeps copying new changes while the old one stays open for business. The AWS Schema Conversion Tool (SCT) is the translator. When the new database is a different kind of engine, it rewrites the blueprint (tables, indexes and built-in code) into the new engine's dialect. Same engine on both sides means you need only the moving crew.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company wants to move a live Oracle database to Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL, a different database engine. Do you think a tool that only copies rows of data would be enough? What else might need changing?
lessons.teach:
AWS Database Migration Service (DMS) is a managed service, meaning AWS runs the servers that do the work. It moves data from a source database to a target database. The source keeps running during the migration, so applications see little downtime. DMS works in two phases. First comes a full load, a one-time copy of all existing data. Then comes ongoing replication, called change data capture (CDC), where every new insert, update or delete on the source is replayed on the target until you switch over.

A homogeneous migration keeps the same database engine on both ends, for example MySQL to Amazon RDS for MySQL. A heterogeneous migration changes engines, for example Oracle to PostgreSQL. Engines differ in data types and in their built-in code languages, so a heterogeneous move first needs the schema translated. The schema is the structure of the database: its tables, columns, indexes, views and stored procedures, which are small programs saved inside the database. The AWS Schema Conversion Tool (SCT) does this translation. It converts what it can automatically and produces a report of the items a person must rewrite by hand.

Here is a worked example: Oracle on-premises to Aurora PostgreSQL. Step 1: SCT reads the Oracle schema, converts it to PostgreSQL, and flags three stored procedures for manual fixes. Step 2: Engineers fix those procedures and create the schema in Aurora. Step 3: DMS runs the full load of all rows. Step 4: CDC keeps Aurora in step while the shop stays open. Step 5: At cutover, the application is briefly paused, the last changes drain across, and the application is pointed at Aurora.

A common mistake is assuming DMS translates everything. DMS moves data. It does not rewrite stored procedures or engine-specific code. If you skip SCT on a heterogeneous move, the data arrives but application features fail at cutover. The reverse mistake is reaching for SCT on a same-engine move, where it adds nothing.

questions.prompt: A concert-ticketing company runs a 40 GB PostgreSQL database in its own data centre. It is moving that database to Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL, and the ticket website must keep selling during the move. The plan is mostly worked out. Step 1: Both ends run PostgreSQL, so this is a homogeneous migration. No schema translation is needed, so the AWS Schema Conversion Tool is not used. Step 2: AWS DMS, the managed migration service, makes a one-time copy of all 40 GB of existing ticket records into RDS. Step 3: ??? Step 4: At cutover the website pauses briefly, the last changes drain across, and the site is pointed at RDS. Which choice correctly fills Step 3?
choices: Run the Schema Conversion Tool on the copied tables so the stored procedures work on RDS
Close the website for the length of Step 2 so that no new sales happen during the copy
DMS change data capture replays each new ticket sale, update or refund on RDS as it happens
Repeat the full 40 GB copy every night until cutover, so RDS is never more than a day behind
questions.why: After the full load, change data capture keeps the target in step by replaying every insert, update and delete from the still-running source until cutover.

questions.prompt: A team is using AWS Database Migration Service (DMS). The one-time copy of all existing rows has just finished. What does DMS do next, until the team switches over to the new database?
choices: Nothing: the source must be shut down, because DMS only works while the source is stopped
Change data capture: it replays each new insert, update or delete from the source onto the target
