Schema conversion: it rewrites the source's stored procedures into the target engine's language
A second full load: it copies every row again to catch anything missed the first time
questions.why: DMS works in two phases, a full load followed by ongoing replication called change data capture, while the source keeps running.

questions.prompt: A bakery chain is moving its MySQL database from an office server to Amazon RDS for MySQL. It has a few stored procedures, which are small programs saved inside the database. Which tooling fits this move?
choices: Neither tool, because AWS migration services only support moves between different engines
The Schema Conversion Tool first to translate the stored procedures, then AWS DMS for the data
The AWS Schema Conversion Tool alone, because it copies both the structure and all of the rows
AWS DMS alone, because the engine is the same on both ends and needs no schema translation
questions.why: This is a homogeneous MySQL-to-MySQL move, so DMS can move the data and SCT would add nothing.

questions.prompt: An insurer moved its Microsoft SQL Server database to Amazon Aurora MySQL using only AWS DMS. All the rows arrived correctly, but at cutover several application features that rely on stored procedures failed. What is the most likely cause?
choices: DMS moves data but does not rewrite engine-specific code; the AWS Schema Conversion Tool was skipped
The full load was too large for DMS, so the stored procedures were dropped to save space
Aurora MySQL cannot hold stored procedures, so this kind of migration can never fully work
Change data capture was left running after cutover and overwrote the stored procedures
questions.why: Changing engines is a heterogeneous migration, which needs SCT to translate the schema and flag code for manual fixes, because DMS only moves the data.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between AWS DMS and the AWS Schema Conversion Tool, when you would need both, and one thing DMS will not do for you.
lessons.modelAnswer: DMS is a managed service that moves the data. It does a full load of existing rows, then uses change data capture to replay new changes while the source database stays live, so the cutover only needs a short pause. SCT handles the structure. When we change engines, say Oracle to PostgreSQL, SCT translates tables, data types, views and stored procedures into the new dialect, and it reports anything it can't convert so we can rewrite it by hand. For a same-engine move like MySQL to RDS MySQL, DMS alone is enough. For an engine change we use SCT first, then DMS. The limit to remember is that DMS doesn't convert schema or database code. If we skip conversion, the rows land fine but procedures break at cutover. SCT also isn't fully automatic, so we should budget time for the manual fixes.
rubricPoints: DMS is a managed service that moves data between databases.
DMS keeps the source running, using a full load followed by ongoing change replication.
SCT converts schema and database code when the engine changes.
Same-engine moves need only DMS; engine changes need SCT and then DMS.
DMS does not translate schema or stored procedures, and SCT may leave items for manual rewrite.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests this by describing a migration and asking which tool or tools fit, so reasoning through homogeneous versus heterogeneous scenarios builds the skill best.

lessons.plain: A VPC (Virtual Private Cloud) is your own private, walled-off network inside AWS, like a fenced office park you rent inside a huge city. Subnets are the individual buildings, each holding some of your servers. Route tables are the signposts at each building telling traffic which road to take. An internet gateway is the main gate to the public street, letting traffic come in from and go out to the internet. A NAT gateway is a one-way exit door: servers in private buildings can step out to fetch things, but strangers on the street cannot walk in through it.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose you have a database server that should never be reachable from the internet, but it still needs to download security updates from the internet. What kind of doorway would you want it to use: one that allows traffic both in and out, or one that only lets it start conversations outward?
lessons.teach:
A VPC (Virtual Private Cloud) is a logically isolated virtual network in an AWS Region that you control. It has a private address range, and nothing gets in or out unless you add a path.

A subnet is a slice of that address range placed in exactly one Availability Zone (one of the separate data-center groups inside a Region). You put resources such as EC2 servers into subnets.

A route table is a list of rules, called routes, that each say "traffic headed to this destination goes to this target." Every subnet is associated with one route table. Every route table automatically includes a local route so resources inside the VPC can reach each other.

An internet gateway is a component you attach to the VPC that lets traffic flow both ways between the VPC and the internet. A subnet is called public when its route table sends internet-bound traffic (destination 0.0.0.0/0, meaning "anywhere") to the internet gateway. Its servers also need public IP addresses.

A NAT gateway (Network Address Translation) is a managed device that sits in a public subnet. It lets servers in a private subnet, one with no route to the internet gateway, start outbound connections. Replies come back, but nobody on the internet can start a connection inward.

Worked example: a web server sits in a public subnet and a database sits in a private subnet. A user's request reaches the internet gateway, the public subnet's route table delivers it to the web server, and the web server queries the database over the local route. When the database needs a patch download, its private route table sends 0.0.0.0/0 traffic to the NAT gateway. The NAT gateway forwards it out through the internet gateway, and the reply returns the same way.

Common mistake: attaching an internet gateway and assuming the subnet is now public. Without a route pointing to it, nothing uses it. A related near-miss is choosing an internet gateway when the need says "outbound only." That need calls for a NAT gateway. In a running system, a missing route means servers silently cannot reach the internet, and a wrong route can expose a database publicly.

questions.prompt: A small news website is building its network on AWS so readers can load articles from a single web server. The team works through these steps. Step 1: create a VPC (a private, isolated virtual network) with its own address range. Step 2: create one subnet (a slice of that address range) in a single Availability Zone. Step 3: attach an internet gateway to the VPC. Step 4: ______. Step 5: launch the web server in that subnet and give it a public IP address. Result: readers on the internet can reach the server. Which action belongs in Step 4?
choices: In the subnet's route table, add a route sending 0.0.0.0/0 traffic to the internet gateway
Create a second subnet in another Availability Zone so the first one becomes public
Create a NAT gateway in the subnet and route all of the subnet's traffic to it
Add a local route to the subnet's route table so the server can reach the internet
questions.why: Attaching an internet gateway does nothing until the subnet's route table sends internet-bound (0.0.0.0/0) traffic to it, and that route is what makes the subnet public.

questions.prompt: A logistics company wants to split its VPC's address range into smaller pieces and place each piece in a specific data-center group so its servers are spread out. What is the term for one of those pieces, and where does it live?
choices: A route table, which can cover several Availability Zones at once
A subnet, which is placed in exactly one Availability Zone
A VPC, which is placed in exactly one Availability Zone
An internet gateway, which is placed in one Availability Zone
questions.why: A subnet is a slice of the VPC's address range, and each subnet sits in exactly one Availability Zone.

questions.prompt: A hospital runs report-generation servers in a private subnet. The servers must send results to an outside partner's web service on the internet. Nobody on the internet should ever be able to start a connection to these servers. Which component fits this need?
choices: A second route table holding only the local route, associated with the private subnet
Public IP addresses on the report servers, with no changes to any route table
An internet gateway with the private subnet's 0.0.0.0/0 route pointing directly to it
A NAT gateway placed in a public subnet, with the private subnet's 0.0.0.0/0 route pointing to it
questions.why: A NAT gateway lets private servers start outbound connections and receive replies, while blocking connections that start from the internet, so it matches an outbound-only need.

questions.prompt: A retailer's customer database sits in a private subnet whose route table sends 0.0.0.0/0 traffic to a NAT gateway. During a cleanup, an engineer changes that route's target to the VPC's internet gateway instead. What is the most important consequence?
choices: Nothing changes, because the local route still controls all traffic leaving the subnet
The database loses the ability to talk to other servers inside the VPC
The subnet becomes a NAT subnet, so outbound traffic now works more quickly
The subnet is now public by definition, which can expose the database to the internet
questions.why: A subnet whose route table sends 0.0.0.0/0 to an internet gateway is public, so this wrong route can expose a database that was meant to stay private.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a server in a private subnet gets software updates from the internet while staying unreachable from outside. Name each VPC component involved and one limit or tradeoff of this setup.
lessons.modelAnswer: Our VPC is our isolated network, split into subnets that each live in one Availability Zone. Each subnet follows a route table, which says where traffic should go. The public subnet's route table sends anything bound for the internet to the internet gateway, which allows traffic both in and out. The private subnet has no route to the internet gateway. Instead, its default route points to a NAT gateway that sits in the public subnet. When the private server requests an update, the NAT gateway forwards the request out through the internet gateway, and the reply comes back. Nobody outside can start a connection to that server. One tradeoff is that the NAT gateway is a paid managed service. It also lives in one Availability Zone, so for resilience you may need one per zone. That means more cost.
rubricPoints: A VPC is an isolated virtual network, and a subnet is a slice of it in one Availability Zone.
Route tables decide where a subnet's traffic goes, and a subnet is public only if its route table points to an internet gateway.
An internet gateway allows two-way traffic between the VPC and the internet.
A NAT gateway sits in a public subnet and gives private subnets outbound-only internet access.
Names a tradeoff such as NAT gateway cost or its single-Availability-Zone scope.

suggested.rationale: Tracing a packet hop by hop through route tables, internet gateways and NAT gateways in a virtual network path tracer is the most direct way to make these components concrete.

lessons.plain: A virtual private cloud (VPC) is your own private, walled-off section of the AWS network. Two kinds of traffic filters protect it. A security group is like a bouncer standing at the door of each individual server: it only has a guest list of who may come in, and it remembers who it let in so their replies can leave freely. A network ACL (access control list) is like a security checkpoint at the gate of a whole neighbourhood, called a subnet: it can both allow and refuse, checks everyone in both directions, and remembers nobody.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose you want to block traffic from one specific troublesome IP address from reaching every server in a section of your network, while still letting everyone else in. Would you rather use a filter that only lets you list who is allowed, or one that also lets you list who is refused? Why?
lessons.teach:
A security group is a virtual firewall (a traffic filter) attached to an individual resource, such as an Amazon EC2 instance (a virtual server). It contains allow rules only; anything not allowed is dropped. It is stateful, meaning it remembers connections: if a request is allowed in, the reply is automatically allowed out, with no extra rule. All of its rules are considered together. By default, a new security group allows no inbound traffic and all outbound traffic.

A network ACL (network access control list) is a filter attached to a subnet, a slice of the VPC that holds resources. It supports both allow and deny rules. Rules are numbered and checked in order from lowest number up; the first match decides. It is stateless, meaning it remembers nothing, so inbound and outbound traffic are each checked separately. The default network ACL allows all traffic both ways.

Why two layers? Defence in depth: the network ACL is a coarse guard for a whole subnet, and the security group is a fine-grained guard per resource.

Worked example: a user visits a web server on port 443 (secure web traffic). Step 1: the packet reaches the subnet, and the network ACL checks its inbound rules; rule 100 allows port 443, so it passes. Step 2: the security group on the server allows inbound 443, so the server receives it. Step 3: the server replies. The security group lets the reply out automatically because it is stateful. Step 4: the network ACL checks its outbound rules separately. If no rule allows the reply's return ports, the reply is dropped.

Common mistake: trying to block one bad IP address with a security group. You cannot, because security groups have no deny rules; use a network ACL deny rule instead. A second classic error is forgetting the network ACL outbound rule for replies, which in a running system shows up as connections that seem to hang or time out even though inbound looks correctly opened.

questions.prompt: A small bakery runs its online ordering site on an EC2 instance (a virtual server) inside a subnet (a slice of the VPC). Repeated bad requests arrive from one IP address, 198.51.100.77. The team works through the fix. Step 1: they note that a security group cannot block this address, because security groups contain allow rules only. Step 2: on the subnet's network ACL they add rule 80, which denies all traffic from 198.51.100.77. Step 3: the network ACL already has rule 100, which allows inbound port 443 (secure web traffic) from any address. Step 4 is missing: a new packet from 198.51.100.77 arrives at the subnet on port 443. What happens at the network ACL, and why?
choices: It is allowed, because rule 100 permits port 443 from anywhere, and in a network ACL an allow rule always takes priority over a deny rule.
It is denied, because the network ACL checks rules in order from the lowest number, rule 80 matches first, and the first match decides, so rule 100 is never reached.
It is allowed, because the instance's security group permits inbound 443, and the security group overrides the network ACL for that instance.
It is denied, because all of the network ACL's rules are considered together and a deny anywhere in the list always beats an allow.
questions.why: Network ACL rules are checked in numbered order from lowest up and the first match decides, so deny rule 80 stops the packet before allow rule 100 is ever checked.

questions.prompt: A team is comparing the two traffic filters available inside a VPC (a private virtual network in AWS). Which description fits a security group?
choices: Attached to an individual resource such as an EC2 instance, supports allow rules only, considers all rules together, and is stateful.
Attached to an individual resource, supports allow and deny rules, and checks inbound and outbound traffic separately with no memory of connections.
Attached to a whole subnet, supports allow rules only, and automatically lets replies out because it remembers connections.
Attached to a subnet, supports allow and deny rules, checks rules in numbered order, and is stateless.
questions.why: A security group is a per-resource filter with allow rules only, all evaluated together, and it is stateful, so replies to allowed requests go out automatically.

questions.prompt: A logistics company opens inbound port 8443 on both its subnet's network ACL and its application server's security group. Users report that connections to the app reach the server but then hang and time out. The server's security group has no extra outbound rules. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The security group needs an outbound rule for the replies, because security groups do not remember connections.
The network ACL has no outbound rule allowing the replies' return ports, and because it is stateless it does not let replies out automatically.
The network ACL needs a deny rule numbered lower than the allow rule so that replies are matched first.
The security group is blocking the requests, because a new security group denies all outbound traffic by default.
questions.why: A network ACL is stateless and checks outbound traffic separately, so without an outbound rule for the return ports the replies are dropped and connections appear to hang, while the stateful security group already lets replies out.

questions.prompt: A developer at a travel agency creates a brand-new security group, adds no rules to it, and attaches it to a new EC2 instance. What traffic does this security group allow?
choices: All traffic is allowed in both directions until rules are added.
No inbound traffic is allowed, and all outbound traffic is allowed.
All inbound traffic is allowed, and no outbound traffic is allowed.
No traffic is allowed in either direction until rules are added.
questions.why: By default a new security group allows no inbound traffic and all outbound traffic; allowing all traffic both ways is the default behaviour of the default network ACL, not of a security group.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between a security group and a network ACL, and describe one situation where only one of them can do the job, plus one tradeoff or limit of each.
lessons.modelAnswer: Both are traffic filters in a VPC, but they sit at different levels and behave differently. A security group is attached to an individual resource like an EC2 instance. It only has allow rules, and it is stateful, so if inbound traffic is allowed, the reply goes back out automatically. A network ACL is attached to a whole subnet. It can allow and deny, its numbered rules are checked lowest first with the first match winning, and it is stateless, so I must allow return traffic in the other direction explicitly. If I need to block one specific IP address, only a network ACL can do it, because security groups cannot deny. The limit of a security group is that lack of deny rules; the limit of a network ACL is extra rule work and easy mistakes, like forgetting outbound return ports so replies are silently dropped. Using both gives layered defence.
rubricPoints: Security groups apply to individual resources; network ACLs apply to subnets.
Security groups are stateful; network ACLs are stateless and need explicit return-traffic rules.
Security groups have allow rules only; network ACLs support allow and deny.
Network ACL rules are evaluated in numbered order, first match wins.
Blocking a specific IP address requires a network ACL deny rule.
Names a limit or tradeoff, such as missing outbound ACL rules dropping replies.

suggested.rationale: Tracing a packet through a subnet's network ACL and an instance's security group in both directions makes the stateful-versus-stateless difference concrete in a way reading alone does not.

lessons.plain: Amazon Route 53 is AWS's managed DNS service. DNS, the Domain Name System, is the internet's phone book: people remember names like shop.example.com, but computers connect using numeric IP addresses. When someone types a name, a DNS service looks up which address it belongs to. Route 53 answers those lookups for you. It can also register domain names, check whether your servers are healthy, and choose which address to give out, for example the nearest or the one still working. Think of a switchboard operator who knows every extension and quietly reroutes calls when a line goes dead.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your website runs in two places, one in the United States and one in Europe. When a visitor in Paris types your web address, how could the system that turns names into addresses help that visitor reach the faster, closer copy?
lessons.teach:
Amazon Route 53 is a managed, highly available DNS (Domain Name System) service. DNS translates human-friendly domain names into IP addresses, the numeric labels computers use to find each other. Route 53 does three jobs. First, domain registration: you can buy and renew a domain name through it. Second, DNS hosting: you create a hosted zone, a container holding the records for one domain. A record maps a name to a value; an A record points a name to an IPv4 address, and a CNAME points one name to another name. Third, health checks: Route 53 regularly tests an endpoint, meaning a server or address, and can stop handing out addresses that fail.

It also offers routing policies, rules for which answer to return. Simple returns one answer. Weighted splits traffic by percentage, useful for testing a new version on 10% of users. Latency-based sends users to the AWS Region that responds fastest for them. Failover sends traffic to a backup only when the primary fails its health check. Geolocation answers based on the user's country or continent.

Worked example: a visitor types shop.example.com. Their device asks a resolver, usually run by their internet provider. The resolver is directed to Route 53, which holds the hosted zone for example.com. Route 53 sees a latency policy, finds that the Europe Region is fastest for this visitor, and returns that Region's address. The browser then connects directly to that address. Route 53 never carries the web traffic itself; it only gives directions.

Common mistake: confusing Route 53 with a load balancer or a content delivery network. A load balancer spreads live traffic across servers inside an application, and a content delivery network caches content near users. Route 53 only answers name lookups. In a running system, answers are cached for a set time called the TTL (time to live), so a changed record or a failover can take that long to reach every user.

questions.prompt: A clinic runs its booking site at book.clinicnorth.org. It uses Route 53 with a failover routing policy, which is a rule that sends traffic to a backup only when the main (primary) endpoint fails its health check. The primary server is in one AWS Region and a backup server is in another. Tonight the primary has been failing its health checks. A patient types book.clinicnorth.org. Step 1: The patient's device asks a resolver, usually run by their internet provider. Step 2: The resolver is directed to Route 53, which holds the hosted zone (the container of records) for clinicnorth.org. Step 3: Route 53 applies the failover policy and sees that the primary's health check is failing. Step 4: ??? Step 5: The patient's browser connects directly to the backup server and the page loads. Which choice correctly fills in Step 4?
choices: Route 53 returns the backup server's address to the resolver as the answer.
Route 53 sends the patient a stored copy of the booking page from a nearby location.
Route 53 splits the patient's requests evenly between the primary and the backup.
Route 53 receives the patient's web request and forwards it on to the backup server.
questions.why: Route 53 only gives directions: under failover it answers with the backup's address, and the browser then connects to that address itself.

questions.prompt: A game studio has released a new version of its matchmaking server. Before switching everyone over, it wants about 20% of players' name lookups to return the new server's address, and 80% to keep getting the old one. Which Route 53 routing policy fits this need?
choices: Latency-based
Geolocation
Weighted
Failover
questions.why: Weighted routing splits answers by percentage, which suits testing a new version on a share of users. Latency-based picks the fastest Region, geolocation picks by country, and failover only switches when the primary is unhealthy.

questions.prompt: A video-streaming startup wants copies of its large video files kept at locations near viewers around the world so downloads start faster. An engineer suggests Route 53 for this. Why is that the wrong fit?
choices: Route 53 would work, but only if the startup's viewers are all inside a single country.
Route 53 can only host records for domains that were registered somewhere outside of AWS.
Route 53 only answers name lookups; keeping cached copies of content near users is what a content delivery network does.
Route 53 is a load balancer, so it spreads traffic across servers rather than across regions.
questions.why: Route 53 is a DNS service that hands out addresses and never stores or carries the content; caching content near users is the job of a content delivery network.

questions.prompt: A logistics company moves its tracking service to a new server and updates the A record for api.fieldtrack.io to point to the new IPv4 address. For a while afterwards, some customers are still reaching the old server, while others reach the new one. What is the most likely reason?
choices: An A record can only point to another name, so the new address was ignored.
The hosted zone automatically applied a weighted policy that splits traffic between the two.
Resolvers cached the old answer, and they keep using it until its TTL (time to live) runs out.
Route 53 is still carrying those customers' web traffic through the old server.
questions.why: DNS answers are cached for the TTL, so a changed record takes up to that long to reach every user. Route 53 never carries the traffic itself, and an A record maps a name to an IPv4 address.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what Amazon Route 53 does and how it could keep a website reachable when one server location goes down. Include one limit or tradeoff of relying on DNS for this.
lessons.modelAnswer: Route 53 is AWS's managed DNS service. DNS turns a name like shop.example.com into the IP address a computer actually connects to. Route 53 can register the domain, hold its records in a hosted zone, and decide which answer to give using routing policies such as weighted, latency-based, geolocation, or failover. For keeping a site reachable, I'd put a health check on the primary location and use a failover policy: while the primary passes, Route 53 returns its address; once it fails, Route 53 starts returning the backup's address instead. The tradeoff is that DNS answers are cached for the TTL, so some users keep getting the old, dead address until their cache expires. Also, Route 53 only gives directions; it doesn't carry or spread the actual traffic the way a load balancer does.
rubricPoints: States that Route 53 is a managed DNS service translating names to IP addresses.
Mentions domain registration and hosted zones holding records.
Describes health checks combined with a failover or other routing policy.
Names caching via TTL as a delay limit on changes or failover.
Distinguishes Route 53 from a load balancer or content delivery network because it only answers lookups.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests picking Route 53 over near-miss services like load balancers or content delivery networks in described scenarios, so reasoning through such situations adds the most.

lessons.plain: Many companies keep some computers in their own buildings and also run systems in AWS, so they need a way to link the two. AWS offers two main options. AWS Site-to-Site VPN builds a scrambled, private tunnel across the ordinary public internet between your office network and your AWS network. AWS Direct Connect is a dedicated physical line from your premises, or a nearby data centre, straight into AWS, which skips the public internet. Think of it like getting to work: the VPN is driving a locked armoured van on public roads, while Direct Connect is having your own private road built.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company needs its office network linked to AWS by tomorrow morning and has only a small budget. Would you choose a connection that travels over the internet they already have, or one that needs a new physical cable installed? Why?
lessons.teach:
AWS Site-to-Site VPN is a managed service that connects a whole on-premises network (computers in your own building) to a virtual private cloud, or VPC, which is your private, isolated network inside AWS. A VPN (virtual private network) uses encryption, meaning data is scrambled so only the two ends can read it, to create a protected tunnel across the public internet. Because it reuses your existing internet line, it can be set up in minutes to hours and costs little. The tradeoff is that the internet is shared, so speed and latency (the delay before data arrives) can vary.

AWS Direct Connect is a dedicated private network connection from your site, or a colocation facility (a shared data centre where AWS has a presence), into AWS. Traffic never crosses the public internet, so bandwidth (how much data per second) is consistent and latency is predictable. It can carry large volumes cheaply per gigabyte. The tradeoff is time and effort: a physical circuit must be ordered and installed, which often takes weeks.

Worked example: a hospital moves 20 terabytes of scans to AWS every night and needs steady performance. Step one, how much data? Very large, every day. Step two, does performance need to be predictable? Yes. Step three, can they wait for installation? Yes, it is a long-term plan. Answer: Direct Connect. Step four, what if that line fails? They add a Site-to-Site VPN as a cheaper backup path, a very common pairing.

A common mistake is assuming Direct Connect is encrypted because it is private. It is not encrypted by default; private means not shared, not scrambled. Teams that need encryption run a VPN over Direct Connect or encrypt at another layer. Another near-miss: Site-to-Site VPN joins networks, not individual laptops; single remote users connect through a different service, AWS Client VPN.

In a running system, choosing the VPN for heavy, latency-sensitive traffic shows up as slow, uneven transfers, while relying on a single Direct Connect line with no backup means one cable fault cuts you off from AWS.

questions.prompt: A regional insurance company already sends its daily claims data into its VPC (its private, isolated network inside AWS) over an AWS Direct Connect line, which is a dedicated private connection that does not cross the public internet. A new compliance rule now says that all claims data must be encrypted (scrambled so only the two ends can read it) while it travels between the office and AWS. Step one: does the rule cover this traffic? Yes, it moves between the office and AWS. Step two: is the Direct Connect traffic already encrypted? No. Direct Connect is private, meaning not shared, but it is not encrypted by default. Step three: ??? Step four: the team confirms the claims data is now scrambled in transit and still gets the steady performance of the dedicated line. What is step three?
choices: Do nothing, because a private dedicated line already counts as encrypted for compliance purposes
Move all the claims traffic onto the public internet, because data that crosses the internet is encrypted automatically
Run an AWS Site-to-Site VPN over the existing Direct Connect line so the traffic is encrypted inside the private connection
Replace Direct Connect with AWS Client VPN, because Client VPN is built for joining whole office networks to a VPC
questions.why: Running a VPN over Direct Connect adds encryption while keeping the dedicated line's consistent performance, which is how teams meet an encryption requirement on Direct Connect.

questions.prompt: A small design agency with one office wants to connect its office network to its VPC (its private network inside AWS) by the end of this week. It moves only a few gigabytes a day, has a small budget, and can accept speed that sometimes varies. Which option fits best?
choices: AWS Client VPN, because it is designed to connect an entire office network
AWS Site-to-Site VPN, because it reuses the existing internet line and can be set up quickly at low cost
AWS Direct Connect, because a dedicated private circuit is the only way to reach a VPC
No connection is possible until a colocation facility is arranged
questions.why: Site-to-Site VPN joins a whole on-premises network to a VPC over the existing internet in minutes to hours at low cost, which fits a small, fast, budget-limited need where variable speed is acceptable.

questions.prompt: A consulting firm has 40 staff who travel and work from hotels on their own laptops. Each person needs a protected connection into the company's VPC (its private network inside AWS). Which service is the right fit?
choices: AWS Client VPN, because it is meant for individual remote users rather than whole networks
AWS Site-to-Site VPN, because any VPN can connect individual laptops
AWS Direct Connect, because it gives each traveller predictable latency
A single Direct Connect line from the head office with a Site-to-Site VPN backup
questions.why: Site-to-Site VPN joins networks, not individual laptops; single remote users connect through AWS Client VPN.

questions.prompt: A logistics company relies on one AWS Direct Connect line (a dedicated private connection into AWS) and nothing else. A construction crew accidentally cuts that cable, and the company loses all access to its AWS systems for a day. Which design choice would most likely have kept it connected?
choices: Adding an AWS Site-to-Site VPN over the internet as a cheaper backup path
Moving the office into a colocation facility while keeping only one line
Turning on encryption for the Direct Connect traffic
Switching to a higher-bandwidth Direct Connect line on the same single cable
questions.why: A single Direct Connect line with no backup means one cable fault cuts you off, so pairing it with a Site-to-Site VPN backup gives a second path when the line fails.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between AWS Site-to-Site VPN and AWS Direct Connect, and describe one tradeoff that would make you pick one over the other.
lessons.modelAnswer: Both connect our own network to our VPC in AWS, but they travel differently. Site-to-Site VPN builds an encrypted tunnel over the public internet we already pay for, so it is quick to set up, often the same day, and cheap. Because the internet is shared, though, speed and delay can wobble. Direct Connect is a dedicated physical connection into AWS that avoids the internet, so bandwidth and latency are consistent and big data transfers are efficient. The catch is it takes weeks to install and costs more up front, and it is not encrypted by default, so we would add encryption if we need it. If we need something fast and modest, I pick the VPN; for heavy, steady, long-term traffic I pick Direct Connect, ideally with a VPN as a backup path in case the line fails.
rubricPoints: Site-to-Site VPN is an encrypted tunnel over the public internet between an on-premises network and a VPC.
Direct Connect is a dedicated private connection that does not use the public internet.
VPN is fast and cheap to set up but performance varies; Direct Connect is consistent but takes weeks to provision.
Direct Connect is not encrypted by default.
A VPN is commonly used as a backup for Direct Connect.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests this as short scenarios where the learner weighs speed of setup, cost, consistency and encryption to pick the right connection and reject the near-miss, so reasoning through situations adds the most.

lessons.plain: Object storage keeps data as whole items, called objects, each with a unique name and some descriptive labels, rather than as files in folders or blocks on a disk. You put an object in and fetch it back by name over the internet. Amazon S3 (Simple Storage Service) is AWS's object storage service. Picture a huge self-storage company. You can rent a unit by the front door that you can open any time, but it costs more. You can also rent a cheaper unit out back, where staff need a while to fetch your box. S3 storage classes are those tiers. Each one balances storage price, access fees and retrieval speed.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company must keep scanned tax records for seven years and expects to look at them perhaps once, if ever. Would you pay more for instant access, or less for storage that takes hours to retrieve, and why?
lessons.teach:
Object storage holds data as objects. An object is the data itself, plus metadata (descriptive labels), plus a key, which is the object's unique name. Objects live in a bucket, a named container. You read and write whole objects over web requests. You do not edit part of an object in place. Amazon S3 is designed for very high durability, meaning the chance of losing stored data is extremely small. Most classes copy data across at least three Availability Zones, which are separate data-centre groups within one Region.

A storage class is a pricing and access tier for an object. Cheaper storage usually brings a retrieval fee (a charge per gigabyte read), a minimum storage duration (you are billed for at least that many days), or a slower retrieval time. S3 Standard suits frequently accessed data and has no retrieval fee. S3 Intelligent-Tiering moves objects between tiers automatically when access patterns are unknown or changing. S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (Standard-IA) costs less to store but charges per retrieval. S3 One Zone-IA is cheaper again but keeps data in a single Availability Zone. S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval is archive pricing with millisecond access. S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval takes minutes to hours. S3 Glacier Deep Archive is the cheapest class and takes up to about twelve hours. S3 Express One Zone gives very low latency in a single zone for performance-hungry workloads.

Worked example. A hospital stores X-rays. In the first month doctors view them daily, so the hospital uses Standard. After that they are viewed a few times a year but must open instantly, so Glacier Instant Retrieval fits. After seven years they are kept only for legal reasons and a day's wait is fine, so Deep Archive fits.

A common mistake is putting frequently read data in an infrequent-access or Glacier class to save money. The retrieval fees then cost more than the storage savings. Another is keeping the only copy of irreplaceable data in One Zone-IA. If that one zone is lost, the data can be lost too.

questions.prompt:
A photo-sharing app plans storage for two kinds of objects, and three of the four decisions are already made.

Step 1: Newly uploaded original photos are opened many times a day for the first few weeks, so they go in S3 Standard, which has no retrieval fee.

Step 2: After a few weeks, originals are opened only a handful of times a year, but they must load immediately when someone opens an old album. They move to S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval, which offers archive pricing with millisecond access.

Step 3: (missing) The app also stores small thumbnail versions of each photo. A thumbnail is read only rarely, but it must appear immediately when it is needed. It can be regenerated at any time from the original, so losing one is only an inconvenience. The team wants the lowest storage price that still allows immediate reads.

Step 4: Originals of deleted accounts must be kept for five years for legal reasons, and a wait of most of a day is acceptable, so they go in S3 Glacier Deep Archive.

Which storage class completes Step 3?
choices: S3 Glacier Deep Archive, because thumbnails are rarely read and this is the cheapest class
S3 Standard, because thumbnails must appear on screen immediately
S3 One Zone-IA, because thumbnails can be regenerated, so keeping them in a single Availability Zone is an acceptable risk in exchange for a lower price
S3 Express One Zone, because thumbnails need fast single-zone access
questions.why: One Zone-IA is cheaper than the multi-zone infrequent-access class and still reads immediately, and keeping data in a single zone is acceptable only because the thumbnails can be re-created from the originals.

questions.prompt: An engineer uploads a file to an Amazon S3 bucket and names it reports/2024/q3-summary.pdf. In object storage terms, what is that name?
choices: The storage class, which is the pricing and access tier of the object
The bucket, which is the named container that holds the object
The metadata, which is the set of descriptive labels attached to the object
The key, which is the object's unique name inside the bucket
questions.why: In object storage, the key is the unique name that identifies an object within its bucket, while metadata is the separate set of descriptive labels.

questions.prompt: A data science team is launching a new shared dataset. They cannot predict how often it will be read. Some files may be read heavily for a while and then not at all, and nobody wants to keep moving files between tiers by hand. Which S3 storage class fits best?
choices: S3 Standard-IA, because it is cheaper to store than S3 Standard
S3 One Zone-IA, because it is cheaper than Standard-IA
S3 Intelligent-Tiering, because it moves objects between tiers automatically when access patterns are unknown or changing
S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval, because files that go unused should be archived
questions.why: Intelligent-Tiering is designed for unknown or changing access patterns: it shifts objects between tiers automatically, so nobody has to guess the pattern or move files by hand.

questions.prompt: A retail company stores the data files behind a sales dashboard. The dashboard reads these files every hour. To cut costs, the team moved the files from S3 Standard to S3 Standard-IA. The next monthly bill was higher than before. What is the most likely reason?
choices: Standard-IA charges a fee for every gigabyte read, and hourly reads made those retrieval fees larger than the storage savings
Standard-IA has a higher price per gigabyte stored than S3 Standard
Standard-IA keeps data in only one Availability Zone, so the company paid for extra copies
Standard-IA takes minutes to hours to return data, so the dashboard was billed for waiting time
questions.why: Infrequent-access classes are cheaper to store but charge for each retrieval, so frequently read data can end up costing more than it did in S3 Standard.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what object storage is and how you would choose between S3 storage classes, naming at least one tradeoff that makes a cheaper class the wrong choice.
lessons.modelAnswer: Object storage saves each piece of data as a whole object in a bucket. Every object has a unique key and some metadata, and you read or write the whole object over web requests. S3 is AWS's version, and it is built for very high durability. Storage classes let us match cost to how often we read the data. Standard is for hot data. Intelligent-Tiering is for unpredictable access. Standard-IA and One Zone-IA are for data we rarely read. The Glacier classes are for archives: Instant Retrieval returns in milliseconds, Flexible Retrieval in minutes to hours, and Deep Archive in up to about twelve hours. The tradeoff is that cheaper classes add retrieval fees, minimum storage durations or slow access. If we read the data often, those fees can cost more than Standard would. One Zone-IA also keeps data in a single zone, so it suits only data we can recreate.
rubricPoints: Defines an object as data plus metadata plus a unique key, stored in a bucket.
Links storage class choice to how often and how fast data must be accessed.
Names at least three classes correctly, including a Glacier tier and its retrieval speed.
States that cheaper classes add retrieval fees, minimum durations or slower access.
Notes that One Zone-IA stores data in a single Availability Zone, so it is less resilient.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests this by describing an access pattern and asking for the right class, so reasoning through scenarios with near-miss options builds the skill best.

lessons.plain: Block storage is a virtual hard drive for a cloud server: the server sees a blank disk it can format and write files to. AWS offers two kinds for its virtual servers. Amazon EBS (Elastic Block Store) is a drive kept on separate, network-connected storage. It survives when the server stops and can be unplugged and moved to another server. Instance store is a disk physically inside the machine hosting your server. It is very fast but temporary. Think of EBS as an external drive you carry between desks, and instance store as a whiteboard that gets wiped when you leave the room.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose one disk lives inside the physical machine running your server and another lives on separate storage reached over the network. If you shut the server down and AWS later starts it on a different physical machine, which disk would you expect to still hold your files, and why?
lessons.teach:
Block storage presents raw storage as a disk that the operating system formats with a file system. It suits operating systems, databases and applications that expect a normal drive. Amazon EC2 is AWS's virtual server service, and an EC2 server is called an instance. An instance can use two kinds of block storage.

An Amazon EBS volume is network-attached block storage that exists independently of any instance. Its lifetime is separate from the server's, so data survives when the instance stops, and you can detach the volume and attach it to another instance. A volume lives in one Availability Zone, which is an isolated data-centre location inside a Region. AWS copies the data within that zone to protect against hardware failure. A volume can only attach to instances in the same zone. You can take a snapshot, which is a point-in-time backup that AWS stores durably and can use to create new volumes, even in other zones. You pay for EBS separately, based on its size.

Instance store is temporary, or ephemeral, block storage on disks physically attached to the host machine running your instance. Because the data does not cross a network, it is very fast, and it comes included with the instance types that offer it. The data survives a reboot. It is lost if the instance stops, hibernates or terminates, or if the disk fails, because a restarted instance may land on a different host.

Here is a worked example. A team runs a database on an instance with both kinds of disk. They put the database files on EBS and a scratch cache on instance store. They stop the instance overnight to save money. In the morning they start it: the database files are intact on EBS, and the cache is empty. The application rebuilds the cache, so nothing important was lost.

A common mistake is to keep the only copy of important data on instance store because it is fast. In a running system, a routine stop or a hardware failure then destroys that data with no snapshot to restore from. Use instance store only for data you can recreate or that is copied elsewhere.

questions.prompt: A small animation studio renders short films on one EC2 instance (an EC2 instance is a virtual server). The instance has two block-storage disks. One is an Amazon EBS volume, which is network-attached storage that exists separately from the server. It holds the source scenes and the finished renders. The other is instance store, which is temporary storage on disks physically attached to the host machine. It holds intermediate frame tiles that the renderer can always regenerate from the source scenes. Step 1: On Tuesday an operating-system patch requires a reboot. Afterwards the frame tiles are still on instance store, because a reboot keeps the data. Step 2: On Friday evening the team stops the instance for the weekend to save money. Step 3: [missing] Step 4: The renderer regenerates the frame tiles from the source scenes, and the team loses no real work. What belongs in Step 3, describing what the team finds when they start the instance on Monday?
choices: Both disks are empty, because stopping an instance wipes every disk that was attached to it.
Both disks are intact, because the frame tiles already survived Tuesday's reboot and a stop works the same way.
The frame tiles are intact, but the EBS volume was detached and must be reattached from another zone.
The source scenes and renders are intact on EBS, but the frame tiles on instance store are gone.
questions.why: EBS data survives a stop because its lifetime is separate from the instance, while instance store data is lost on a stop, since the restarted instance may land on a different host.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes an Amazon EBS volume?
choices: Temporary block storage on disks physically inside the host machine, included in the price of certain instance types.
Block storage that attaches to instances in any Availability Zone in a Region without needing a copy.
A point-in-time backup that AWS stores durably and uses to create new disks in any zone.
Network-attached block storage that lives in one Availability Zone and keeps its data when the instance it is attached to stops.
questions.why: An EBS volume is network-attached block storage with its own lifetime, tied to a single Availability Zone, so its data survives an instance stop.

questions.prompt: A logistics company has a 200 GB Amazon EBS volume of shipment records attached to an instance in Availability Zone A. (An Availability Zone is an isolated data-centre location inside a Region.) It now needs the same data on a new instance running in Availability Zone B. What should it do?
choices: Copy the records onto the new instance's instance store, which can be reached from any zone.
Reboot the original instance so AWS moves the volume to the zone with the most capacity.
Take a snapshot of the volume, then create a new volume from that snapshot in zone B and attach it.
Detach the volume from the first instance and attach it directly to the new instance in zone B.
questions.why: An EBS volume can only attach to instances in its own zone, but a snapshot can be used to create a new volume in a different zone.

questions.prompt: A research lab keeps a temporary dataset on instance store, which is ephemeral block storage on the host machine's own disks. Which of these events would leave that dataset in place?
choices: Rebooting the instance.
Hibernating the instance.
Stopping the instance.
Failure of the underlying disk.
questions.why: Instance store data survives a reboot, but it is lost if the instance stops, hibernates or terminates, or if the disk fails.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate asks whether to put a new application's database on EBS or instance store. Explain the difference in your own words and name the tradeoff that decides it.
lessons.modelAnswer: Both give the server a disk it can format, but they differ in where the disk lives and how long the data lasts. An EBS volume sits on separate storage reached over the network, so its data survives when the instance stops. We can detach it, move it to another instance in the same Availability Zone, and take snapshots for backup. Instance store is a disk physically inside the host machine. It is very fast and included in the instance price, but the data disappears if the instance stops, hibernates or terminates, or the disk fails. Only a reboot keeps it. The tradeoff is durability against speed and cost. For a database whose data we cannot lose, EBS is the right choice. Instance store fits only caches, scratch space, or data that is copied elsewhere and can be rebuilt.
rubricPoints: Says both are block storage that the instance uses like a disk.
States that EBS persists independently of the instance and can be detached, reattached and snapshotted.
States that instance store is physically attached, very fast and temporary, and is lost on stop, hibernate, terminate or disk failure.
Notes that an EBS volume is tied to one Availability Zone.
Names the tradeoff of durability versus speed and cost, and picks EBS for important data.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests this by describing a workload and asking which disk fits, so reasoning through scenarios that turn on whether data must survive a stop is the most useful practice.

lessons.plain: File storage is a shared folder in the cloud: a tree of directories and files that several computers can open at once, just like a shared drive at an office. Amazon EFS (Elastic File System) is AWS's managed shared folder for Linux machines; it grows and shrinks as you add or delete files. Amazon FSx is a family of managed file systems built on well-known existing file system software, such as one for Windows networks and one for very fast scientific computing. Think of EFS as the general office shared drive and FSx as specialist drives for particular tools and teams.
lessons.guessPrompt: Three Linux web servers all need to read and write the same folder of customer-uploaded photos at the same time. Would you give each server its own private disk, or one shared folder they all mount, and why?
lessons.teach:
A file system stores data as files inside folders and lets programs open, edit, and lock files by path. File storage in AWS means a managed service runs that file system for you, and many servers connect to it over the network at the same time. Managed means AWS handles the hardware, patching, and replication.

Amazon EFS is a managed file system for Linux that speaks NFS (Network File System, the standard Linux protocol for sharing folders over a network). It is elastic: capacity grows and shrinks automatically, you never pre-size it, and you pay for what you store. By default it keeps data across multiple Availability Zones (separate data centre groups in a Region), so servers in different zones can share it.

Amazon FSx is a family of managed file systems, each built on a familiar existing product. FSx for Windows File Server speaks SMB (the Windows file-sharing protocol) and joins Active Directory (Microsoft's user and permission directory). FSx for Lustre is a very high-speed file system for high performance computing and machine learning, and can work with data in Amazon S3. FSx for NetApp ONTAP and FSx for OpenZFS suit teams already using those storage systems.

Worked example: a company runs four Linux web servers in two Availability Zones, and all must see the same uploads folder. Step one: the need is shared, simultaneous file access, so file storage. Step two: the servers are Linux, so the protocol is NFS. Step three: no special product is required, so EFS fits. If the servers were Windows with Active Directory permissions, step two would give SMB and the answer would become FSx for Windows File Server.

Common mistake: picking Amazon EBS (block storage, a virtual disk normally attached to one instance in one zone) for shared data. Each server then holds its own copy, and a photo uploaded through one server is missing on the others. Amazon S3 is the other near miss: it stores objects through an API rather than being mounted as an ordinary shared folder.

questions.prompt: A genomics research lab runs 150 Linux compute nodes for a large analysis job. The nodes must all read the same huge set of input files at once and need very high throughput. The raw data already sits in Amazon S3. Step one: many nodes need shared, simultaneous access to the same files, so this is file storage, not a separate virtual disk per node. Step two: the deciding requirement is very high speed for high performance computing, plus working directly with data held in S3. Step three is missing. Which choice correctly completes step three?
choices: Choose Amazon EFS, because the nodes run Linux and EFS is the general managed file system for Linux over NFS.
Choose Amazon FSx for Windows File Server, because it joins Active Directory and shares files over SMB.
Choose Amazon FSx for Lustre, because it is the very high-speed managed file system built for HPC and can work with data in S3.
Choose an Amazon EBS volume for each node, because a local virtual disk gives each node the fastest access to its data.
questions.why: Step two named very high speed for HPC and S3 integration, which is exactly what FSx for Lustre is built for, while EFS is the general-purpose Linux option.

questions.prompt: A team is told that Amazon EFS is "elastic." What does that mean for how they plan and pay for it?
choices: It can be attached to exactly one server at a time, but that server can be swapped quickly.
They must choose a fixed size when creating it, and can only grow it later by taking the file system offline.
Capacity grows and shrinks automatically as files are added or removed, so they never pre-size it and pay for what they store.
It automatically moves files to another AWS Region whenever one Region becomes busy.
questions.why: Elastic in EFS means capacity adjusts automatically with no pre-sizing, and billing follows the amount actually stored.

questions.prompt: A regional law firm is moving its office file shares to AWS. Staff use Windows computers, the shares are accessed over SMB, and folder permissions are controlled by the firm's existing Active Directory. Which service fits best?
choices: Amazon EBS
Amazon S3
Amazon EFS
Amazon FSx for Windows File Server
questions.why: FSx for Windows File Server is the managed file system that speaks SMB and joins Active Directory, while EFS uses NFS for Linux, S3 is object storage via an API, and EBS is a single-instance disk.

questions.prompt: A small startup runs three Linux application servers. Each server has its own Amazon EBS volume, and each stores a "reports" folder there. A user saves a report through one server, but when their next request reaches a different server, the report is missing. What is the cause and the better choice?
choices: The EBS volumes are too small; increasing their size will let the servers share the reports folder.
The servers should mount Amazon S3 as an ordinary shared folder in place of EBS, since S3 is the standard shared file system.
The folder needs FSx for Lustre, because the problem is that EBS is too slow to copy files between servers.
EBS is block storage normally attached to one instance, so each server has its own separate copy; a shared file system such as Amazon EFS lets all servers see the same folder.
questions.why: An EBS volume is a virtual disk for one instance, so data written on one server never appears on the others, whereas EFS is shared by many Linux servers over NFS at the same time.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose between Amazon EFS, an Amazon FSx option, and Amazon EBS for a workload, and name one limit or tradeoff of each choice.
lessons.modelAnswer: First I ask whether several servers need the same files at once. If only one server needs a fast private disk, EBS is the fit, but it is normally attached to one instance in one Availability Zone, so it cannot act as a shared folder. If many servers share files, I want managed file storage. For Linux servers using NFS with no special requirements, EFS works: it grows automatically, spans Availability Zones, and bills for what is stored, but it is aimed at Linux and NFS, not Windows SMB shares. If the servers are Windows and need Active Directory permissions, FSx for Windows File Server fits. If the job is high performance computing or machine learning needing very fast throughput, FSx for Lustre fits. The tradeoff with FSx is that each option is specialised, so I pick it to match a specific protocol or product rather than as a general default.
rubricPoints: File storage lets many servers mount and share the same folders at the same time.
EFS is managed, elastic NFS file storage for Linux that spans Availability Zones.
FSx is a family of managed file systems built on specific products, such as Windows File Server and Lustre.
FSx for Windows suits SMB and Active Directory; FSx for Lustre suits high performance computing and machine learning.
EBS is a near miss because it is a block disk normally attached to one instance in one zone.
S3 is a near miss because it is object storage accessed through an API, not a mounted shared folder.

suggested.rationale: This objective is tested as pick-the-service scenarios, so reasoning through described needs and rejecting near misses like EBS and S3 builds the skill best.

lessons.plain: AWS Storage Gateway is a bridge between the computers in your own building and storage in the AWS cloud. You install a small appliance in your office, either a virtual machine or a hardware box. Your existing servers talk to it the way they already talk to a local file server, disk or tape drive. Behind the scenes, the gateway keeps the data in AWS. Think of a library branch: popular books stay on the local shelf, and the full collection lives in a big central warehouse. You get almost unlimited cloud capacity without rewriting your applications.
lessons.guessPrompt: A small office keeps running out of space on its file server. Staff open recent files all day but rarely touch files older than a year. If you could keep only some data in the office and the rest in the cloud, which data would you keep locally, and why?
lessons.teach:
AWS Storage Gateway is a hybrid storage service. Hybrid means part of the setup runs on-premises, in your own building, and part runs in AWS. You run a gateway appliance locally. It presents storage using standard protocols, which are agreed ways for computers to talk. These include NFS and SMB, the common protocols for sharing files over a network, and iSCSI, a protocol that makes remote storage look like a local disk. The gateway then stores the data durably in AWS services such as Amazon S3, which is object storage.

It comes in a few types. An S3 File Gateway gives you file shares whose files become objects in S3. A Volume Gateway gives you block storage, meaning raw disks, over iSCSI. It has two modes. In cached mode, the full data lives in AWS and only frequently used data is kept locally. In stored mode, the full copy stays local and is backed up to AWS as snapshots, which are point-in-time copies. A Tape Gateway pretends to be a tape library, so old backup software can write virtual tapes to cloud storage.

These setups work because of a cache, which is a small, fast local copy of recently used data. Most reads hit a small set of hot files. Serving those locally avoids latency, the delay of a round trip to the cloud.

Worked example: an office uses an S3 File Gateway. A user opens yesterday's report. The gateway finds it in its local cache, which is a cache hit, and returns it at once. Next, the user opens a 2019 file. It is not cached, which is a cache miss, so the gateway fetches it from S3, serves it a little more slowly, and keeps a local copy.

A common mistake is confusing Storage Gateway with Amazon EFS. EFS is a file system for servers already running in AWS, while Storage Gateway serves machines on-premises. It is also not a network link itself, because it uses your internet or private connection. In a running system, a cache that is too small, or a slow link, means frequent misses and sluggish file access for users.

questions.prompt: A regional law firm runs an AWS Storage Gateway Volume Gateway in cached mode. It presents a 10 TB disk to the firm's on-premises file server over iSCSI, and the gateway's local cache holds 500 GB. Step 1: A paralegal opens this week's case notes. Those blocks are in the local cache, so this is a cache hit and they are returned at once. Step 2: A partner opens a contract archived in 2016. Those blocks are not in the local cache, so this is a cache miss. Step 3: ??? Step 4: The partner sees the contract after a short delay, and the gateway keeps a local copy so the next open is fast. Which choice correctly fills in Step 3?
choices: The gateway redirects the request to Amazon EFS, which holds the older files for on-premises users.
The gateway reports the blocks as lost, because cached mode keeps only frequently used data and discards the rest.
The gateway fetches the missing blocks from AWS, where cached mode keeps the full copy of the data.
The gateway reads the blocks from its full local copy of the volume and then sends a snapshot of them to AWS.
questions.why: In cached mode the full data lives in AWS and only hot data is kept locally, so a cache miss is served by fetching the blocks from AWS and then keeping a local copy.

questions.prompt: A shipping company's decades-old backup software can only write to a tape library. The company wants those backups to land in cloud storage without replacing or reconfiguring the software. Which option fits best?
choices: S3 File Gateway, presenting an SMB file share whose files become S3 objects
Volume Gateway in stored mode, keeping a full local disk with snapshots in AWS
Tape Gateway, which pretends to be a tape library and writes virtual tapes to cloud storage
Amazon EFS, a file system shared by servers already running in AWS
questions.why: A Tape Gateway looks like a tape library to the old backup software, so the software keeps working unchanged while the virtual tapes are stored in the cloud.

questions.prompt: A startup runs all of its application servers inside AWS and has no on-premises machines. Those servers need a shared file system they can all mount. Which choice fits, and why is the near-miss wrong?
choices: S3 File Gateway, because it gives file shares backed by S3, which suits servers that already run inside AWS.
Amazon EFS, because it is a file system for servers already running in AWS; Storage Gateway is meant to serve on-premises machines.
Tape Gateway, because writing virtual tapes is the usual way for servers in AWS to share files with each other.
Volume Gateway in cached mode, because keeping hot data on a local appliance speeds up servers running in AWS.
questions.why: EFS is the file system for servers already in AWS, while Storage Gateway is a hybrid service whose job is to serve machines in your own building.

questions.prompt: A clinic uses an S3 File Gateway on-premises. Staff complain that opening files is often sluggish, and monitoring shows most file reads are cache misses travelling over the clinic's modest internet connection. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The shares use SMB instead of NFS, and SMB always forces every read to go to the cloud.
The local cache is too small for the files staff use, so many reads must cross a slow link to S3.
Amazon S3 is losing objects, so the gateway has to rebuild each file before it can open it.
The gateway itself is the network link to AWS, so its built-in connection to the cloud must be failing.
questions.why: A cache that is too small, or a slow link, causes frequent misses, and each miss needs a round trip to the cloud, which makes file access sluggish for users.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what AWS Storage Gateway does and when you would choose it. Include one limit or tradeoff, and say why Amazon EFS would be the wrong pick for an on-premises office.
lessons.modelAnswer: Storage Gateway lets our on-premises servers keep using familiar file shares, iSCSI disks or tape backups while the real data lives in AWS. We run a gateway appliance in our building, and it speaks NFS, SMB or iSCSI locally while storing data in services like S3. In cached mode, only the hot data sits on local disk and everything else is in the cloud, so we gain near-unlimited capacity without changing applications. Stored mode keeps the full copy locally and backs it up to AWS. The tradeoff is that anything not in the cache has to be fetched over our network link. If the cache is too small or the link is slow, users notice delays. EFS is the wrong pick here because it is a file system for compute running inside AWS, not a bridge for machines in our office.
rubricPoints: Defines Storage Gateway as a hybrid service connecting on-premises systems to AWS storage.
Mentions that it presents standard protocols such as NFS, SMB or iSCSI, so applications need no rewrite.
Names at least one gateway type: file, volume or tape.
Explains cached mode, where hot data is kept local and the full data set is in AWS.
States a tradeoff such as cache misses, cache size or dependence on the network link.
Distinguishes it from Amazon EFS, which serves workloads already inside AWS.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests picking Storage Gateway over near-miss services like EFS or S3 in a described hybrid scenario, so reasoning through situations adds the most and no mission or planned engine covers it.

lessons.plain: An S3 lifecycle policy is a set of standing instructions you attach to a storage bucket, such as: after 30 days move these files to a cheaper shelf, and after a year throw them away. Amazon S3 is AWS's object storage, a service that holds files of any kind. Lifecycle rules carry out those moves and deletions automatically. AWS Backup is a different tool: a central control room that takes scheduled safety copies of data across many AWS services and keeps them for as long as you say. Think of a filing clerk who archives old paperwork (lifecycle) versus a fireproof vault that keeps copies (Backup).
lessons.guessPrompt: Your team keeps application logs in cloud storage. They are read often in the first month, almost never after that, and must be deleted after one year. Would you rather have a person move and delete them by hand, or set a rule once? What could go wrong with each approach?
lessons.teach:
An S3 lifecycle policy is a set of rules on an Amazon S3 bucket (a container for stored objects, meaning files plus their metadata). Each rule matches objects, for example by a name prefix like logs/, and performs one of two kinds of action. A transition action moves objects to another storage class, which is a price-and-access tier: S3 Standard for frequently read data, S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (Standard-IA) for data read rarely but needed quickly, and S3 Glacier classes for cheap archives that can be slower to retrieve. An expiration action deletes objects once they reach a set age. This saves money because data usually gets colder with age, and the rules run without anyone remembering to act.

Worked example: a rule on logs/ says move to Standard-IA at 30 days, move to Glacier Flexible Retrieval at 90 days, and expire at 365 days. A log uploaded on 1 January sits in Standard and is read heavily. Around 31 January it moves to Standard-IA, so storage is cheaper but each read costs a little more. Around 1 April it moves to Glacier, cheapest of the three, but a retrieval takes minutes to hours. Around 1 January the next year it is deleted.

AWS Backup is a managed service that centralizes backups. A backup is a separate point-in-time copy you can restore from. You write a backup plan, which sets the schedule and how long copies are kept. Copies are stored in a backup vault, a protected container. The plan can cover many services, such as EBS disk volumes, RDS and Aurora databases, DynamoDB tables, EFS file systems and S3, and can copy backups to another Region or another account for disaster recovery and audit needs.

Common mistake: treating a lifecycle policy as a backup. It moves or deletes the only copy; it does not make a second one. If an expiration rule is set to 30 days instead of 365, real data disappears from a running system. Use lifecycle rules for cost and retention, and AWS Backup for recoverable copies.

questions.prompt: A veterinary clinic stores scanned patient forms in an S3 bucket under the prefix scans/. Its lifecycle rule says: transition to S3 Standard-IA at 45 days, transition to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval at 180 days, and expire at 730 days. Trace a form uploaded on 1 March. Step 1: Until about mid-April it sits in S3 Standard, where staff read it often. Step 2: Around 15 April it moves to Standard-IA, so storage gets cheaper but each read costs a little more. Step 3: Around late August, what happens? Step 4: Around 1 March two years later, the form is deleted. Which choice correctly completes Step 3?
choices: A second copy is made in Glacier while the Standard-IA copy stays as a backup
The form moves back to S3 Standard because it has not been read lately
The form moves to Glacier Flexible Retrieval: cheapest storage, slower retrieval
AWS Backup copies the form into a backup vault and removes the original
questions.why: At 180 days the transition action moves the only copy of the form to Glacier Flexible Retrieval, the cheapest tier, where retrieval can take minutes to hours, and no second copy is created.

questions.prompt: An online retailer wants daily point-in-time copies of its RDS database, its EBS disk volumes and its DynamoDB tables. It wants the copies kept for 35 days under one central schedule, and copied to a second Region for disaster recovery. Which AWS service fits this need?
choices: Moving the data into S3 Standard-IA
An S3 lifecycle rule that transitions data to Glacier
An S3 lifecycle policy with an expiration action
AWS Backup, using a backup plan and a backup vault
questions.why: AWS Backup centrally schedules and keeps separate restorable copies across services such as RDS, EBS and DynamoDB, and it can copy them to another Region, while lifecycle rules only move or delete the existing objects.

questions.prompt: A finance team adds an S3 lifecycle rule to the prefix reports/ with an expiration action set to 14 days. They believe this keeps their reports safely backed up. What actually happens to a report on day 14?
choices: It stays in place, and a copy is written to another Region
It is deleted, and no other copy exists to restore from
It is copied into a backup vault, and the original is kept
It is moved to Glacier so it can be restored later
questions.why: An expiration action deletes the only copy once the object reaches the set age, because a lifecycle policy never makes a second copy, so the reports are simply gone.

questions.prompt: A video studio keeps raw footage under the prefix raw/ in an S3 bucket. Editors use the footage heavily for about 60 days and almost never after that. The studio wants the files moved automatically to a cheaper storage tier at 60 days and deleted after 3 years, without anyone having to remember to do it. What should it use?
choices: An S3 lifecycle policy with a transition action and an expiration action
An AWS Backup plan that keeps copies for 3 years
Keeping all the footage in S3 Standard and deleting files by hand
A backup vault copied to a second AWS account
questions.why: A lifecycle policy on the raw/ prefix can automatically transition the objects to a cheaper storage class at 60 days and expire them at 3 years, which handles both cost and retention.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between an S3 lifecycle policy and AWS Backup, when you would pick each, and one limit or tradeoff of using a lifecycle policy to save money.
lessons.modelAnswer: A lifecycle policy is a set of rules on an S3 bucket that act on objects as they age. It can transition them to cheaper storage classes, like Standard-IA or Glacier, or expire them, which deletes them. I would use it for data that cools over time, like logs that are read a lot for a month and then rarely, with a deletion date to meet a retention rule. AWS Backup is a managed, central service that takes scheduled point-in-time copies across many services, such as EBS, RDS, DynamoDB, EFS and S3, keeps them in a vault, and can copy them to another Region or account. I would use it when I need to restore after deletion or corruption, or to prove backup compliance. The tradeoff with lifecycle is that colder classes cost more per read and Glacier retrieval can be slow. It also never makes a second copy, so a wrong expiration rule simply destroys data.
rubricPoints: A lifecycle policy automatically transitions S3 objects to other storage classes or expires them based on age.
Its purpose is lowering storage cost and enforcing retention without manual work.
AWS Backup centrally schedules and retains point-in-time copies across multiple AWS services in a vault.
AWS Backup supports cross-Region or cross-account copies for disaster recovery and compliance.
A lifecycle policy is not a backup; expiration deletes the only copy.
Colder storage classes trade cheaper storage for higher or slower retrieval.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests choosing between lifecycle rules, AWS Backup and near-miss options from a described need, which is best practiced by reasoning through scenarios rather than by a hands-on mission.

lessons.plain: AWS offers two kinds of artificial intelligence help. One is a workshop: Amazon SageMaker AI gives you the tools to build, train and run your own machine learning model, which is software that learns patterns from example data. The other is a shelf of ready-made tools, each already trained to do one job, such as understanding speech, reading documents, spotting objects in photos or holding a chat conversation. Amazon Lex is one of those ready-made tools; it powers chatbots. Think of baking your own bread versus buying a loaf: you bake only when no shop sells what you need.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company wants a website chat window where customers type questions and a bot asks follow-up questions to book an appointment. Would you guess they should train their own machine learning model, or use a ready-made chatbot service, and why?
lessons.teach:
AWS AI/ML services come in two layers. Machine learning (ML) means software that learns patterns from example data instead of following hand-written rules; the learned result is called a model. Amazon SageMaker AI is the build-your-own layer: a managed platform where data scientists prepare data, train a model and host it so applications can use it. You supply the data and the expertise.

Above it sit pre-trained AI services. These are ready-made models you call through an API (a request your program sends over the network), with no training needed. Each does one task. Amazon Lex builds chatbots and voice bots: it works out what a user wants, called an intent, and asks follow-up questions. Amazon Transcribe turns speech into text. Amazon Polly turns text into lifelike speech. Amazon Translate converts text between languages. Amazon Comprehend reads text for meaning, such as sentiment (positive or negative tone) and names of people or places. Amazon Rekognition analyzes images and video for objects, faces or unsafe content. Amazon Textract pulls printed and handwritten text and form fields out of scanned documents. Amazon Bedrock gives API access to foundation models, which are large general-purpose models that generate or summarize text.

Why the split works: most businesses need a common task done well, so a shared pre-trained model is cheaper and faster than training one. SageMaker AI is for problems unique to your own data.
