Worked example: a retailer wants customers to type "where is my order?" and have a bot ask for the order number. Step 1: is the core task a back-and-forth conversation? Yes, so Lex. Step 2: rule out near-misses. Transcribe only converts speech to text. Polly only speaks. Comprehend scores text but never replies. SageMaker AI could work, but it means training a model for an already-solved problem. Answer: Lex.

Common mistake: picking SageMaker AI whenever "machine learning" appears. If a pre-trained service matches the task, that is the expected answer. In a running system, the custom route means data collection, training and hosting costs before anything works, while the pre-trained service is usable on day one.

questions.prompt: A city council has 4,000 scanned paper permit applications. Each one has handwritten answers in boxes such as applicant name, street address and requested date. The council wants those answers captured automatically. Step 1: Name the core task. It is pulling handwritten text and form fields out of scanned documents. Step 2: [missing] Step 3: Rule out the near-misses. Amazon Rekognition analyzes images for objects, faces or unsafe content, not form fields. Amazon Comprehend reads text for meaning, but only after the text has already been extracted. Amazon SageMaker AI could work, but the council would have to train its own model for a problem that is already solved. Which choice correctly completes Step 2?
choices: Choose Amazon SageMaker AI, because reading handwriting requires machine learning.
Choose Amazon Comprehend, because it reads text and picks out names and places.
Choose Amazon Rekognition, because the applications are scanned images.
Choose Amazon Textract, the pre-trained service that pulls text and form fields from scanned documents.
questions.why: Textract is the pre-trained service whose one task is pulling printed and handwritten text and form fields out of scanned documents, and that is exactly the core task named in Step 1.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes a pre-trained AI service on AWS, such as Amazon Translate or Amazon Polly?
choices: A managed platform where you supply your own data, then train and host your own model.
A chatbot framework that every other AWS AI service has to be called through.
A ready-made model that performs one task, called through an API with no training needed.
A large general-purpose model that you must fine-tune before it can return any result.
questions.why: Pre-trained AI services are ready-made, single-task models that your program calls through an API (a request sent over the network), with no training step. The build-your-own platform described in the first choice is SageMaker AI.

questions.prompt: A travel booking app wants to read its written hotel descriptions aloud in a natural-sounding voice for users with low vision. Which AWS service fits this need?
choices: Amazon Polly
Amazon Lex
Amazon Translate
Amazon Transcribe
questions.why: Polly turns text into lifelike speech. Transcribe does the reverse, turning speech into text. Translate changes text from one language to another. Lex builds conversational bots, but the task here is only to speak existing text.

questions.prompt: A company wants to find the negative-toned reviews among 20,000 written product reviews. The team plans to collect labeled reviews, then train and host a custom model in Amazon SageMaker AI. What is the main problem with this plan?
choices: Amazon Comprehend would also need training on the company's reviews, so neither option is quicker.
SageMaker AI can only work with images and video, so it cannot process written reviews.
Amazon Comprehend already detects sentiment, so the custom route adds data, training and hosting costs before anything works.
Amazon Rekognition is the correct service, because it flags unsafe or negative content.
questions.why: Comprehend is a pre-trained service that already detects sentiment, which is the positive or negative tone of text, so it is usable on day one. Picking SageMaker AI for an already-solved task is the common mistake, because it means paying for data collection, training and hosting before the system works.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you decide between Amazon SageMaker AI and a pre-trained service like Amazon Lex, and name one limit or tradeoff of each choice.
lessons.modelAnswer: AWS gives us two routes. Pre-trained services such as Lex for chatbots, Transcribe for speech to text, Polly for text to speech, Rekognition for images, Comprehend for text meaning and Textract for documents are models AWS already trained; we just call them through an API. SageMaker AI is a managed platform for building, training and hosting our own model. I first ask whether the task is a common one a pre-trained service already does. If a customer chat bot is needed, Lex fits, and Polly or Transcribe would be near-misses because they only speak or only listen. The tradeoff: pre-trained services are fast and cheap to start but only do their fixed task. SageMaker AI handles problems unique to our data, but it needs training data, ML skills, time and ongoing hosting cost.
rubricPoints: States that SageMaker AI is for building, training and hosting your own model.
States that pre-trained services like Lex are ready-made and called through an API.
Correctly names Lex as the conversational chatbot service.
Distinguishes at least one near-miss such as Polly, Transcribe or Comprehend from Lex.
Names a tradeoff: pre-trained services are limited to their task, custom models cost data, skill and time.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests matching a described need to the right AI service and rejecting near-misses, which is best practiced by reasoning through short scenario questions.

lessons.plain: Analytics services help you turn piles of raw data into answers. Think of a busy kitchen: deliveries keep arriving at the back door (Amazon Kinesis catches data the moment it is produced), a prep cook cleans and labels ingredients so they can be found (AWS Glue tidies data and keeps a catalogue of what exists), the chef answers questions by pulling exactly what is needed from the shelves (Amazon Athena runs questions written in SQL, a standard query language, against stored files), and the waiter presents the finished plate (Amazon QuickSight turns results into charts and dashboards people can read).
lessons.guessPrompt: A shop already stores a year of sales records as files in cloud storage and wants to ask "which product sold most in March?" without setting up and running a database server. What kind of tool would you want: one that streams live data, one that queries files where they sit, or one that draws charts?
lessons.teach:
These four services each cover one stage of an analytics flow. Amazon Kinesis is a managed streaming service: it ingests data continuously, in near real time, such as clickstreams, app logs or sensor readings, so it can be processed within seconds instead of waiting for a nightly batch. AWS Glue is a serverless ETL service; ETL means extract, transform, load, which is pulling data out of a source, reshaping or cleaning it, and writing it somewhere useful. Glue also keeps the Glue Data Catalog, a central list describing what datasets exist and their columns, and its crawlers are jobs that scan storage to fill that catalog automatically. Serverless means AWS runs the servers and you pay for the work done. Amazon Athena is a serverless query service that runs SQL directly against files stored in Amazon S3, AWS's object storage, with no database to load or manage; you pay roughly by the amount of data each query scans. Amazon QuickSight is a business intelligence (BI) service, meaning it builds interactive dashboards and charts for people who make decisions.

Worked example: a delivery company wants a live view of late trucks. Step one, trucks send GPS readings every few seconds into Kinesis. Step two, the stream is saved to S3 as files. Step three, a Glue crawler scans those files and records their structure in the Data Catalog, and a Glue job cleans bad readings. Step four, Athena uses that catalog to answer "which routes averaged more than 10 minutes late this week?" in SQL. Step five, QuickSight charts the result for managers.

Common mistake: picking Kinesis whenever the word "data" appears. If the data already sits in S3 and the need is ad hoc questions, Athena fits; Kinesis is for data still arriving. Likewise Glue prepares and catalogs data but is not where people view charts, which is QuickSight. In a running system, careless Athena queries that scan every file on each run raise costs, which is why data is often organized so queries read less.

questions.prompt: A chain of 40 garden-supply shops uploads one sales file per shop to Amazon S3 every night. The files arrive in batches, so nothing needs processing within seconds. Step 1: the nightly files land in S3. Step 2: a Glue crawler scans the files and records their columns (store, product, date, quantity) in the Glue Data Catalog. Step 3: a Glue job fixes the mixed date formats and writes clean copies back to S3. Step 4 is missing. The data analyst needs to answer one-off SQL questions such as "Which shop sold the most watering cans in April?" directly against the cleaned files, without loading them into a database first. Which choice completes Step 4?
choices: Use Amazon Athena to run the SQL query against the files in S3, using the table structure the crawler recorded in the Data Catalog.
Run the Glue crawler again, because the crawler returns query results once it has scanned the files.
Send the cleaned files into Amazon Kinesis so the analyst can query them as they stream in.
Open Amazon QuickSight and type the SQL question there, because QuickSight is where queries against S3 files run.
questions.why: Athena is the serverless query service that runs SQL directly on files in S3 and uses the Data Catalog to know their structure, so no database needs to be loaded.

questions.prompt: In AWS Glue, what does a crawler do?
choices: It scans data in storage and fills in the Glue Data Catalog with what datasets exist and what columns they have.
It continuously takes in live data such as sensor readings and makes them available within seconds.
It runs SQL queries against files in Amazon S3 and charts you for the data scanned.
It draws interactive charts and dashboards for decision makers.
questions.why: A crawler is a Glue job that scans storage and records dataset descriptions in the Data Catalog automatically; streaming is Kinesis, charts are QuickSight, and SQL queries are Athena.

questions.prompt: A wind farm has 300 turbines that each send vibration readings every two seconds. Engineers want the readings taken in continuously so a fault can be spotted within seconds, not after a nightly batch. Which service fits the ingestion need, and why is the near-miss wrong?
choices: Amazon Athena, because it queries data as soon as any file exists; Kinesis is only for clickstreams.
Amazon QuickSight, because dashboards update live; Kinesis is only for app logs.
AWS Glue, because ETL jobs run continuously on arriving data; Kinesis only stores data in S3.
Amazon Kinesis, because it ingests continuously arriving data in near real time; Athena is for questions about data already sitting in S3.
questions.why: Kinesis is the managed streaming service for data still arriving that must be processed within seconds, while Athena answers ad hoc queries about data already stored in S3.

questions.prompt: A media company's Athena bill keeps climbing. Each time analysts ask about a single day of viewing logs, their queries read every log file the company has ever stored in S3. What is the most sensible fix?
choices: Move the logs into Amazon Kinesis, because streaming data costs nothing to query.
Rebuild the reports in Amazon QuickSight, because dashboards remove the charge for scanning data.
Run the Glue crawler every hour, because a fresher Data Catalog makes Athena scan fewer files on its own.
Organize the data in S3 so that each query only needs to read the files relevant to the question, which lowers the data scanned.
questions.why: Athena charges roughly by the amount of data each query scans, so organizing data so queries read fewer files directly reduces cost.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, in your own words, how Kinesis, Glue, Athena and QuickSight differ and fit together, and name one limit or tradeoff, for example when Athena is the wrong choice or what drives its cost.
lessons.modelAnswer: They are four stages of one pipeline. Kinesis is for data that is still arriving: it collects streams like clicks or sensor readings in near real time. Glue is the preparation stage: it runs serverless extract-transform-load jobs to clean and reshape data, and its Data Catalog, filled by crawlers, records what datasets exist and their columns. Athena answers questions with SQL directly against files in S3, with no database server to run. QuickSight turns results into dashboards for business users. A tradeoff: Athena charges by data scanned, so querying huge unorganized files repeatedly gets expensive, and it is meant for analysis, not as the live database behind an application. Also, if data already sits in S3 and nobody needs second-by-second updates, adding Kinesis is unnecessary complexity.
rubricPoints: Kinesis ingests and processes streaming data in near real time.
Glue performs serverless ETL and maintains a Data Catalog, filled by crawlers.
Athena runs serverless SQL queries directly on data in S3 without managing a database.
QuickSight is the BI service for dashboards and visualizations.
Names a tradeoff, such as Athena cost driven by data scanned or Kinesis being unnecessary for data already at rest.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests matching a described need to the right analytics service versus its near-miss, which is best practiced by reasoning through scenario questions.

lessons.plain: Application integration means letting separate pieces of software pass work and news to each other without being tightly wired together. AWS offers three main tools. Amazon SQS is a managed queue: like a ticket rail in a restaurant kitchen, orders wait in line until a cook is free to take one. Amazon SNS is a managed notification service: like a group text, one message goes out to every subscriber at once. Amazon EventBridge is a managed event router: like a mailroom clerk who reads each envelope and sends it to the right department based on rules. All three let parts of a system fail, slow down or grow without breaking each other.
lessons.guessPrompt: An online shop's checkout sometimes gets 50 times its normal orders in a minute, and the payment-processing program can only handle a few per second. If you could put something between checkout and payments, what would you want it to do with the extra orders?
lessons.teach:
Decoupling means building parts of a system so they do not call each other directly; a service in the middle carries the messages. A message is a small piece of data describing work or news. The sender is the producer; the receiver is the consumer.

Amazon SQS (Simple Queue Service) is a managed queue: producers drop messages in, and messages wait, stored durably, until a consumer pulls one, processes it and deletes it. Each message is handled by one consumer. This absorbs bursts, because a slow or offline consumer simply works through the backlog later.

Amazon SNS (Simple Notification Service) is managed publish/subscribe. A producer publishes to a topic, a named channel, and SNS pushes a copy immediately to every subscriber: queues, functions, email addresses, phone numbers or web endpoints. This is called fan-out: one message, many receivers.

Amazon EventBridge is a managed event bus. An event is a record that something happened, from your apps, AWS services or software-as-a-service partners. Rules match events by their content and send each one to chosen targets. It also supports schedules. Pick it when routing depends on what the event says.

Worked example: a customer places an order. Step 1, checkout publishes "order placed" to an SNS topic. Step 2, SNS fans out copies to the shipping queue, the email service and the analytics queue. Step 3, the shipping queue in SQS holds the copy until the warehouse program is free, so a surge just lengthens the queue. Had the shop needed "send only orders over 1,000 dollars to fraud review", an EventBridge rule filtering on order amount would fit.

Common mistake: choosing SNS when the receiver might be busy or down. SNS pushes and moves on; it is not a place for work to wait to be picked up. In a running system that is how work goes missing. Buffering work for later means SQS, and pairing SNS with SQS gives both fan-out and buffering.

questions.prompt: A video-sharing site, ClipHarbor, must react when a user uploads a video. Thumbnails must be made right away, and the video must also be converted into smaller formats by a pool of conversion servers that are often busy for several minutes at a time. Step 1: the upload service publishes a "video uploaded" message to an Amazon SNS topic (a named publish/subscribe channel). Step 2: SNS pushes a copy at once to each subscriber, which here are a thumbnail function and an Amazon SQS queue for conversion work. Step 3: ??? Step 4: on a busy evening, 4,000 uploads arrive in an hour, the conversion queue grows long, and the servers clear the backlog overnight without losing any work. Which statement correctly fills in Step 3?
choices: The SQS queue sends a copy of each message to every conversion server, so all servers convert every video together.
The SQS queue stores the message durably until one conversion server pulls it, converts the video, then deletes the message.
An EventBridge rule holds the message and checks its content until it decides a conversion server has become available.
SNS keeps the message on the topic and keeps pushing it until a conversion server finally has free capacity to accept it.
questions.why: SQS is the managed queue where messages wait until a single consumer pulls, processes and deletes each one, which is what lets the backlog be worked through later.

questions.prompt: A hospital's lab system emits an event every time a test result is ready, about 20,000 a day. Only results whose content is marked "critical" should be sent to the on-call doctor's paging system; everything else goes to a records archive. Which AWS service fits this routing need best?
choices: Amazon SQS, because a queue stores every result until the pager pulls it
Amazon SNS, because a topic pushes every result to every subscriber at once
Amazon EventBridge, because rules can match events on their content and send each to chosen targets
Amazon SQS paired with SNS, because fan-out plus buffering covers routing
questions.why: EventBridge is the managed event bus whose rules filter on what the event says, so only "critical" results reach the pager while SNS and SQS do not route by content on their own.

questions.prompt: A concert-ticket website receives about 30,000 purchase requests in the first minute of a big sale, but its payment program can only process about 600 per minute. Each purchase must be processed exactly once by one payment worker, and none may be lost. Which service should sit between the website and the payment program?
choices: Amazon EventBridge, so a schedule runs the payment program once per minute
Amazon SNS, so each purchase is pushed immediately to every payment worker
Amazon SQS, so purchases wait in a durable queue until a worker pulls each one
Amazon SNS with an email subscription, so staff can process overflow by hand
questions.why: SQS absorbs the burst by holding messages durably until a single consumer pulls and processes each one, so the slower payment program works through the backlog without losing any.

questions.prompt: A payroll team connects its timesheet app directly to an Amazon SNS topic, with the payroll calculation server subscribed as a web endpoint. The server is switched off for maintenance every night from midnight to 3 a.m., and timesheets submitted during those hours are never processed. What is the best explanation and fix?
choices: SNS cannot send to web endpoints; replace it with an EventBridge schedule that delivers timesheets each night at midnight.
SNS sends each message to only one subscriber; switch to SQS fan-out so that every server receives its own copy.
SNS pushes and moves on rather than holding work; subscribe an SQS queue to the topic so timesheets wait until the server pulls them.
SNS stores messages only for a short time; add more web endpoints so that at least one copy is delivered during maintenance.
questions.why: SNS is not a place for work to wait, so an offline receiver misses messages, and pairing SNS with an SQS queue adds the buffering that holds timesheets until the server is back.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose between SQS, SNS and EventBridge for a new feature, and name one thing each one is not good at.
lessons.modelAnswer: All three decouple producers from consumers, so one part can slow down or fail without dragging the others down. I pick SQS when work needs to wait in line: it stores messages until a consumer pulls them, which smooths bursts, but each message goes to one consumer, so it is not a broadcast tool. I pick SNS when one message must reach many receivers at once; it pushes copies to every subscriber of a topic, but it does not hold work for a consumer that is offline, so I put an SQS queue behind it when work must not be lost. I pick EventBridge when events from my apps, AWS services or partners need routing by their content, using rules that send matching events to targets, or when I need a schedule. Its tradeoff is that it is a router, not a buffer, so it also often pairs with a queue.
rubricPoints: States that all three decouple parts of a system so they do not call each other directly.
Describes SQS as a queue that holds messages until one consumer pulls and processes each.
Describes SNS as publish/subscribe that pushes one message to many subscribers (fan-out).
Describes EventBridge as an event bus that routes events by content using rules, including from AWS services and partners.
Names a limit, such as SNS not storing work for offline consumers or SQS not broadcasting.
Mentions combining services, such as SNS fanning out into SQS queues.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests telling three near-miss services apart from a described need, so reasoning through short scenarios that force a choice and a rejection builds the skill best.

lessons.plain: Some AWS services are not building blocks for engineers but ready-made business tools. Amazon Connect is a cloud contact center: a company uses it to run a customer phone and chat help desk without buying phone hardware, routing callers to available agents and paying only for the minutes used. Amazon SES (Simple Email Service) is a managed email-sending service: an application hands it messages such as receipts, password resets or newsletters, and SES delivers them at scale. Think of Connect as renting a fully staffed switchboard room, and SES as hiring a postal service for your app's letters.
lessons.guessPrompt: A small online shop wants customers to be able to phone a support line and reach whichever agent is free, without installing any phone equipment. It also wants its website to automatically email an order receipt after each purchase. Would you guess the same AWS service handles both jobs, or two different ones? Why?
lessons.teach:
Amazon Connect is a cloud-based contact center service. A contact center is the system a business uses to handle customer phone calls and chats: answering, playing menus, queuing callers and routing them to human agents. With Connect, an administrator claims a phone number, designs a contact flow (the scripted path a caller follows, such as 'press 1 for billing'), and agents answer from a web browser. It is pay-as-you-go, billed by usage minutes, so there is no switchboard hardware or long telephony contract.

Amazon SES (Simple Email Service) is a managed service for sending email from applications. Transactional email is a one-to-one message triggered by an event (a receipt or password reset); marketing email is a bulk campaign. SES handles both at high volume and can also receive incoming mail. AWS runs the mail servers and helps protect sender reputation, the trust score mailbox providers use to decide whether your mail lands in the inbox or spam.

Why this works: both remove undifferentiated heavy lifting. Running phone switching or mail servers yourself is costly and specialised; renting them as a managed service lets a team focus on its customers.

Worked example: a customer buys shoes. Step 1, the store's application calls SES with the receipt text and customer address. Step 2, SES sends the email. Step 3, the shoes are late, so the customer phones the support number. Step 4, Connect answers, plays the contact flow menu, and routes the call to a free agent's browser. Two needs, two services.

Common mistake: choosing Amazon SNS (Simple Notification Service) for customer email. SNS is a publish-subscribe messaging service that fans one message out to many subscribers, and while it can send plain notification emails, it is not built for formatted, branded customer email at volume. If the need is 'send email from my app', the answer is SES. Likewise, a voice or chat help desk with human agents points to Connect, not to a chatbot service alone.

In a running system, picking the near-miss means rebuilding features the right service gives for free, such as call queuing or email deliverability controls.

questions.prompt: A veterinary clinic chain with 12 branches wants two things handled on AWS without buying mail servers or phone hardware. Here is the plan, step by step. Step 1: when a pet's vaccination is due in 7 days, the clinic's booking application calls Amazon SES (Simple Email Service, a managed service for sending email from applications) with the reminder text and the owner's address. Step 2: SES sends the transactional email, a one-to-one message triggered by an event. Step 3: the owner wants to change the time, so they phone the clinic's support number. Step 4: ______. Which choice correctly completes Step 4?
choices: Amazon Connect answers on the claimed number, plays the contact flow menu and routes the caller to a free agent's browser
Amazon SNS publishes the incoming call to every subscribed staff member at the same moment
Amazon SES receives the phone call, turns it into an email and places it in a shared inbox for clinic staff
A chatbot service alone answers the call and closes it without ever involving a human receptionist
questions.why: A voice help desk with menus, queuing and routing to human agents is the job of Amazon Connect, a cloud contact center service, not of an email or publish-subscribe messaging service.

questions.prompt: An administrator setting up Amazon Connect for an insurance company builds a 'contact flow'. What is a contact flow?
choices: The scripted path a caller follows, such as a menu saying 'press 2 for claims'
A list of subscribers that receives a copy of every published message
The trust score mailbox providers use to decide inbox or spam
A bulk email campaign sent to every policyholder at once
questions.why: In a contact center (the system that answers, queues and routes customer calls and chats), a contact flow is the scripted path a caller follows through menus to the right agent.

questions.prompt: An online ticketing startup needs its application to send about 150,000 branded, formatted emails a day: order confirmations, password resets and a weekly promotional newsletter. It wants AWS to run the mail servers and help keep the emails out of spam folders. Which service fits best?
choices: Amazon Connect, because it handles customer communications through agents
A chatbot service, because it can reply to customers automatically
Amazon SES, because it is a managed service for sending transactional and marketing email from applications at volume
Amazon SNS, because it fans one message out to many subscribers
questions.why: Sending formatted, branded email from an application at high volume, both one-to-one transactional and bulk marketing, is exactly what Amazon SES is built for, with deliverability support included.

questions.prompt: A furniture retailer sends its order receipts through a messaging setup that has no deliverability controls, and over a few weeks more of its customers' receipts start landing in spam folders. Which idea best explains what is going wrong and what the near-miss choice costs them?
choices: Their publish-subscribe topic has too many subscribers, so every message is marked as a duplicate
Their sender reputation, the trust score mailbox providers use to place mail in the inbox or spam, is suffering, and without a service like SES they must rebuild deliverability features themselves
Their contact flow is too long, so customers hang up before reaching an agent
Their pay-as-you-go usage minutes have run out, so mail is downgraded to spam
questions.why: Whether email reaches the inbox depends on sender reputation, and picking a service not built for customer email means rebuilding the deliverability controls Amazon SES provides.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, in your own words, when you would pick Amazon Connect and when you would pick Amazon SES, and name one near-miss service someone might wrongly choose and why it falls short.
lessons.modelAnswer: Both are managed business applications, so we rent the capability instead of running hardware or servers. Amazon Connect is a cloud contact center: we get phone numbers and chat, design contact flows like 'press 1 for billing', queue callers, and route them to agents who work from a browser, paying per usage minute. Amazon SES is for sending email from our application, such as receipts and password resets or bulk marketing campaigns, and AWS runs the mail infrastructure and helps protect our sender reputation so mail reaches inboxes. The near-miss is Amazon SNS: it is pub-sub messaging that fans one message out to subscribers, and although it can send basic notification emails, it is not the tool for formatted customer email at scale, so 'app sends customer email' means SES. The tradeoff is less control: we work within each service's features and pricing rather than customising our own phone or mail system.
rubricPoints: Amazon Connect is a cloud contact center for customer calls and chat routed to agents.
Amazon SES is a managed service for sending application email, transactional or bulk.
Both are pay-as-you-go managed services that remove hardware or server management.
SNS is a near-miss for email because it is pub-sub notification, not customer email delivery.
Names a tradeoff, such as less customisation in exchange for not running the infrastructure.

suggested.rationale: This objective is about recognising which catalogue service fits a described business need, which is best learned by reading clear definitions and near-miss contrasts rather than a hands-on lab.

lessons.plain: These three AWS services help teams ship software and understand it once it is running. AWS CodeBuild is a managed build service: it takes your source code, compiles it, runs your tests, and packages the result. AWS CodePipeline is a release orchestrator: it moves each code change through a series of steps, from new code to tested build to deployed application. AWS X-Ray is a tracing service: it follows a single user request as it hops between parts of your application and shows where time was spent. Think of a car factory. CodeBuild is one workstation, CodePipeline is the assembly line connecting the workstations, and X-Ray is a tracker that follows one finished car on the road.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your web app is built from five small services that call each other, and users say checkout is slow. Which would help you more: a tool that shows the total CPU use of each server, or a tool that follows one checkout request through every service and times each hop? Why?
lessons.teach:
AWS CodeBuild is a managed build service. A build is the step that turns source code into something runnable: compiling it, running automated tests, and producing an artifact, the packaged output such as a zip file or container image. Managed means AWS runs the build machines for you, starts them on demand, and bills by the build minutes you use, so you keep no idle build servers.

AWS CodePipeline is a continuous delivery service. Continuous delivery means every code change automatically flows through the same ordered stages, typically source, build, test, and deploy, so releases are repeatable instead of manual. CodePipeline does not compile anything itself; it orchestrates, passing work to other tools such as CodeBuild for the build stage.

AWS X-Ray is a distributed tracing service. A trace is the recorded journey of one request across many components, with the time spent in each. This matters when an application is split into microservices, small services that call one another over the network.

Worked example. A developer pushes a change to the code repository. Step one: CodePipeline notices the new commit in its source stage. Step two: it hands the code to CodeBuild, which compiles it and runs the tests; all pass, so an artifact is produced. Step three: CodePipeline moves the artifact to its deploy stage and the new version goes live. Step four: users report slow checkouts. The team opens X-Ray, sees a trace where the checkout service waits three seconds on the payment service, and knows exactly where to look.

Common mistake: swapping these up with near-miss services. Amazon CloudWatch collects metrics, logs, and alarms, telling you that something is slow or failing, but X-Ray shows which hop inside a request is slow. Likewise, if a question describes compiling and testing, the answer is CodeBuild; if it describes automating the whole release flow end to end, the answer is CodePipeline.

questions.prompt: A parcel-tracking company runs its website as several microservices (small services that call one another over the network). A CloudWatch alarm fires because the average response time of the 'where is my parcel' page has risen from 200 milliseconds to 1.8 seconds. Here is how the team works through it. Step 1: The CloudWatch alarm tells them that the page is slow, but not which part of a request is causing it. Step 2: [missing]. Step 3: They see that the route-calculation service spends 1.5 seconds waiting on the map-lookup service, so they focus their fix there. Which action is the missing Step 2?
choices: Rerun the CodeBuild project so the route-calculation code is compiled and tested again
Open AWS X-Ray and inspect the trace of one slow request to see the time spent in each service
Check the CodePipeline stage history to find which deploy stage ran slowly
Add another CloudWatch metric that records the page's total response time every minute
questions.why: X-Ray records a trace of one request's journey across services, with the time spent in each, which is exactly what reveals the slow hop that CloudWatch alone cannot pinpoint.

questions.prompt: AWS CodeBuild is described as a managed build service. What does 'managed' mean here?
choices: You rent a dedicated build server for a fixed monthly fee and install your own compilers on it
It records how long each microservice takes while handling a single request
AWS runs the build machines for you, starts them when a build is needed, and bills by the build minutes used, so you keep no idle build servers
It arranges the order of release stages and passes each change to other tools
questions.why: Managed means AWS operates the build machines on demand and charges only for the build minutes you consume.

questions.prompt: A payroll software company has 12 developers. Every Friday, one of them copies files to the servers by hand, and releases often go wrong. The company wants every merged change to flow automatically through the same ordered stages (source, build, test, deploy) so releases are repeatable. Which AWS service fits this need?
choices: AWS CodeBuild
AWS CodePipeline
AWS X-Ray
Amazon CloudWatch
questions.why: CodePipeline is the continuous delivery service that automates the whole release flow end to end through ordered stages. CodeBuild only handles the build step, which is compiling and testing.

questions.prompt: An architect proposes using AWS CodePipeline on its own to compile the company's code and run its automated tests, with no other tool attached to the build stage. What is wrong with this plan?
choices: AWS X-Ray must be added to CodePipeline before any code can be compiled
CodePipeline does not compile or test anything itself; it orchestrates the stages and hands that work to a build service such as CodeBuild
CodePipeline compiles code but cannot run tests, so Amazon CloudWatch has to run them
CodePipeline can only release container images, so it cannot work with compiled code
questions.why: CodePipeline orchestrates the release flow. Compiling, testing and producing an artifact is the job of a build service like CodeBuild.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what CodeBuild, CodePipeline, and X-Ray each do and how they fit together, and name one thing each one does not do so they don't pick the wrong service.
lessons.modelAnswer: CodeBuild is a managed build service: it compiles our code, runs our tests, and produces an artifact, and we pay only for build minutes instead of keeping build servers idle. CodePipeline is the release conveyor belt: whenever we push a change, it runs the same stages in order, source, build, test, deploy, and calls CodeBuild for the build step. The catch is that CodePipeline orchestrates but does not compile anything, and CodeBuild builds but does not decide the release order. X-Ray is for after the code is live: it traces one request across our microservices and times each hop, so we can see which service is slow. It is not a general metrics and alarms tool; that is CloudWatch, which tells us something is wrong but not which hop in the request caused it.
rubricPoints: CodeBuild compiles code, runs tests, and produces artifacts as a managed, pay-per-use service.
CodePipeline orchestrates the ordered release stages and delegates the build work rather than doing it.
X-Ray traces individual requests across services to find where latency or errors occur.
Distinguishes X-Ray from CloudWatch, which handles metrics, logs, and alarms.
Shows how the pieces connect: pipeline calls build, then tracing helps after deployment.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests picking the right developer tool from a described need versus near misses like CloudWatch, so reasoning through scenario questions builds the matching skill best.

lessons.plain: End-user computing means giving people the screens and tools they work with from the cloud, instead of installing everything on each laptop. The work runs on AWS computers; the person's own device just shows pictures of it and sends back clicks and keystrokes. Think of it like streaming a film instead of owning the disc. AWS offers three levels. Amazon WorkSpaces streams a whole desktop. Amazon AppStream 2.0 streams just one or a few applications. WorkSpaces Secure Browser streams only a web browser. Choosing well means asking how much the user actually needs.
lessons.guessPrompt: A design studio wants freelancers to use one expensive 3D modelling program for a month, through a web browser, without ever getting a full company desktop. Would you give them a complete virtual desktop, a streamed single application, or a locked-down browser, and why?
lessons.teach:
End-user computing is delivering a user's working environment from servers in the cloud. The processing and data stay in AWS, and the user's device (a laptop, thin client or tablet) only receives a video-like stream of the screen and sends input back. Because data never has to live on the device, a lost laptop leaks little, and IT can update one central image instead of hundreds of machines.

Amazon WorkSpaces is a managed virtual desktop service, sometimes called desktop as a service. Each user gets a full Windows or Linux desktop that is usually persistent, meaning their files, settings and installed tools are still there tomorrow. It replaces a physical office PC.

Amazon AppStream 2.0 is a managed application streaming service. Instead of a whole desktop, users open specific applications, often in a browser, that run on a shared pool of cloud machines called a fleet. Sessions are typically non-persistent: when a user logs off, that machine is reset for the next person. It suits giving many people temporary access to one demanding program.

WorkSpaces Secure Browser is a managed, isolated web browser. Users reach internal websites and software-as-a-service tools (applications delivered over the web) through a browser that runs in AWS, so nothing from those sites is stored on the device.

Worked example: a company hires 50 contractors for three months. Step one, ask what they need. They only use the company's internal web portal and a hosted ticketing tool. Step two, rule out a full desktop: WorkSpaces would be more than they need. Step three, rule out application streaming: there is no installed program to stream. Step four, choose WorkSpaces Secure Browser.

A common mistake is reaching for WorkSpaces whenever you hear "remote access." If the need is one application, AppStream 2.0 is the better fit; if it is only websites, the secure browser is. Over-provisioning full desktops means paying for and patching environments nobody uses fully.

questions.prompt: A university runs a 12-week engineering course. Its 180 students need one heavy 3D modelling program that is normally installed on lab PCs. They need nothing else, and nobody needs to keep a personal setup between sessions. Step one: the need is a single installed program, used temporarily by many people. Step two: rule out WorkSpaces Secure Browser, because this is an installed program, not a website. Step three: [missing]. Step four: choose Amazon AppStream 2.0, which streams that one program from a shared fleet. What is step three?
choices: Rule out cloud delivery entirely, because demanding programs must run on the student's own device.
Rule out AppStream 2.0, because its sessions reset at log off and students would lose their work.
Choose WorkSpaces, because any remote access to a demanding program calls for a virtual desktop.
Rule out WorkSpaces, because a full, usually persistent desktop for each student is more than they need.
questions.why: The students need one program, not a whole persistent desktop each, so WorkSpaces would be over-provisioning and is ruled out before AppStream 2.0 is chosen.

questions.prompt: A small accounting firm is retiring the 25 office PCs its staff use every day. Each accountant needs a complete Windows desktop, and their files, settings and installed tools must still be there when they log in the next morning. Which service fits best?
choices: Amazon AppStream 2.0
A shared fleet that resets at log off
WorkSpaces Secure Browser
Amazon WorkSpaces
questions.why: WorkSpaces is a managed virtual desktop service that gives each user a full, usually persistent desktop, which is exactly a replacement for an office PC.

questions.prompt: A retail chain gives 300 seasonal store staff full Amazon WorkSpaces desktops, but the staff only ever open a web-based rota tool and an online training site. What is the main problem with this choice?
choices: WorkSpaces stores all data on the staff's own devices, so it is less secure.
AppStream 2.0 would have been the right choice, because it streams websites.
The chain pays for and patches full desktops nobody uses fully; a secure browser fits.
Desktops cannot reach websites, so the staff cannot open either tool.
questions.why: When the need is only websites, WorkSpaces Secure Browser fits, and full desktops mean paying for and maintaining environments that go largely unused.

questions.prompt: A field engineer reaches all of her work tools through end-user computing on a tablet, and the tablet is stolen. Why does this usually leak little company data?
choices: The processing and data stay in AWS, and the tablet only receives a stream of the screen.
End-user computing deletes the tablet's data when it is reported stolen.
The tablet keeps an encrypted copy of every file that only IT can unlock.
Her desktop image is updated centrally, which also wipes the lost device.
questions.why: In end-user computing the work runs and the data lives on cloud servers, so the device holds only a video-like stream and little to leak.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate asks why we would not just give everyone an Amazon WorkSpaces desktop. Explain in your own words how WorkSpaces, AppStream 2.0 and WorkSpaces Secure Browser differ, and name one tradeoff or limit that should steer the choice.
lessons.modelAnswer: All three keep the real work and data in AWS and just stream the screen to the user's device, so a lost laptop holds little and IT updates things centrally. The difference is scope. WorkSpaces gives each person a full, usually persistent Windows or Linux desktop, like a cloud office PC. AppStream 2.0 streams only specific applications from a shared fleet, and sessions are typically reset when the user logs off, which fits lots of temporary users of one program. WorkSpaces Secure Browser streams just an isolated web browser for internal sites and web-based tools. The tradeoff is that a full desktop is the most flexible but also the most to pay for and maintain; if someone only needs one app or a few websites, giving them a whole desktop wastes money and widens what you must secure. Match the service to the smallest thing the user actually needs.
rubricPoints: States that all three run in AWS and stream the screen, keeping data off the user's device.
Describes WorkSpaces as a full, usually persistent virtual desktop.
Describes AppStream 2.0 as streaming specific applications, typically non-persistent, from a shared fleet.
Describes WorkSpaces Secure Browser as an isolated browser for internal websites and web-based tools.
Names a tradeoff such as a full desktop costing and exposing more than a single app or browser needs.

suggested.rationale: No mission or planned engine covers virtual desktops, and the exam tests this by giving a user need and asking you to pick the right service over its near-miss neighbours, so reasoning through scenarios teaches it best.

lessons.plain: Two AWS services help you build the parts of a system that people and machines touch directly. AWS Amplify is a toolkit plus a hosting service for building web and mobile apps: it gives the app sign-in, data and file storage, and puts the website online, without you running servers. AWS IoT Core is a managed meeting point for connected devices, such as sensors, meters or smart locks. They connect, send readings to the cloud and receive commands back. Think of Amplify as the shop front customers walk into, and IoT Core as the loading dock where machines check in.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company has 50,000 temperature sensors in refrigerated trucks that must send a reading every minute, plus a phone app that drivers use to view those readings. Which part would you expect needs a service built for managing huge numbers of small machines, and which part needs a service for building an app people use?
lessons.teach:
AWS Amplify is a set of tools and a managed hosting service for the frontend, meaning the part of an application a person sees and touches, either a website or a mobile app on a phone. Amplify connects that frontend to common backend features (the server-side parts), such as user sign-in, a data store and file storage, and it can build and publish a website every time developers save new code. It works because most apps need the same few building blocks, so Amplify supplies them ready-made instead of making a small team assemble servers.

AWS IoT Core is a managed service for the Internet of Things (IoT), meaning physical devices with sensors and a network connection. Each device gets its own identity, usually a digital certificate, so the service knows exactly which device is talking. Devices send small messages, often using MQTT, a lightweight messaging protocol suited to weak networks and low-power hardware. IoT Core receives the messages and uses rules, which are instructions saying where each kind of message should go, to forward data to other AWS services such as a database or storage. It can also send commands back to devices.

Worked example: a refrigerated-truck company. Step 1: a sensor in truck 412 connects to IoT Core using its certificate. Step 2: it publishes a message saying 3 degrees. Step 3: a rule forwards that reading to a database. Step 4: the drivers' phone app, built and hosted with Amplify, signs the driver in and shows the reading. Step 5: if the temperature climbs, a command goes back through IoT Core to the truck.

Common mistake: choosing Amplify because the question says mobile, when the real need is connecting many machines. A phone app used by a person is an Amplify job; a fleet of sensors reporting on their own is an IoT Core job. Picking wrongly in a real system means devices without individual identities and no efficient way to handle millions of tiny messages, which leaves you with a security weakness and a scaling problem.

questions.prompt: A vineyard installs 800 soil-moisture probes across its fields. Here is how one reading travels. Step 1: probe 57 connects to AWS IoT Core (a managed service for networked physical devices) using its own digital certificate. Step 2: it publishes a small MQTT message (MQTT is a lightweight messaging protocol suited to weak networks) saying 18 percent moisture. Step 3: missing. Step 4: the vineyard manager opens a website built and hosted with AWS Amplify (a managed service for app frontends), signs in, and sees the stored reading. Step 5: when moisture drops too low, a command goes back through IoT Core to open an irrigation valve. Which choice correctly completes Step 3?
choices: Amplify rebuilds and republishes the manager's website so that the new reading is written into the site's code.
An IoT Core rule, which says where this kind of message should go, forwards the moisture reading to a database.
Probe 57 signs in through Amplify's user sign-in feature so that the service can tell which probe sent the reading.
The manager's website receives the MQTT message straight from the probe and keeps it without any AWS service in between.
questions.why: IoT Core uses rules to forward incoming device messages to other AWS services, such as a database, where the Amplify-hosted website can later read and display them.

questions.prompt: A city library has two developers. They want a website and a phone app where members sign in, reserve books and upload profile photos, and they want the website republished automatically every time they save new code. They do not want to assemble servers themselves. Which AWS service fits best?
choices: AWS IoT Core, because each member needs their own digital certificate to connect
AWS Amplify for the website only, with AWS IoT Core needed for the phone app
AWS Amplify, because it hosts the frontend and supplies sign-in and storage ready-made
AWS IoT Core, because members will connect to it from their mobile phones
questions.why: This is a person-facing website and mobile app needing sign-in, file storage and automatic publishing, which is exactly what Amplify (frontend tools and managed hosting) provides.

questions.prompt: In AWS IoT Core, why is each connected device usually given its own digital certificate?
choices: So Amplify can rebuild the website whenever a device changes its settings
So the device can sign a person in to a phone app on their behalf
So the service knows exactly which individual device is sending each message
So the device can send larger messages than MQTT would normally allow
questions.why: The certificate is the device's individual identity, letting IoT Core know precisely which device is talking.

questions.prompt: A wind-farm operator has 50,000 turbine sensors, each reporting a tiny reading every few seconds with no person involved. Because the maintenance crew uses a phone app, an engineer proposes handling the sensors with AWS Amplify instead of AWS IoT Core. What is the likely consequence for the running system?
choices: The sensors would lack individual identities and there would be no efficient way to handle millions of tiny messages
The crew's phone app could no longer be hosted, because Amplify can only serve websites
The sensors would gain stronger security, because Amplify gives every sensor a certificate
Nothing important changes, because the two services do the same job for any networked machine
questions.why: A fleet of self-reporting sensors is an IoT Core job; using Amplify instead leaves devices without individual identities and no efficient handling of huge numbers of small messages, creating a security weakness and a scaling problem.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide between AWS Amplify and AWS IoT Core when a requirement mentions apps or devices, and name one thing each service does not do for you.
lessons.modelAnswer: I ask who is on the other end. If it is a person using a website or phone app, that is Amplify: it gives the frontend ready-made sign-in, data and file storage, and hosts and republishes the site when code changes. If it is a machine, such as a sensor, meter or lock, sending readings on its own, that is IoT Core: each device gets its own identity, sends small messages over a light protocol like MQTT, and rules forward those messages to other services, with commands able to flow back. Many systems use both, devices into IoT Core and people viewing results in an Amplify app. The limits: Amplify is not built to manage thousands of devices or their per-device certificates, and IoT Core does not build or host a user interface. It also only routes data, so you still need a separate place to store and analyse it.
rubricPoints: Amplify builds, connects and hosts web and mobile frontends used by people.
IoT Core securely connects large numbers of physical devices to the cloud.
Each IoT device has its own identity and sends small messages, often over MQTT.
IoT Core rules route device messages to other services and commands can go back to devices.
The deciding question is whether a person or a machine is the client.
Names a limit, such as Amplify not managing device fleets or IoT Core not providing a user interface or storage.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests this by describing a need and offering near-miss services, so reasoning through scenario questions that mix apps and devices builds the right instinct best.

lessons.plain: When you rent virtual servers in AWS, you choose not only the server size but also how you pay for it. AWS offers several purchasing options. You can pay by the second with no promise, commit to a year or three for a discount, bid for spare capacity that may be taken back, rent a whole physical machine for yourself, or hold capacity in reserve. It is like getting to work: pay a taxi fare each trip, buy an annual train pass, grab cheap standby seats that can be cancelled, or lease a private car.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a cloud provider has spare servers sitting idle, why might it rent them to you at a very deep discount, and what catch would you expect in return?
lessons.teach:
A purchasing option is the billing model for compute, meaning virtual servers (Amazon EC2 instances). The server is the same in each case; price, commitment and guarantees change.

On-Demand: pay per second or hour with no commitment. It is the most flexible and the most expensive per hour. Reserved Instances (RIs): a 1-year or 3-year commitment to a specific instance configuration in exchange for a large discount. Savings Plans: a 1-year or 3-year commitment to spend a fixed amount per hour on compute. You get a similar discount, but it applies more flexibly. Compute Savings Plans also cover AWS Fargate (managed containers) and AWS Lambda (serverless functions). Spot Instances: AWS's unused capacity at up to roughly 90% off. AWS can reclaim it after a two-minute warning, so the work must tolerate interruption. Dedicated Hosts: an entire physical server reserved for you. You can see its sockets and cores, which matters for software licenses counted per core and for strict compliance. Dedicated Instances: your instances run on hardware no other customer uses, but you do not control or see the physical host. Capacity Reservations: hold capacity in one specific Availability Zone (an isolated data center group) with no long-term term. You pay the On-Demand rate whether or not you use it.

Worked example with made-up prices. A server costs 10 credits per hour On-Demand and runs all 8,760 hours of a year, so the cost is 87,600 credits. A 1-year commitment at 40% off gives 6 credits per hour, or 52,560 credits, which saves 35,040. If the server instead ran only 2,000 hours, On-Demand would cost 20,000. The commitment still costs 52,560, so it would lose money.

Common mistake: treating a Capacity Reservation as a discount. It guarantees that capacity is available but saves nothing by itself; you would combine it with a Savings Plan or RI for that. Another mistake is running a critical database on Spot. When AWS reclaims the capacity, the database stops.

questions.prompt:
A design studio runs one rendering server. It costs 5 credits per hour On-Demand and will run 6,000 hours this year. The studio is offered a 1-year commitment at 30% off.

Step 1: On-Demand cost = 5 x 6,000 = 30,000 credits.
Step 2: Committed hourly rate = 5 x 0.70 = 3.5 credits per hour.
Step 3: (missing) Find the yearly cost of the commitment.
Step 4: Compare the two costs. The commitment costs 660 credits more, so the studio should stay On-Demand.

What is the correct Step 3?
choices: 5 x 8,760 = 43,800 credits, because a commitment is billed at the full rate for the year
30,000 x 0.30 = 9,000 credits, because the discount is the amount you pay
3.5 x 6,000 = 21,000 credits, because you pay only for the hours the server runs
3.5 x 8,760 = 30,660 credits, because the commitment is paid for every hour of the year
questions.why: A 1-year commitment is paid for all 8,760 hours of the year at the discounted rate, whether or not the server runs, so it costs 3.5 x 8,760 = 30,660 credits.

questions.prompt: A hospital runs a database product that is licensed per physical CPU core. Its auditors also want proof of exactly which physical server hosts the workload. Which EC2 purchasing option fits?
choices: Dedicated Hosts
Capacity Reservations
Spot Instances
Dedicated Instances
questions.why: Only Dedicated Hosts reserve a whole physical server for you and let you see its sockets and cores, which per-core licensing and strict compliance need.

questions.prompt: A retailer has a steady compute spend that it expects to keep for three years. The spend is split across EC2 virtual servers, AWS Fargate (managed containers) and AWS Lambda (serverless functions), and the mix keeps shifting. Which option gives a large discount that covers all three?
choices: Spot Instances for all three services
A Compute Savings Plan with a fixed hourly spend commitment
On-Demand pricing with no commitment
Reserved Instances for one specific instance configuration
questions.why: A Compute Savings Plan commits to a fixed hourly compute spend, and its discount applies flexibly across EC2, Fargate and Lambda, while a Reserved Instance is tied to one instance configuration.

questions.prompt: A ticketing company buys a Capacity Reservation in one Availability Zone for a big sales weekend and expects its bill to drop. Which statement about this plan is correct?
choices: The bill drops because Capacity Reservations are discounted like Spot capacity
The capacity is guaranteed, but it is billed at the On-Demand rate even when unused, so it saves nothing on its own
The reservation requires a 1-year or 3-year term, so the discount only appears later
The reservation is free whenever the reserved instances are not running
questions.why: A Capacity Reservation guarantees capacity in one Availability Zone at the On-Demand rate whether or not you use it; to save money you would combine it with a Savings Plan or Reserved Instance.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between Reserved Instances or Savings Plans, Spot Instances, and a Capacity Reservation, including the tradeoff each one asks you to accept.
lessons.modelAnswer: All of these change how we pay for the same EC2 servers. On-Demand is the baseline: no commitment, but the highest hourly rate. Reserved Instances and Savings Plans give a big discount if we commit for one or three years. RIs tie us to a configuration, while Savings Plans commit us to an hourly spend and are more flexible. The catch is that we pay even if usage drops. Spot is the cheapest because it uses spare capacity, but AWS can take it back with a two-minute warning, so it only suits interruptible work like batch jobs. A Capacity Reservation guarantees capacity in a specific Availability Zone, but it is billed at On-Demand rates whether we use it or not, so it buys certainty rather than savings. Dedicated Hosts and Dedicated Instances are for isolation or per-core licensing, and they cost more.
rubricPoints: States that On-Demand has no commitment and the highest hourly price.
Explains that RIs and Savings Plans trade a 1- or 3-year commitment for a discount, and that Savings Plans are more flexible.
Explains that Spot is deeply discounted but can be reclaimed with a short warning.
Notes that a Capacity Reservation guarantees capacity at On-Demand price and is not a discount.
Distinguishes Dedicated Hosts (whole visible physical server, per-core licensing) from Dedicated Instances (isolated hardware, no host control).

suggested.rationale: Comparing the same workload's yearly cost under each purchasing option in fictional credits makes the commitment-versus-flexibility tradeoffs concrete.

lessons.plain: Cloud providers sell the same computer time in different ways, and the cheapest way depends on two questions about your work: how predictable it is, and whether it can be stopped partway without harm. It is like paying for a commute. If you ride every day, a yearly pass is cheapest. If you ride only now and then, you pay per trip. If you can wait for empty seats at odd hours, you ride very cheaply, but you may be asked to get off. Picking a purchasing option means matching how you will use computers to the price model that rewards that pattern.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company runs a website that must stay up all day, every day, for the next three years, and also runs a nightly batch job that can simply be restarted if it stops. Would you pay for both the same way? Which one do you think could use the cheapest, least reliable kind of capacity?
lessons.teach:
A purchasing option is the pricing model you choose for compute capacity, meaning the virtual servers AWS calls EC2 instances. The right option depends on two traits of a workload. Predictability is whether you know how much capacity you will need and for how long. Interruption tolerance is whether the work can be stopped by the provider and resumed or retried without damage.

On-Demand means paying per second or hour with no commitment. It costs the most per hour but suits unpredictable, short, or brand-new workloads you cannot yet size. Reserved Instances and Savings Plans trade a one-year or three-year commitment for a large discount. A Reserved Instance commits to a particular kind of instance; a Savings Plan commits to spending a set dollar amount per hour on compute. Both suit steady, predictable workloads that run continuously. Spot Instances use AWS's spare capacity at the deepest discount, but AWS can reclaim them with about two minutes' warning. They suit flexible, interruption-tolerant work such as batch processing or rendering. Dedicated Hosts, which are whole physical servers reserved for you, are chosen for licensing or compliance needs rather than for predictability.

This works because AWS rewards whatever helps it plan. A commitment lets AWS plan capacity, and accepting interruption lets AWS sell idle machines.

Worked example: a shop has three workloads. First, its database runs all the time for years: predictable and not interruptible, so a Reserved Instance or Savings Plan. Second, a two-week holiday promotion of unknown size: unpredictable and short, so On-Demand. Third, nightly image resizing that can rerun: interruption tolerant, so Spot.

A common mistake is putting a database, or any work that cannot stop safely, on Spot because it is cheapest. When AWS reclaims the capacity, the work halts mid-task, which can mean an outage or lost work. The opposite mistake, running a steady three-year workload on On-Demand, never breaks anything but overpays every month.

questions.prompt: A city library plans compute for three workloads. Its catalog search website runs around the clock and will keep doing so for at least three years. This is predictable and cannot be interrupted, so it goes on a Savings Plan. Its overnight job that converts scanned books to text saves its progress and can simply rerun if stopped. This is interruption tolerant, so it goes on Spot Instances. Its new e-book lending pilot will run for about one month, and nobody yet knows how many readers will use it. Which purchasing option completes the plan for the pilot?
choices: Spot Instances, because the pilot is short and Spot is the cheapest option
A one-year Reserved Instance, because the pilot will need a fixed amount of capacity
On-Demand, because the pilot is short and its size cannot yet be predicted
A Dedicated Host, because a new service needs its own physical server
questions.why: On-Demand needs no commitment, which fits short, brand-new work whose size is unknown, while a one-year commitment would outlast a one-month pilot.

questions.prompt: An online ticket seller runs its payment-processing service on Spot Instances because they have the deepest discount. A payment cannot be safely stopped halfway through. What is the most likely problem?
choices: AWS will automatically move the service to a Reserved Instance when Spot capacity runs out
The service must commit to one or three years of use, which it cannot cancel if sales drop
The service will run without trouble but will cost more each month than it would on On-Demand
AWS can reclaim the capacity with about two minutes' warning, so payments may halt mid-task and cause an outage or lost work
questions.why: Spot capacity can be reclaimed at short notice, so work that cannot stop safely is at risk of being interrupted mid-task.

questions.prompt: A hospital wants to run a medical-records application on AWS. Its software license, and a compliance rule it must follow, both require the application to run on a whole physical server set aside only for the hospital. Which purchasing option addresses this need?
choices: On-Demand, because paying with no commitment avoids licensing restrictions
Dedicated Hosts, because they are whole physical servers reserved for one customer
Spot Instances, because spare capacity is kept separate from other customers
A Savings Plan, because committing to an hourly spend reserves hardware for you
questions.why: Dedicated Hosts are chosen for licensing or compliance needs that call for a physical server reserved for you, not for workload predictability.

questions.prompt: A logistics company has a reporting system that has run steadily all day, every day, for years and will continue for at least three more. It pays for this system On-Demand. What is the consequence of this choice?
choices: Nothing breaks, but the company overpays every month compared with a commitment-based discount
The company is locked into a three-year contract that it cannot change if needs shift
The system may be stopped with about two minutes' warning whenever AWS needs the capacity back
The system is not allowed to run continuously, because On-Demand is meant only for short jobs
questions.why: Steady, predictable work on On-Demand runs safely but misses the large discount that a Reserved Instance or Savings Plan gives in exchange for a commitment.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide between On-Demand, a Reserved Instance or Savings Plan, and Spot for a new workload, and name the risk or tradeoff each choice carries.
lessons.modelAnswer: I ask two questions: do we know how much we will need over the next year or more, and can the work survive being stopped? If usage is steady and long-lived, like a database that runs all the time, I commit with a Reserved Instance or Savings Plan for a big discount; the tradeoff is that we pay for the term even if our needs shrink. If usage is unpredictable, short, or we are still learning its size, On-Demand gives total flexibility, but it is the most expensive per hour. If the work is flexible and can be retried, like batch jobs, Spot is cheapest, but AWS can take the capacity back with about two minutes' warning, so it must never hold anything that cannot be interrupted safely. Often one system mixes all three.
rubricPoints: Names predictability and interruption tolerance as the two deciding traits.
Matches steady, long-running workloads to Reserved Instances or Savings Plans and notes the commitment risk.
Matches unpredictable or short-term workloads to On-Demand and notes its higher price.
Matches interruptible, flexible work to Spot and warns it can be reclaimed with short notice.
Warns against putting non-interruptible work such as databases on Spot.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests this by describing a workload and asking for the best option, so reasoning through several short scenarios builds the matching skill fastest.

lessons.plain: A Reserved Instance is not a server you own. It is a billing discount: you promise to pay for a certain kind of virtual machine for one or three years, and AWS charges you less whenever matching usage appears. Flexibility is about how loosely 'matching' is judged. Think of a prepaid gym pass. One pass works only at one branch at one time slot, a looser pass works at any branch, and a family pass lets anyone in the household use it. Reserved Instances come in similar versions. When several AWS accounts are grouped into one organization, a pass bought by one account can be used by another account in that organization.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company buys a discount for one large virtual machine for a year, then replaces it with two half-size machines of the same type. Do you think the discount is wasted, partly used, or fully used? Why?
lessons.teach:
A Reserved Instance (RI) is a discount you buy by committing to a specific kind of Amazon EC2 instance for one or three years. EC2 is AWS's rentable virtual machine service. The RI never starts a machine. Each hour, AWS checks your running machines and applies the discount to any that match the RI's attributes.

Flexibility is decided by three things. The first is scope. A zonal RI is tied to one Availability Zone, meaning one data-center location within a Region. It also reserves capacity there, but it matches only that exact instance size. A regional RI applies in any Availability Zone of its Region, but it does not reserve capacity. The second is size flexibility. A regional RI for Linux with default (shared) tenancy covers any size in the same instance family. AWS weighs sizes with normalization factors: large counts as 4 units, xlarge as 8, and 2xlarge as 16. The third is the offering class. A Standard RI gives the bigger discount and can be modified, for example by changing its Availability Zone or splitting its size, and it can be resold on the RI Marketplace. A Convertible RI gives a smaller discount but can be exchanged for a different instance family, operating system or tenancy.

Here is a worked example. Suppose you buy one regional Linux m5.xlarge RI, which is 8 units. You then run two m5.large machines, each worth 4 units. Adding them gives 4 plus 4, which equals 8, so both are fully discounted. If you instead run one m5.2xlarge, worth 16 units, half its hours are discounted and the other half bill at On-Demand rates.

Inside AWS Organizations, all member accounts share one consolidated bill. An RI applies first to usage in the account that bought it. Any leftover discount then flows to matching usage in other accounts in the organization. The management account can turn this sharing off for chosen accounts.

A common mistake is assuming RIs always reserve capacity. Only zonal RIs do. The consequence is that a team relying on regional RIs during an outage in one zone may find no spare capacity, even though it is still paying for the commitment.

questions.prompt: A media startup buys one regional Reserved Instance for Linux with default (shared) tenancy for the r5.2xlarge size. Its normalization factor is 16 units. This hour the startup runs one r5.xlarge (8 units) and one r5.large (4 units) in the same Region. Step 1: The reservation covers 16 units per hour. Step 2: Running usage is 8 + 4 = 12 units, all in the same r5 family. Step 3: [missing]. Which choice correctly completes Step 3?
choices: Since 12 units is no more than 16, both machines are fully discounted, and 4 units of the reservation go unused in this account.
Only the r5.xlarge is discounted, because a reservation applies to just one running machine at a time.
Neither machine is discounted, because no running machine is exactly the r5.2xlarge size that was reserved.
Each machine is discounted for 12/16 (75%) of its hour, and the remaining 25% of each bills at On-Demand rates.
questions.why: A regional Linux shared-tenancy RI is size-flexible within its family, so 12 units of usage fit fully inside 16 units of discount, leaving 4 units unused.

questions.prompt: A hospital group uses AWS Organizations, a service that groups several AWS accounts under one consolidated bill. Its Imaging account bought a regional Linux c5.xlarge Reserved Instance, but this hour Imaging runs no c5 machines. The Billing account in the same organization is running one c5.xlarge in the same Region, and the management account has not turned off RI sharing. What happens to the discount this hour?
choices: The unused discount flows to the Billing account's matching c5.xlarge, so that machine is billed at the reserved rate.
The discount is split evenly across every account in the organization, whether or not they run matching machines.
The discount is wasted, because a Reserved Instance only ever applies inside the account that bought it.
The Billing account receives the discount only if the management account was the one that bought the Reserved Instance.
questions.why: An RI applies first in the buying account, and any leftover discount then flows to matching usage in other accounts of the organization unless the management account has turned sharing off for them.

questions.prompt: A payment processor must be sure it can launch its servers in one specific Availability Zone (a single data-center location within a Region) even during a busy period or a problem elsewhere. Which purchase gives it a capacity reservation there, not just a discount?
choices: Any Reserved Instance, since every RI reserves capacity in each zone of its Region
A zonal Reserved Instance for that Availability Zone
A regional Standard Reserved Instance in that Region
A regional Convertible Reserved Instance in that Region
questions.why: Only zonal RIs reserve capacity, and only in their one Availability Zone; regional RIs give a discount across zones but reserve no capacity.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm wants a three-year Reserved Instance discount. However, it expects to move its workload to a different instance family and possibly a different operating system within the first year. Which offering class fits best, and what is the trade-off?
choices: Standard, because it gives the bigger discount and can be exchanged for any instance family or operating system
Zonal, because tying the RI to one Availability Zone allows its instance family to change freely
Standard, because it can be resold on the RI Marketplace, which also changes its operating system automatically
Convertible, because it can be exchanged for a different family or operating system, in return for a smaller discount
questions.why: Convertible RIs can be exchanged for a different instance family, operating system or tenancy, but they give a smaller discount than Standard RIs.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a Reserved Instance's discount decides which machines it covers, including across accounts in an AWS Organization, and name one tradeoff between the flexible and the rigid options.
lessons.modelAnswer: An RI is a billing discount, not a machine. Every hour AWS checks running instances and applies the discount to whatever matches. A zonal RI matches one exact size in one Availability Zone, but it also reserves capacity there. A regional RI works in any zone in the Region and, for Linux with shared tenancy, across sizes in the same family using normalization units, but it reserves no capacity. A Standard RI gives a bigger discount and allows only modest changes. A Convertible RI costs more but can be exchanged for another family or OS. In an Organization with consolidated billing, the buying account uses the discount first, and any unused part flows to matching usage in other member accounts unless the management account disables sharing. The tradeoff is that more flexibility gives up either the capacity guarantee or part of the discount.
rubricPoints: States that an RI is a billing discount applied to matching usage, not a running machine.
Distinguishes zonal scope (capacity reserved, exact size) from regional scope (any zone, size flexible, no capacity reserved).
Explains size flexibility within an instance family using normalization units.
Contrasts Standard and Convertible RIs as discount versus exchange flexibility.
Explains that unused RI discounts are shared across accounts under consolidated billing, and that sharing can be turned off.
Names a tradeoff such as lower discount or no capacity guarantee in exchange for flexibility.

suggested.rationale: Applying RIs of different scopes and sizes to a simulated multi-account fleet, and watching which hours get discounted, makes the matching rules concrete better than reading alone.

lessons.plain: Data transfer cost is what a cloud provider charges for moving data from one place to another, as opposed to storing it or computing with it. AWS charges differently depending on direction and distance. Data coming into AWS from the internet is generally free. Data going out to the internet is billed per gigabyte. Moving data between two AWS Regions (separate geographic areas) costs money, and even moving it between data centers inside one Region can. Think of a toll road that lets you drive into the city free but charges you to leave, and charges a small fee to cross between districts.
