lessons.guessPrompt: A company uploads 1 TB of files into AWS and later sends 1 TB of files from AWS out to customers on the internet. Which of those two transfers do you think AWS charges for, and why might a provider price it that way?
lessons.teach:
Data transfer pricing is the per-gigabyte charge for moving data, billed separately from compute and storage. Four directions matter. Inbound means data arriving into AWS from the internet, and it is generally free, because AWS wants it to be easy to bring workloads in. Outbound means data leaving AWS to the internet (often called egress), and it is charged per GB, with the rate falling as volume rises and a small free monthly allowance. Region to Region means data sent from one AWS Region (an independent geographic location such as one in Virginia and one in Ireland) to another, and the sending Region charges for it. Within a Region, a Region contains several Availability Zones, which are separate data centers with their own power and networking. Traffic between resources in the same Availability Zone using private addresses is usually free, while traffic crossing between Availability Zones is charged a small amount per GB, typically in each direction.

Worked example: a web app runs in one Region. In a month, users upload 200 GB, which is inbound and free. The app serves 500 GB of pages and images to users, which is outbound and charged. It copies 50 GB of backups to a second Region for disaster recovery, which is Region to Region and charged by the source Region. Its servers in one Availability Zone send 100 GB to a database in another Availability Zone, which is cross-AZ and charged. Only the uploads cost nothing. A content delivery network (CDN), such as Amazon CloudFront, caches content close to users and can lower outbound costs, because transfer from AWS services into the CDN is not charged and its own delivery rates are often cheaper.

A common mistake is assuming that anything "inside AWS" is free. In a running system, a chatty design that spreads tightly coupled components across Availability Zones, or replicates heavily between Regions, can produce a data transfer bill larger than the servers themselves. Data transfer is therefore a design decision as well as a billing detail.

questions.prompt: A photo-printing startup runs its service in a single AWS Region (an independent geographic location). Last month: customers' phones uploaded 300 GB of photos into AWS, which is inbound and free. The print-processing servers in Availability Zone A sent 120 GB to a storage cluster in Availability Zone B. An Availability Zone is a separate data center inside the Region with its own power and networking. Customers downloaded 60 GB of finished proofs, which is outbound to the internet (egress) and charged per GB. The startup also copied 25 GB of order records to a second Region, which is Region to Region and charged by the sending Region. Missing step: how is the 120 GB sent from Availability Zone A to Availability Zone B treated?
choices: Free, because the data never leaves AWS's own network
Charged as Region-to-Region transfer, paid by the receiving zone
Charged a small per-GB amount, because it crosses between Availability Zones
Free, because both zones belong to the same Region
questions.why: Traffic that crosses between Availability Zones, even inside one Region, is charged a small per-GB amount, typically in each direction; only same-zone traffic on private addresses is usually free.

questions.prompt: A research lab moves 2 TB of sensor readings from its own office over the internet into Amazon S3, a managed object storage service. Which data transfer direction is this, and how is it generally priced?
choices: Cross-Availability-Zone, charged in each direction
Inbound, which is generally free
Outbound, which is charged per GB
Region to Region, charged by the source
questions.why: Data arriving into AWS from the internet is inbound, and AWS generally does not charge for it so that bringing workloads in is easy.

questions.prompt: An online course provider streams large video files from AWS to students worldwide, and its outbound (egress) bill keeps growing. Which change most directly targets that cost?
choices: Ask students to upload their own copies of videos
Copy the videos to a second Region each night
Move the servers into a single Availability Zone
Serve the videos through a content delivery network such as Amazon CloudFront
questions.why: A content delivery network caches content close to users; transfer from AWS services into it is not charged and its delivery rates are often cheaper, lowering outbound costs.

questions.prompt: A retailer splits its checkout system into many small services that call each other constantly, and spreads them evenly across three Availability Zones in one Region. Its monthly data transfer charge now exceeds its server charge. What is the most likely cause?
choices: Frequent traffic crossing between Availability Zones is charged per GB
Traffic inside one Availability Zone is billed per request
The Region charges a flat fee for each Availability Zone used
Inbound traffic from shoppers is billed at a high rate
questions.why: Cross-AZ traffic carries a small per-GB charge, so a chatty design spread across zones can rack up a data transfer bill larger than the servers themselves.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, in your own words, which kinds of data movement AWS charges for and which are usually free, and name one tradeoff a team faces when it spreads a system across Availability Zones or Regions.
lessons.modelAnswer: AWS bills data movement separately from servers and storage. Bringing data in from the internet is generally free, but sending data out to the internet is charged per gigabyte, getting cheaper per GB at higher volumes. Sending data from one Region to another costs money, charged by the Region it leaves. Even inside one Region, traffic between Availability Zones, which are separate data centers, is charged a little per GB, while traffic within the same zone over private addresses is usually free. The tradeoff is resilience versus cost: running across multiple zones or Regions protects you from a data center or regional outage, but every byte crossing those boundaries adds to the bill. So we should keep chatty components close together where we can, replicate only what we need, and consider a CDN like CloudFront to cut outbound costs to users.
rubricPoints: Inbound data from the internet is generally free.
Outbound data to the internet is charged per GB, with tiered rates.
Region-to-Region transfer is charged, by the sending Region.
Cross-Availability-Zone traffic is charged, while same-zone private traffic is usually free.
Names a tradeoff such as resilience across zones or Regions versus added transfer cost.
Mentions a mitigation such as keeping chatty parts together or using a CDN.

suggested.rationale: A cost model in fictional credits would let the learner route data between internet, zones and Regions and see which paths add to the bill, which is the core judgment this objective needs.

lessons.plain: Cloud storage is not one price. It is a menu of tiers that trade the cost of keeping data against the cost and speed of getting it back. Think of a self-storage company: a unit by the front door costs more per month but you can grab things any time, while a cheap warehouse across town charges a fee and makes you wait whenever you want a box back. AWS prices its storage the same way. Frequently used data belongs in the convenient, pricier tier, and rarely touched data belongs in the cheap, slower tier. Choosing well means matching each tier to how often the data is actually read.
lessons.guessPrompt: You must keep tax records for seven years and expect never to open them. Would you expect the cheapest place to keep them to also be instant and free to read back, or slow and charged per read? Why would a provider price it that way?
lessons.teach:
Storage pricing on AWS is a bill built from a few meters. Storage is charged per gigabyte-month, meaning one gigabyte kept for one month. Requests are charged per batch of reads or writes. Retrieval fees are charged per gigabyte read back from colder tiers. Amazon S3, a managed object store that keeps files as objects in containers called buckets, offers storage classes, which are price tiers. S3 Standard suits frequently read data. S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (Standard-IA) and S3 One Zone-IA suit data read rarely but needed fast; One Zone-IA is cheaper because it keeps data in a single Availability Zone, one isolated group of data centers, so it is less resilient. S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval, Glacier Flexible Retrieval (minutes to hours) and Glacier Deep Archive (up to about half a day, the cheapest) are archive tiers. S3 Intelligent-Tiering moves objects between tiers automatically for a small monitoring fee, useful when access is unpredictable. Lifecycle rules move or delete objects on a schedule. Colder classes also have a minimum storage duration: delete early and you still pay the minimum.

It works because holding idle data is cheap for AWS, while serving it costs effort, so colder tiers charge less to keep and more to read.

Worked example with made-up round prices: 1,000 GB of logs. Standard costs 2 credits per GB-month with no retrieval fee, so 2,000 a month. Standard-IA costs 1 credit per GB-month plus 1 credit per GB retrieved. Reading 100 GB a month gives 1,000 + 100 = 1,100, a saving. Reading all 1,000 GB gives 1,000 + 1,000 = 2,000, no saving; read more and IA loses.

Other storage bills differently. Amazon EBS, a virtual disk attached to one server, charges for the size you provision even if it is empty. Amazon EFS, a shared network file system, charges for what you actually store and has its own infrequent-access class.

The common mistake is choosing the lowest per-GB class for data read often: retrieval fees and minimum durations erase the saving, and an archive tier can delay a restore by hours during an outage.

questions.prompt:
A design studio keeps 500 GB of finished project files and wants to know whether moving them from S3 Standard to S3 Standard-IA saves money. Using made-up round prices: Standard costs 4 credits per GB-month with no retrieval fee, and Standard-IA costs 2 credits per GB-month plus 2 credits per GB retrieved. The studio reads back about 200 GB a month.

Step 1: Standard cost = 500 GB x 4 = 2,000 credits a month.
Step 2: Standard-IA storage cost = 500 GB x 2 = 1,000 credits a month.
Step 3: Standard-IA retrieval cost = ?
Step 4: Standard-IA total = 1,000 + Step 3. Compare it with 2,000 to see whether IA saves money.

What is the result of Step 3?
choices: 400 credits, because 200 GB read back x 2 credits per GB
1,000 credits, because retrieval is charged on all 500 GB stored
200 credits, because one credit is charged per GB read back
0 credits, because Standard-IA has no retrieval fee
questions.why: Retrieval fees are charged only on the gigabytes actually read back, so 200 GB x 2 credits = 400, giving a 1,400-credit IA total that beats Standard's 2,000.

questions.prompt: A team uploads a batch of test files to an S3 storage class that has a 90-day minimum storage duration (a minimum period you are billed for, even if you delete sooner). They delete the files after 20 days. How are they billed for storage?
choices: For 20 days, because storage is billed only while the data exists
For 20 days plus a retrieval fee for the deleted gigabytes
For the full 90-day minimum, even though the files existed only 20 days
For nothing, because files deleted before the minimum are free
questions.why: Colder classes have a minimum storage duration, and deleting early still costs the full minimum.

questions.prompt: A news website stores millions of images in Amazon S3, a managed object store. Some images are viewed heavily for a few days, others suddenly become popular again months later, and nobody can predict which. Which storage class best fits this unpredictable access while keeping costs down?
choices: S3 Glacier Deep Archive, since it is the cheapest per gigabyte
S3 One Zone-IA, since storing in one Availability Zone is always cheapest overall
S3 Standard only, since any other class adds unpredictable fees
S3 Intelligent-Tiering, which moves objects between tiers automatically for a small monitoring fee
questions.why: Intelligent-Tiering is designed for unpredictable access, shifting objects to cheaper or faster tiers automatically in exchange for a small monitoring fee.

questions.prompt: An engineer creates a 1,000 GB Amazon EBS volume (a virtual disk attached to one server) but stores only 100 GB of data on it. A colleague stores 100 GB on Amazon EFS (a shared network file system). Which statement about their bills is correct?
choices: Both are charged for 100 GB, because AWS bills only for data actually written
The EBS volume is charged for 100 GB and EFS for the full file system limit
Both are charged for 1,000 GB, because AWS bills for the largest possible size
The EBS volume is charged for the 1,000 GB provisioned; EFS is charged for the 100 GB stored
questions.why: EBS charges for the size you provision even if it sits empty, while EFS charges for what you actually store.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate wants to move all the team's S3 data to Glacier Deep Archive because it has the lowest price per gigabyte. Explain to them how S3 storage pricing actually works and when that move would backfire.
lessons.modelAnswer: S3 pricing has more than one meter. You pay per gigabyte-month to store data, per request, and in the colder classes a retrieval fee per gigabyte read back. Deep Archive has the lowest storage price, but reading data costs extra and can take up to about half a day, and there is a minimum storage duration, so deleting early still bills the minimum. That is great for compliance records nobody opens. It backfires for data we read often or need quickly: retrieval fees can exceed the storage saving, and a restore during an incident would be stuck waiting for hours. A better plan is to keep hot data in Standard, move rarely read data to Standard-IA or a Glacier tier with lifecycle rules, and use Intelligent-Tiering where we cannot predict access, accepting its small monitoring fee.
rubricPoints: Names the pricing meters: storage per GB-month, requests, and retrieval fees.
States that colder classes trade lower storage price for higher retrieval cost and slower access.
Mentions minimum storage duration charges on colder classes.
Matches classes to access frequency, using lifecycle rules or Intelligent-Tiering for changing or unknown patterns.
Identifies the risk of slow restores from archive tiers when data is needed urgently.

suggested.rationale: Pricing the same dataset across tiers with different read volumes in fictional credits makes the storage-versus-retrieval tradeoff concrete in a way reading alone cannot.

lessons.plain: AWS Cost Explorer and AWS Budgets are two free-to-start tools for keeping an eye on what you spend in AWS. Cost Explorer is a rear-view mirror with charts. It lets you look back at past spending, slice it by service, account or day, and see a rough forecast of where the trend is heading. AWS Budgets is a smoke alarm. You set a limit you care about, such as 500 dollars a month, and it warns you when actual or forecast spending crosses that line. One answers "where did the money go?" and the other answers "tell me before we overspend."
lessons.guessPrompt: Your team's AWS bill was twice what you expected last month. Would you rather have a tool that shows charts of last month's spending broken down by service, or a tool that emails you when spending passes a limit? Which one helps you find the cause, and which one helps stop it happening again?
lessons.teach:
AWS Cost Explorer is a reporting tool for analysing spending you have already done. It shows cost and usage as charts and tables over a time range you choose, and lets you group or filter the data. Grouping means splitting one total into parts, for example by service (compute, storage, databases), by linked account, by Region, or by tag. A tag is a label you attach to a resource, such as project=checkout. Cost Explorer can also show a forecast, an estimate of future spend projected from your past pattern. It answers analysis questions: what did we spend, on what, and is it trending up?

AWS Budgets is an alerting tool. A budget is a threshold you define for cost, usage or savings coverage over a period, usually monthly. When actual spend, or forecast spend, crosses a percentage of that threshold, Budgets notifies people by email or through a notification service. It can also trigger a budget action, an automatic response such as applying a restrictive permission policy. It answers control questions: will we go over, and who needs to know?

Why two tools? Looking back and watching forward are different jobs. Charts do not wake anyone up, and an alert does not explain a cause.

Worked example. A startup sets a monthly budget of 1,000 dollars with an alert at 80 percent of forecast. On day 10 the forecast reaches 1,300 dollars, so Budgets emails the team lead. She opens Cost Explorer, filters to this month and groups by service. Database spend has tripled since day 7. She then groups by tag and finds a test database someone left running at a large size. She removes it, and the forecast drops back under the budget.

A common mistake is to think Budgets stops spending by default. A plain budget only notifies. Resources keep running and charging unless you configure an action or someone responds. In a running system, an unanswered alert is the same as no alert, and the bill keeps growing.

questions.prompt: A design agency runs three linked accounts, named design, render and admin. It sets a monthly AWS budget of 2,400 dollars, with an alert at 90 percent of actual spend. Step 1: On day 18, actual spend passes 2,160 dollars, and Budgets emails the operations manager. Step 2: (missing). Step 3: The resulting chart shows that compute spend in the render account jumped last week. She then groups that account's costs by tag and finds rendering servers tagged project=promo-video still running after the project ended. Step 4: She shuts those servers down, and spending flattens. Which action is the missing Step 2?
choices: She raises the budget threshold in AWS Budgets to 3,000 dollars, so the alert stops firing and the team can investigate later.
She opens AWS Cost Explorer, filters to the current month and groups the costs by linked account to see where the money went.
She does nothing yet, because the budget alert has already paused the resources that pushed spend past the threshold.
She views only the Cost Explorer forecast for next month, which tells her which resource is causing the extra spend.
questions.why: Budgets only says that a threshold was crossed, so the next step is to analyse past spend in Cost Explorer, filtering and grouping by linked account, which produces the chart described in Step 3.

questions.prompt: A finance analyst at a logistics company asks: "Over the last six months, how much did we spend on storage compared with databases, and is storage cost trending up?" Which tool is built to answer this question?
choices: AWS Budgets, because a budget action can split the bill into services automatically.
Neither tool, because AWS only shows a single total figure on each monthly bill.
AWS Cost Explorer, because it charts past cost and usage and can group it by service.
AWS Budgets, because it compares monthly spend against a threshold you define.
questions.why: Cost Explorer is the reporting tool for spending that has already happened, and it can group costs by service over a time range you choose to show trends.

questions.prompt: A university research lab has a monthly cloud allowance of 3,000 dollars. The lab director says: "I don't need charts. I just want an email if we look likely to go over this month." What should the lab set up?
choices: A tag such as project=research on every resource, because tags send alerts when costs grow.
An AWS Budgets budget of 3,000 dollars with an alert based on forecast spend, sent to the director by email.
A Cost Explorer report grouped by Region, which the director checks at the end of each month.
A Cost Explorer forecast, because a forecast emails people automatically when spend rises.
questions.why: Budgets is the alerting tool: it notifies people when actual or forecast spend crosses a percentage of a threshold you define, which answers the question "will we go over?"

questions.prompt: A retail company created a monthly budget of 5,000 dollars in AWS Budgets, with an email alert at 100 percent of actual spend. No budget action was configured, and the alert email went to a mailbox that nobody reads. The month ended at 8,200 dollars. Why did spending continue past 5,000 dollars?
choices: Budgets always stops resources at 100 percent, so the extra cost must have come from a different AWS account.
A plain budget only sends notifications. Resources kept running and charging because no action was set up and nobody responded to the alert.
Cost Explorer was not enabled, and Budgets needs Cost Explorer turned on before it can stop resources.
Budgets can only alert on forecast spend, so an alert based on actual spend never fires.
questions.why: By default a budget only notifies people. Spending stops only if a budget action is configured or someone acts on the alert, so an unread alert works the same as having no alert.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between AWS Budgets and AWS Cost Explorer, which question each one answers, and one limit of each that means you need both.
lessons.modelAnswer: Cost Explorer is for looking back. It charts what we have spent and lets us group it by service, account, Region or tag, so we can find out where the money went. It also gives a rough forecast based on past trends. Budgets is for watching forward. We set a threshold, say 2,000 dollars a month, and it alerts us when actual or forecast spend crosses a percentage of it. It can also run a configured action. Each has a limit. Cost Explorer will not tell anyone anything unless someone opens it, so it cannot catch a surprise in time. Budgets can tell us we are heading over, but it does not explain why. By default it also does not stop resources from running, so someone still has to act. In practice a Budgets alert fires, and then we use Cost Explorer to find the cause.
rubricPoints: Cost Explorer analyses and visualises past cost and usage, with grouping and filtering.
Cost Explorer offers a forecast but does not alert anyone on its own.
AWS Budgets sets thresholds and sends alerts on actual or forecast spend.
Budgets only notifies by default and does not stop spending unless an action is configured.
The two work together: an alert from Budgets, then diagnosis in Cost Explorer.

suggested.rationale: A cost model in fictional credits would let the learner set a threshold, watch an alert fire, and then break spending down to find the cause, which practises both tools' questions directly.

lessons.plain: The AWS Pricing Calculator is a free website where you describe what you plan to run in the AWS Cloud and it tells you roughly what that will cost, before you have spent anything. Think of it like a car-repair quote: you list the parts and hours, the shop shows a price, and you decide whether to go ahead. You pick the services you want, say where in the world they will run, and how big and how busy they will be. It adds everything up into a monthly figure you can save, share or compare with other options.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a website asked you to list the servers and storage you plan to rent, how many hours they will run and in which location, what two or three things would you expect it to give back to you?
lessons.teach:
The AWS Pricing Calculator is a free, web-based estimating tool. It lets you build a cost estimate for planned AWS usage without creating or running anything, and you do not need an AWS account to use it. An estimate is a forecast based on the numbers you type in, not a bill.

It works because AWS publishes a price for each unit of each service, such as an hour of a virtual server (a rented computer) or a gigabyte-month of storage (one gigabyte kept for one month). Prices can differ by Region, meaning the geographic area of data centres you choose. The calculator multiplies your planned quantities by those unit prices for the Region you picked, then adds the services together. You can group services, export the result as a file, or share it as a link so a manager or customer sees the same numbers.

Worked example using made-up prices. You plan two virtual servers at 0.10 dollars per hour, running all month. The calculator treats a month as about 730 hours. Step one: 2 servers times 0.10 times 730 equals 146 dollars. Step two: you add 100 gigabytes of storage at 0.08 dollars per gigabyte-month, which is 8 dollars. Step three: the monthly total is 154 dollars. Step four: the twelve-month view shows 154 times 12, or 1,848 dollars. You could now copy the estimate, choose a different Region or server size, and compare the two totals side by side.

A common mistake is treating the estimate as a promise. It only covers what you entered, so forgetting an item, such as data leaving AWS, or choosing the wrong Region, gives a number that is too low. It also leaves out taxes.

In a running system, a poor estimate leads to a surprise bill and a budget that was approved on the wrong figure. A careful estimate lets a team compare designs and agree on a cost before any resource exists.

questions.prompt: A small charity wants to estimate its monthly AWS cost with the AWS Pricing Calculator before building anything. It plans 3 virtual servers (rented computers) at a made-up price of 0.05 dollars per hour, running all month. It also plans 200 gigabytes of storage at 0.10 dollars per gigabyte-month (one gigabyte kept for one month). The calculator treats a month as about 730 hours. Step one: the server cost is ____. Step two: storage is 200 times 0.10, which is 20 dollars. Step three: the monthly total is the server cost plus 20 dollars. Step four: the twelve-month view is that monthly total times 12. What belongs in step one?
choices: 109.50 dollars, because 3 servers times 0.05 dollars times 730 hours
3.60 dollars, because 3 servers times 0.05 dollars times 24 hours
36.50 dollars, because 0.05 dollars times 730 hours
0.15 dollars, because 3 servers times 0.05 dollars
questions.why: The calculator multiplies the quantity (3 servers) by the hourly unit price (0.05 dollars) by the hours in a month (about 730), which gives 109.50 dollars.

questions.prompt: A founder of a new mobile game studio has no AWS account yet. She wants a rough monthly cost for her planned servers and storage before she commits to anything. Which statement about the AWS Pricing Calculator is correct?
choices: She can use it for free without an AWS account, and it gives her a forecast based on the numbers she enters, not a bill.
It is free, but the figure it gives is a guaranteed price that AWS must honour for her first year.
She must first create an AWS account and launch the servers so the calculator can measure their real usage.
It charges a small fee per estimate, which is later taken off her first AWS bill.
questions.why: The Pricing Calculator is a free web tool that needs no account and creates nothing; it only forecasts cost from the quantities you type in.

questions.prompt: A logistics company built an estimate in the AWS Pricing Calculator using one Region (a geographic area of AWS data centres). It then deployed the same servers and storage in a different Region, and the real monthly cost did not match the estimate. What is the most likely reason?
choices: The calculator rounds every total to the nearest hundred dollars.
The calculator ignores storage and only prices servers, so the difference came from storage.
AWS unit prices can differ by Region, so the estimate was based on the wrong Region's prices.
Estimates expire after one month, so the old estimate was no longer valid.
questions.why: The calculator multiplies quantities by the unit prices for the Region you pick, and those prices can differ between Regions.

questions.prompt: A retail team's Pricing Calculator estimate came to 500 dollars a month, and their manager approved that budget. After launch the bill was noticeably higher, even though they used exactly the servers and storage they had entered. Their app sends a lot of data out of AWS to customers. What best explains the gap?
choices: The calculator treats a month as 365 hours, so server costs were undercounted.
Sharing the estimate as a link resets the prices to an older price list.
The calculator always adds taxes, which made the estimate too high rather than too low.
They did not enter the data leaving AWS, and the estimate only covers what you enter; it also leaves out taxes.
questions.why: An estimate only includes the items you enter and excludes taxes, so forgetting data leaving AWS makes the figure too low and can lead to a surprise bill.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what the AWS Pricing Calculator is for and how it produces its number, and name at least one limit on how far its figure can be trusted.
lessons.modelAnswer: The Pricing Calculator is a free web tool for planning costs before we build anything. We don't even need an AWS account. We pick each service we intend to use, choose the Region, and enter sizes and quantities, for example two servers running about 730 hours a month plus 100 gigabytes of storage. It multiplies those quantities by the published unit prices for that Region and adds them up into a monthly total and a twelve-month total. We can save, export or share the estimate and copy it to compare options, such as a different Region or server size. The limit is that it is only as good as our inputs. If we forget something like outbound data transfer, guess usage wrong or pick the wrong Region, the real bill will differ. It also leaves out taxes, so it is a forecast, not a guaranteed price.
rubricPoints: States it is a free tool for estimating cost before resources are created, with no AWS account required.
Explains that it multiplies planned quantities by per-unit prices for the chosen Region and sums them.
Mentions monthly or yearly totals and that estimates can be saved, shared, exported or compared.
Names a limit: the estimate depends on accurate inputs and is not a bill or guarantee.
Gives a consequence, such as a surprise bill when items are missed or the wrong Region is chosen.

suggested.rationale: Building an estimate from unit prices and quantities in fictional credits lets the learner practise exactly what the calculator does, including seeing how a missed item changes the total.

lessons.plain: AWS Organizations is a service for managing many AWS accounts as one group. Consolidated billing is its money feature: one account, called the management account, receives a single bill and pays for every account in the group. Usage from all accounts is added together, so the group can reach cheaper volume prices sooner, and every charge still shows which account caused it. Think of a family phone plan: one person pays one bill, the shared data total earns a better rate, and the statement still lists each person's usage line by line.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company runs three separate AWS accounts that each use a moderate amount of storage. If they were combined under one bill, why might the total cost go down even though nobody uses less storage?
lessons.teach:
AWS Organizations is a service that lets you group several AWS accounts and manage them centrally. The account that creates the group is the management account (once called the payer account); the others are member accounts. You can sort member accounts into organizational units (OUs), which are folders that group accounts, for example by department or by environment.

Consolidated billing means the management account gets one combined bill and one payment method covers all member accounts. It costs nothing extra. It works in your favour because many AWS prices are tiered: the more you use of a service, the lower the unit price for usage past each threshold. Organizations treats the whole group's usage as one customer's usage when applying those tiers.

Worked example with made-up prices: storage costs 3 credits per terabyte for the first 50 TB each month, then 2 credits per terabyte after that. Account A stores 30 TB and Account B stores 30 TB. Billed separately, each pays 30 x 3 = 90, total 180. Consolidated, the group stores 60 TB: the first 50 TB cost 150 and the remaining 10 TB cost 20, total 170. Same usage, 10 credits saved.

Cost allocation means attributing spending to whoever caused it. Consolidated billing keeps an itemized breakdown per member account, so finance can see that Account B spent more than Account A and charge each team back. Finer splits, by project or owner inside an account, use cost allocation tags, which are a separate topic.

A common mistake is believing consolidated billing merges the accounts. It does not: each member account keeps its own resources, users and permissions, and security boundaries stay in place. Only billing is combined. In a running organization, the management account is legally responsible for paying every member account's charges, so it should be tightly protected and used for billing and governance rather than for running workloads.

questions.prompt:
A design studio uses AWS Organizations (a service that groups several AWS accounts under one management account) with consolidated billing (one combined bill for the whole group). It has three member accounts. Made-up prices: data transfer costs 5 credits per GB for the first 100 GB each month, then 4 credits per GB after that. Usage this month: Account X 40 GB, Account Y 50 GB, Account Z 30 GB.

Step 1: Billed separately, each account stays under 100 GB, so each pays 5 per GB: 200 + 250 + 150 = 600 credits.
Step 2: Consolidated, the group's usage counts as one customer: 40 + 50 + 30 = 120 GB. The first 100 GB cost 100 x 5 = 500 credits.
Step 3: ?
Step 4: The group saves 20 credits on the same usage.

Which choice correctly completes Step 3?
choices: The remaining 20 GB cost 20 x 5 = 100, so the total is 600 credits
Each account gets its own first 100 GB, so the total stays 600 credits
The remaining 20 GB cost 20 x 4 = 80, so the total is 580 credits
All 120 GB move to the lower tier: 120 x 4 = 480 credits in total
questions.why: Only the usage past the 100 GB threshold gets the lower 4-credit price, so 500 + 80 = 580, which is 20 less than 600.

questions.prompt: A retailer joins its Marketing and Logistics AWS accounts into one organization with consolidated billing. A Marketing engineer asks whether she can now open the Logistics account's databases using her Marketing login. What is the correct answer?
choices: Yes. Consolidated billing merges member accounts, so users can reach all resources in the group.
No. Each member account keeps its own resources, users and permissions; only billing is combined.
No, because consolidated billing deletes existing users and they must be recreated in the management account.
Yes, but only if both accounts are placed in the same organizational unit (OU).
questions.why: Consolidated billing combines only the bill; security boundaries between member accounts stay in place.

questions.prompt: A university runs each faculty (Engineering, Medicine, Arts) in its own member account under one AWS Organizations management account with consolidated billing. Finance wants to charge each faculty for exactly what its account spent. What already gives them this information?
choices: Moving all three faculties into one shared account so spending appears on one line
Cost allocation tags, which are the only way to see spending per member account
Placing each faculty in an OU, because OUs produce separate invoices and payment methods
The itemized per-account breakdown that consolidated billing keeps
questions.why: Consolidated billing keeps an itemized breakdown per member account, which supports charging each team back; tags are for finer splits inside an account.

questions.prompt: A startup's management account (the account that created the organization and pays the combined bill) has spare capacity, so a developer proposes running the company's main web application in it. What is the best response?
choices: Avoid it: this account is legally responsible for all members' charges, so keep it protected and use it for billing and governance
Fine, because workloads in the management account are excluded from the combined bill
Avoid it: the management account cannot launch any resources at all
Fine, because the management account is billed at a lower tier than member accounts
questions.why: The management account pays for every member account, so it should be tightly protected and reserved for billing and governance rather than workloads.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what consolidated billing in AWS Organizations does for a company with many accounts, how costs can still be traced to each team, and one limit or tradeoff they should understand.
lessons.modelAnswer: AWS Organizations lets us group all our AWS accounts under one management account. With consolidated billing, that management account gets a single bill and pays for every member account, at no extra charge. Because AWS adds up usage across the whole group, we hit cheaper volume tiers sooner than any single account would, so the same usage can cost less. We don't lose visibility either: the bill is itemized per member account, so finance can charge each team for its own account, and we can group accounts into organizational units by department. The tradeoff is responsibility: the management account is on the hook for everyone's charges, so it must be locked down and not used for everyday workloads. Also, consolidated billing only combines payment; it doesn't merge accounts or share permissions, and splitting costs inside one account needs tags.
rubricPoints: The management account receives and pays one combined bill for all member accounts.
Usage is aggregated across accounts so volume pricing tiers are reached sooner, at no extra fee.
Costs remain itemized per member account, enabling allocation or chargeback to teams.
Accounts stay separate for resources and permissions; only billing is combined.
The management account carries payment responsibility and should be protected.

suggested.rationale: Pricing several accounts separately versus combined in fictional credits makes the volume-tier saving and per-account allocation concrete.

lessons.plain: Cost allocation tags and the Cost and Usage Report are how you find out who spent what on AWS. A tag is a label you attach to something you rent, such as a server or a storage bucket, written as a name and a value, like Team = checkout. Once you switch the tag on for billing, AWS can split your bill by that label. The AWS Cost and Usage Report is the most detailed record of your spending: a large spreadsheet-style file, delivered to storage you own, with one row per charge. Think of tags as sticky notes on shopping items, and the report as the itemized receipt that shows each note.
lessons.guessPrompt: Two teams share one AWS account and the monthly bill arrives as a single total. Before any teaching, how might you work out what each team spent?
lessons.teach:
A cost allocation tag is a tag that has been switched on for billing. A tag is a key-value label, such as Project = mobile-app, attached to an AWS resource (anything you create and pay for, such as a virtual server or a database). Tags come in two kinds. User-defined tags are ones you create. AWS-generated tags are added by AWS itself, such as one recording who created a resource. A tag only shows up in billing data after someone activates it in the billing settings. In a group of accounts managed with AWS Organizations, the management account, which is the account that pays for the group, does this. Activation can take up to a day to take effect, so plan to tag and activate early.

The AWS Cost and Usage Report (CUR) is the most detailed billing data AWS offers. It is a set of files delivered to an Amazon S3 bucket, which is AWS's managed file storage, and you own that bucket. Each line item, meaning one row, describes a charge: the service, the usage amount, the price, the time period (hourly, daily or monthly), and optionally the resource ID and a column for each activated tag. You analyze it with query or spreadsheet tools, for example Amazon Athena, which runs SQL queries directly on files in S3.

Worked example: Checkout and Search share an account. Step 1: tag every resource with Team = checkout or Team = search. Step 2: activate Team as a cost allocation tag. Step 3: set up the CUR with resource IDs included. Step 4: next month, sum the cost column grouped by the Team column. The bill now splits into Checkout, Search, and an empty-tag group.

Common mistake: tagging resources but never activating the tag, or tagging inconsistently. Tags are case-sensitive, so team and Team count as different keys. Either way, real spending lands in the untagged group and nobody can be charged back for it. That turns budget conversations into guesswork.

questions.prompt: Harbor Logistics runs several AWS accounts grouped under AWS Organizations. A team lead in one member account (an account that belongs to the group but does not pay the bill) wants the warehouse and delivery departments' costs shown separately. Here is how the work went. Step 1: she labels every virtual server and database in her account with the tag Dept = warehouse or Dept = delivery, using exactly that spelling and capitalization. Step 2: a week later she opens the Cost and Usage Report files in the S3 bucket and finds no Dept column at all, so every charge sits in one undivided group. Step 3: she confirms the tags are still on the resources, so the labels themselves are fine. Step 4: ??? Step 5: after waiting up to a day, the next report includes a Dept column and the charges split into warehouse, delivery, and an untagged group. What is Step 4?
choices: Use Amazon Athena to add a Dept column to the existing report files in the S3 bucket
Re-tag every resource with dept in lowercase, because billing only reads lowercase tag keys
Change the Cost and Usage Report from hourly to monthly time periods so that tag columns are included
Ask the management account, which pays for the group, to activate Dept as a cost allocation tag in the billing settings
questions.why: A tag appears in billing data only after it is activated in the billing settings, which in AWS Organizations is done by the management account, and activation can take up to a day.

questions.prompt: What turns an ordinary tag (a key-value label on an AWS resource) into a cost allocation tag?
choices: It has been activated in the billing settings so that it shows up in billing data
Its key is written entirely in capital letters
It is attached to at least one virtual server or database
It was created by AWS itself rather than by a user
questions.why: A cost allocation tag is simply a tag that has been switched on for billing. Both user-defined and AWS-generated tags can be activated, and neither the resource type nor the capitalization is what qualifies a tag.

questions.prompt: A design studio queries its Cost and Usage Report with Amazon Athena and groups the cost by tag. The results show env = prod at $500, Env = prod at $200, and an empty-tag group at $300. Why does production spending appear in two separate rows?
choices: The $200 row is AWS-generated and the $500 row is user-defined, so they can never be combined
The report was delivered hourly, so each row is a different hour
Tags are case-sensitive, so env and Env are treated as two different keys, and the studio should standardize on one spelling
Athena splits any group of charges larger than $500 into two rows
questions.why: Tag keys are case-sensitive, so inconsistent capitalization creates separate keys and splits the spending. Using one consistent spelling fixes the problem.

questions.prompt: A finance analyst at a charity wants line-by-line billing data that shows each charge's service, usage amount, price and time period, and optionally the resource ID. She also wants to run her own SQL queries on it. What should she use?
choices: An AWS-generated tag that records who created each resource
The AWS Cost and Usage Report, delivered as files to an S3 bucket the charity owns and queried with a tool such as Amazon Athena
A user-defined tag named Finance attached to each resource
The management account's activation settings, which display each charge as a row
questions.why: The Cost and Usage Report is AWS's most detailed billing data. It is delivered as files to an S3 bucket you own, and you can query it with SQL using Amazon Athena. Tags and their activation settings only label resources; they do not produce the billing data.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how cost allocation tags and the Cost and Usage Report together let you charge each team for its AWS spending, and name one limit or tradeoff of this approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: We put a key-value label, like Team = checkout, on every resource we create. Labels alone do nothing for billing. The paying account has to activate that key as a cost allocation tag, and only then does it appear in billing data. The Cost and Usage Report is AWS's most detailed billing export. It drops files into an S3 bucket we own, with one line per charge, and it can include resource IDs and a column for each activated tag. We query those files, say with Athena, and total costs per team. The limit is that it only works as well as our tagging discipline. Untagged resources, tags typed with different capitalization, and the delay after activation all leave spending we can't assign. The report is also large and raw, so someone has to build the queries.
rubricPoints: A tag is a key-value label on a resource, and it must be activated before it appears in billing data.
In AWS Organizations, the management account activates cost allocation tags.
The Cost and Usage Report is the most detailed billing data, with line items delivered to an S3 bucket the customer owns.
The report can include activated tags and resource IDs, so costs can be grouped by team or project.
Untagged or inconsistently tagged resources, and the delay after activation, leave unallocated cost.

suggested.rationale: On the exam this objective appears as a scenario where you must pick the most detailed billing data or a way to split costs by team, so reasoning through such situations adds the most.

lessons.plain: AWS Support plans are tiers of help you can buy from AWS, a bit like choosing between a free helpline, a paid mechanic you email, and a dedicated pit crew. Every account gets free customer service for account and billing questions, plus public documentation and community forums. Paid tiers add access to technical experts, faster promised response times, round-the-clock phone help, and eventually a named advisor who knows your setup. Each step up costs more, so the skill is matching what a customer actually needs, such as how fast help must arrive when production breaks, to the cheapest tier that delivers it.
lessons.guessPrompt: A small company runs its customer-facing website on AWS. They want to phone an AWS engineer at 3 a.m. if the site goes down, but they do not need a dedicated advisor. Should they pick the cheapest paid plan, a middle plan, or the most expensive plan, and why?
lessons.teach:
An AWS Support plan is a paid or free level of help attached to an account. Three ideas separate the plans. A response time is AWS's target for first replying to a support case, which is a ticket you open describing a problem. A Technical Account Manager (TAM) is an AWS engineer who gives proactive guidance on your architecture. The Concierge team is a billing and account specialist group for big customers. AWS Trusted Advisor is a tool that checks your account against best practices.

Basic is free: account and billing customer service, documentation, AWS re:Post (a community question site), the AWS Health Dashboard, and a small set of Trusted Advisor checks. You cannot open technical cases. Developer adds business-hours email access to support staff, suited to testing and early development. Business is the lowest tier with 24/7 phone, email, and chat with engineers, the full set of Trusted Advisor checks, and under one hour response when a production system is down. Enterprise On-Ramp adds a pool of TAMs, the Concierge team, and about 30 minutes for a business-critical system down. Enterprise adds a designated TAM of your own, about 15 minutes for business-critical outages, and help planning large events.

This works because AWS prices support by how much attention you consume: faster promises and named people cost more.

Worked example: a retailer runs production on AWS, needs a human by phone any hour, and wants every Trusted Advisor check. Step one: Basic and Developer lack 24/7 phone, so drop them. Step two: Business meets both needs. Step three: no TAM or 15-minute target was requested, so Enterprise tiers are overspend. Answer: Business.

A common mistake is confusing Enterprise On-Ramp with Enterprise: On-Ramp shares a pool of TAMs, while only Enterprise gives a designated one. Another is assuming Developer covers production emergencies. In a running system, choosing too low a tier means an outage at night waits for email during business hours, which can turn a short incident into a long, costly one. Exact prices and times can change, so check AWS's current pages.

questions.prompt: A video-streaming company runs its main platform on AWS. Its managers want proactive architecture advice from Technical Account Managers (TAMs, AWS engineers who guide your design), and they are happy to share a pool of them rather than have one assigned. They also want the Concierge team (AWS billing and account specialists) and roughly a 30-minute response when a business-critical system goes down. They did not ask for a TAM of their own or a 15-minute target. Step one: Basic, Developer, and Business offer no TAM access, so drop them. Step two: ??? Step three: Enterprise adds a designated TAM and about 15-minute responses that were not requested, so it would be overspend. Answer: Enterprise On-Ramp. Which statement correctly fills step two?
choices: Enterprise On-Ramp meets every need, because it gives the company a designated TAM of its own.
Developer meets every need, because email access to support staff covers architecture advice.
Enterprise On-Ramp meets every need: a shared pool of TAMs, the Concierge team, and about 30 minutes for business-critical outages.
Business meets every need, because its 24/7 phone access with engineers counts as TAM guidance.
questions.why: Enterprise On-Ramp is the tier that adds a shared pool of TAMs, the Concierge team, and a roughly 30-minute target for business-critical outages, which matches every stated need.

questions.prompt: A bank is choosing between Enterprise On-Ramp and Enterprise. What is the key difference in how each plan provides Technical Account Managers (TAMs)?
choices: Both plans give a designated TAM; they differ only in price.
Enterprise On-Ramp gives access to a shared pool of TAMs, while Enterprise gives you a designated TAM of your own.
Enterprise On-Ramp provides no TAM at all, while Enterprise provides a shared pool of them.
Enterprise On-Ramp gives a designated TAM, while Enterprise gives access to a pool of TAMs.
questions.why: On-Ramp shares a pool of TAMs across customers, and only Enterprise assigns a designated TAM to your account.

questions.prompt: A small design agency is building a test app on AWS with nothing in production yet. Its developers want to email AWS support staff with technical questions during business hours, at the lowest cost that allows this. Which plan fits?
choices: Business, because it is the lowest tier with any human technical help.
Developer, because it adds business-hours email access to support staff for testing and early development.
Basic, because it includes re:Post and documentation.
Enterprise On-Ramp, because it includes the Concierge team.
questions.why: Basic cannot open technical cases, while Developer is the cheapest plan that adds business-hours email to support staff for early development.

questions.prompt: A startup runs its live payments service on AWS under the Developer plan. The service goes down at 2 a.m. on a Saturday. What is the most likely consequence of this plan choice?
choices: Their case can only reach support by email during business hours, so the outage may wait until then; Business would give 24/7 phone and chat with under one hour response.
The Concierge team takes over the technical outage, because Developer includes it.
Nothing changes, because every paid plan includes 24/7 phone support for production outages.
A designated TAM is paged automatically and responds within about 15 minutes.
questions.why: Developer offers only business-hours email, so a night or weekend production outage can wait for help, while Business is the lowest tier with 24/7 engineer access and an under-one-hour target for production systems down.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide which AWS Support plan a customer needs, and name the tradeoff that stops you from simply recommending the top plan every time.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start from what the customer must have, then pick the cheapest plan that covers it. Basic is free and handles billing and account questions, docs, and community help, but no technical cases. Developer adds business-hours email support, fine for building and testing. Once real production is involved and someone needs to reach an engineer by phone at any hour with roughly a one-hour response for a down system, Business is the floor; it also unlocks all Trusted Advisor checks. If they want proactive architecture guidance from a pool of Technical Account Managers plus the Concierge billing team, Enterprise On-Ramp fits; if they need their own designated TAM and the fastest outage response, around 15 minutes, that's Enterprise. The tradeoff is cost: each tier's minimum monthly price rises steeply, so recommending Enterprise to a startup wastes money, while picking too low a tier leaves outages waiting for help.
rubricPoints: Basic is free and covers billing, account help, docs, and community but no technical cases.
Developer gives business-hours email support for non-production work.
Business is the lowest tier with 24/7 phone access and full Trusted Advisor checks.
Enterprise On-Ramp offers a pool of TAMs while Enterprise gives a designated TAM and fastest response.
Choose the cheapest plan that meets the need because cost rises steeply by tier.

suggested.rationale: The unit goal is naming the right plan for a described customer, so reasoning through short exam-style scenarios after reading the tier differences builds that skill best.

lessons.plain: When you use AWS you will constantly have questions: how should I design this, why is this error happening, has anyone solved this before? AWS publishes several free libraries of help, each built for a different kind of question. Whitepapers are long, careful reports on big ideas. Blogs carry news and walkthroughs. AWS Prescriptive Guidance gives tested, step-by-step plans for projects like migrations. The AWS Knowledge Center answers common support questions. AWS re:Post is a public question-and-answer forum. Think of a city library: the reference shelf, the newspaper rack, the how-to manuals, the help desk's FAQ sheet, and the community notice board.
lessons.guessPrompt: If you hit a confusing error that thousands of other customers have probably hit before, would you rather read a 60-page design report or a short page written by the vendor's support staff answering that exact problem? Why?
lessons.teach:
AWS offers five free self-help resources, and the exam expects you to match a need to the right one.

AWS whitepapers are long, formal documents written by AWS and partners that explain architecture, security, cost and best practices in depth. The AWS Well-Architected Framework, a set of design principles for building reliable, secure, efficient and cost-effective systems, is published this way. Use whitepapers when you need to understand a concept or strategy thoroughly.

AWS blogs are articles about new features, announcements, customer stories and practical walkthroughs. They are good for staying current.

AWS Prescriptive Guidance is a library of proven strategies, guides and patterns. A pattern is a step-by-step recipe for a specific job, such as moving a database to AWS. It focuses on migration and modernization projects, meaning moving existing systems to the cloud and updating them.

The AWS Knowledge Center is a collection of articles and videos written by AWS that answer the questions AWS Support receives most often, like how to fix a common error.

AWS re:Post is a community question-and-answer site, moderated by AWS, where anyone can ask a question and get answers from other users, AWS experts and staff. It replaced the old AWS Forums.

Worked example: a team gets an "access denied" error uploading to storage. Step 1: is this a common, known problem? Likely yes, so check the Knowledge Center. Step 2: if their case is unusual and no article fits, post it on re:Post. Step 3: later, planning to move their whole on-premises database, they use Prescriptive Guidance patterns. Step 4: to learn why the design should spread across multiple locations, they read a whitepaper.

Common mistake: mixing up the Knowledge Center and re:Post. The Knowledge Center is written by AWS for frequent questions; re:Post is community-driven questions and answers. In practice, picking the right resource first saves hours and avoids paying for a support case you did not need.

questions.prompt: A regional insurance company, Harbor Mutual, is starting to use AWS. Its cloud lead matches each need to a free self-help resource. Need A: the CFO wants a thorough, formal explanation of design principles for building cost-effective systems. This calls for a whitepaper, such as the AWS Well-Architected Framework. Need B: the team wants to hear about a storage feature AWS announced this week, along with a customer story. This calls for AWS blogs. Need C: they plan to move 40 legacy claims applications to the cloud and want a proven, step-by-step recipe for each move. This calls for AWS Prescriptive Guidance patterns. Need D: an engineer has an unusual question about combining two services in an odd way. She has searched the AWS-written articles for frequent questions and found nothing that fits. She wants answers from other users and AWS experts. Which resource completes Need D?
choices: AWS Knowledge Center, because it holds AWS-written answers to support questions
An AWS whitepaper, because it explains architecture topics in depth
AWS re:Post, because it is a community question-and-answer site moderated by AWS
AWS Prescriptive Guidance, because it gives step-by-step patterns
questions.why: re:Post is the community Q&A site where anyone can ask a question and get answers from other users, AWS experts and staff, which fits an unusual question with no existing AWS article.

questions.prompt: Which AWS self-help resource is a collection of articles and videos written by AWS that answer the questions AWS Support receives most often?
choices: AWS blogs
AWS Prescriptive Guidance
AWS re:Post
AWS Knowledge Center
questions.why: The Knowledge Center is AWS-written content built around the most frequent questions sent to AWS Support.

questions.prompt: A product manager at a travel-booking startup wants a quick, regular way to keep up with newly launched AWS features and read practical walkthroughs. She does not need a deep, formal study. Which resource fits best?
choices: AWS Knowledge Center
AWS blogs
AWS whitepapers
AWS Prescriptive Guidance
questions.why: AWS blogs cover new features, announcements, customer stories and walkthroughs, so they suit staying current.

questions.prompt: A new hire at a logistics firm says: "AWS re:Post is where AWS publishes its own official articles for the most common support questions." What is wrong with this statement?
choices: It describes the Knowledge Center; re:Post is a community Q&A site moderated by AWS
Nothing; re:Post and the AWS Forums are both official AWS article libraries
It describes whitepapers; re:Post holds formal architecture documents
It describes Prescriptive Guidance; re:Post holds migration patterns
questions.why: AWS writes the Knowledge Center articles for frequent questions, while re:Post is a community-driven question-and-answer site that replaced the old AWS Forums.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide between whitepapers, blogs, Prescriptive Guidance, the Knowledge Center and re:Post for a question, and name one limit of relying on community answers.
lessons.modelAnswer: I pick by the kind of question. If I need deep understanding of a principle, like cost optimization or resilient design, I read a whitepaper, such as the Well-Architected Framework. If I want to know what is new or see a quick walkthrough, I check the blogs. If I'm planning a project like migrating a database, Prescriptive Guidance gives me tested strategies and step-by-step patterns. If I hit a common error, the Knowledge Center has AWS-written answers to the questions Support sees most. If my problem is unusual, I ask on re:Post, the AWS-moderated community Q&A site. The limit of re:Post is that answers come partly from other users, so they may be slow, incomplete or not fit my setup, and there is no guaranteed response time. For an urgent production problem, a paid support plan is the reliable route.
rubricPoints: Whitepapers are in-depth AWS documents on architecture and best practices.
Blogs cover announcements, news and practical walkthroughs.
Prescriptive Guidance offers proven strategies and step-by-step patterns, especially for migration and modernization.
The Knowledge Center holds AWS-written answers to frequently asked support questions.
re:Post is a moderated community Q&A site with answers from users and AWS experts.
Community answers have no guaranteed accuracy or response time, unlike paid support.

suggested.rationale: This objective is a catalogue of free resources and what each is for, best learned by reading and matching needs to resources rather than through a hands-on mission.

lessons.plain: These are three AWS tools that tell you when something needs your attention, from two different directions. AWS Trusted Advisor looks inward at your own setup. It runs automatic checks and flags things you could improve, such as wasted spending or a storage bucket anyone can read. The AWS Health Dashboard looks at AWS's side: outages, maintenance and other events that affect AWS services or your specific resources. The AWS Health API delivers those same events to your own programs. Think of a car: Trusted Advisor is the mechanic's inspection of how you maintain it, and Health is the recall notice from the manufacturer.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your website suddenly slows down. One tool tells you that you configured something poorly. Another tells you the cloud provider is having a problem in your area. Why would you want both, rather than just one?
lessons.teach:
AWS Trusted Advisor is an automated advisor. It inspects your account against best practices and reports findings in categories that include cost optimization, performance, security, fault tolerance (surviving a failure), service limits (the maximum amount of a resource AWS lets an account use, also called quotas), and operational excellence. Every account gets a core set of checks, mainly some security checks and the service limit checks. The full set of checks, plus programmatic access, comes with the Business, Enterprise On-Ramp or Enterprise support plans.

The AWS Health Dashboard reports events on AWS's side. It has two views. Service health is a public view of the general status of AWS services in each Region (a geographic area of AWS data centers). Your account health is a personalized view of events that touch your own resources, such as planned maintenance on the hardware under one of your virtual servers. The AWS Health API is a programmatic interface to those account events, so your tools can react automatically, for example by sending them to an event-routing service. Full use of the API also requires Business, Enterprise On-Ramp or Enterprise support.

Worked example. First, Trusted Advisor flags a load balancer receiving no traffic, which is a cost finding. Second, it flags a storage bucket open to the public, which is a security finding. Third, it warns that the account is close to its limit on virtual servers, which is a service limit finding. Each one is something you fix in your own setup. Separately, account health shows that AWS will retire the hardware under one of your servers next week. That is an AWS event, and your job is to move the server before that date.

A common mistake is checking only the public service health page during trouble. It can show all green while one of your resources has a problem, because only account health is specific to you. In a running system, wiring the Health API into alerts helps catch planned retirements and maintenance before customers notice.

questions.prompt:
A regional chain of veterinary clinics runs its booking system on AWS and pays for the Business support plan. Its IT lead is working through this week's alerts.

Step 1: Trusted Advisor (an automated advisor that checks the account against best practices) reports two database servers with almost no activity for a month. This is a cost optimization finding in the clinic's own setup, so the team plans to shut them down.

Step 2: The account health view of the AWS Health Dashboard (the personalized view of AWS-side events that affect your own resources) shows AWS will perform maintenance on the hardware under the main booking database in nine days. This is an AWS event, so the team schedules time to prepare before that date.

Step 3 (missing): The lead wants future notices like the one in Step 2 to page the on-call engineer automatically, with no one having to open a web page. Which approach fits?
choices: Downgrade to the basic core checks, since automatic alerts on AWS events are included free for every account.
Turn on the Trusted Advisor service limit checks, because they report every AWS maintenance event affecting the account.
Assign someone to refresh the public service health page each morning, since it lists maintenance for each customer's servers.
Connect the AWS Health API to an event-routing service that forwards account events to the paging tool, which the Business plan allows.
questions.why: The AWS Health API is the programmatic interface to account events, so tools can react automatically, and full use of it comes with the Business, Enterprise On-Ramp or Enterprise plans.

questions.prompt: A small accounting firm on the most basic support level wants to know whether it is getting close to the maximum number of IP addresses AWS allows its account to use. Which tool and category report this, and is it available to them?
choices: Trusted Advisor's service limit checks, which are part of the core set every account gets.
The AWS Health API, which reports quota usage but only on Enterprise support.
Trusted Advisor's cost optimization checks, which require the Business plan or higher.
The public service health view, which shows each account's quota usage by Region.
questions.why: Service limits (also called quotas) are a Trusted Advisor category, and the service limit checks are in the core set available to every account.

questions.prompt: An online tutoring company sees errors on its video servers in one Region. An engineer opens the public service health view and sees every service marked healthy, so he concludes AWS has no issue affecting them. What is wrong with this conclusion?
choices: He should have run Trusted Advisor instead, because it reports AWS outages in each Region.
The public view only covers security events, so it cannot show problems with servers.
The public view shows general status only; account health could still show an event affecting their specific servers.
Nothing; if the public view shows all green, no AWS event can be affecting their resources.
questions.why: Only the account health view is specific to your own resources, so the public service health page can be all green while one of your resources has a problem.

questions.prompt: A furniture retailer's cloud team gets only a handful of Trusted Advisor results, mostly security and service limit checks. They want the full set of checks, including cost optimization and fault tolerance, and they want to pull results into their own reporting tools. What do they need?
choices: The AWS Health API, which replaces Trusted Advisor checks with AWS event data.
A Business, Enterprise On-Ramp or Enterprise support plan, which unlocks the full checks and programmatic access.
Nothing extra; every account already gets all checks, but they must be enabled one by one.
The account health view of the AWS Health Dashboard, which lists cost and fault tolerance findings.
questions.why: Every account gets only a core set of Trusted Advisor checks; the full set plus programmatic access comes with the Business, Enterprise On-Ramp or Enterprise plans.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between Trusted Advisor and the AWS Health Dashboard and API, when you would reach for each, and one limit or tradeoff, such as what a free account does not get.
lessons.modelAnswer: Trusted Advisor looks at our own account. It runs automated best-practice checks and flags idle resources costing money, security gaps like a publicly readable bucket, weak fault tolerance, and resources nearing their service limits. Those are things we fix ourselves. The Health Dashboard reports AWS-side events. Its public service health view shows the general status of each service by Region, and its account health view shows events affecting our specific resources, such as scheduled hardware retirement. The Health API sends those account events to our automation so we can alert or react without anyone watching a screen. One limit is that on the free Basic plan, Trusted Advisor only runs the core checks, mostly security and service limits. The full check set and full use of the Health API need Business, Enterprise On-Ramp or Enterprise support. Also, the public status page can look fine while our own resources are affected.
rubricPoints: Trusted Advisor runs automated best-practice checks on your own account and suggests fixes.
Names Trusted Advisor categories such as cost, security, fault tolerance, performance and service limits.
The Health Dashboard reports AWS-side events, with a public service health view and a personalized account health view.
The Health API delivers account events to programs for automated alerting or response.
Basic support gets only core Trusted Advisor checks, and the full checks and Health API need Business-level support or higher.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests choosing the right tool from a short scenario, so reasoning through situations such as an idle resource, a nearly reached limit or a hardware retirement notice builds the needed distinction best.

lessons.plain: Not every cloud problem has to be solved by you alone. AWS surrounds its platform with three kinds of outside help. The AWS Partner Network is a program of vetted companies, consultants and software makers who build on AWS and can do the work for you. AWS Marketplace is an online catalogue where you can find, buy and launch ready-made software from other vendors, billed through your AWS account. AWS Professional Services is AWS's own team of experts you hire for big projects. Think of renovating a house: you can hire a certified contractor, buy pre-built kitchen units from a showroom, or bring in the manufacturer's own engineers.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company wants to run a well-known commercial firewall product on AWS without negotiating a separate contract, and wants the charge to appear on its normal AWS bill. Where would you guess it should look?
lessons.teach:
The AWS Partner Network (APN) is a global program for companies that build on AWS. Two broad kinds of partner exist. Consulting or services partners are firms that design, migrate, build and manage systems for customers. Software or technology partners make products that run on or integrate with AWS. Partners can earn badges called competencies, which show proven expertise in an area such as security, migration or a particular industry. The program works because a customer short on skills can rent proven expertise, and the badges make partners easier to judge.

AWS Marketplace is a curated digital catalogue of third-party software, data and services. Its value is speed and simpler buying. Many listings deploy straight into your account, sometimes as a ready-to-run server image (a saved machine template). The vendor's charges appear on your AWS bill instead of a separate invoice. Pricing models vary: free, hourly or per-use, yearly contracts, and bring-your-own-license (BYOL), where you use a license you already own. Private offers let a buyer negotiate custom terms with a seller.

AWS Professional Services is a consulting team employed by AWS itself. It helps large organisations with major efforts such as data-centre migrations, often working alongside APN partners.

Worked example: a retailer must move 300 servers to AWS in six months and needs a security scanner. Step one, it lacks migration staff, so it hires an APN consulting partner holding a migration competency. Step two, it finds a scanner on AWS Marketplace, subscribes, and launches it into its account. Step three, the scanner's hourly fee appears on next month's AWS bill. Step four, because the project is large and strategic, AWS Professional Services advises the overall plan.

A common mistake is confusing Marketplace with AWS's own services or with Support plans. Marketplace software is sold by third parties, and the seller usually supports it, not AWS. In a running system, Marketplace subscriptions keep charging until you cancel them. A forgotten subscription is a quiet, recurring cost.

questions.prompt: A regional bus company is moving 40 servers to AWS and wants a ready-made route-analytics product. Step one: it has no cloud engineers, so it hires an APN consulting partner holding a migration competency (a badge showing proven expertise). Step two: it finds the analytics product on AWS Marketplace, a curated catalogue of third-party software. The company already bought a license for this exact product from the vendor last year and does not want to pay for it twice. Step three (missing): which Marketplace pricing model should it pick? Step four: it launches the product into its account, and any remaining Marketplace charges appear on its AWS bill.
choices: A private offer, so it can negotiate new custom terms with the seller
Hourly per-use pricing, so it pays only while the product runs
A Business Support plan, so AWS covers the product's license
Bring-your-own-license (BYOL), using the license it already owns
questions.why: BYOL is the Marketplace pricing model that lets a buyer use a license it already owns instead of paying for the software again.

questions.prompt: A design studio subscribes to a video-encoding tool sold by a third-party vendor on AWS Marketplace. The tool starts failing. Who usually provides support for that tool?
choices: The studio's AWS Support plan, because the fee is on the AWS bill
An APN partner chosen automatically by AWS
AWS Professional Services, because the tool runs in AWS
The vendor that sells the tool on Marketplace
questions.why: Marketplace software is sold by third parties, and the seller usually supports it, not AWS, even though the charge appears on the AWS bill.

questions.prompt: An insurance firm wants to hire an outside company to tighten the security of its AWS setup, and it wants an easy way to tell which firms have proven expertise in security. What should it look for?
choices: A bring-your-own-license offer from a seller
A security product with a free Marketplace listing
An APN partner holding a security competency
An AWS Support plan that includes security reviews
questions.why: Competencies are badges APN partners earn to show proven expertise in an area such as security, which makes partners easier to judge.

questions.prompt: A charity's finance officer notices the same monthly charge for a third-party mapping tool on its AWS bill. The team that used the tool stopped using it four months ago. What best explains the charge?
choices: APN partner competencies carry a recurring yearly fee
The Marketplace subscription keeps charging until cancelled
Marketplace tools stop billing only after AWS deletes them
AWS Professional Services bills for past advice monthly
questions.why: Marketplace subscriptions keep charging until you cancel them, so a forgotten subscription becomes a quiet, recurring cost.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between the AWS Partner Network, AWS Marketplace and AWS Professional Services, and name one limit or tradeoff of using Marketplace software.
lessons.modelAnswer: They're three ways to get outside help on AWS. The AWS Partner Network is a program of outside companies. Consulting partners do work for us, like migrations. Technology partners make software that runs on AWS. Competency badges show which partners have proven skill in an area. AWS Marketplace is a catalogue where we can find and subscribe to third-party software and data. A lot of it launches straight into our account, and the charge lands on our AWS bill. It supports hourly, contract and bring-your-own-license pricing. AWS Professional Services is AWS's own consulting team, usually brought in for large projects such as big migrations. The tradeoff with Marketplace is that the software comes from another vendor. Support for it usually comes from that seller, not AWS. Also, subscriptions keep billing until someone cancels them, so unused ones become a hidden recurring cost.
rubricPoints: Defines the AWS Partner Network as third-party consulting and technology companies, with competencies showing proven expertise.
Defines AWS Marketplace as a catalogue of third-party software and data that deploys into your account.
States that Marketplace charges appear on the AWS bill and mentions pricing models such as hourly, contract or BYOL.
Identifies AWS Professional Services as AWS's own consulting team for large projects.
Names a limit, such as seller-provided support or subscriptions billing until cancelled.

suggested.rationale: This objective is vocabulary about AWS programs and catalogues, and no mission or planned engine exercises it, so reading and recalling the distinctions is the best fit.
