lessons.plain: AWS Trust and Safety is the team inside AWS that handles complaints when someone uses AWS computers to cause harm, such as sending spam, scanning other people's networks, hosting phishing pages or malware, or flooding a site with traffic. Anyone can report this, even people who are not AWS customers, and you do not need a paid support plan. Think of it like reporting a rented van being driven dangerously: you tell the rental company, not the driver. The company contacts its own customer, investigates, and can stop the misuse, while the customer's identity stays private.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your website's logs show thousands of failed login attempts coming from an IP address that belongs to AWS. Who do you think you should tell, and what information would help them act on it?
lessons.teach:
Abuse means using AWS resources to harm others or break AWS's acceptable use rules. Resources are the things customers rent, such as virtual servers and storage. Common types are spam email, port scanning (probing another network for open entry points), denial-of-service attacks (flooding a target with traffic until it fails), intrusion attempts, phishing or malware hosting, and hosting content the poster has no right to share. The AWS Trust and Safety team receives these reports, usually through an online abuse report form or the abuse email address AWS publishes. Reporting is open to anyone and needs no paid support plan.

It works because AWS knows which customer account is using a given IP address at a given moment, while an outside victim does not. AWS can therefore contact the account owner, require a fix, and restrict the resource if needed.

Worked example. First, your server logs show repeated SSH login failures (SSH is a remote login method). Second, you check the source IP and confirm it falls inside AWS's published address ranges. Third, you gather evidence: source IP, exact timestamps with time zone, the destination you own, and a short log excerpt. Fourth, you submit it to Trust and Safety. Fifth, AWS investigates and contacts the account owner. You will not be told who that customer is.

The reverse also happens. If your own instance is compromised and starts attacking others, AWS may send you an abuse notice. You are expected to respond promptly and fix the cause. If you ignore it, AWS can restrict or suspend the resource, which can take your workload offline.

A common mistake is opening a technical support case or waiting for a support plan to cover abuse. Abuse reports go to Trust and Safety, which is a separate channel available to everyone. Another mistake is sending a report with no timestamps or logs, which slows the investigation.

questions.prompt: A small design studio runs one virtual server on AWS. One morning they receive an abuse notice from AWS. It says their server's IP address sent about 4,000 unsolicited emails overnight. Here is how they handle it. Step 1: they confirm the IP address in the notice belongs to their own server. Step 2: they find an old contact-form script that attackers took over to send spam. Step 3: (missing). Step 4: they reply to the notice and explain what they found and what they changed. Which action belongs in Step 3?
choices: Leave the server running unchanged until AWS says what to do next
Promptly remove or patch the hijacked script so the server stops sending spam
Ask AWS to tell them which person or company reported the spam
Open a technical support case and wait for a paid support plan to handle the spam problem
questions.why: When AWS sends an abuse notice, you are expected to respond promptly and fix the cause; ignoring it risks AWS restricting or suspending the server.

questions.prompt: A local charity uses only the free Basic level of AWS support. Its firewall logs show that a single IP address inside AWS's published address ranges probed hundreds of its ports in ten minutes. Probing a network like this to look for open entry points is called port scanning. What should the charity do?
choices: Send a report with the IP, timestamps and log lines to the AWS Trust and Safety team, using the abuse form or the published abuse email
Open a technical support case about the scanning traffic
Upgrade to a paid support plan first, because only paying customers can report abuse
Do nothing, because AWS only accepts abuse reports from the owner of the attacking account
questions.why: Abuse reports go to Trust and Safety, a separate channel that anyone can use with no paid support plan.

questions.prompt: An online game company is flooded with traffic from an IP address in AWS's ranges, and its servers keep failing. This kind of flooding is called a denial-of-service attack. Why is reporting it to AWS more useful than the company trying to track down the attacker itself?
choices: AWS knows which customer account was using that IP at that moment, so it can contact the owner, require a fix, and restrict the resource if needed
AWS publishes the name of every customer, so the company can then contact the attacker directly
AWS automatically blocks all traffic between AWS customers once any report arrives
Only AWS can legally read the company's server logs
questions.why: An outside victim cannot tell who was using an AWS IP address at a given moment, but AWS can, which lets it act against the right account.

questions.prompt: A university IT team emails AWS Trust and Safety: "A server of yours attacked our network sometime last week. Please stop it." They give no IP address, no timestamps and no logs. What is the most likely result?
choices: AWS must reject the report because the university has no paid support plan
AWS shuts down every server that contacted the university last week
AWS replies with the name of the customer who owns the attacking server
The investigation is slowed, because AWS needs the source IP, exact times with time zone, the targeted destination and a log excerpt to find the right resource
questions.why: Reports without timestamps or logs slow the investigation, because AWS uses those details to find which account was using the IP at that time.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what the AWS Trust and Safety team does, when you would contact it, and one limit of what it will do for the person reporting.
lessons.modelAnswer: AWS Trust and Safety handles reports that AWS resources are being misused, for example to send spam, scan networks, launch denial-of-service floods, try break-ins, or host phishing pages and malware. If we see an attack coming from an AWS IP address, we report it through the abuse form or AWS's abuse email. We don't need a support plan, and we don't open a normal support case. A good report includes the source IP, exact timestamps with the time zone, what was targeted, and log excerpts. One limit is that AWS won't tell us who owns the offending account, and we won't control how fast they act. The reverse matters too: if one of our instances gets compromised and AWS sends us an abuse notice, we must respond quickly. Otherwise they can restrict the resource and take our service down.
rubricPoints: Trust and Safety handles reports of AWS resources being used for abuse such as spam, scanning, DoS, intrusion, phishing or malware.
Reports go through the abuse form or abuse email, are open to anyone, and need no paid support plan.
A useful report includes source IP, timestamps, the target, and log evidence.
AWS contacts the account owner but does not reveal the owner's identity to the reporter.
If your own resource is reported, you must respond, or AWS may restrict or suspend it.

suggested.rationale: This objective is a factual matter of which team and channel handle abuse and what to include, so reading and recalling it is enough.

scenarios.title: Harbor Lane Bakeries Outgrows Its Server Closet
scenarios.scenario:
Harbor Lane Bakeries is a fictional chain of 12 bakeries that takes most of its orders through its own website. Today the website and its order database run on four physical servers in a small, air-conditioned closet at head office. The company bought those servers outright three years ago. A one-time, up-front purchase of long-lived equipment like this is called a capital expense.

The finance director, Priya, has a quote to buy six more servers before the holiday season. In most of the year the four existing servers sit about 20% busy. For roughly three weeks in December, orders jump to about five times normal and the site slows to a crawl. Last spring a power cut at head office took the website offline for an afternoon. The marketing team also wants to try a new loyalty-points feature, but the IT lead, Marcus, says ordering and setting up a test server would take about six weeks.

Harbor Lane is considering moving the website to AWS (Amazon Web Services), a cloud provider that rents computing power, storage, and databases over the internet and charges for what you use. The order database runs on commercial database software. Harbor Lane already owns licenses for it, which are the legal rights to use the software. On AWS it could either reuse those licenses, called bring your own license (BYOL), or rent servers where the license cost is included in the hourly price, called license-included.

Priya has asked you for a short briefing. Answer each part in plain language.

1. Priya asks: "What does the cloud actually change about how we pay?" Explain the trade of capital expense for variable expense (cost that rises and falls with how much you use). Say which of Harbor Lane's current costs are fixed (paid whether or not the servers are busy) and name at least two on-premises costs (costs of running your own equipment on your own site) that a move to AWS is meant to remove.

2. Marcus lists three problems: the website went down during the power cut, it slows down every December, and a test server takes six weeks to arrive. Match each problem to the one benefit among high availability, elasticity, and agility that addresses it. Define each benefit in a sentence, and show why they are not three words for the same thing.

3. Harbor Lane already owns database licenses that still have two years of support left. Compare BYOL with license-included for this database and recommend one, giving your reason.

4. After the move, Marcus says: "We'll pick the right server size once during migration and then we're done." Explain rightsizing (matching the size of rented resources to what the workload actually needs) and why it has to be repeated. Use Harbor Lane's own numbers.
subParts: Capital vs variable expense and costs removed
modelAnswer: Today Harbor Lane pays a capital expense: it buys servers up front, before it knows exactly how busy they will be, and owns them for years. On AWS it would pay a variable expense instead: it rents capacity by the hour or second and pays more in a busy month and less in a quiet one. The cost changes shape from a large, guessed, up-front lump into a smaller bill that tracks real use. Fixed costs today include the purchase price of the four servers (and the six on the quote), the closet's air conditioning and power, and the staff time to maintain the hardware. All of these are paid even though the servers sit about 20% busy most of the year. On-premises costs a migration is meant to remove include buying and replacing server hardware, running and cooling the server room, physical security and space for it, and the staff hours spent racking, repairing, and patching hardware. Worked trace: buying six servers for a three-week December peak means paying all year for capacity used about 6% of the year. Renting extra capacity for those three weeks means paying for it only during those weeks. The common mistake is to say the cloud is 'just cheaper'. The real point is that you stop paying in advance for guessed capacity and pay for what you actually use.

The power-cut outage maps to high availability: the system keeps running when one part fails. On AWS this is done by running copies in more than one separate data center, so losing one location does not take the site offline. The December slowdown maps to elasticity: capacity automatically grows when demand rises and shrinks when it falls. Here that means adding servers for the roughly fivefold holiday spike and removing them in January. The six-week wait maps to agility: how fast the team can try something new. On AWS a test server can be started in minutes, used for the loyalty-points trial, and switched off if the idea fails. They are distinct because each solves a different problem. A site can be highly available yet not elastic, staying up through a failure but still slowing under a fivefold load. It can be elastic yet not agile, scaling well while new projects still wait weeks for approval. Calling them all 'scalable and flexible' would hide which problem is being fixed.

With BYOL, Harbor Lane reuses the database licenses it already owns. It pays AWS only for the compute, so the hourly rate is lower, but it must make sure its license terms allow use on cloud servers and keep tracking compliance itself. With license-included, the license cost is built into the hourly price. That is simpler and can be switched off at any time, but Harbor Lane would effectively pay for the license twice while its owned licenses are still valid. Recommendation: use BYOL for now, provided the license terms permit cloud use, because the company has already paid for licenses with two years of support left. Then reconsider license-included when those licenses come up for renewal. The common mistake is to ignore existing licenses and pay again for software already owned. Choosing license-included without checking can quietly raise the monthly bill.

Rightsizing means choosing the smallest and cheapest resource that still handles the workload well, then adjusting it as needs change. It cannot be done once because the workload keeps changing. Harbor Lane runs at about 20% for most of the year and about five times normal in December. New features such as loyalty points add load, and AWS regularly offers new server types that may be cheaper for the same work. Worked trace: if Marcus sizes servers for the December peak and never revisits them, Harbor Lane pays for peak capacity for roughly 49 weeks a year when it needs a fraction of it. That rebuilds the waste of the server closet, just on a monthly bill. If he sizes for a quiet month and never revisits, the site slows down again at the next peak. The consequence for a running system is that, without regular reviews (for example, monthly checks of how busy each server really is), costs drift upward or performance drifts downward. Rightsizing should be a routine, scheduled check, combined with elasticity for the predictable peak.

scenarios.title: Bramblewood Bakeries Moves Its Online Ordering to AWS
scenarios.scenario:
Bramblewood Bakeries is a fictional regional bakery chain that has just moved its online ordering website to AWS. A cloud provider like AWS rents out computing resources over the internet, and you pay for what you use. You have joined as a junior cloud engineer.

The website uses three AWS services. Amazon EC2 provides virtual servers, which are rented computers in AWS data centers that you control, including the operating system. The operating system is the base software, such as Linux, that everything else runs on. Amazon RDS is a managed relational database service, meaning AWS runs the database software for you while you store your tables of orders and customers in it. AWS Lambda runs small pieces of code, called functions, only when an event triggers them, with no servers for you to manage. Bramblewood uses a Lambda function to send order confirmation emails.

In your first week you notice four problems. First, nobody agrees who is supposed to apply security patches, which are software updates that fix known weaknesses. Second, Bramblewood takes card payments, and an outside auditor wants evidence that AWS's own data centers and infrastructure meet recognized security standards. Third, the owner signs in every day as the root user, the all-powerful identity created with the AWS account. The root user also has access keys, which are long-lived credentials that let programs act as that identity. In addition, a developer typed the database password directly into the website's code. Fourth, last night a database backup, called a snapshot, was deleted, and nobody knows who did it.

Your manager asks you to write short answers to these tasks:
1. Using the AWS shared responsibility model, explain who patches the operating system and the database or runtime software for EC2, RDS, and Lambda, and name one thing Bramblewood still owns for each service.
2. Tell the auditor where to get AWS's compliance reports, and explain what those reports do and do not prove about Bramblewood.
3. Fix the root user and the hardcoded database password. Name the specific controls and services you would use and say why.
4. Name the AWS service that will show who deleted the snapshot, and name one other service that helps Bramblewood spot this kind of problem in the future.
subParts: Responsibility line for EC2, RDS and Lambda
modelAnswer:
The shared responsibility model splits security into two parts. AWS is responsible for security of the cloud: the physical data centers, hardware, networking, and the virtualization layer underneath every service. The customer is responsible for security in the cloud: what it builds, stores, and configures. The line moves depending on how much the service manages for you.

For EC2, Bramblewood patches the guest operating system and any software it installs, because it controls the whole virtual server. AWS only covers the hardware and virtualization underneath. Bramblewood also owns its firewall settings, such as security groups, and its data.

For RDS, AWS patches the underlying operating system and the database software, although Bramblewood can choose the maintenance timing. Bramblewood still owns its data, its database user accounts and passwords, who can reach the database over the network, and whether encryption is turned on.

For Lambda, AWS manages the servers, the operating system, and the language runtime. Bramblewood owns its function code, the permissions the function is given, and the data the function handles.

A strong answer states that the more managed the service, the more AWS takes on, and that the customer always keeps its data, identities, and access settings.

The auditor should use AWS Artifact. Artifact is a self-service portal in the AWS console where customers download AWS's compliance reports, such as independent audit reports and payment card industry attestations, and review or accept certain agreements.

These reports prove that AWS's side of the shared responsibility model, its infrastructure and data centers, has been checked against those standards. They do not prove that Bramblewood's own setup is compliant. Bramblewood must still show evidence for its own responsibilities, such as how it controls access, protects card data, encrypts data, and configures its services.

A strong answer also notes that compliance requirements can vary by industry, such as card payments, by geography, and by which individual AWS services are used. Bramblewood should therefore check that the services it relies on are covered for the standard it needs.

For the root user: turn on multi-factor authentication (MFA), which requires a second proof such as a code from a phone or a hardware key in addition to the password. Delete the root user's access keys. Stop using root for daily work and lock its credentials away. Root should be kept for the short list of tasks only it can do, such as changing core account settings or closing the account.

Give people their own identities instead. Use AWS IAM Identity Center, a central place for workforce sign-in, or IAM users placed in IAM groups. IAM stands for Identity and Access Management, the service that controls who can do what. Grant permissions through policies written to least privilege, meaning each person gets only the permissions their job needs.

For the database password: treat it as exposed and change it. Store the new password in AWS Secrets Manager, a service that keeps secrets encrypted, controls who can read them, and can rotate them automatically. The website should fetch the password at runtime using an IAM role, which provides temporary permissions to an application. The password should never sit in the code.

The consequence of not fixing this is serious. Anyone who obtains the root keys or the code could take over the account or read every customer order.

AWS CloudTrail is the service to use. It records API activity in the account, meaning the actions taken through the console, command line, or software. Each record shows which identity acted, what action it took, when, and from which IP address. Bramblewood would look up the snapshot deletion event to see who deleted it.

Any one of these is an acceptable second service. Amazon GuardDuty continuously analyzes account activity and network logs to detect suspicious behavior, such as stolen credentials being used, and raises findings. AWS Config records the configuration history of resources and can flag changes that break a rule. Amazon CloudWatch can alarm on specific events or metrics. AWS Security Hub gathers security findings from these services in one place.

A strong answer distinguishes the two jobs. CloudTrail answers who did what, while a detection or monitoring service raises an alert next time.

scenarios.title: Tidewell Outfitters moves its online shop to AWS
scenarios.scenario:
Tidewell Outfitters is a fictional, mid-sized company that sells camping gear through its website. Today the whole shop runs on two servers in a closet at head office. Last month a power cut there took the site offline for six hours on a busy Saturday. Management has decided to move the shop to AWS, and you have joined the small team doing the work. Your lead, Priya, wants a short written recommendation for four decisions before anything is built.

Some terms you will need. A Region is a separate geographic area where AWS runs data centers. An Availability Zone (AZ) is one or more data centers inside a Region, with its own power and networking, set apart from the other AZs in that Region so that one failure does not spread to the others. An EC2 instance is a virtual server you rent from AWS. A load balancer is a service that receives incoming visitor traffic and spreads it across several servers, sending traffic only to servers that pass its health checks. Auto scaling is a feature that adds or removes servers automatically as demand rises and falls.

Here are the facts Priya has collected. Traffic is calm on weekdays but triples during weekend sales. The shop keeps orders, customers and stock levels in a relational database, which means a database that stores data in tables with rows and columns that link to each other. No one on the team is a database administrator, so nobody wants to handle patching, backups or failover (switching to a standby copy when the main copy fails) by hand. Each order produces a PDF invoice. Staff open invoices often during the first 30 days, almost never after that, but the law requires the company to keep them for seven years. Finally, when an order is placed, the website must hand the job to a separate warehouse system that prints packing slips. That warehouse system sometimes goes offline for a few minutes, and orders must not be lost while it is down.

1. Describe how to run the web servers so that the failure of one data center does not take the shop offline, and so that the weekend traffic spikes are handled without paying for idle servers all week.
2. Recommend where to run the relational database: on a database you install yourselves on an EC2 instance, or on a managed AWS database service. Name the service you choose and explain why the other option is the weaker fit here.
3. Recommend where to store the PDF invoices and how to keep storage costs low over the seven years without anyone moving files by hand.
4. Name the AWS service that should carry orders from the website to the warehouse system so nothing is lost while the warehouse is offline, and explain why Amazon SNS is the near-miss rather than the right answer.
subParts: High availability and elasticity for web servers
Decoupling the website from the warehouse
modelAnswer: Run the web servers as EC2 instances spread across at least two Availability Zones in the same Region, with a load balancer in front of them. Because each AZ has its own power and networking, a failure in one AZ, like the closet power cut, leaves the instances in the other AZ running, and the load balancer sends visitors only to healthy instances. Add auto scaling so the group adds instances when traffic rises at weekends and removes them when it falls. That is elasticity: you pay for extra servers only while they are needed. A common mistake is putting several instances in one AZ and calling it highly available. That still has a single point of failure, so one AZ outage takes the whole shop down. Using more than one Region is not required for this need; multiple Regions are for things like disaster recovery or data sovereignty.

Use a managed relational database. Amazon RDS (Relational Database Service) fits well, and Amazon Aurora, AWS's own high-performance relational engine run as a managed service, is also an acceptable choice. With a managed service, AWS handles routine patching and automated backups, and you can turn on a standby copy in a second AZ (a Multi-AZ setup) so failover happens automatically. Hosting the database yourself on EC2 is the weaker fit because the team would have to install, patch, back up and fail over the database by hand. Nobody on the team has those skills, so a mistake could mean lost orders or a long outage. Self-hosting on EC2 makes sense mainly when you need operating-system-level control that a managed service does not allow, and that is not the case here. Amazon DynamoDB is a near-miss because it is a NoSQL key-value database, which stores items by key instead of in linked tables, while the shop's data is relational.

Store the invoices in Amazon S3, AWS's object storage service, which holds files as objects in buckets and is built for very high durability, meaning data is very unlikely to be lost. Start new invoices in S3 Standard, which suits the frequent access in the first 30 days. Then add an S3 lifecycle policy, a rule that moves or deletes objects automatically based on their age. Have it move invoices to a cheaper class for rarely accessed data after 30 days, such as S3 Standard-Infrequent Access, or an S3 Glacier archive class for the long retention. Have it delete them after seven years. This cuts cost with no manual work. A common mistake is leaving everything in S3 Standard forever, which means paying the highest storage price for seven years of files nobody opens. Another mistake is archiving too early: Glacier classes can take time to retrieve data and charge for retrieval, so files still in daily use should not go there. EBS block storage is the wrong fit because it is a disk attached to a single instance, not a cheap long-term store for millions of files.

Use Amazon SQS (Simple Queue Service), a managed message queue. The website puts each order into the queue as a message, and the message waits there until the warehouse system reads it and finishes processing it. If the warehouse is offline for a few minutes, the orders simply pile up in the queue and are processed when it comes back, so nothing is lost and the website does not have to wait. This is called decoupling: the two systems no longer depend on each other being up at the same moment. Amazon SNS (Simple Notification Service) is the near-miss because it is a publish/subscribe service that pushes each message out to its subscribers right away. It is designed for fanning one message out to many receivers, not for holding work in a queue until a slow or offline consumer is ready. Amazon EventBridge, an event bus that routes events to targets by rule, is also not the best answer here, because the need is a buffer that holds work, not event routing.

scenarios.title: Cutting Surprise Cloud Bills at Brightkettle Foods
scenarios.scenario:
Brightkettle Foods is a small fictional company that sells weekly recipe boxes online. You have just joined as a junior cloud engineer, and your manager, Priya, hands you four problems.

First, the company runs its online shop on Amazon EC2. EC2 is AWS's service for renting virtual servers, called instances. The shop's web servers run 24 hours a day, every day, at a steady size, and the company expects to keep them for at least the next three years. Today they are billed On-Demand, meaning Brightkettle pays a full hourly or per-second rate with no commitment. Separately, every night a batch job resizes thousands of recipe photos. The job saves its progress often, so if a server disappears partway through, the job simply restarts later. Nobody minds if the photos are ready a few hours late.

Second, last month's AWS bill was almost double what finance expected. Priya wants two things: to understand which services caused last month's jump, and to be warned automatically before this month's spending passes 5,000 US dollars.

Third, the marketing team and the warehouse team share the same AWS account, and finance wants the bill split by team. Engineers have started adding a label to each resource, a key-value pair called a tag, such as team=marketing or team=warehouse. These tags do not yet appear in any billing report.

Fourth, the shop is now the company's main source of revenue. Leadership wants to be able to reach AWS technical support engineers by phone or chat at any hour, with a response in under one hour if the production shop goes down. They do not need a named advisor assigned to the company, and they want to keep the support bill as low as possible.

1. Recommend a compute purchasing option for the always-on web servers and a different one for the nightly photo job, and explain why each fits.
2. Name the AWS tool that explains last month's cost jump and the AWS tool that warns before the 5,000 US dollar limit is crossed, and say what question each answers.
3. Explain what must happen for the team tags to appear in billing data, and one limit to expect.
4. Recommend the AWS Support plan that meets leadership's needs at the lowest cost, and explain why the cheaper plan below it is not enough.
modelAnswer: For the always-on web servers, choose a commitment-based discount: a Savings Plan or Reserved Instances. A Savings Plan is a promise to spend a fixed amount per hour on compute for one or three years in exchange for a lower rate. A Reserved Instance is a one- or three-year commitment to a particular instance configuration, also at a discount. Both fit because the servers run steadily for years, so Brightkettle will use what it commits to and save a lot compared with On-Demand. A three-year term gives the deepest discount. Compute Savings Plans are the more flexible choice if the instance type might change later. For the nightly photo job, choose Spot Instances. These are spare AWS capacity sold at a large discount, but AWS can reclaim them with about two minutes' warning. They fit because the job saves progress, can restart, and has no strict deadline. A common mistake is putting the web servers on Spot. If AWS reclaims the capacity, the shop goes offline and customers cannot order.

Use AWS Cost Explorer to explain last month's jump. Cost Explorer shows past and current spending in charts that you can filter and group by service, account, or tag. It answers the question 'Where did my money go, and what is the trend?' It can also forecast future spending. Use AWS Budgets for the warning. A budget is a spending or usage threshold you set, such as 5,000 US dollars per month. AWS Budgets sends an alert by email or notification when actual or forecasted costs cross it. It answers the question 'Tell me before I go over my limit.' A common mistake is expecting Cost Explorer to send alerts. It only shows data, so without a budget nobody would be warned until the bill arrives.

The tags must be activated as cost allocation tags in the AWS Billing and Cost Management console. A cost allocation tag is a tag that AWS includes in billing data. Only the account that pays the bill, the management account in an AWS Organization, can activate them. After activation, costs can be grouped by team in Cost Explorer and appear in the AWS Cost and Usage Report, which is the most detailed billing data file AWS provides. One limit to expect is that tags only begin tracking costs from activation onward. Earlier spending is not split by team, and it can take up to about a day for tags to show up. Resources that were never tagged will appear as untagged, so the engineers must tag everything consistently.

Recommend the Business Support plan. It gives 24/7 access to AWS cloud support engineers by phone, chat, and email, with a response target of under one hour when a production system is down. It also unlocks the full set of AWS Trusted Advisor checks, which are automated recommendations about cost, security, and performance. It meets every requirement without paying for a named Technical Account Manager, which is an AWS advisor assigned to your company and comes only with the higher Enterprise On-Ramp and Enterprise plans. The cheaper Developer plan is not enough. It offers email access to support during business hours only, with no phone or chat, and its fastest response targets are measured in hours, not under one hour for a production outage. If the shop failed at night on the Developer plan, Brightkettle could not reach an engineer quickly, and every hour of downtime would mean lost orders.
